G's mother has one brother, making that brother G's maternal uncle. G's father has one brother, the paternal uncle. The child of either uncle is G's cousin, because a cousin is defined as the child of a parent's sibling. Whether the uncle is maternal or paternal does not change the relationship; both are first cousins. Hence H is G's first cousin.

Anna and Ben are half‑siblings, sharing only one parent. Their children, Clara and David, each have that shared parent as a grandparent. They therefore share a single grandparent, not a full pair. First cousins normally share both grandparents; when only one grandparent is common, the precise term is “half‑first cousins.” Hence the most accurate standard English term is half‑first cousins.

John's mother and Mary are sisters, making Mary John's aunt. Mary's son Peter is therefore John's first cousin. Lily is John's daughter, one generation below John, so she is one generation removed from Peter, yielding the relationship of first cousin once removed.

John’s father Peter has a brother Mark, making Mark John’s paternal uncle (blood). Mark’s wife Susan is therefore the spouse of John’s paternal uncle, which fits the definition of a sibling’s spouse (an in‑law). Hence Susan is John’s aunt‑in‑law. No blood aunt or cousin relationship exists.

John and Mark are brothers, making their children Peter and Lily first cousins. Emma is Peter’s daughter, one generation below Peter. A first cousin of a parent is a first cousin once removed to the child. Therefore Lily’s precise relation to Emma is first cousin once removed.

M is mother of siblings N and O. O's child is R, making R the niece/nephew of N. Q is married to R, so Q is the spouse of N's niece/nephew. The standard term for the spouse of a niece or nephew is "niece‑in‑law" (or nephew‑in‑law). Therefore Q's relation to N is niece‑in‑law.

R's mother has one brother (M's brother = maternal uncle). That uncle's daughter S makes S R's first cousin. R's father has one sister (F's sister = paternal aunt). That aunt's son T also makes T a first cousin of R. Since S and T are the same person, the maternal uncle and paternal aunt are married and share a child. Thus S is simultaneously the child of R's maternal uncle and paternal aunt, which makes S R's first cousin (no other standard term applies).

M and N are siblings, so they share one set of grandparents. O and P are siblings, sharing another set of grandparents. X is child of M (from the first sibling pair) and O (from the second pair); Y is child of N (first pair) and P (second pair). Thus X and Y each have the same two sets of grandparents, meaning they are first cousins through both parental lines. This is the definition of double first cousins, the most precise term.

M and N are siblings, so they share the same set of grandparents (call them Grandparents A). W and H are siblings, sharing another set of grandparents (Grandparents B). D1 is the child of M (descended from A) and W (descended from B). S1 is the child of N (also descended from A) and H (also descended from B). Therefore D1 and S1 share both sets of grandparents, making them first cousins through both parents – i.e., double first cousins.

Z is the child of Y's maternal uncle (the only brother of Y's mother) making Z a first cousin on the mother's side. Z is also the child of Y's paternal aunt (the only sister of Y's father) making Z a first cousin on the father's side. Being a cousin through both parental lines means Z shares both sets of grandparents with Y, which is the definition of a double first cousin.

N's spouse's mother is N's mother‑in‑law. M is described as the sibling of that mother‑in‑law. The sibling of a mother‑in‑law is the aunt/uncle of N's spouse, but there is no standard English term for the spouse's aunt/uncle in relation to N. Hence the relationship is only an affinal chain, not a direct standard kinship term.

John’s mother is sibling of Mary’s father, so John and Mary share that pair of grandparents. John’s father is sibling of Mary’s mother, giving them the second pair of shared grandparents. They therefore share both sets of grandparents, which defines double first cousins (children of two sibling pairs). Hence the precise term is double first cousins.

A is the child of R's maternal uncle (mother's brother). B is the child of R's paternal aunt (father's sister). The uncle and aunt come from different parental lines and, given no intermarriage, have no common ancestors. Therefore A and B share no blood relation; they are not cousins or half‑cousins.

M's mother’s sole brother is M's maternal uncle; his child is L. M's father’s sole sister is M's paternal aunt; her child is also L. Thus L is the child of M's maternal uncle and paternal aunt. A child of an uncle or aunt is a first cousin. Because the same person is both maternal and paternal cousin, L is a double first cousin, but the standard kinship term is still "first cousin".

Emma's father and Liam's mother are siblings, making Emma and Liam first cousins through that side. Additionally, Liam's father and Emma's mother are siblings, creating another first‑cousin link. Because they are first cousins via both parental lines, they are double first cousins.

Mara and Lyle are half‑siblings, sharing only one parent. Their children each descend from that shared parent’s line, giving Cora and Dax a single common grandparent. Thus they are cousins, but only half‑cousins because they inherit only one grandparent in common. The precise term is half‑first cousins.

N’s father’s sister is N’s paternal aunt, and N’s mother’s brother is N’s maternal uncle. Their child M is the offspring of both the paternal aunt and maternal uncle. Therefore M is the child of N’s paternal aunt (making M a first cousin on the father’s side) and also the child of N’s maternal uncle (making M a first cousin on the mother’s side). Since M shares both sets of grandparents with N, the relationship is a double first cousin.

Anna is Mary's mother, so she is John’s mother‑in‑law. After Mary's father and John’s mother die, Anna marries John’s father Peter, making her Peter’s wife and thus John’s step‑mother. Since she simultaneously fulfills both roles, the specific kinship term is not uniquely determined.

M and N are siblings, so their children O (M's daughter) and Q (N's son) are first cousins. S is Q's child, placing S one generation below Q. A child of a first cousin is a first cousin once removed relative to the other cousin. Therefore S is O's first cousin once removed.

A’s mother’s brother B is A’s maternal uncle. B’s daughter C is therefore A’s first cousin (children of siblings of a parent). C’s son D is the child of A’s first cousin, which makes D a first cousin once removed (one generation down from the cousin relationship). This is a standard English kinship term.

M is the child of N's maternal aunt (sister of N's mother) and also the child of N's paternal uncle (brother of N's father). If those two siblings are married, their child is simultaneously N's first cousin on the mother's side and on the father's side. This situation defines double first cousins—children of two pairs of siblings. The other options do not match the described dual relationship.

X's mother’s brother (maternal uncle) and X's father’s sister (paternal aunt) each are a sibling of one of X’s parents. Their child is therefore X’s first cousin through the mother and also X’s first cousin through the father. Sharing both sets of grandparents makes this a double first cousin relationship.

Peter and Anna are first cousins (children of siblings John and Mary). Their child Lily is therefore Peter's daughter. Since Lily is also the child of his cousin Anna, she is his first cousin once removed as well. The option that captures both relations is the most precise.

R’s paternal grandfather and S’s maternal grandfather are brothers, meaning they share the same parents (a common great‑grandparent for both R and S). Therefore R and S each descend from that shared great‑grandparent, but through different lines (R via his father’s father, S via her mother’s father). Sharing a great‑grandparent defines a second‑cousin relationship. No closer or affinal ties exist.

John and Mary are siblings. John’s son Kevin is therefore Mary’s nephew. Kevin’s daughter Emma (with Linda) is the child of Mary’s nephew, making Emma the child of a niece/nephew. In standard kinship terms, the child of a niece or nephew is a grandniece (also called great‑niece). No blood relation through Linda changes this designation; the primary line is through Kevin. Hence Emma is Mary’s grandniece.

Y is the brother of X's mother, making Y X's maternal uncle. Z is the sister of X's father, making Z X's paternal aunt. Their child W is therefore the child of X's maternal uncle (a first cousin) and also the child of X's paternal aunt (another first cousin). Since W is a first cousin to X through both parental lines, they are double first cousins, sharing both sets of grandparents. The other options do not fit: they are not siblings, not removed, and a kinship term exists.

Mo (M's mother) and U are siblings, making V (U's daughter) M's first cousin. The child of a first cousin is a first cousin once removed relative to the original cousin's child. Therefore V is a first cousin once removed to M's child W.

M and N share the same parents, and O and P share another set of parents. X is child of M (from the first set) and O (from the second set); Y is child of N (same first set) and P (same second set). Therefore X and Y have both sets of grandparents in common, making them first cousins through both parents—a double first‑cousin relationship.

Adam and Brian are brothers, so they share the same parents. Clara and Diana are sisters, sharing their own parents. Ethan’s father (Adam) and Fiona’s father (Brian) have the same parents, making those parents Ethan’s paternal grandparents and Fiona’s paternal grandparents. Likewise, Ethan’s mother (Clara) and Fiona’s mother (Diana) share the same parents, who are Ethan’s maternal grandparents and Fiona’s maternal grandparents. Thus Ethan and Fiona share both sets of grandparents, which is the definition of double first cousins.

Lily's father (Adam) and Mark's father (Ben) are brothers, making Lily and Mark first cousins on their fathers' side. Likewise, Lily's mother (Clara) and Mark's mother (Dana) are sisters, making them first cousins on their mothers' side. Sharing both sets of grandparents means they are double first cousins.

Mary's brother Peter's daughter Laura is Mary's niece. Laura's child Sophie is therefore the child of Mary's niece, which makes Sophie Mary's grand‑niece (great‑niece). No other standard kin term applies.
Robert's sister Helen is Emma's aunt. Helen's son Victor is therefore Emma's first cousin. Victor's daughter Sarah is one generation below Victor, making her Emma's first cousin once removed.

P is the child of Q's maternal uncle (the mother's only brother) and also the child of Q's paternal aunt (the father's only sister). Thus P is a first cousin of Q through the mother and also a first cousin through the father, making them double first cousins. No other relationship fits.

Mary and Tom are siblings, so their children Alice and Ben are first cousins. Clara is Alice's child, one generation below Alice. Therefore Clara is one generation removed from the cousin relationship with Ben, making her Ben's first cousin once removed.

L's father has one sister, making her L's paternal aunt. L's mother has one brother, making him L's maternal uncle. These two siblings-in-law marry and have a child M. M is the child of L's paternal aunt, so M is L's first cousin on the father's side. M is also the child of L's maternal uncle, so M is L's first cousin on the mother's side. Being a first cousin through both parental lines makes M a double first cousin of L, which is the most precise term.

Mary and Linda are sisters, so John and Emma share Mary’s parents as grandparents via Mary (John’s mother) and Linda (Emma’s mother). Peter and Thomas are brothers, so John and Emma also share Peter’s parents as grandparents via Peter (John’s father) and Thomas (Emma’s father). Thus Emma is John’s first cousin on both the maternal and paternal sides, i.e., double first cousins.

N’s father and P are brothers, making P N’s paternal uncle. N’s mother and Q are sisters, making Q N’s maternal aunt. P and Q are married and their child M is thus the child of N’s paternal uncle and maternal aunt simultaneously. Therefore M is N’s first cousin on both the paternal and maternal sides, which is the definition of a double first cousin.

John’s brother Peter is Sam’s father, making Sam the son of John’s sibling. In standard kinship terms, the child of one’s brother is a nephew. Eva’s marriage to Sam does not affect the blood relationship between Sam and John, and in‑law terms are to be ignored. Therefore Sam’s direct blood relation to John is nephew.

M and N are siblings, so their children O and R are first cousins. Q is the child of R, making Q the next generation down from O's cousin. The relationship between a person and the child of his/her cousin is defined as a first cousin once removed. Hence O is Q's first cousin once removed.

Alice and Carl share only one parent (George), making them half‑siblings. Emma is Alice's child and Frank is Carl's child. Children of half‑siblings are termed half‑first cousins, as they are one generation removed from a half‑sibling relationship. Therefore the most precise kinship term is half‑first cousins.

Mary and Paul are siblings, making Paul John’s maternal uncle. Paul’s daughter Lisa is therefore John’s first cousin. Lisa’s son Tom is one generation below Lisa, so he is one generation below John’s first cousin, which is the definition of a first cousin once removed.

Y's mother’s brother is Y’s maternal uncle; Y’s father’s sister is Y’s paternal aunt. X is the child of that uncle and that aunt. Therefore X shares both sets of Y’s grandparents – the maternal grandparents via the uncle and the paternal grandparents via the aunt. Sharing both grandparent pairs defines a double first cousin. The relation is uniquely determined.

Alan is John’s maternal uncle, so his daughter Clara is John’s first cousin on his mother’s side. Beth is John’s paternal aunt, so her son David is John’s first cousin on his father’s side. Both possible selections are first cousins, making the kinship term uniquely first cousin.

Maya and Omar are siblings. Omar’s wife Priya is Maya’s sister‑in‑law. Rahul is Priya’s brother, making him the brother‑in‑law of Maya’s brother, i.e., Maya’s brother‑in‑law’s brother. This relation has no standard English kinship term. Consequently, their children L (Maya’s child) and Kiran (Rahul’s child) also share no standard term. The only appropriate choice is “No standard kinship (no relation)”.

J's father and L are siblings, so L is J's aunt. The child of an aunt (or uncle) is the standard definition of a first cousin. The constraints (no adoption, monogamy, no remarriage) eliminate any half‑sibling or ambiguous relations, making the relationship determinable as first cousin.

X is the child of Y's maternal uncle (the only brother of Y's mother), making X a first cousin to Y on the mother's side. X is also the child of Y's paternal aunt (the only sister of Y's father), making X a first cousin to Y on the father's side as well. Being first cousins through both parental lines defines a double first cousin relationship.

W's brother's child is W's niece/nephew. M, as that child's child, is the grandchild of W's brother, i.e., the grandniece/grandnephew of W. Similarly, the sister's child is also W's niece/nephew, and N, being that child's child, is likewise a grandniece/grandnephew. Since both possible choices (M or N) share the same precise kinship to W, the relation is uniquely the grandniece/grandnephew.

John’s mother’s brother Mike is John’s maternal uncle, making Mike’s daughter Lisa John’s first cousin. John’s father’s sister Anna is John’s paternal aunt, making Anna’s son Mark also John’s first cousin. Lisa and Mark are unrelated to each other, so Sam (their child) is the child of two of John’s first cousins. A person’s first cousin’s child is a first cousin once removed. Therefore Sam is John’s first cousin once removed.

M and N are full siblings, and O and P are full siblings. X’s parents are M and O; Y’s parents are N and P. Therefore X and Y share both sets of grandparents (the parents of M/N and the parents of O/P). Sharing both pairs of grandparents makes them double first cousins, not half‑cousins.

M and N are siblings. Their children O (M's daughter) and R (N's daughter) are therefore first cousins. Q is R's son, placing him one generation below R. Thus Q is the child of O's first cousin, making O and Q first cousins once removed.

M is married to L. L's brother N is M's brother‑in‑law. N's spouse O is also an in‑law. O's sibling Q is a sibling‑in‑law, and Q's child R is a child of that sibling‑in‑law. This chain involves multiple affinal links with no direct standard term in English kinship; the relationship is not covered by great‑uncle, cousin, or uncle‑in‑law categories.

A and C are siblings, sharing parents P1 and P2. B and D are siblings, sharing parents Q1 and Q2. X is child of A & B; Y is child of C & D. Consequently X and Y each have the same four grandparents (P1, P2, Q1, Q2). They are therefore first cousins through both parental lines, i.e., double first cousins, the most specific term.

L and K are siblings, so their children M and N are first cousins. N is the mother of O, making O one generation below N. The child of your first cousin is your first cousin once removed. Therefore M’s relation to O is first cousin once removed.

L’s children D and S are siblings. D’s child C and S’s child N are therefore first cousins. M is C’s child, placing M one generation below C. Since N is in the same generation as C, M is one generation removed from N, making them first cousins once removed.

Y is M's maternal uncle (mother's brother) and Z is M's paternal uncle (father's brother). Their child C is therefore the child of M's maternal uncle, making C a first cousin on the maternal side, and also the child of M's paternal uncle, making C a first cousin on the paternal side. Being a first cousin through both parents defines a double first cousin, the most specific term.

John and Jane are siblings, so their parents are Alex's paternal grandparents and Bella's paternal grandparents. Mary and Mark are siblings, so their parents are Alex's maternal grandparents and Bella's maternal grandparents. Thus Alex and Bella share both sets of grandparents, making them the children of two pairs of siblings. This relationship is called double first cousins.

N's father has a sibling who is one parent of M, and N's mother has a sibling who is the other parent of M. Thus the two siblings (one from each of N's parental families) are married to each other, and their children (N and M) share both sets of grandparents. This is the definition of double first cousins.

Alice's sister Clara is Frank's mother, making Frank the child of Alice's sibling. Regardless of Frank's father being Edward (Clara's husband and Alice's brother‑in‑law), the direct blood link is through Clara, so Frank is Alice's niece/nephew.

Liam and Maya share only their father George, making them half‑siblings. Their children, Noah (Liam’s child) and Zoe (Maya’s child), therefore share only one grandparent (George) and not the other grandparents. This matches the definition of half‑first cousins, who have a single common grandparent because their parents are half‑siblings.

John and Mary are siblings. Their children, Kevin and Lisa, are first cousins. Paul is Lisa's son, placing him one generation below Lisa. Therefore Kevin and Paul are separated by one generation while sharing a common ancestor (their grandparents), which defines a first‑cousin once‑removed relationship.

L's father and P are brothers, making P L's paternal uncle. L's mother and Q are sisters, making Q L's maternal aunt. P and Q are married (their only child is M), so M is the child of L's paternal uncle and also the child of L's maternal aunt. Thus M is simultaneously L's first cousin on the father's side and first cousin on the mother's side, i.e., a double first cousin.

Clara is the daughter of George. George's brother is Peter, making Peter Clara's paternal uncle. Anna is married to Peter, so Anna is Clara's aunt by marriage (aunt‑in‑law). The reciprocal relationship is that Clara is the niece of Anna, again by marriage, i.e., niece‑in‑law.
P is the parent of M and N. M's child A is P's grandchild, and A's child C is therefore P's great‑grandchild. The same holds via N's line. Thus C is a great‑grandchild of M's parent.

John and Mary are siblings. Mary’s son Peter is John’s nephew; John’s daughter Lisa is his child. Peter and Lisa (first cousins) have a child Emma. Emma is the child of John’s daughter, making her John’s granddaughter. Although she is also the child of John’s nephew (great‑niece), the direct line through his own child gives the standard term granddaughter.

Carl’s father John and Dana’s father Anna are siblings, sharing the same paternal grandparents. Carl’s mother Mary and Dana’s mother Ben are also siblings, sharing the same maternal grandparents. Thus Carl and Dana share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins, the most precise term.

M and N are siblings, sharing the same parents (Grandparents G1 & G2). O and P are siblings, sharing another set of parents (Grandparents G3 & G4). X is child of M (who descends from G1 & G2) and O (who descends from G3 & G4). Y is child of N (descends from G1 & G2) and P (descends from G3 & G4). Therefore X and Y share both sets of grandparents, i.e., they are children of two different sibling pairs. This relationship is precisely called double first cousins.

N's father has one sister, who is N's paternal aunt. N's mother has one brother, who is N's maternal uncle. These two relatives marry and have a child M. M is therefore the child of N's paternal aunt (making M a first cousin on the father's side) and also the child of N's maternal uncle (making M a first cousin on the mother's side). Being a first cousin through both parental lines makes M a double first cousin of N.

M and N are siblings, so their children O and R are first cousins. R's child S is one generation below O. Therefore O and S are first cousins separated by one generation, i.e., first cousins once removed.

Z is the daughter of Y, who is X's maternal uncle, making Z X's maternal first cousin. V is the son of W, who is X's paternal aunt, making V X's paternal first cousin. Y and W are siblings of X's parents, not siblings to each other, so they have no common ancestors. Consequently V and Z share no grandparent or ancestor; they are not cousins, half‑cousins, or otherwise related by blood before any marriage.

R’s mother’s brother U is R’s maternal uncle. U’s daughter V is therefore R’s first cousin. R’s son W is one generation below R. Since V is in the same generation as R, V is one generation above W, making V the first cousin of W’s parent. In kinship terms, that relation is a first cousin once removed. The family constraints guarantee a unique determination.

X and Y are double first cousins, meaning they share both pairs of grandparents. The children of first cousins are second cousins, because they share great‑grandparents. Since X and Y share two distinct grandparental lines, their children P and Q share both corresponding great‑grandparental lines, making them double second cousins. This is more precise than simply "second cousins" and is a recognized term, so option A is correct.

R's paternal grandmother's brother is R's great‑uncle. The great‑uncle's child (S) is first cousin to R's father (the grandmother's child). Since R is one generation below his father, R and S are first cousins once removed. Hence the relation is uniquely determined.

Alex's father John and Emma's mother Linda are siblings, making Emma a first cousin on the paternal side. Alex's mother Mary and Emma's father Kevin are also siblings, making Emma a first cousin on the maternal side. Because Emma shares both sets of grandparents with Alex (John’s parents and Mary’s parents), they are cousins through two sibling pairs. This relationship is called a double first cousin.

X's father and Y's mother are brother and sister, i.e., siblings. X is the child of the father, Y is the child of the mother. Therefore X and Y are the children of two siblings, which makes them first cousins. They do not share both sets of grandparents from both parental lines, so they are not double cousins, nor are they half‑cousins, and they are not siblings.

John and Mary are half‑siblings, sharing only one parent. Their children each descend from one of those half‑siblings, so Lily and Peter share exactly one grandparent (the common parent of John and Mary). In kinship terms, children of half‑siblings are half‑first cousins, distinct from full first cousins who share both grandparents. Therefore the precise term is half‑first cousins.

John and Mike share both parents, making them full brothers. Their respective children, X (John's child with his second wife Beth) and Ethan (Mike's child), are therefore the children of two full siblings. In standard kinship terms, children of siblings are first cousins. No half‑sibling or other complexities affect this relationship, so the precise term is first cousin.

Anna's mother married Ben, making Ben Anna's stepfather. Carl is Ben's biological son from an earlier marriage, so Carl is the child of Anna's stepfather. Since they share no biological parent, Carl is Anna's stepbrother, the correct kinship term.

X's mother has exactly one sibling, a sister named Y. A sister of one's mother is defined as a maternal aunt. The statement that X's father is unrelated to Y only confirms Y is not the father's relative, reinforcing that Y is not a spouse or sibling of the father, but remains the mother's sister. Hence Y's relation to X is aunt.

John and Mary are full siblings. John’s son Michael and Mary’s son Peter are therefore first cousins. Sarah is Michael’s daughter, making her one generation below Peter. The child of a first cousin is a first cousin once removed of the other cousin. Hence Peter and Sarah are first cousins once removed.

Mike is the brother of John's mother, making Mike John's maternal uncle. Therefore Mike's daughter Sarah is John's first cousin on the mother's side. The extra detail about Sarah's husband being the child of John's paternal aunt only adds an in‑law connection, which is ignored for blood relations. Hence Sarah is John's first cousin.

N is M's mother. N's brother O is M's maternal uncle. O's daughter P is therefore M's first cousin (maternal side). The extra detail about P marrying Q (M's paternal cousin) does not change the blood relationship between P and M; it only adds an affinal link. Since a standard kinship term exists for their blood tie, the precise relation is "first cousin".

M and N are half‑siblings, sharing only one parent. Their respective children, P and Q, are the offspring of those half‑siblings. The standard kinship classification treats the children of full siblings as first cousins; when the sibling relationship is half, the cousin relationship is correspondingly half, i.e., half‑first cousins. No other marital connections are involved, so the precise term is half‑first cousins.

John's mother has one brother; that brother's only child Alice is the child of John's maternal uncle, making Alice John’s first cousin. John’s father has one sister; that sister's only child Bob is the child of John's paternal aunt, also making Bob John’s first cousin. Regardless of whether X is Alice or Bob, the relationship to John is the same: first cousin.

Lily's father Peter is John’s brother, so Lily shares John’s parents as paternal grandparents with Sam. Lily’s mother Anna is Mary’s sister, so Lily shares Mary’s parents as maternal grandparents with Sam. Hence Lily and Sam have both sets of grandparents in common, making them double first cousins.

J’s father’s sister is J’s paternal aunt; her child is a first cousin of J. J’s mother’s brother is J’s maternal uncle; his child is also a first cousin of J. If the aunt and uncle are married, their child M is simultaneously the offspring of both a paternal aunt and a maternal uncle, sharing both sets of grandparents with J. This makes M and J double first cousins.

R's spouse S has brother T (R's brother‑in‑law). T's wife U is R's sister‑in‑law. V is U's mother, i.e., the mother of R's sister‑in‑law. English kinship does not have a standard term for the mother of a sister‑in‑law, so the correct choice is 'No standard kinship term'.

The described person is a son of Q’s spouse’s paternal grandmother. That grandmother’s children include the spouse’s father, but may also include other sons who are the spouse’s paternal uncles. Since we cannot tell whether L is the father or a sibling of the father, L could be Q’s father‑in‑law or uncle‑in‑law. Therefore the exact term is not uniquely determinable.

Alan and Brian are brothers and Clara and Diana are sisters, so Ethan (son of Alan & Clara) and Fiona (daughter of Brian & Diana) share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins. George is Ethan's son and Hannah is Fiona's daughter. The children of first cousins are second cousins; when the first cousins are double first cousins, their children share all four great‑grandparents, making them double second cousins. Hence George and Hannah are double second cousins.

M and H share only one parent (their father), making them half‑sisters. The children of siblings are first cousins; when the siblings are half‑siblings, their children are half‑first cousins. Since A is M's child and B is H's child, B is A's half‑first cousin. The relationship is determinable, not a removed cousin.

R’s maternal uncle U’s daughter S is R’s maternal first cousin. R’s paternal aunt T’s son V is R’s paternal first cousin. S and V (two unrelated first cousins of R) marry and have child C. A child of one’s first cousin is one generation removed from the cousin relationship, i.e., a first cousin once removed. Hence C is R’s first cousin once removed.

M and N are siblings. Therefore N's child Q is M's niece/nephew. R is Q's daughter, making R the child of M's niece/nephew. The child of a niece/nephew is called a great‑niece (or great‑nephew). Thus R is M's great‑niece.

Peter's father John and Susan's mother Mary are full siblings, giving Peter and Susan a set of shared grandparents. Additionally, Peter's mother Laura and Susan's father Kevin are full siblings, providing a second set of shared grandparents. Thus Peter and Susan are first cousins through both parental lines, i.e., double first cousins. They are not half‑first cousins because they share both grandparent pairs, and they are not second cousins.

L's mother and her sister are siblings, so the sister is L's maternal aunt. The aunt's only child is L's first cousin. That cousin's only child, M, is one generation below the cousin, making M a first cousin of L's parent’s generation, i.e., a first cousin once removed. Hence the precise kinship term is 'first cousin once removed.'

M and N are siblings, so their children (O and R) are first cousins. R's child Q is one generation down from R. Therefore O, who is R's first cousin, is one generation above Q, making O and Q first cousins once removed. They are not siblings of any parent (aunt/uncle), nor are they second cousins, and they do share blood, so the correct choice is C.

The child of R's maternal uncle (mother's brother) is R's first cousin on the mother's side. Likewise, the child of R's paternal aunt (father's sister) is R's first cousin on the father's side. Both relationships are standard first cousins, with no half‑sibling implication given. Hence, whichever of P or Q is chosen, S is a first cousin of R.

J's father's sister is J's paternal aunt; her child is J's first cousin on the father's side. J's mother's brother is J's maternal uncle; his child is J's first cousin on the mother's side. Since the aunt and the uncle are married and have the same child M, M is simultaneously the child of both a paternal aunt and a maternal uncle. U is the brother of M's mother, making him M's maternal uncle. Therefore M is U's nephew or niece. Although U is also the husband of M's paternal aunt (uncle‑in‑law), the direct blood relationship already provides a standard term, nephew/niece, which precisely describes M's relation to U.

L and K share only one parent (their mother M) and have different fathers, making them half‑siblings. The children of half‑siblings are called half‑first cousins. X is L's child and Y is K's child, so X and Y are half‑first cousins, not full first cousins, second cousins, or double first cousins.

Since L is the only child of both father and mother, the father's only child and the mother's only child are both L. M is defined as the child of that child (L), and N is likewise the child of that child (L). Therefore both M and N are children of L, making them siblings (assuming they are distinct individuals).

Paul's daughter Lily is Mark's mother, making Mark Paul’s grandson. Mark’s son Tom is therefore Paul’s great‑grandson (Paul → Lily → Mark → Tom). Although Tom is also the child of Paul’s niece Emma (making him a grandnephew), the direct line of descent yields the standard term great‑grandson, which is the most precise relationship.

X's mother and her brother are the only children of their parents (no multiple siblings). The brother's only child is X's first cousin. That cousin's son Y is the child of X's first cousin, which by definition is a first cousin once removed. The constraints guarantee no alternative lineage, so the relationship is determined.

John and Mary are siblings. Mary's son Peter is John’s nephew. John’s son Michael is Peter’s first cousin (children of siblings). Lisa is Michael’s daughter, making her one generation below Michael. Since Peter is first cousin to Michael, he is one generation above Lisa, which defines a first cousin once removed relationship.
The woman's only sibling is her brother. His child, Zoe, is therefore the daughter of her brother. In standard kinship terms, a sibling's daughter is a niece. No other listed relationship fits.

John is Alex's father, so Charlie, Alex's child, is John's grandson. John is also Paul’s brother, making Paul’s son Ben John’s nephew. Charlie, as Ben’s child, is therefore John’s grand‑nephew (great‑nephew). Because both lines of descent are valid and not ignored, Charlie holds both relations to John simultaneously. The most precise description is the double relationship.

P’s paternal grandmother is his father’s mother. Her sister is the father’s aunt, i.e., P’s great‑aunt. The child of that great‑aunt is the father’s cousin. Thus M is a cousin of P’s father. A cousin of one’s parent is a first cousin once removed to the child, so M is P’s first cousin once removed.

X is the child of Y's paternal aunt (the father's only sister) making X a first cousin on Y's father's side. X is also the child of Y's maternal uncle (the mother's only brother) making X a first cousin on Y's mother's side. Since the aunt and uncle are from different families and are stated to be unrelated, X is related to Y through both parental lines, i.e., a double first cousin.

M and N are full siblings, sharing both parents (grandparents A and B for their children). P and Q are also full siblings, sharing both parents (grandparents C and D for their children). X’s parents are M (grandparents A&B) and P (grandparents C&D). Y’s parents are N (grandparents A&B) and Q (grandparents C&D). Thus X and Y share both sets of grandparents, making them cousins through two distinct sibling pairs. This is the definition of double first cousins, the most precise kinship term for this situation.

M and N are siblings, so their children O (M's daughter) and R (N's daughter) are first cousins. R's child Q is one generation below R. Therefore O is the first cousin of Q's parent, making O a first cousin once removed to Q.

Mark and Luke are brothers, so they share the same parents. Nina and Olivia are sisters, sharing their own parents. Alice is the child of Mark (son of the brothers' parents) and Nina (daughter of the sisters' parents). Ben is the child of Luke (son of the brothers' parents) and Olivia (daughter of the sisters' parents). Thus Alice and Ben share both sets of grandparents: the parents of Mark/Luke and the parents of Nina/Olivia. Sharing both grandparents makes them double first cousins.

John and Peter are full brothers, and Anna and Mary are full sisters. Emma is the child of John (brother of Peter) and Anna (sister of Mary). Liam is the child of Peter (brother of John) and Mary (sister of Anna). Therefore Emma and Liam share both sets of grandparents—the parents of John and Peter, and the parents of Anna and Mary. Sharing both paternal and maternal grandparents makes them double first cousins, not merely first, half‑first, or second cousins.

Y’s father’s sister is Y’s paternal aunt. Her only child is Y’s first cousin (same generation). X is the child of that cousin, placing X one generation below Y. In kinship terms this is a first cousin once removed. The monogamous, non‑adopted context ensures no half‑relations or ambiguity.

John and Kate share a mother but have different fathers, making them half‑siblings. Sam is John’s child and Lily is Kate’s child. Children of siblings are first cousins; when the siblings are half‑siblings, their children are half‑first cousins. This is the most specific term applicable, as no further relationship ambiguity exists.

M and N are siblings, so they share one set of grandparents. O and P are siblings, sharing another set of grandparents. X's parents are M (child of the first set) and O (child of the second set). Y's parents are N (child of the first set) and P (child of the second set). Therefore X and Y inherit both sets of grandparents in common, making them children of two sibling pairs – the definition of double first cousins.

M and N are siblings, making their children A and B first cousins. D is B's spouse, so D is married to A's cousin. In standard English kinship, there is no direct term for the spouse of a cousin; "cousin‑in‑law" is not a standard kinship term. Therefore D has no standard direct relation to A, only an affinal connection.

M and N are siblings, sharing grandparents A1/A2. O and P are siblings, sharing grandparents B1/B2. X’s parents are M (child of A1/A2) and O (child of B1/B2); Y’s parents are N (child of A1/A2) and P (child of B1/B2). Therefore X and Y have both sets of grandparents in common, being the children of two distinct sibling pairs. This is the definition of double first cousins.

A is married to B, making B A's spouse. B's sister C is A's sister-in-law. C's husband D is the spouse of A's sister-in-law, which is not covered by the allowed in-law categories (only siblings' spouses, not spouse's siblings' spouses). E is D's sister, extending the chain further. No standard English kinship term directly describes E's relation to A under the given constraints.

Emma's father Adam and Frank's father Ben are brothers, making Emma and Frank first cousins on their paternal side. Their mothers Clara and Diana are sisters, so Emma and Frank are also first cousins on their maternal side. Sharing both sets of grandparents means they are double first cousins, the most precise term.

N’s father (F) has one sister (S). S is N’s paternal aunt. M is S’s child, making M the child of N’s aunt. If F and S are full siblings, M is N’s first cousin; if they are half‑siblings, M is a half‑cousin. The statement only says “sister,” which could denote either a full or half sister, and provides no information about their shared parentage. Therefore the precise kinship (first cousin vs. half‑cousin) cannot be determined.

N’s father’s sister is N’s paternal aunt; N’s mother’s brother is N’s maternal uncle. Their child M is therefore the child of N’s paternal aunt and also the child of N’s maternal uncle. Consequently M is a first cousin to N via the paternal line (child of father’s sibling) and also a first cousin via the maternal line (child of mother’s sibling). Sharing both sets of grandparents makes M a double first cousin of N, not a half‑cousin or indeterminate.

M and N are siblings, so they share the same parents. D is M's daughter, Q is N's son. Therefore D and Q are children of two siblings, making them first cousins. The marriage of D to P (Q's son) does not alter their blood relationship. Hence Q is D's first cousin.

M and N are siblings, so they share the same parents. X and Y are also siblings, sharing another set of parents. A’s grandparents are the parents of M (P1, P2) and the parents of X (Q1, Q2). B’s grandparents are the parents of N (P1, P2) and the parents of Y (Q1, Q2). Thus A and B have both sets of grandparents in common, making them children of two sibling pairs who married each other. This relationship is defined as double first cousins.

P's daughter (D) and son (S) are siblings. Their children, M (child of D) and Q (child of S), are first cousins because they share grandparents P. R is Q's child, making R one generation below Q. Therefore M is the first cousin of R's parent, which defines a "first cousin once removed" relationship. The correct choice is B.

M is R's maternal uncle (mother's brother) and S is R's paternal aunt (father's sister). Their child X is therefore the offspring of R's maternal uncle, making X a first cousin on the mother's side, and also the offspring of R's paternal aunt, making X a first cousin on the father's side. This double first‑cousin relationship still classifies X as a first cousin (not an aunt/uncle, half‑cousin, or indeterminate).

X is the child of Y's maternal uncle (mother's brother) and also the child of Y's paternal aunt (father's sister). Thus X is Y's cousin on both the maternal and paternal sides. When two cousins share both sets of grandparents because their parents are two pairs of siblings, they are double first cousins. The spouses are unrelated, satisfying the double first‑cousin definition. Therefore the most precise term is double first cousin.

M’s father is N’s paternal uncle (father’s brother) and M’s mother is N’s maternal aunt (mother’s sister). Thus N and M are first cousins through the paternal line and also first cousins through the maternal line. Since they share both sets of grandparents, they are double first cousins.

M and N are full brothers, sharing both parents; S and T are full sisters, sharing both parents. X is child of M (brother) and S (sister), while Y is child of N (brother) and T (sister). Thus X and Y have the same paternal grandparents (parents of M/N) and the same maternal grandparents (parents of S/T). Sharing both sets of grandparents makes them double first cousins, the most specific term.

M and Q are brothers, so their children are first cousins. J is M's child; P is Q's child. Marriage links (J-L, L-N, N-P) are irrelevant because only blood relations count. Therefore P and J are first cousins.

Adam and Brian are brothers, so Ethan and Fiona share the same paternal grandparents. Clara and Diana are sisters, so they also share the same maternal grandparents. Thus the two children have both sets of grandparents in common, which is the definition of double first cousins.

L and N are siblings, so their children M (of L) and O (of N) are first cousins. P is O's child, placing P one generation below O. A first cousin's child is a first cousin once removed relative to the original cousin. Therefore M and P are first cousins once removed.

M's mother has a brother T, making T M's maternal uncle. T's daughter S is therefore M's first cousin (child of an uncle). The additional detail that S marries X, who is M's paternal cousin, does not alter the blood relationship; S remains M's first cousin. Hence the appropriate kinship term is "first cousin."

X’s father A and Y’s father B are brothers, so X and Y share the same paternal grandparents. Likewise, X’s mother C and Y’s mother D are sisters, giving them the same maternal grandparents. Because the children share both sets of grandparents (the result of two sibling pairs marrying each other), they are double first cousins, a more specific term than plain first cousins.

Bm (mother's brother) is a sibling of Q's mother, so Bm's child P is Q's first cousin on the maternal side. Fs (father's sister) is a sibling of Q's father, so Fs's child P is Q's first cousin on the paternal side. Because P is a cousin of Q through both parental lines, the relationship is a double first cousin.

Ethan and Fiona are double first cousins because their fathers are brothers and their mothers are sisters, so they share both sets of grandparents. Grace and Henry are each one generation down from Ethan and Fiona. Children of first cousins are second cousins; because Ethan and Fiona are double first cousins, their children share both sets of great‑grandparents, making them double second cousins. Hence the most precise term is double second cousins.

M is child of P's father's sister (paternal aunt) making M a first cousin on the paternal side. M is also child of P's mother's brother (maternal uncle) making M a first cousin on the maternal side. Since the paternal aunt and maternal uncle are married, M is the child of two siblings from each family, which defines a double first cousin relationship.

Q is the biological child of O from an earlier marriage. R is the biological child of O and P. Thus Q and R share one parent (O) but have different other parents. Sharing a single parent defines a half‑sibling relationship, not a full sibling (both parents shared) nor a step‑sibling (no blood link). They are not cousins because they are not children of siblings. Therefore the correct term is half‑sibling.

Emma's husband Noah has a sister Zoe, making Zoe Emma's sister‑in‑law. Maya is Zoe's daughter, i.e., the child of Emma's spouse's sibling. In English kinship, the child of a sibling‑in‑law is referred to as a niece‑in‑law. Therefore Maya is Emma's niece‑in‑law.

L’s sister S and brother B each have exactly one child, and those children are the same person (C). Thus C is both L’s niece/nephew (child of a sibling). M is the child of C, making M the grandchild of S and B, i.e., the child of L’s niece/nephew. In standard kinship terms, the child of a niece/nephew is a grandniece or grandnephew of the original aunt/uncle. Therefore M is L’s grandniece/grandnephew.

C and D are sisters; A and B are brothers. Each sister marries a brother, and each couple has a child. M and N therefore share both sets of grandparents (maternal and paternal). This is the definition of double first cousins, who are first cousins through both parents.

P and Q are brothers, so their children share the same paternal grandparents. R and S are sisters, so their children share the same maternal grandparents. X and Y therefore share both sets of grandparents, making them children of two sibling pairs, i.e., double first cousins, which is more specific than plain first cousins.

M’s mother and N’s father are siblings, so M and N are children of those siblings – they are first cousins. O is the child of N, placing O one generation below N. The child of a first cousin is a first cousin once removed relative to the original cousin. Therefore O is M’s first cousin once removed.

Ethan's mother Clara and Felix's mother Diana are sisters, making Ethan and Felix first cousins through their shared maternal grandparents. Their fathers are unrelated, so they do not share a second set of grandparents required for double first cousins. They are not half‑first cousins because the mothers are full siblings, not half‑siblings.

Adam and Brian are brothers, so their children share the same paternal grandparents. Clara and Diana are sisters, so their children also share the same maternal grandparents. Ethan (son of Adam + Clara) and Fiona (daughter of Brian + Diana) are therefore first cousins through both their fathers and their mothers, making them double first cousins.

R's mother has exactly one brother, making him R's maternal uncle. The child of that uncle is R's first cousin. R's father has exactly one sister, making her R's paternal aunt. The child of that aunt is also R's first cousin. Since the same person P is described as the child of both the maternal uncle and the paternal aunt, P is R's first cousin (on both sides). Hence the precise kinship term is "first cousin".

M's paternal grandmother is M's father's mother. Her brother is M's great‑uncle. The great‑uncle's child is a first cousin of M's father (they share the same grandparents). Since N is a first cousin of M's father, N is one generation above M, making N M's first cousin once removed. The relationship is uniquely determined under the given family constraints.
M's father's sister is M's paternal aunt. Her daughter is M's first cousin. The child of that cousin (X) is one generation removed from M, making X M's first cousin once removed.

Lily's father John and Sam's father Mark are full brothers, and Lily's mother Anna and Sam's mother Beth are full sisters. Thus Lily and Sam are children of two sibling pairs, sharing both sets of grandparents. This relationship is termed double first cousins, which is more specific than ordinary first cousins.
Y's mother’s brother is Y’s maternal uncle. The uncle’s child X is therefore the child of Y’s uncle, which makes X Y’s first cousin under standard kinship terminology.

Mary is John’s sister, so her son David is John’s nephew. Emma is John’s daughter. Their child Lily is therefore the child of John’s daughter, making Lily John’s granddaughter. Simultaneously Lily is the child of John’s nephew, which makes her John’s great‑niece (the child of a nephew). Hence Lily holds both relations.

X’s father A and Y’s mother B are siblings, making X and Y first cousins on that side. Likewise, X’s mother D and Y’s father C are siblings, giving another first‑cousin link. Since they share both sets of grandparents, they are double first cousins.
N is married to P. R is P's sister, making R the sibling of N's spouse. In standard kinship terminology, the sister of one's spouse is a sister‑in‑law. No other direct term applies.

M (X's mother) is the only daughter of Y, making Y M's parent. Y's brother Z is therefore M's uncle. Z's son W is M's first cousin. Since X is M's child, X is one generation below M, making X and W first cousins once removed.

R's mother has one brother, making him R's maternal uncle. The uncle's daughter S is R's first cousin. S's son T is the child of R's first cousin, which by kinship terminology is a first cousin once removed (one generation down). Therefore the relationship is uniquely determined as first cousin once removed.

John's father and Mary's mother are siblings, giving John and Mary one shared set of grandparents. Likewise, John's mother and Mary's father are siblings, giving them a second shared set of grandparents. Sharing both paternal and maternal grandparents makes them double first cousins, the precise term.

B is A's parent. B's sister C is A's aunt by blood. C is married to D, whose mother is E. Therefore E is the mother of A's aunt's husband. This makes E related to A only through an affinal chain (spouse of aunt's parent), for which standard English kinship terminology provides no direct term.

Alice and Ben share the same parents (GP1). Carol and Dan share the same parents (GP2). Alice marries Dan, producing Emma; Ben marries Carol, producing Frank. Emma’s grandparents are GP1 (through Alice) and GP2 (through Dan). Frank’s grandparents are GP1 (through Ben) and GP2 (through Carol). Hence Emma and Frank share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins.

M and N are half‑siblings, sharing only mother O. Their children P and Q therefore each have O as a grandparent, but they have different other grandparents. First cousins share both grandparents; when only one grandparent is shared (due to half‑sibling parents), the correct term is half‑first cousins. Hence the precise relationship is half‑first cousins.

Alice and Ben share a mother, so their children Clara and David are half‑cousins. Clara marries Edward. Fiona is Edward's sister, making her the sibling of Clara's spouse. In kinship terms, a sibling of one's spouse is a sister‑in‑law. Therefore Fiona's precise relation to Clara is sister‑in‑law.

John and Mary are siblings, sharing grandparents G1. Anne and Paul are siblings, sharing grandparents G2. X is child of John (G1 grandparent) and Anne (G2 grandparent). Y is child of Mary (G1) and Paul (G2). Thus X and Y share both sets of grandparents, making them children of two sibling pairs, i.e., double first cousins.

John and Mary are siblings. Anna and Tom are also siblings. John (brother of Mary) marries Anna (sister of Tom), and Mary (sister of John) marries Tom (brother of Anna). Thus Lily’s parents are a sibling pair (John & Mary) married to another sibling pair (Anna & Tom). Lily and Sam therefore share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins.

M and O are brothers, so they share the same parents. N and P are sisters, so they also share the same parents. L is the child of M (father) and N (mother); Q is the child of O (father) and P (mother). Therefore L and Q have the same paternal grandparents (the parents of M and O) and the same maternal grandparents (the parents of N and P). Sharing both sets of grandparents makes them double first cousins, the most precise term.

A and B are siblings, as are C and D. A (child of grandparents G1) marries C (child of grandparents G2), while B (child of G1) marries D (child of G2). Their children X (A+C) and Y (B+D) therefore share both sets of grandparents G1 and G2, making them first cousins through each parent pair—i.e., double first cousins.

Susan is Kevin's mother. Michael is Susan's brother, making him the sibling of Kevin's mother. In English kinship, a mother's brother is a maternal uncle. Other connections (Thomas as Kevin's uncle by marriage) do not affect Michael's direct blood relation to Kevin.

A and B are children of two sibling pairs: M and N are full siblings, as are X and Y. A’s father (M) and B’s father (N) are siblings, making them first cousins on the paternal side. Likewise, A’s mother (X) and B’s mother (Y) are siblings, making them first cousins on the maternal side. Sharing both sets of grandparents means they are first cousins through two independent lines, i.e., double first cousins.

John and Mary are Peter's parents. Mary’s brother Tom is therefore the brother of Peter’s mother, making Tom Peter’s maternal uncle. The fact that Tom is married to Lisa (John’s niece) does not affect his direct kinship to Peter, and no other relationship (paternal uncle, cousin, or no kinship) fits.

A's mother and B's father are half‑siblings, meaning they share exactly one parent. That shared parent is a grandparent to both A and B. Since A and B are each the child of one of those half‑siblings, they are cousins who share only one grandparent, which defines a half‑first cousin relationship. No other intermarriages affect this calculation, so the kinship is determinable.

M and N are siblings, so they share one set of grandparents (call them A). O and P are siblings, sharing another set of grandparents (call them B). M marries O, producing child X, who has grandparents A (through M) and B (through O). N marries P, producing child Y, who also has grandparents A (through N) and B (through P). Thus X and Y share both sets of grandparents, making them children of two distinct sibling pairs. This relationship is defined as double first cousins.

M and N are siblings, so their children O and R are first cousins. R's child Q is one generation below R. The child of your first cousin is your first cousin once removed. Hence O is first cousin once removed to Q, ignoring the marriage.

A's mother’s brother is A’s maternal uncle; his daughter B is A’s maternal first cousin. A's father’s sister is A’s paternal aunt; her son C is A’s paternal first cousin. B and C (both first cousins of A) marry and have child D. The child of a first cousin is a first cousin once removed from the original person. Since D is the child of A’s first cousin (via B and also via C), D is A’s first cousin once removed.

Q's mother has one brother, who is Q's maternal uncle. P is his child, making P a first cousin on the maternal side. Q's father has one sister, his paternal aunt, whose child P also is, making P a first cousin on the paternal side as well. Hence P is a (double) first cousin of Q, uniquely determined.

P's mother is sibling of Q's father, so they share one pair of grandparents. P's father is sibling of Q's mother, so they share a second pair of grandparents. Thus P and Q have both sets of grandparents in common, making them children of two sibling couples. This is the definition of double first cousins, more specific than ordinary first cousins and distinct from half‑first or second cousins.

M is the child of N's paternal aunt (father's only sister) making M a first cousin on the father's side. M is also the child of N's maternal uncle (mother's only brother) making M a first cousin on the mother's side. The two parents (paternal aunt and maternal uncle) are married, so M shares both sets of grandparents with N, i.e., two parallel first‑cousin relationships. This is the definition of a double first cousin.

The elder brother and younger brother are siblings, and their wives are sisters. Their children (the son and daughter) therefore share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins. The grandchildren are each one generation down from these double first cousins, so they are second cousins who share all four great‑grandparents – i.e., double second cousins.

John is the father of Peter, making Peter his son. Peter and Lisa (John's niece) have a child Sam. Since Sam is the child of John’s son, Sam is John’s direct descendant: his grandson. Although Sam is also the child of John’s niece (making him a great‑nephew), the direct lineage term "grandson" is more precise and unambiguous.

M is the child of P's paternal aunt (sister of P's father) making M a first cousin via the father's side. M is also the child of P's maternal uncle (brother of P's mother) making M a first cousin via the mother's side. The two parents (paternal aunt and maternal uncle) are each siblings of one of P's parents, i.e., a pair of siblings from the father's family married a pair of siblings from the mother's family. This creates double first cousins, where the cousins share both sets of grandparents. Hence M is a double first cousin of P.

Sam is the child of Lily, Paul’s daughter, making Sam Paul’s grandchild. Sam is also the child of Maya, Paul’s niece (daughter of his brother Quinn), making Sam Paul’s great‑niece. No single standard English kinship term simultaneously denotes both roles, so the correct choice is that no single term applies.

L’s father’s only sister is L’s paternal aunt. The child of that aunt (M) is L’s first cousin. Similarly, L’s mother’s only brother is L’s maternal uncle, and the child of that uncle (N) is also L’s first cousin. Hence both M and N are first cousins of L, uniquely determined.

Anna and Ben are siblings, sharing grandparents P1 and P2. Clara and Dan are siblings, sharing grandparents Q1 and Q2. Emma is the child of Anna (P‑family) and Dan (Q‑family). Frank is the child of Ben (P‑family) and Clara (Q‑family). Thus Emma and Frank each have the same two sets of grandparents (P1,P2 and Q1,Q2). Children of two sibling pairs are double first cousins, the most precise term among the choices.

John’s father is sibling of Mary’s mother, making John the child of Mary’s maternal uncle – a first cousin. John’s mother is sibling of Mary’s father, making John also the child of Mary’s paternal aunt – another first cousin. Since both of John’s parents are siblings of both of Mary’s parents, they share both sets of grandparents, which is the definition of double first cousins.

P is the mother of O. Since Q is the child of O, Q is the child of P's child, which makes Q P's grandchild. This direct parent‑child lineage is the most precise standard term, superseding other possible indirect descriptors.

John and Mary are siblings, sharing grandparents GP1/GP2. Lisa and Tom are siblings, sharing grandparents GP3/GP4. Alice’s parents are John (child of GP1/GP2) and Lisa (child of GP3/GP4). Bob’s parents are Mary (child of GP1/GP2) and Tom (child of GP3/GP4). Therefore Alice and Bob share both sets of grandparents, making them children of two sibling pairs. This precise relationship is termed double first cousins.

A and B share only their mother, so they have one set of common grandparents (the mother’s parents). Their children C and D therefore share exactly those grandparents, but not the other set. Hence C and D are first cousins who share only one grandparent, i.e., half‑first cousins. The most precise term is "half‑first cousins."

John and Lisa are siblings, so their children Mike and Anna are first cousins (they share the same grandparents). Clara is Mike's daughter and Ben is Anna's son, placing them one generation below Mike and Anna. Children of first cousins are second cousins, sharing the same great‑grandparents (John and Lisa's parents). They are in the same generation, so no "removed" term applies, and they share both great‑grandparents, not just one, eliminating the half‑cousin case.

Adam and Bob are brothers, so their children share paternal grandparents. Eve and Fay are sisters, so their children share maternal grandparents. Carl’s father is Adam and mother is Eve; Dana’s father is Bob and mother is Fay. Thus Carl and Dana share both sets of grandparents, making them first cousins on both sides – the definition of double first cousins.

B’s mother’s brother C is B’s maternal uncle. C’s wife D is described as the sister of A’s father. In standard kinship, a father’s sister is a paternal aunt of A. This relation exists independently of any in‑law connections, providing a direct term. Therefore D is A’s aunt.

Mary's brother and Mary’s sister share the same parents, making them siblings. John is the son of Mary’s brother, and Lisa is the daughter of Mary’s sister. Therefore John and Lisa are the children of two siblings, which by standard kinship terminology makes them first cousins.

Mary and Nina become step‑siblings when Ellen marries Victor, because each is the biological child of one spouse. John is Mary's husband, so his connection to Nina is through his spouse's step‑sibling. There is no established term for a husband's relationship to his spouse's step‑sibling; it is merely an affinal link without a standard kinship label.

Clara and Ethan share the same mother (Alice) but have different fathers (Bob and Dave). In standard kinship terminology, children who share one parent but not both are half‑siblings. No other relationships apply, so the correct choice is half‑siblings.

L and M are half‑siblings, sharing only their mother. Their children A and B are therefore the offspring of half‑siblings. Such offspring share exactly one grandparent (the common mother) rather than both, which is the definition of half‑first cousins. First cousins would require their parents to be full siblings, and second cousins would require a generation gap of two. The relationship is determinable, so the precise term is half‑first cousins.

M and N are siblings, so they share the same parents (paternal grandparents of X and Y). A and B are also siblings, sharing another set of parents (maternal grandparents of X and Y). X’s parents are M and A; Y’s parents are N and B. Hence X and Y share both sets of grandparents, making them first cousins on both paternal and maternal lines – i.e., double first cousins.

C is mother of X, making her Z's grandmother. C is also sister of D, who is Y's mother, so C is Y's aunt; consequently she is Z's great-aunt. Thus Z is related to C as both grandmother and great‑aunt, a double relationship.

A is K's paternal aunt (father's sister) and B is K's maternal uncle (mother's brother).
