M and N are half‑brothers (share only father A). Their children X and Y therefore share only one grandparent (A). Children of half‑siblings are classified as half‑first cousins, distinct from full first cousins who share both grandparents. Hence X and Y are half‑first cousins.

X's parents are the father's brother (sharing the father's parents) and the mother's sister (sharing the mother's parents). Y's parents are the father's sister (sharing the father's parents) and the mother's brother (sharing the mother's parents). Thus X and Y have the same paternal grandparents and the same maternal grandparents, i.e., they share both sets of grandparents. This is the definition of double first cousins.

M and N share the same parents, and P and Q share another set of parents. X is the child of M (a child of the first set) and P (a child of the second set). Y is the child of N (the sibling of M) and Q (the sibling of P). Therefore X and Y have both sets of grandparents in common, making them first cousins through two sibling links. This is the definition of double first cousins.

X's father Alan and Y's father Brian are brothers, sharing the same paternal grandparents. X's mother Claire and Y's mother Diana are sisters, sharing the same maternal grandparents. Thus X and Y have both sets of grandparents in common, making them the children of two sibling pairs. This is the definition of double first cousins.

Tom and Sam are brothers; Anna and Beth are sisters. Their children Carl and Dana are double first cousins, sharing both sets of grandparents. Emma is Carl's child and Fiona is Dana's child. Children of first cousins are second cousins; because Carl and Dana are double first cousins, their children share both sets of great‑grandparents, making Emma and Fiona double second cousins.

A and C are full brothers, sharing the same parents. B and D are full sisters, also sharing the same parents. M is the child of A (brother) and B (sister), while N is the child of C (brother) and D (sister). Therefore M and N share both sets of grandparents (the parents of A/C and the parents of B/D). This makes them children of two sibling pairs, i.e., double first cousins, the most precise term.

Peter is Anna's biological father, making him Sam's maternal grandfather. He is also Mary's husband, so he is John's step‑father; John's child Sam therefore gives Peter the status of step‑grandfather on the paternal side. Hence Peter holds both a biological and a step grandparent relationship to Sam.

X is the child of Y's father's brother, making X a first cousin of Y on the paternal side. Z is the child of Y's mother's sister, making Z a first cousin of Y on the maternal side. The paternal and maternal families are unrelated (no intermarriage), so X's parent and Z's parent share no common ancestors. Consequently X and Z share no blood relation; they are not cousins, half‑cousins, or otherwise related.

My mother’s brother is my maternal uncle; his child is my maternal first cousin. My father’s sister is my paternal aunt; her child is my paternal first cousin. Since the same person Y is child of both the maternal uncle and paternal aunt, those two siblings must be married, making Y a double first cousin (cousin through both parental lines). The relationship is uniquely determined under the given constraints.

R and S are siblings, so their children T and U are first cousins (they share the same grandparents). V is T's child and W is U's child. Children of first cousins are second cousins, because they share the same great‑grandparents. Therefore V and W are second cousins.

P's paternal aunt (father's sister) and P's maternal uncle (mother's brother) are Q's parents. Through the aunt, Q is the child of P's father's sibling, making Q a first cousin on the paternal side. Through the uncle, Q is the child of P's mother's sibling, also a first cousin on the maternal side. Being first cousins via both parental lines makes Q a double first cousin of P, a recognized term.

Lisa's father John and Tom's father Mark are brothers, making Lisa and Tom first cousins through their paternal line. Likewise, Lisa's mother Anna and Tom's mother Beth are sisters, making them first cousins through their maternal line as well. Sharing both sets of grandparents qualifies them as double first cousins, not half‑cousins or unrelated.

X's mother and Y are siblings, making Y X's maternal uncle. Y's daughter Z is therefore X's first cousin by blood. Z's marriage to X's paternal uncle W adds no blood connection, so the only blood relationship between X and Z remains that of first cousins.

X and Y share only one parent, making them half‑siblings. Their children M and N each descend from one of these half‑siblings, so M and N share only one grandparent (the mother common to X and Y). First cousins share both grandparents; when only one grandparent is common, the correct term is half‑first cousins. Thus the precise relation is half‑first cousins.

U is R's maternal uncle (mother's brother) and V is R's paternal aunt (father's sister). They marry and have child C. C is the child of R's maternal uncle, making C a first cousin on the mother's side, and also the child of R's paternal aunt, making C a first cousin on the father's side. Sharing both sets of grandparents, C is a double first cousin of R.

M is mother of N and O, so N and O are siblings. O's son R is therefore N's nephew. Q is married to R, making Q the spouse of N's nephew. The spouse of one's nephew is referred to as a niece‑in‑law (niece by marriage). Hence Q's precise kinship term to N is niece‑in‑law.

R’s mother’s brother (M) is R’s maternal uncle. The child of that uncle (X) shares both grandparents with R, making X a direct first cousin on the maternal side. No half‑relationship is indicated, so the precise term is "first cousin".

Ethan's father Adam and Fiona's father Brian are brothers, and Ethan's mother Clara and Fiona's mother Diana are sisters. Thus Ethan and Fiona share both paternal grandparents (through their fathers) and maternal grandparents (through their mothers). Sharing both sets of grandparents makes them double first cousins, the most precise term.

X and Y each have a father who are brothers (A and B) and a mother who are sisters (C and D). Therefore X and Y share both sets of grandparents: the parents of A/B and the parents of C/D. Sharing both paternal and maternal grandparents makes them first cousins on two separate lines, i.e., double first cousins, not half or second cousins.

John and Jane are siblings, sharing grandparents P1 and P2. Anna and Adam are siblings, sharing grandparents Q1 and Q2. Tom is child of John (descendant of P1,P2) and Anna (descendant of Q1,Q2). Sue is child of Jane (descendant of P1,P2) and Adam (descendant of Q1,Q2). Therefore Tom and Sue share both sets of grandparents, making them first cousins through both parental lines—a double first‑cousin relationship.

Emma's paternal uncle Tom has a daughter Lily, making Lily Emma's first cousin. Emma's maternal uncle has a son Michael, also Emma's first cousin. Lily and Michael (two of Emma's first cousins, unrelated by blood) marry and have Noah. A child of one's first cousin is defined as a first cousin once removed. Since Noah is the child of Emma's first cousin on both sides, the appropriate term is still first cousin once removed.

John and Mary are siblings, sharing the same parents. Mary’s son Tom and John’s son Peter are therefore first cousins (children of siblings). Sarah is Peter’s daughter, placing her one generation below Peter. Consequently, Tom (cousin of Peter) is a first cousin once removed from Sarah, who is Peter’s child. This matches option C.

F is child of A (who is sibling of C) and B (who is sibling of D). E is child of C and D. Thus F and E each descend from the same paternal grandparents (parents of A and C) and the same maternal grandparents (parents of B and D). Sharing both sets of grandparents makes them double first cousins, the precise term among the choices.

M and N are siblings, so they share the same parents. X and Y are also siblings, sharing a different set of parents. A’s father (M) and B’s father (N) are brothers, making A and B first cousins on their paternal side. Likewise, A’s mother (X) and B’s mother (Y) are sisters, making A and B first cousins on their maternal side as well. Because they are first cousins through both parents, they are double first cousins, the most precise term.

R is L's maternal uncle (mother's brother) and S is L's paternal aunt (father's sister). Their only child M is therefore both the child of L's maternal uncle and the child of L's paternal aunt. M shares L's maternal grandparents (through R) and L's paternal grandparents (through S). Hence M and L are first cousins on both sides, i.e., double first cousins, the most precise term.
R is O's father. Q is R's sister, making Q O's paternal aunt. Therefore O is Q's niece (or nephew). This matches choice A.

M and N are half‑siblings, sharing one parent P. That parent P is a grandparent of both X (through M) and Y (through N). X and Y therefore share exactly one grandparent, not both. Children of full siblings are first cousins (share two grandparents). When only one grandparent is shared, the correct term is half‑first cousins (or first cousins, half‑blood). Hence the most precise relation is half‑first cousins.

X's mother and Y's father are siblings, meaning they share a parent. X is the child of one sibling, Y is the child of the other sibling. Children of siblings are first cousins. The extra condition about marriage does not affect the blood relationship.

M and N are siblings, so they share the same parents (grandparents A for their children). O and Q are also siblings, sharing another set of parents (grandparents B). X is child of M (from family A) and O (from family B). Z is child of N (family A) and Q (family B). Thus X and Z have both sets of grandparents in common, meaning they are children of two different sibling pairs. This defines double first cousins.

Ethan's mother Clara and Fiona's mother Diana are sisters, making Ethan and Fiona maternal first cousins. Their fathers, Adam and Brian, are not siblings—only brothers‑in‑law—so there is no paternal sibling link. Double first cousins require both parents to be siblings, which is not the case. Therefore the correct classification is simple first cousins.

Mary's daughters are Anna and Emma, making them sisters. Emma's child is Clara, so Clara is the daughter of Anna's sister, i.e., Anna's niece. A niece is the child of a sibling; therefore Anna is the aunt of Clara. No other listed relationship fits.

John and Mary are siblings, so their children Peter and Susan are first cousins. Kevin is Peter's son and Michael is Susan's son; they are the children of first cousins, which makes them second cousins.

John’s mother’s brother Mark is John’s maternal uncle. Mark’s daughter Lisa is John’s first cousin. Lisa marries a man M. M’s sister is Sarah’s mother, making M Sarah’s maternal uncle (by blood). Lisa, as M’s wife, is sister‑in‑law to Sarah’s mother, which makes her the aunt‑in‑law of Sarah. Hence Lisa’s relation to Sarah is aunt‑in‑law.

M and F share only a mother, making them half‑siblings. Their children C1 and C2 are each one generation down from half‑siblings, so they are the offspring of half‑siblings. In standard English kinship terminology, such offspring are called half‑first cousins (sometimes just half‑cousins). Therefore the precise relation is half‑first cousins.

A is X's maternal uncle, so A's daughter Y is X's maternal first cousin. B is X's paternal aunt, so B's son Z is X's paternal first cousin. Y and Z are unrelated to each other, but each is a first cousin of X. Their child W is therefore the child of X's first cousin, which by standard kinship terminology is a first cousin once removed. No half‑relationship or double‑cousin applies.

Alan and Brian are brothers; Clara and Diana are sisters. Their children Ethan and Fiona therefore share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins. The next generation—Paul (Ethan's child) and Quinn (Fiona's child)—are the children of double first cousins, which makes them double second cousins.

Adam and Brian are brothers; Clara and Diana are sisters. Their children X and Y therefore share both sets of grandparents, making X and Y double first cousins. The children of X (P) and Y (Q) each descend one generation further, so they share both sets of great‑grandparents. Sharing great‑grandparents defines second cousins; sharing both sets makes them double second cousins. Hence the most precise term is double second cousins.

B is A's maternal uncle (mother's brother) and D is A's paternal aunt (father's sister). Their child would be A's maternal first cousin via B and paternal first cousin via D. Since C and E are the same person, that child is both cousins, meaning A's parents' siblings married each other. This produces a double first cousin, who shares both sets of grandparents with A.

Adam and Ben are brothers, so their children share the same paternal grandparents. Clara and Diana are sisters, so their children share the same maternal grandparents. Ethan and Fiona therefore have both sets of grandparents in common, making them first cousins through both parents—a double first‑cousin relationship.

M and N are full siblings. Their children, D (M's son) and B (N's son), are first cousins because their parents are siblings. C is D's daughter, one generation below D. Therefore C is one generation below B's first cousin, making B and C first cousins once removed. This matches option A.

Ethan's father Adam and Fiona's father Brian are brothers, making Ethan and Fiona first cousins on their paternal side. Likewise, Ethan's mother Clara and Fiona's mother Diana are sisters, making them first cousins on their maternal side as well. Because they are first cousins through both parents, they are double first cousins.

A is R's paternal aunt (father's sister) and B is R's maternal uncle (mother's brother). Their child X is simultaneously the child of R's aunt and uncle, making X a first cousin on the father's side and also a first cousin on the mother's side. Sharing two distinct lines of first‑cousin relationship defines a double first cousin.

John's father Michael is Laura's brother, making Michael and Laura share the same parents. John's mother Sarah is David's sister, so Sarah and David share another set of parents. Emily's parents are Laura and David. Therefore John and Emily each have one parent who is a sibling of one of Emily's parents, and the other parent is a sibling of the other parent. They share both sets of grandparents, which defines a double first cousin relationship.

X is the child of R's maternal uncle (mother's brother) making X a first cousin on the maternal side. X is also the child of R's paternal aunt (father's sister) making X a first cousin on the paternal side as well. Being a first cousin through both parents defines a double first cousin, the most specific term.

X's mother’s brother Y is X’s maternal uncle. Y’s daughter Z is therefore X’s first cousin (children of siblings). Z’s son W is the child of X’s first cousin, which makes W a first cousin once removed to X (one generation apart). Hence the precise kinship term is "first cousin once removed".

M and N are siblings, so their children O, P, and R are first cousins. R’s child Q is one generation below R. A child of a first cousin is a first cousin once removed from the original cousin. Therefore Q is the first cousin once removed of O.

M and N share only their mother, making them half‑siblings. Their children A and B each have that mother as a grandparent, but they have different other grandparents. Thus A and B share exactly one grandparent, not both, which defines a half‑first cousin relationship—the most precise term among the choices.

M and N are full siblings, so they share the same parents. X and Y are also full siblings, sharing their own parents. A is the child of M (father) and X (mother); B is the child of N (father) and Y (mother). A and B are first cousins through their fathers (M and N) and also first cousins through their mothers (X and Y). Because they are related as first cousins on both paternal and maternal sides, they are double first cousins, the most specific term.

A and B are brothers, so they share the same parents. C and D are sisters, sharing their own parents. X is child of A (brother) and C (sister); Y is child of B (brother) and D (sister). Therefore X and Y have both sets of grandparents in common, making them first cousins through both parental lines – i.e., double first cousins.

Kevin is the brother of Paul. Paul is the father of Lisa, making Paul Lisa's father. Therefore Kevin, as Paul's brother, is Lisa's paternal uncle by blood. No other relationship changes this, and the term "uncle" correctly captures the direct blood tie.

A is mother of B, and also mother of E (since E’s parents are A and C). B’s father is not specified as C, so B and E share only one parent, A. Sharing a single biological parent defines a half‑sibling relationship. They are not full siblings (different fathers), not step‑siblings (no marriage between parents creating a blended family), nor cousins (different generational line).

Adam and Beth are siblings, and Clara and Daniel are siblings. X is child of Adam (family1) and Clara (family2); Y is child of Beth (family1) and Daniel (family2). Thus X and Y each have the same two grandparents from Adam/Beth's parents and the same two grandparents from Clara/Daniel's parents. Sharing both sets of grandparents makes them double first cousins, the most precise term.

M and N are siblings, so they share the same parents. O and P are another set of siblings, sharing a different set of parents. M marries O, N marries P. Their children A (from M + O) and B (from N + P) therefore have the same paternal grandparents (parents of M and N) and the same maternal grandparents (parents of O and P). Sharing both sets of grandparents makes them double first cousins, i.e., children of two sibling couples.

M and N are siblings, and O and Q are also siblings. M marries O while N marries Q. Thus X’s parents (M and O) are each siblings of Y’s parents (N and Q). X and Y therefore share both sets of grandparents – the parents of M/N and the parents of O/Q. Sharing both paternal and maternal grandparents defines double first cousins, which is more specific than ordinary first cousins.

M and N are siblings, making their children O and R first cousins. Q is R's child, so Q is one generation below R. Therefore O is the first cousin of Q's parent, which defines a first cousin once removed relationship.

C and D are siblings, so their children B and E are first cousins. A is B's child, placing A one generation below B. Thus A is one generation removed from the cousin relationship with E, making A and E first cousins once removed.

R's paternal aunt S's child C1 is R's first cousin. R's maternal uncle U's child C2 is also R's first cousin. X is the child of C1 and C2. The child of one's first cousin is a first cousin once removed. Since X is the offspring of two of R's first cousins, X is still a first cousin once removed to R. The other options do not match this kinship level.

M is the child of N's paternal aunt (father's only sister) and also the child of N's maternal uncle (mother's only brother). Thus M is the offspring of two siblings of N's parents, making M a first cousin on both the father's and mother's sides—a double first cousin.

A is the child of M's maternal uncle, making A a first cousin of M on the mother's side. B is the child of M's paternal aunt, making B a first cousin of M on the father's side. The two cousins derive from unrelated sibling lines of M's parents, so A and B share no common ancestor and have no standard blood kinship term. Under the limited in‑law definitions given, they are linked only through an affinal chain, not by a direct kinship term.

Lisa is John’s daughter, making her child Sam John’s grandchild. Simultaneously, Tom is John’s nephew (son of John’s brother Mark), so Sam is also John’s great‑nephew. However, the direct line of descent gives a standard term: grandson. Hence the precise relation is grandson.

A is the father of E, who is G's parent, making A G's grandfather via the direct line. Although A is also B's brother, making him great‑uncle to F and thus great‑uncle to G, the direct lineage term (grandfather) is more precise than the collateral relation.

John is Lily's stepfather because Lily is Anna's daughter from a previous marriage. Lily is Sam's mother, so Sam is the child of John's stepdaughter. The child of a stepchild is a step-grandchild. Hence Sam is John’s step‑grandchild, matching choice B.

M is the child of J's paternal aunt (sister of J's father) and also the child of J's maternal uncle (brother of J's mother). For M to have both these parents, the aunt and uncle must be married. Thus J's father’s sister married J's mother’s brother, creating two parallel sibling links between the families. Their offspring (M) shares both sets of grandparents with J, making M a double first cousin rather than a regular first cousin, half‑cousin, or second cousin.

N’s father’s sister is N’s paternal aunt; her child is N’s paternal first cousin. N’s mother’s brother is N’s maternal uncle; his child is N’s maternal first cousin. The puzzle states these two siblings each have a single child, and that child is the same person M. Hence M is simultaneously the child of N’s paternal aunt and maternal uncle, making M both a paternal and maternal first cousin – a double first cousin.

L and R are half‑sisters, sharing only one parent (their mother). Their children S and D therefore share only that one grandparent (the mother of L and R). First cousins share both grandparents; when only one grandparent is common, the relationship is termed half‑first cousins. No other family ties affect this, so the precise kinship is half‑first cousins.

Ethan's mother Anna and Fiona's mother Beth are full sisters, making Ethan and Fiona first cousins through their mothers. Likewise, Ethan's father Carl and Fiona's father Dan are full brothers, making them first cousins through their fathers as well. Sharing both sets of grandparents defines a double first‑cousin relationship.

Anna and Diana are sisters; Ben and Carl are brothers. Each sister married a brother. Claire's parents are Anna (sister of Diana) and Ben (brother of Carl). Ethan's parents are Diana and Carl. Therefore Claire and Ethan share the same maternal grandparents (parents of Anna and Diana) and the same paternal grandparents (parents of Ben and Carl). Sharing both sets of grandparents makes them double first cousins, not just ordinary first cousins or half‑cousins.
U is R's maternal uncle, making U's daughter R's first cousin. V is the child of that cousin, which is defined as a first cousin once removed relative to R. The relationship is uniquely determined.

M and N are brothers; P and Q are sisters. Their children X and Y share both sets of grandparents, making X and Y double first cousins. The next generation—A (child of X) and B (child of Y)—are therefore the children of double first cousins, which defines them as double second cousins.

A is the child of X and W; B is the child of Y and Z. X and Y are siblings, so A and B share one set of grandparents through their fathers (or mothers). W and Z are also siblings, giving A and B a second shared set of grandparents through their mothers (or fathers). Sharing both paternal and maternal grandparental lines makes them double first cousins, not just ordinary first cousins or half‑first cousins.

P and Q are siblings, so their children R (P's son) and S (Q's daughter) are first cousins. T is S's son, i.e., the child of R's first cousin. The relationship between a person and the child of his/her first cousin is defined as first cousin once removed. Therefore T is R's first cousin once removed.

Mary’s children are John and Anna, making Tom their father as John’s father is Tom and Mary is John’s mother. Tom also fathered Brian with a previous spouse, so Brian shares Tom as a biological parent with Anna but has a different mother. Sharing one parent makes them half‑siblings, not step‑siblings (which require no blood link) nor cousins. Therefore the precise kinship term is half‑sibling.

L, S, and B are siblings, sharing the same parents (the great‑grandparents of M and N). S's child C₁ and B's child C₂ are first cousins (they share grandparents). M and N are each one generation further down: they are the children of C₁ and C₂ respectively, making M and N great‑grandchildren of L's parents. Sharing great‑grandparents but not grandparents defines second cousins.

L's sister's son S is L's nephew; L's brother's daughter D is L's niece. S and D (first cousins) have a child M. M is therefore the child of L's nephew/niece, which makes M L's grand‑nephew (or great‑nephew/niece), a standard kinship term.

M and N share the same parents; P and Q share another set of parents. When each sibling pair marries the other sibling pair, their children inherit both sets of grandparents from both sides. X’s paternal grandparents are M/N’s parents, and maternal grandparents are P/Q’s parents; Y has the same two sets of grandparents. Sharing both sets of grandparents makes X and Y double first cousins, not just first cousins or any half/second cousin relationship.

Mary and Carl are siblings, so Carl is John’s maternal uncle. Carl’s daughter Nina is therefore John’s first cousin. Nina’s son Kevin is one generation below John, making Kevin John’s first cousin once removed. Kevin’s daughter Sara is another generation below John, so the removal count increases by one more generation, yielding a first cousin twice removed relationship between John and Sara.

John and Paul are brothers; Mary and Linda are sisters. Their children Alex and Bella are therefore first cousins through both parents, i.e., double first cousins. Sam is Alex's child and Tina is Bella's child. Children of first cousins are second cousins, and children of double first cousins are double second cousins because they share both sets of great‑grandparents. Hence Sam and Tina are double second cousins.

John and Mark are brothers, so their children share the same paternal grandparents. Lisa and Nina are sisters, so their children share the same maternal grandparents. Alex and Bella therefore have both sets of grandparents in common, making them first cousins on the father's side and also first cousins on the mother's side. This dual relationship defines double first cousins.

John and Paul are brothers, and their wives Mary and Lisa are sisters, making Tom and Sara double first cousins (they share both paternal and maternal grandparents). The children of first cousins are second cousins; because Tom and Sara are double first cousins, their children Emma and Noah are second cousins through two distinct lines, i.e., double second cousins.

M and N are siblings. S is the child of M, making S the niece/nephew of N. Q is N's spouse, so Q is not a blood aunt/uncle but the spouse of S's aunt/uncle. The standard English term for such a relation is "aunt/uncle-in-law". Hence the correct choice is D.

L is parent of D and sibling of S, making D the niece of S. S's child Sson is thus D's first cousin. M is D's child and N is Sson's child, so they are the children of first cousins, which makes M and N second cousins.

A and B are siblings sharing one set of grandparents, while C and D are another set of siblings sharing a different set of grandparents. X is child of A (from the first sibling pair) and C (from the second pair); Y is child of B (first pair) and D (second pair). Thus X and Y share both sets of grandparents, making them first cousins through two distinct sibling connections—i.e., double first cousins.

A and C are half‑siblings because they share only their father G. X is A's child and Y is C's child. Children of half‑siblings share only one grandparent (G), making them half‑first cousins. Therefore the precise kinship term is half‑first cousins.

N is the sister of M's father, making N M's paternal aunt. O, N's daughter, is therefore M's first cousin. P, as O's son, is the child of M's cousin, which is defined in kinship as a first cousin once removed. The other options do not match this relationship.

Ben is Alex's paternal uncle (father's brother) and Clara is Alex's maternal aunt (mother's sister). Their child Dana is therefore the child of Alex's uncle on one side and aunt on the other. Dana shares Alex's paternal grandparents through Ben and Alex's maternal grandparents through Clara, giving them both sets of grandparents in common. This matches the definition of double first cousins, not a single first cousin or other variant.

N is the father of P, who is one of Q's parents, making N Q's grandfather. N is also the sibling of M, who is the mother of O, the other parent of Q. Being the sibling of Q's grandparent (M) makes N a great‑uncle of Q. Thus N holds both relations simultaneously, which is the most precise description.

Anna and Ben share the same parents, and Carl and Diana share another set of parents. Eva is child of Anna (sibling of Ben) and Carl (sibling of Diana). Frank is child of Ben (sibling of Anna) and Diana (sibling of Carl). Therefore Eva and Frank have both sets of grandparents in common: the parents of Anna/Ben and the parents of Carl/Diana. Sharing both grandparent pairs makes them double first cousins, not just regular or half‑first cousins.

John and Mark are full brothers. Their children Tom and Lily are therefore first cousins. Sara is Tom's child, placing her one generation below Tom. A cousin of a parent is a first cousin once removed. Hence Lily, Tom's cousin, is Sara's first cousin once removed.

X’s father Adam and Y’s father Brian are brothers, sharing both paternal grandparents. X’s mother Clara and Y’s mother Dana are full sisters, sharing both maternal grandparents. Thus X and Y share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins, the most precise term.

Alan and Brian share the same mother. Alan's daughter Clara is Ethan's mother, making Ethan Alan's grandson. Since Alan's mother is one generation above Alan, Ethan is one generation further down, i.e., the great‑grandson of Alan's mother.

Alan is Tom's maternal uncle, so his daughter Beth is Tom's first cousin on the mother's side. Carl is Tom's paternal uncle, so his daughter Dana is Tom's first cousin on the father's side. In either case the child of an uncle is a first cousin of the nephew/niece. Thus S, whether Beth or Dana, is Tom's first cousin.

M and N are full siblings, so they share both parents. O and Q are full siblings, also sharing both parents. X is the child of M (sibling of N) and O (sibling of Q). Y is the child of N (sibling of M) and Q (sibling of O). Thus X and Y each have the same two sets of grandparents: the parents of M/N and the parents of O/Q. They are first cousins through both parental lines, i.e., double first cousins, which is more specific than ordinary first cousins.

N and O share mother M, making them siblings. O's son R is therefore N's nephew. Q is married to R, making Q the spouse of N's nephew. In standard English kinship, the spouse of one's nephew is termed a niece‑in‑law.

K and M are siblings. Their children J (son of K) and N (son of M) are first cousins. O is N's daughter, one generation below N. Therefore O is the child of J's first cousin, making O J's first cousin once removed.

R is married to S, making S R's spouse. S's brother T is R's brother‑in‑law. T's son U is the child of R's brother‑in‑law, which is the definition of a nephew‑in‑law (the nephew of one’s spouse). Hence U is R's nephew‑in‑law.

John and Linda are siblings. Linda's son Kevin is therefore John's nephew and Mary's first cousin. Sara is Kevin's daughter, placing her one generation below Mary. A first cousin's child is a first cousin once removed. Hence Sara is Mary's first cousin once removed.

X's mother’s brother is X’s maternal uncle, and X's father’s sister is X’s paternal aunt. Their child Y is therefore the child of X’s maternal uncle (making Y a first cousin on the mother’s side) and also the child of X’s paternal aunt (making Y a first cousin on the father’s side). Being first cousins through both parental lines defines a double first cousin, which is more precise than a simple first cousin.

X's mother has one brother A, making A X's maternal uncle. A's daughter C is therefore X's maternal first cousin. X's father has one sister B, making B X's paternal aunt. B's son D is X's paternal first cousin. Whether Y is C or D, Y is a first cousin of X. Hence the kinship is uniquely a first cousin.

M is the sister of L's mother, which makes her an aunt. The clause that M and L's mother share only one parent tells us they are half‑sisters, not full sisters. Therefore M is an aunt who is a half‑sister of the mother, i.e., a half‑aunt. The appropriate standard term among the options is "Half‑aunt".

Aaron and Ben are brothers, so they share the same parents. Clara and Diana are sisters, sharing their own parents. Xavier is the child of Aaron and Clara; Yvonne is the child of Ben and Diana. Thus Xavier and Yvonne have both sets of grandparents in common (the brothers' parents and the sisters' parents). Lisa and Anna share the same father (John) but have different mothers, making them half‑siblings. Their other family connections (Mark's marriage to Anna) do not alter their direct sibling relationship. Therefore the precise term is half‑sister.

John and Mary are siblings, so their parents are Anna's paternal grandparents and Ben's maternal grandparents. Linda and Tom are also siblings, making them Anna's maternal grandparents and Ben's paternal grandparents. Thus Anna and Ben share both sets of grandparents, being the children of two distinct sibling pairs. This is the definition of double first cousins, not half or indeterminate.

M and N share only a mother, making them half‑siblings. Their respective children, X and Y, are the offspring of half‑siblings. In kinship terminology, the children of full siblings are first cousins, while the children of half‑siblings are termed half‑first cousins (or first cousins, half‑blood). Therefore the most precise description of X and Y’s relationship is half‑first cousins.

John's sister Mary has a son Peter, making Peter John’s nephew. John’s brother Thomas has a daughter Laura, making Laura John’s niece. Peter and Laura (first cousins) have a child Sam. Sam is therefore the child of John’s nephew and also the child of John’s niece. The child of a nephew or niece is called a grandnephew (or great‑nephew) for a male descendant. Hence Sam is John’s grandnephew.

M and N are half‑siblings, sharing one parent. The children of full siblings are first cousins. When the parents are only half‑siblings, the degree of cousinship remains first, but the blood relationship is halved, yielding the term “half‑first cousins.” Therefore S and T are half‑first cousins.

A and B are half‑siblings, sharing only one parent. The children of full siblings are first cousins. When the siblings share only one parent, their children share only one set of grandparents (the common parent’s parents). Thus X and Y are first cousins but of half‑blood, i.e., half‑first cousins.

W is X's maternal aunt (sister of X's mother) and Z is X's paternal uncle (brother of X's father). Their child V is therefore a child of X's aunt on one side and uncle on the other, making V a first cousin through the mother and also a first cousin through the father. Being first cousins on both parental lines defines a double first cousin.

John and Mary are siblings, so their parents are Lila's paternal grandparents and Milo's maternal grandparents. Alan and Beth are siblings, so their parents are Lila's maternal grandparents and Milo's paternal grandparents. Thus Lila and Milo share both sets of grandparents, making them the children of two pairs of siblings. This is the definition of double first cousins.

Z is described as the child of M’s mother’s only brother (M’s maternal uncle) and also the child of M’s father’s only sister (M’s paternal aunt). Under monogamy, these two relatives must be married and are Z’s parents. Hence Z is the child of M’s maternal uncle (making Z a first cousin on the maternal side) and also the child of M’s paternal aunt (making Z a first cousin on the paternal side). Being a first cousin through both parental lines defines a double first cousin. The relationship is uniquely determined.

M and N are siblings, so their children O, P, and R are first cousins. R is the parent of Q, making Q one generation below R. Therefore O, being a first cousin of Q's parent, is a first cousin once removed to Q. No other listed relationship fits.

R's spouse S has brother T (R's brother‑in‑law). T's wife U is also R's sister‑in‑law. U's brother V is the sibling of R's sister‑in‑law, which is not a direct in‑law relation under the limited set. W, as V's wife, is therefore linked to R only through this extended affinal chain and has no standard direct kinship term.

M and N are full siblings, so they share the same paternal grandparents. W1 and W2 are also full siblings, sharing the same maternal grandparents. A’s parents are M and W1; B’s parents are N and W2. Consequently, A and B share both sets of grandparents (the grandparents of M/N and the grandparents of W1/W2). Sharing both grandparent pairs defines double first cousins, which is more specific than ordinary first cousins.

A and B share the same parents (P1, M1); C and D share another set of parents (P2, M2). X’s parents are A (child of P1/M1) and C (child of P2/M2). Y’s parents are B (child of P1/M1) and D (child of P2/M2). Therefore X and Y each have both P1/M1 and P2/M2 as grandparents, meaning they share *both* sets of grandparents. This is the definition of double first cousins, i.e., children of two sibling pairs who marry each other’s siblings.

John’s maternal uncle Tom’s daughter Lily is John’s maternal first cousin. John’s paternal aunt Mary’s son Alex is John’s paternal first cousin. Lily and Alex’s child Sam is therefore the child of John’s first cousin (via either side). In kinship terms, the child of one’s cousin is a first cousin once removed. No sibling or aunt/uncle relationship applies, and the relation is determinable.

N’s father’s sister is N’s paternal aunt. The mother of that aunt is also the mother of N’s father (they share the same mother under standard full‑sibling assumptions). Therefore M is the mother of N’s father, i.e., N’s grandmother.

M is R's maternal uncle (mother's brother) and S is R's paternal aunt (father's sister). Their child C is therefore R's child of his maternal uncle (first cousin) and also child of his paternal aunt (first cousin). Being a first cousin on both parental sides makes C a double first cousin of R, the most precise standard term.

M is L's maternal uncle (mother's brother). N's sister is L's paternal aunt (father's sister). M marries N's sister, so their daughter S is child of L's maternal uncle and paternal aunt. Therefore S is L's first cousin on both maternal and paternal sides, i.e., a double first cousin.

M and N are siblings, so they share the same parents. O and P are also siblings, sharing their own parents. X’s father (M) is a sibling of Y’s father (N), and X’s mother (O) is a sibling of Y’s mother (P). Thus X and Y are first cousins through both paternal and maternal lines, i.e., they are double first cousins, sharing both sets of grandparents.

M and N are siblings, making their children O (M's daughter) and P (N's son) first cousins. R is married to P, so R is the spouse of O's cousin. Within the allowed kinship scope, the spouse of a cousin is termed a "cousin-in-law." The other options do not fit: R is not an aunt, nor a first cousin once removed, and there is a recognized term for this relation. Hence the precise term is cousin-in-law.

M is Y's maternal aunt (sister of Y's mother) and N is Y's paternal uncle (brother of Y's father). X, child of M and N, is therefore Y's cousin through the mother’s side and also through the father’s side. Since the two cousin relationships involve both parents, X is a double first cousin of Y.

K's mother and L's father are siblings, making K and L first cousins (their parents are siblings). L's child M is one generation below L. The relationship between a person and the child of their first cousin is defined as a first cousin once removed. This matches a standard kinship term, so the correct choice is B.

A and B are half‑siblings, sharing only their father. Therefore they share only one grandparent. Their children, C and D, each inherit that single shared grandparent, making them first cousins on the half‑blood side. The precise term for cousins who share only one grandparent is half‑first cousins.

M and N are siblings, sharing grandparents G1 and G2. O and P are siblings, sharing grandparents G3 and G4. X is child of M (grandparents G1,G2) and O (grandparents G3,G4). Y is child of N (same G1,G2) and P (same G3,G4). Hence X and Y share both sets of grandparents, making them first cousins through each parent – i.e., double first cousins.

A's father and his brother are siblings, making the brother A's paternal uncle. The uncle's daughter B is therefore A's first cousin. B's son C is the child of A's first cousin, which is the definition of a first cousin once removed (one generation down). The marriage of C to A's daughter D does not alter the blood relationship between C and A. Hence C is A's first cousin once removed.

R's mother (M) has exactly one sibling. That sibling is the parent of S. Therefore M and S's parent are siblings. R is the child of M. Children of siblings are first cousins, regardless of the genders involved. Hence S is R's first cousin, a uniquely determined relationship.

John and Mark are brothers. Mark is the father of Dana. Dana and her cousin Carl have a child Ethan. Since Dana is Ethan's mother, Mark, as Dana's father, is Ethan's maternal grandfather. Therefore Ethan is Mark's grandson.

Adam and Brian are brothers; Clara and Diana are sisters. Ethan is the child of Adam (brother) and Clara (sister), while Fiona is the child of Brian (brother) and Diana (sister). Thus Ethan and Fiona share both paternal grandparents (parents of Adam and Brian) and maternal grandparents (parents of Clara and Diana). Sharing both sets of grandparents makes them double first cousins, the most specific term among the options.

Y's father is the brother of X's father, making Y the child of X's paternal uncle – a first‑cousin relationship. The other condition (X's maternal uncle married to Y's sister) only establishes an aunt/uncle by marriage and does not alter the blood relation. Hence the precise kinship is first cousins.

M and N share only one parent, so they are half‑siblings. Their children A and B each inherit the shared grandparent (the mother of M and N) but have different other grandparents. Cousins who share both grandparents are first cousins; those who share only one grandparent are half‑first cousins. Thus the precise term for A and B's relationship is half‑first cousins.

M and N are full siblings, as are O and P. X is child of M (family A) and O (family B). Y is child of N (family A) and P (family B). Therefore X and Y share both sets of grandparents – the parents of M/N and the parents of O/P. Sharing two grandparent pairs makes them double first cousins, the most precise term among the options.

M's father is R. Q is R's sister, making Q M's paternal aunt. The other connections (Q being mother of P, who is married to O, N's sister) do not change the direct relation between Q and M. Since aunt is a standard kinship term and not an in‑law, the correct choice is C.

R's father’s sister is, by blood, R’s paternal aunt. The same S is married to T, who is R’s mother’s brother, i.e., R’s maternal uncle. Thus S is also an aunt by marriage on the maternal side. In standard kinship terminology, any sister of a parent or the spouse of a parent’s sibling is called an “aunt.” Therefore the appropriate single term for S relative to R is Aunt.

Mary is John's sister, so her son Tom is John's nephew. Tom marries John's daughter Anna, making Anna both John's daughter and Tom's wife. Their child Lily is therefore John's granddaughter through Anna (direct descendant) and also his grand‑niece through Tom (child of his nephew). Both terms are correct, but the direct descendant term "granddaughter" is the standard primary relation. Hence the appropriate answer is Granddaughter.

B is A's maternal uncle, making C A's maternal first cousin. E is A's paternal aunt, making D A's paternal first cousin. B and E are unrelated siblings of A's parents, so C and D share no common ancestor. Their only link is C's marriage to D, making them affinal, not blood, relatives.

M and S are siblings; W and N are siblings. M marries W, and S marries N. Their children D (M + W) and C (S + N) therefore have both sets of grandparents in common: they share the same maternal grandparents (parents of M and S) and the same paternal grandparents (parents of W and N). Hence D and C are cousins through two sibling links, i.e., double first cousins.

M and N are siblings, so they share both parents. P and Q are siblings, sharing both of their parents. M marries P, N marries Q. Their children X (of M&P) and Y (of N&Q) each have grandparents from both sibling pairs. Thus X and Y share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins, the most precise term.

Adam and Brian are brothers, so Ethan and Fiona share the same paternal grandparents. Clara and Diana are sisters, so they also share the same maternal grandparents. Because the cousins share both sets of grandparents, they are double first cousins, not just regular first cousins or half‑cousins.

L's mother has exactly one brother, the maternal uncle. L's father has exactly one sister, the paternal aunt. R is the child of both these distinct individuals, meaning R is the offspring of L's maternal uncle and L's paternal aunt. Consequently, R is simultaneously L's maternal first cousin (child of maternal uncle) and paternal first cousin (child of paternal aunt). The term that captures both relationships is "double first cousin."

R's mother has one brother (maternal uncle). His daughter A is the child of R's maternal uncle, making A R's first cousin. R's father has one brother (paternal uncle). His son B is the child of R's paternal uncle, also making B R's first cousin. Whether X is A or B, the relationship to R is the same: first cousin.

L’s father’s sibling is a paternal aunt/uncle; L’s mother’s sibling is a maternal aunt/uncle. M is the child of both these distinct siblings. Thus M is L’s first cousin on the father’s side and also L’s first cousin on the mother’s side, making M a double first cousin.

Clara and Ethan are each the child of a brother-sister pair: their fathers are brothers (sharing paternal grandparents) and their mothers are sisters (sharing maternal grandparents). Thus they share both sets of grandparents, making them first cousins on both the paternal and maternal sides. This relationship is called double first cousins, the most precise term among the options.

Mark is John’s maternal uncle, so his daughter Lisa is John’s first cousin on his mother’s side. John’s father’s sister is his paternal aunt, and her son Tom is John’s first cousin on his father’s side. Therefore Lisa and Tom share no blood kinship; their only connection is through marriage via John, which is not covered by standard direct kinship terms.

John’s maternal grandfather has two children: John’s mother and Lisa. Lisa is therefore John’s maternal aunt (sister of his mother). Tom is married to Lisa, making him the husband of John’s aunt. Ethan’s father (Adam) and Fiona’s father (Brian) are brothers, giving them the same paternal grandparents. Ethan’s mother (Clara) and Fiona’s mother (Diana) are sisters, giving them the same maternal grandparents. Thus Ethan and Fiona share both sets of grandparents, making them first cousins on both the paternal and maternal sides—i.e., double first cousins.

John and Mary are siblings. Mary's son Peter is John’s nephew. John’s son Michael is Mary’s nephew, making Peter and Michael first cousins. Susan is Michael’s daughter, so she is one generation below Michael. Therefore Peter, being Michael’s first cousin, is one generation above Susan, making them first cousins once removed.

N's father’s sister is N’s paternal aunt, and N's mother’s brother is N’s maternal uncle. They are married, and M is their child. Thus M is the child of N’s paternal aunt (making M a first cousin on the father's side) and also the child of N’s maternal uncle (making M a first cousin on the mother's side). Being a first cousin through both parental lines makes M a double first cousin of N.

X and Y each have a father who are brothers (A and B) and a mother who are sisters (C and D). Therefore X and Y share both paternal grandparents (the parents of A and B) and maternal grandparents (the parents of C and D). Sharing two sets of grandparents makes them first cousins through both parents, i.e., double first cousins.

John is Susan's father, making Lily his granddaughter via Susan. Peter, Mary's son, is John’s nephew, so Lily is also John’s great‑niece. However, the direct line of descent (blood) defines Lily as John’s granddaughter, which is the primary kinship term used.

M and N are siblings, so they share the same parents. P and Q are also siblings, sharing their own parents. X is the child of M and P, while Y is the child of N and Q. X’s parent M is a sibling of Y’s parent N, giving them a first‑cousin link. Simultaneously, X’s other parent P is a sibling of Y’s other parent Q, providing a second, parallel first‑cousin link. Because they are first cousins through both parental lines, they are double first cousins.

Y’s father’s sister is Y’s paternal aunt. X is the child of that aunt, making X the child of Y’s aunt, which is the definition of a first cousin. The extra condition about X’s mother not being related to Y’s mother rules out half‑sibling connections, confirming the relationship is purely cousin.

P’s mother’s brother is P’s maternal uncle. His daughter is P’s first cousin (they share grandparents). The daughter’s son is the next generation down from that cousin, making him P’s first cousin once removed (a one‑generation difference from the first cousin).

Lily's father John and Mark's mother Mary are full siblings, sharing one set of grandparents. Lily's mother Anna and Mark's father Ben are also full siblings, sharing another set of grandparents. Emma is the child of Adam's son David, making her Adam's grandchild. She is also the child of Clara, who is Adam's first cousin; the child of a first cousin is a first cousin once removed. Both relationships hold simultaneously, and no single standard term captures both, so the most precise description is that she is both a grandchild and a first cousin once removed.

John is the biological father of Alex. Alex is the biological father of Sam. Therefore Sam is the child of John's son, making Sam John’s grandson by blood. The marriage to Bella (John’s step‑daughter) does not affect the blood relationship.

L’s mother is the sister of N’s father, so they share one set of grandparents. L’s father is the brother of N’s mother, providing a second set of shared grandparents. Thus each of L’s parents is a sibling of each of N’s parents, which is the definition of double first cousins. The relationship is therefore C.

Anna is aunt to both Diana (her sister's child) and Ethan (her brother's child). Fiona is the child of Diana and Ethan, making her the daughter of Anna's niece/nephew. M (V's mother) and her brother are siblings. The brother's only child is U, making U the child of M's sibling, i.e., U is V's first cousin. Anna is Ben's mother. Ben is married to Clara, making Clara Anna's daughter‑in‑law (an affinal relation). Clara's father is David; David's sister Eva is Clara's paternal aunt. M's mother has exactly one brother; that brother is M's maternal uncle. N is his child, making N the child of M's maternal uncle, i.e., M's first cousin. John and Peter are brothers, so they share the same paternal grandparents. Mary and Susan are sisters, sharing the same maternal grandparents. Tom is the child of John (paternal line) and Mary (maternal line); Lily is the child of Peter (paternal line) and Susan (maternal line). Bob and Alice are siblings (both Mary’s brother and sister). Their children, John (Bob’s son) and Susan (Alice’s daughter), are therefore the children of two siblings. In standard kinship terminology, the children of siblings are first cousins. No half‑sibling information is provided, so they are not half‑first cousins, and they are not a generation removed (second cousins). Thus the precise term is first cousins.

M’s father has only M, so M has no paternal siblings. M’s mother has exactly one sister, N, making N M’s maternal aunt (no remarriage or adoption). N’s only child, P, is the child of M’s aunt, which by standard kinship terminology is M’s first cousin. No other relationship fits the given constraints.

John's maternal uncle's daughter Lily is John's first cousin. John's paternal aunt's son Peter is also John's first cousin. Lily and Peter each are one generation above Sam, making Sam the child of John's cousins. In standard kinship, the child of a first cousin is a first cousin once removed. The fact that the two cousins are from different parental lines does not change the classification.

A and B share only one parent, making them half‑siblings. The children of full siblings are first cousins. When the parents are half‑siblings, their children are still first cousins but share only half the usual genetic relatedness, which is expressed by the term “half‑first cousins.” Thus the precise kinship term for C and D is half‑first cousins.

J's paternal aunt (father's sister) has a daughter. That daughter is J's paternal first cousin. J's maternal uncle (mother's brother) has a son, who is J's maternal first cousin. L is the child of those two cousins. A child of one's cousin is a first cousin once removed. Since L is the child of J's paternal first cousin (and also of J's maternal first cousin), L is J's first cousin once removed.

M and N are full siblings, so their children (X and Y) are first cousins through that side. O and P are also full siblings, making X and Y first cousins through the other side as well. Because they share both sets of grandparents, they are first cousins twice over—i.e., double first cousins.

M and N are full siblings, so X and Y share their paternal grandparents. O and P are also full siblings, so X and Y share their maternal grandparents as well. Thus X and Y have both sets of grandparents in common, making them cousins through two sibling pairs. This relationship is called double first cousins, the most precise term among the choices.

Anna is Tom's mother, so Lily, as Tom's child, is Anna's granddaughter. Although Lily is also the child of Anna's niece Mary (making her a great‑niece), the direct parent‑child line via Anna's son gives the standard term granddaughter.

John and Mary are full siblings, and Anna and Bob are also full siblings. X’s parents (John and Anna) and Y’s parents (Mary and Bob) are each pair of siblings, so X and Y share both sets of grandparents. Sharing both grandparent pairs makes them first cousins on two lines, i.e., double first cousins.

John's mother’s brother is John’s maternal uncle; his daughter Lisa is John’s first cousin. John’s father’s sister is his paternal aunt; her son Mark is also John’s first cousin. Sam is the child of Lisa and Mark, who are John’s first cousins. The child of a first cousin is a first cousin once removed, so Sam is John’s first cousin once removed.

L and M are half‑siblings, sharing only one parent. The children of full siblings are first cousins. When the siblings are half‑siblings, their children are related as half‑first cousins, reflecting the single shared grandparent line. Thus S and D are half‑first cousins.

Mark's brother is John. John’s spouse is Anna. In English kinship, a sibling’s spouse is referred to as a sister‑in‑law (or brother‑in‑law). The definition of in‑law here includes siblings’ spouses, so Anna is Mark’s sister‑in‑law.

P's mother's mother is P's maternal grandmother. M is described as the brother of that grandmother. The sibling of a grandparent is the great-uncle (also called granduncle). Therefore M is P's great‑uncle.

R's spouse S has a brother T, making T R's brother‑in‑law. T's wife U is R's sister‑in‑law. V is U's brother, i.e., the sibling of R's sister‑in‑law. English kinship terms only cover direct affinal relations (spouse, spouse's parents/siblings, siblings' spouses, children's spouses). The relation V to R is a second‑degree affinal link with no standard direct term, so the correct choice is the option stating no standard direct relation.

M and N are siblings. Their children (O and R) are first cousins. Q is R's child, i.e., one generation below R. Therefore O is one generation above Q relative to the cousin line, making O and Q first cousins once removed.

A and B share the same parents, and C and D share another set of parents. Each child inherits one set of grandparents from the A/B side and the other set from the C/D side. Since X and Y have both sets of grandparents in common, they are children of two sibling pairs, which defines double first cousins.

X and Y are brothers, so they share the same parents. M and N are sisters, so they also share the same parents. P’s father (X) and Q’s father (Y) are siblings, making P and Q first cousins on their paternal side. Likewise, P’s mother (M) and Q’s mother (N) are siblings, making them first cousins on their maternal side. Because they are first cousins through both parents, they are double first cousins, the most precise term.

Z is the child of L's maternal uncle (the only brother of L's mother) and L's paternal aunt (the only sister of L's father). Since monogamy, these two are married, making Z the offspring of both sides of L's family. Z is therefore a first cousin through the maternal line and also a first cousin through the paternal line, i.e., a double first cousin. The relationship is uniquely determined under the given constraints.

M's mother has a sister (the aunt) who is married to N. N and the aunt have one child, P, making P M's first cousin. P's mother is the aunt, whose brother is Q. Since the aunt and M's mother are sisters, their brother Q is also a sibling of M's mother. Therefore Q is M's mother's brother, i.e., M's maternal uncle. The correct relation is Uncle (mother's brother).

Emma's mother and Tom are siblings, making Tom Emma's maternal uncle. Tom's daughter Lily is therefore Emma's first cousin. Noah is Emma's son, so Lily is a first cousin of Noah's mother. A cousin of a parent is a "first cousin once removed" to the child. Hence Lily is Noah's first cousin once removed.

F_A is brother of M_B, so they share one pair of grandparents. F_B is brother of M_A, sharing a second pair of grandparents. Thus A and B have both sets of grandparents in common, meaning each is the child of a sibling of the other's parent on both sides. This defines double first cousins, the most specific term among the choices.
Mary and John are siblings, making each other's children first cousins. Anna is Mary's daughter and Ben is John's son, so their relationship is that of first cousins.

R's maternal uncle's daughter S is R's maternal first cousin. R's paternal aunt's son T is R's paternal first cousin. S and T are unrelated to each other, each being a first cousin of R. Their child U is therefore the child of R's first cousin on both sides. In kinship terms, the child of your (any) first cousin is your first cousin once removed. Hence U is R's first cousin once removed.

N’s mother has exactly one brother, i.e., N’s maternal uncle. M is described as the child of that brother. The child of an uncle/aunt is a first cousin to the niece/nephew. No shared parent exists, so they are not siblings or half‑siblings, and they are related, eliminating “No relation.” Hence M is N’s first cousin.

Y and Z are siblings. Z is parent of W, so W is the child of Z. X is child of Y, making X the child of Z's sibling. In genealogical terms, the child of a sibling of one's parent is a first cousin. The relationship does not depend on genders or other variables, so the kinship term is uniquely determined as first cousin.

R's mother has one brother M, whose only child is S. R's father has one sister N, whose only child is also S. Since monogamy prohibits multiple spouses, M and N must be married, making S the child of R's maternal uncle and paternal aunt. Therefore S is R's cousin on both the mother's and father's sides—a double first cousin. The relationship is uniquely determined as first cousin.

John and Lisa are full siblings, sharing both parents. Their children are therefore first cousins. Tom is John’s child; Susan is Lisa’s child. Hence Tom and Susan are first cousins, regardless of their marriage.

M’s mother and N’s father are siblings, but the sibling relationship may be full or half. If they are full siblings, M and N are first cousins; if they are half‑siblings, M and N are half‑first cousins. Since the information does not specify which case holds, the exact kinship term cannot be uniquely determined.

R is the sister of M's mother, making her M's maternal aunt by blood. She is also married to M's paternal uncle, which would also make her an aunt by marriage. In standard English kinship, both blood and marital aunts are simply called "aunt," so the appropriate term is Aunt.

X is the child of R's maternal uncle, making X a first cousin of R on the mother's side. Y is the child of R's paternal uncle, making Y a first cousin of R on the father's side. Since R's mother and father have no blood relation, X and Y share no common ancestor; their only possible link would be through R's parents, which do not exist. Hence X and Y are not blood relatives.

M is the child of P’s father’s sister, making M P’s paternal first cousin. M is also the child of P’s mother’s brother, making M P’s maternal first cousin. Since the two parents (the paternal aunt and maternal uncle) are married, M is related to P as a first cousin on both sides – a double first cousin. No half‑relationship is implied, so the most precise term is double first cousin.

A’s mother M and C’s mother S are sisters, making C a first cousin of A on the maternal side. Likewise, A’s father F and C’s father T are brothers, making C a first cousin of A on the paternal side.
