R's mother has one brother M (maternal uncle). R's father has one sister S (paternal aunt). X is the sole child of M and also the sole child of S, meaning M and S are X's parents. Thus X is the child of R's maternal uncle and simultaneously the child of R's paternal aunt. In standard kinship, the child of an uncle or aunt is a first cousin. Since the same person fulfills both roles, X is R's first cousin (a double first cousin, but still classified as a first cousin). No other relationship fits the given facts, so the relation is uniquely determined as first cousin.

M and N are full siblings, so they share the same parents. X and Y are also full siblings, sharing another set of parents. A is the child of M (son of the first set of grandparents) and X (daughter of the second set). B is the child of N (son of the first set) and Y (daughter of the second set). Therefore A and B have both sets of grandparents in common, making them first cousins through both their fathers and their mothers. This precise relationship is called double first cousins.

Alan and Beth are siblings, sharing grandparents G1. Diane and Carl are also siblings, sharing grandparents G2. Alan marries Diane, and Beth marries Carl. Their children, Ethan (Alan + Diane) and Fiona (Beth + Carl), each have the same two sets of grandparents (G1 and G2). Sharing both sets of grandparents makes them the children of two sibling pairs, which is the definition of double first cousins.

M and N are siblings, so their children share the same paternal grandparents. X and Y are also siblings, so the children share the same maternal grandparents. Thus A and B share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins, the most precise term.

Lily is the child of Tom's son Ben, making her Tom's grandchild. She is also the child of Tom's niece Amy (Tom's sibling's child), which makes her Tom's great‑niece (sometimes called grand‑niece). No single standard term covers both roles, so the precise description must list both relations.

M and N are full siblings, sharing both parents. O and R are also full siblings, sharing both parents. X is child of M (sibling of N) and O (sibling of R). Y is child of N and R. Therefore X and Y each have the same two sets of grandparents: the parents of M/N and the parents of O/R. Sharing both sets of grandparents makes them the children of two sibling pairs, which is the definition of double first cousins.

P’s mother is the sister of Q’s father, so they share the same parents. Those parents are Q’s paternal grandparents and also P’s maternal grandparents. Hence Q’s father and P’s mother are siblings, making Q and P the children of those siblings. By definition, children of siblings are first cousins. No other marriages affect this relationship, so the relationship is uniquely determined as first cousins.

X’s father and V are siblings, making V X’s paternal aunt. V’s son W is therefore the child of X’s aunt, i.e., X’s paternal first cousin. The marriage of W to Z does not alter the blood tie between W and X. Hence W is X’s first cousin.

M’s children are J and K. K has a daughter P, making P a direct descendant of M: P is K’s daughter and therefore M’s grandchild. The marriage connections (J‑L, L‑N, N‑P) do not change this blood line; P is not married to any of M’s children, so she is not a daughter‑in‑law, nor is she a niece. Hence P’s relation to M is granddaughter.

Alice’s maternal uncle (her mother’s brother) and Alice’s paternal uncle (her father’s brother) marry. Their child Ben is the offspring of both uncles. Ben is therefore Alice’s first cousin through her mother’s side and also her first cousin through her father’s side. Having two independent first‑cousin relationships makes Ben a double first cousin of Alice.

John and Mary are siblings. Mary's son Peter is John's nephew. John's daughter Lisa is Mary's niece. Therefore Peter and Lisa are children of siblings, which by standard kinship terminology makes them first cousins. No other relationship fits given the constraints.

Adam and Brian are brothers; Clara and Diana are sisters. Their children Ethan and Fiona are therefore first cousins on both paternal and maternal sides—double first cousins. The children of first cousins are second cousins. Since Ethan and Fiona are double first cousins, their children Greg and Hannah share both sets of great‑grandparents, making them double second cousins, a more specific relationship than plain second cousins.

M and N are siblings, so they share the same set of grandparents (call them G1). O and P are siblings, sharing another set of grandparents (G2). A is child of M (from G1) and O (from G2). B is child of N (from G1) and P (from G2). Therefore A and B share both sets of grandparents, G1 and G2, making them first cousins through two sibling links. This is the definition of double first cousins.

R's mother and father are unrelated. R's maternal uncle (mother's brother) has daughter S, making S R's maternal first cousin. R's paternal aunt (father's sister) has daughter T, making T R's paternal first cousin. The uncle and aunt are unrelated, so S and T have no common ancestor. Consequently they share no blood relationship; there is no standard term for their connection.

Adam and Ben are brothers, so their children Carl and Diana share the same paternal grandparents. Emma and Fiona are sisters, so the children also share the same maternal grandparents. Thus Carl and Diana have both sets of grandparents in common, making them cousins through two sibling pairs. This relationship is called double first cousins, which is more specific than ordinary first cousins.

Y's father has a single brother. The child of that brother (X) is the child of Y's father's sibling, which by definition is a first cousin. The puzzle does not indicate a half‑sibling relationship, and standard usage of "brother" implies a full sibling, so the relation is uniquely a first cousin.

M's maternal uncle's wife is Aunt X, making her M's aunt by marriage. Y is Aunt X's sister, i.e., the sibling of M's aunt-in-law. This relationship is neither a blood tie nor a direct affinal tie covered by standard English kinship terms (spouse, spouse's parents/siblings, siblings' spouses, children's spouses). Therefore Y has no standard direct relation to M; the connection exists only through an affinal chain.

Adam and Brian are brothers, so they share the same parents. Clara and Diana are sisters, sharing their own parents. Ethan is the child of Adam (brother) and Clara (sister), while Fiona is the child of Brian (brother) and Diana (sister). Thus Ethan and Fiona share both sets of grandparents (the parents of Adam/Brian and the parents of Clara/Diana). Sharing two lines of descent makes them double first cousins, not merely first cousins or half‑cousins.

Beth is Alex's sister, so Beth's son Carl is Alex's nephew. Emma is Carl's daughter, making her the child of Alex's nephew. The child of a nephew (or niece) is a grandniece, also called great‑niece. Marriage of Emma to Alex's son does not alter her blood relationship to Alex.

M's mother has only M, so she cannot be N's wife. N is married to M's maternal aunt, making N the aunt's husband. N and M's father together have a son P, meaning P's parents are M's father and N. Thus P shares M's father but has a different mother (N, not M's mother). Sharing only one parent makes them half‑siblings, so P is M's half‑brother.

R's father’s sister is R’s aunt. Her son S is R’s first cousin. S’s daughter T is one generation below S, making T the child of R’s first cousin. In standard terminology, a person’s first cousin’s child is a first cousin once removed. Hence T is R’s first cousin once removed.

John and Mary are half‑siblings, sharing only their mother. Therefore they share one grandparent (the mother's parents). Their children Tom and Lisa each descend from one of these half‑siblings, so Tom and Lisa share exactly one grandparent. Cousins who share both grandparents are first cousins; those who share only one are termed half‑first cousins. Hence Tom and Lisa are half‑first cousins.

Mary and Tom are siblings, so their children Peter and Linda are first cousins. Alex is Peter's child, one generation down from Peter. Therefore Alex is one generation removed from Linda, making Linda Alex's first cousin once removed. This matches the standard term.

Y is X's maternal uncle (mother's brother). Y's daughter Z is therefore X's first cousin. Z's son W is the child of X's first cousin, making W a first cousin once removed relative to X (one generation down).

R's father has one brother (paternal uncle) and R's mother has one brother (maternal uncle). X is the child of one of these brothers, but we don't know which. In either case, X is the child of an uncle of R. The child of an uncle is a first cousin. Whether the two brothers are distinct or the same person does not change the relationship; X remains R's first cousin. Hence the relation is uniquely first cousin.

Peter and Linda are blood siblings. Emma is the daughter of Linda, making Emma the child of Peter's sister. In standard kinship, the child of one's sibling is a niece or nephew. The other connections (through John and Mary) are marriage relations, but the blood link already defines Emma as Peter's niece. No other term applies.

M and N are siblings, so their children (O and R) are first cousins. Q is R's child, one generation below R. Therefore O and Q are first cousins separated by one generation, i.e., first cousins once removed.

A and B are brothers; C and D are sisters. Their children E and F are therefore double first cousins (they share both paternal and maternal grandparents). G is E's child, H is F's child. Children of first cousins are second cousins; since E and F are double first cousins, their children share both lines of great‑grandparents, making G and H double second cousins.

P and Q are half‑siblings, sharing only one parent (their mother). That mother is a grandparent to both R (through P) and S (through Q). Because their parents are half‑siblings, R and S share a single grandparent, making them half‑first cousins – the precise term distinguishing them from full first cousins who share both grandparents.

The two children each have a father who is the brother of the other's father, and a mother who is the sister of the other's mother. Thus they share both paternal grandparents (through their fathers) and maternal grandparents (through their mothers). Sharing both sets of grandparents makes them first cousins on two distinct parental lines, i.e., double first cousins.

S's mother has exactly one brother, who is S's maternal uncle. R is that uncle's child. In standard English blood‑relation terms, the child of one's uncle or aunt is a first cousin. No adoption or non‑monogamy alters this relationship, so the kinship is determinable and is a first cousin.

M is X's maternal uncle (mother's brother). His daughter A is the child of X's maternal uncle, making A X's first cousin on the mother's side. The marriage between A and B (X's paternal cousin) does not alter the blood relation between A and X. Therefore A is X's first cousin.

M and N are siblings. Their children A and D (from M) marry B and E (from N) respectively. Thus C’s parents are A (M’s child) and B (N’s child); F’s parents are D (M’s child) and E (N’s child). Both C and F therefore have the same two grandparents (M and N) through both parental lines. Children who share both sets of grandparents are double first cousins.

B and C are the only siblings, making them full siblings. A is B's child, D is C's child. Children of siblings are first cousins. No half‑sibling information is given, so the precise term is first cousin.

P's father's sister (paternal aunt) marries P's mother's brother (maternal uncle). Their child M is the offspring of P's paternal aunt and maternal uncle, making M simultaneously the child of a sibling of P's father and a sibling of P's mother. Hence M is P's first cousin on both the paternal and maternal sides, which is defined as a double first cousin.

John and Mark are brothers, so they share the same parents (paternal grandparents for both X and Y). Anna and Beth are sisters, sharing the same parents (maternal grandparents for both X and Y). Thus X and Y have both sets of grandparents in common, making them first cousins through their fathers and also first cousins through their mothers. This dual relationship is defined as double first cousins.

Ethan and Fiona are double first cousins (their fathers are brothers and their mothers are sisters). Their children, Ethan Jr. and Fiona Jr., are therefore the offspring of double first cousins. The standard term for the offspring of double first cousins is double second cousins, as they are second cousins through two distinct ancestral lines.

M and N are siblings; P and O are siblings. M marries P, N marries O. X is child of M + P, Y of N + O. X and Y therefore share both sets of grandparents (the parents of M/N and the parents of P/O). Sharing both maternal and paternal grandparents makes them double first cousins, not merely half or removed. The relation is determinable.

Adam is Ethan's father, making Lily, Ethan's child, Adam's grandchild. Through the cousin marriage, Lily is also Adam's great‑niece (child of Adam's niece Fiona), but the direct line relationship—grandchild—is the most precise standard term. The other options do not match the direct generational link.

Edward is Fiona's brother, making him Alice's maternal uncle. Alice is Ben's mother, so Edward is the brother of Ben's maternal grandmother, i.e., the sibling of a grandparent. The standard term for a sibling of a grandparent is great‑uncle (also called granduncle). Other links (brother‑in‑law of Ben's father) do not create a direct kinship term. Hence Edward is Ben's great‑uncle.

J's father's sister is J's paternal aunt; her child is J's first cousin on the father's side. J's mother's brother is J's maternal uncle; his child is J's first cousin on the mother's side. Because M is the child of both a paternal aunt and a maternal uncle, M is simultaneously J's cousin through both parental lines, making M a double first cousin of J.

M, S1, S2, and B are siblings, sharing the same two parents. C is M's child and E is S2's child. Children of siblings are first cousins regardless of whom the siblings marry. The extra marriages (S1 to H1 and B to H1's sister) involve a different family and do not alter the shared ancestry of C and E. Thus their relationship is precisely first cousins.

Sam’s father John and Lily’s father Peter are brothers, making Sam and Lily first cousins on their paternal side. Sam’s mother Mary and Lily’s mother Anna are sisters, making them also first cousins on their maternal side. Sharing both sets of grandparents qualifies them as double first cousins, a more specific term than plain first cousins.

A’s brother C is a blood sibling of A. The child E is the offspring of C, making E the child of A’s sibling. In standard kinship terms, the child of one’s sibling is a niece or nephew. The fact that C’s spouse D is also B’s sister does not affect the blood relationship; E’s connection to A is through C alone. Therefore E is A’s niece/nephew.

A and B are full brothers; C and D are full sisters. X is child of A + C, Y of B + D. Hence X and Y share the same paternal grandparents (parents of A and B) and also the same maternal grandparents (parents of C and D). Sharing both sets of grandparents makes them first cousins on both sides, i.e., double first cousins. They are not half‑first cousins (which would require only one shared grandparent set) nor second cousins.

Peter's daughter Anna is John's niece. John (Peter's brother) and Anna have Sam. Sam is therefore Peter's grandson through Anna and also Peter's nephew as the child of his brother John. Both relations hold simultaneously.

M and N are brothers, so they have the same parents. P and Q are sisters, sharing another set of parents. A’s father (M) and B’s father (N) are siblings, making A and B first cousins on their fathers’ side. Likewise, A’s mother (P) and B’s mother (Q) are siblings, making them first cousins on their mothers’ side. Sharing both paternal and maternal grandparents defines double first cousins, the most precise term.

M's brother is J's maternal uncle, so his son P is J's first cousin. L is J's spouse; L's sister K is J's sister‑in‑law. K's husband P is therefore J's brother‑in‑law (spouse's sister's husband). Hence P holds two relations to J: first cousin by blood and brother‑in‑law by marriage, with no single term covering both.

John and Mary share the same parents. Peter, their other sibling, has a daughter Anna, making Anna the niece of both John and Mary. John marries Anna, and their child Sam is therefore the child of Mary's brother (John) and Mary's niece (Anna). Consequently, Sam is simultaneously Mary's nephew/niece (child of her brother) and Mary's grandniece/grandnephew (child of her niece). This dual relationship is described as a double niece/nephew.

M and N are half‑siblings, sharing one parent. Their children A and B each have that shared parent as a grandparent, but they do not share the other grandparent. Therefore A and B are first cousins through a single common grandparent, i.e., half‑first cousins. This matches the standard term for children of half‑siblings.

M and N are full siblings; O and P are full siblings. M marries O and N marries P, forming two sibling-sibling marriages. Their children X (of M and O) and Y (of N and P) therefore share both sets of grandparents (the parents of M/N and the parents of O/P). This is the definition of double first cousins, who are first cousins through both parental lines. No half‑relations or more distant connections apply.

M's father has a sister, making her M's paternal aunt. The aunt's children, including P, are the children of M's aunt, which by definition are M's first cousins. No shared parent exists, so they aren't siblings or half‑siblings, and they are not a generation removed, so not second cousins.

X's maternal uncle is X's mother’s brother. The uncle’s son Y is therefore X’s first cousin. Z is X’s daughter, i.e., one generation below X. The child of a first cousin is a first cousin once removed, which is the precise standard term for the relationship between Y and Z.

A and B are half‑siblings, sharing one parent. That shared parent is a grandparent of both C and D. Since C and D are the children of A and B respectively, they are first cousins, but they share only a single grandparent rather than a pair. Thus they are half‑first cousins.

M and N are siblings (share grandparents A and B). O and P are siblings (share grandparents C and D). M marries O, N marries P. Their children X (M + O) and Y (N + P) each have the same two sets of grandparents: A/B via M/N and C/D via O/P. Sharing both sets of grandparents makes X and Y double first cousins, the most specific term.

Aaron and Beth are half‑siblings because they share only their father Frank. Their children, Clara (Aaron’s child) and David (Beth’s child), are therefore the children of half‑siblings. Children of half‑siblings are termed half‑first cousins, since they share only one set of grandparents (the parents of Frank) and not the other set. This relationship is uniquely defined, making option A the correct choice.

M and N are siblings, so they share the same set of parents (Grandparents G1). O and P are siblings, sharing another set of parents (Grandparents G2). X is child of M (from G1) and O (from G2); Y is child of N (also from G1) and P (also from G2). Therefore X and Y have both G1 and G2 as common grandparents, i.e., they are children of two different sibling pairs. This is precisely the definition of double first cousins.

Adam and Brian are brothers; Clara and Diana are sisters. Adam+Clara have Ethan, Brian+Diana have Fiona. Ethan and Fiona share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins. Their children, Paul (son of Ethan) and Quinn (child of Fiona), are one generation removed, so they are the children of double first cousins. Children of first cousins are second cousins; because the parental cousins are double first cousins, Paul and Quinn share both sets of great‑grandparents, making them double second cousins.

Clara and David are double first cousins, sharing both sets of grandparents (their mothers are sisters and their fathers are brothers). Their children Lily and Mark are therefore the children of double first cousins, which makes Lily and Mark double second cousins (they share both pairs of great‑grandparents).

M and N are half‑siblings, sharing only one parent. The children of full siblings are first cousins. When the parents are half‑siblings, their children share only one line of descent (the common grandparent) and thus are classified as half‑first cousins, the standard term for this level of relationship. No other marriages are involved, so the relationship is uniquely determined.

M is mother of N, O, and T, so they are siblings. N is married to P. P’s sister Q is therefore the sibling of N’s spouse. In standard English, a spouse’s sibling is called a sister‑in‑law (or brother‑in‑law). No other listed term fits this relationship.

A's mother has one brother (maternal uncle) and A's father has one brother (paternal uncle). Each uncle has exactly one child. Whether B is the child of the maternal uncle or the paternal uncle, B is the child of A's uncle, which by standard kinship terminology is a first cousin. The relationship is the same in either case, so it is uniquely determined as a first cousin.

B1 and B2 are brothers; S1 and S2 are sisters. Their children P and Q are thus double first cousins (they share both sets of grandparents). The next generation, R (child of P) and S (child of Q), inherit this double relationship one degree further: they share all great‑grandparents (the parents of the shared grandparents). Hence R and S are double second cousins, not merely second cousins or half‑relations.

Adam and Brian are brothers, making their children first cousins on the paternal side. Clara and Diana are sisters, making their children first cousins on the maternal side as well. Because Ethan and Fiona share both sets of grandparents (paternal and maternal), they are cousins through two sibling pairs, which is the definition of double first cousins.

B and C are siblings. A is B's child; D is C's child, making A and D first cousins. E is D's daughter, one generation below D. Therefore A is one generation removed from the cousin relationship with E, i.e., a first cousin once removed.

M is L's maternal uncle, so P (M's child) is L's first cousin. N is K's paternal aunt, so Q (N's child) is K's first cousin. The kinship between P and Q depends on how L and K are related, which is not specified. Without that link, the exact relationship cannot be fixed; it could range from siblings to various degrees of cousinship. Therefore the relation is not uniquely determinable.

M's mother has one brother A; A's daughter N is M's maternal first cousin. M's father has one sister B; B's son P is M's paternal first cousin. Both N and P are first cousins of M, regardless of which is chosen as Q. No other relation fits, and the relation is uniquely determined.

R's paternal aunt's son S is R's first cousin. R's maternal uncle's daughter T is also R's first cousin (from the other side). S and T marry and have child U. For any first cousin, their child is a first cousin once removed. Hence R is a first cousin once removed to U through S, and likewise through T. The relationship is therefore first cousins once removed.

E and F have the same mother D, as D bore both children with different fathers. Sharing a parent makes them half‑siblings. Although their fathers are half‑siblings, which would also make them half‑first cousins, the closer relationship (shared parent) is more precise. Therefore the correct term is half‑siblings.

M and N are full siblings, as are X and Y. A is the child of M (father) and X (mother); B is the child of N (father) and Y (mother). Therefore A and B share both a set of paternal grandparents (parents of M and N) and a set of maternal grandparents (parents of X and Y). This makes them first cousins on both sides, i.e., double first cousins, which is more specific than ordinary first cousins.

John is Mary's brother, making Mary's children (Peter and Anna) John's nieces/nephew. Anna's daughter Sophie is therefore the child of John's niece, which is the definition of a grand-niece (niece's daughter). No other direct kinship term fits better.

M and N are siblings, so their children X and Y are first cousins through that side. S and R are also siblings, making X and Y first cousins through the other side as well. Because they share both sets of grandparents, they are cousins twice over, i.e., double first cousins.

M and N are brothers, making their children L and O first cousins. O's child is P, so P is the child of L's cousin. In kinship terms, the child of one's cousin is a first cousin once removed. The extra family details do not affect this relationship.

M and N are siblings, so their children are first cousins. O is M's daughter, R is N's daughter. Therefore O and R are first cousins. The extra information about R's child Q and P's child does not alter their direct relationship.

M and N are siblings, so they share the same two parents (grandparents of X and Y). O and P are also siblings, sharing another pair of parents (the other set of grandparents). X is child of M and O; Y is child of N and P. Hence X and Y share both sets of grandparents, making them first cousins through two sibling pairings, i.e., double first cousins.

M and N are siblings. Their children Q (M's daughter) and P (N's daughter) are therefore first cousins. R is Q's son, placing him one generation below Q. The relationship between a person and the child of their first cousin is defined as first cousin once removed. No alternative kinship fits given the constraints, so the relation is uniquely determined.

R's mother’s brother is R’s maternal uncle. The uncle’s daughter is the child of R’s aunt/uncle, which by standard kinship terminology is a first cousin. No half‑sibling or second‑cousin relationship applies.

Adam and Ben are full brothers, sharing both parents. Clara and Diana are full sisters, sharing both parents. Their children, Ethan (son of Adam + Clara) and Fiona (daughter of Ben + Diana), therefore have the same paternal grandparents (through Adam and Ben) and the same maternal grandparents (through Clara and Diana). Thus they share both sets of grandparents, making them first cousins on both the father's side and the mother's side – i.e., double first cousins.

Ethan’s father Adam and Fiona’s father Ben are brothers, making Ethan and Fiona first cousins on their paternal side. Their mothers Clara and Diana are sisters, making them also first cousins on their maternal side. Sharing both sets of grandparents qualifies them as double first cousins, the most precise term.

Y's mother and her brother are siblings. The brother's child X is therefore Y's first cousin. Z is Y's child. The relationship between a person and the child of their first cousin is a first cousin once removed (one generational difference). Hence X and Z are first cousins once removed.

Eva's father Adam and Frank's father Brian are brothers, making Eva and Frank first cousins through their fathers. Likewise, Eva's mother Clara and Frank's mother Diana are sisters, making them first cousins through their mothers as well. Sharing both sets of grandparents qualifies them as double first cousins, the most precise term.

M’s father is a sibling of N’s father, making him N’s paternal aunt/uncle. M’s mother is a sibling of N’s mother, making her N’s maternal aunt/uncle. Thus M is the child of both N’s paternal and maternal aunts/uncles. They share both sets of grandparents, which defines a double first‑cousin relationship. No intermarriage among the siblings ensures the two parental lines are distinct, confirming the double first‑cousin status.

Peter is John’s maternal uncle (mother’s brother) and Mary is John’s paternal aunt (father’s sister). Their child Emma is John’s cousin through his mother’s side via Peter and also cousin through his father’s side via Mary. Because Emma shares both sets of John’s grandparents, they are related through two distinct sibling links, making them double first cousins.

Alex’s mother’s brother (M) is Alex’s maternal uncle, so M’s child (C1) is Alex’s first cousin. Alex’s father’s sister (F) is Alex’s paternal aunt, so F’s child (C2) is also Alex’s first cousin. C1 and C2 marry and have Sam. The child of a first cousin is a first cousin once removed relative to the original person. Therefore Sam is Alex’s first cousin once removed (the same relation through both sides).

M is R's maternal uncle (mother's brother) and F is R's paternal uncle (father's brother). In either case, the child of an uncle is R's first cousin. The relationship does not depend on whether S is M's child or F's child, so the relation is uniquely determined as first cousin.

Alice's mother and Bob's father are half‑siblings: they share one parent (their mother) but have different fathers. That common parent is a grandparent to both Alice (through her mother) and Bob (through his father). Therefore Alice and Bob share exactly one grandparent, not both, making them first cousins who share only one grandparent. The precise term for such cousins is half‑first cousins. No other family links exist, so the relation is uniquely determined.

John's sister Emma has a son Tom, making Tom John’s nephew. Lisa is married to Tom, so she is the spouse of John’s nephew, which is the definition of a niece‑in‑law. Other connections (through Susan) do not yield a standard term within the allowed set. Therefore the correct relation is niece‑in‑law.

Alex's mother and Martin are siblings, making Martin Alex's maternal uncle. Martin's son Ethan is therefore the child of Alex's uncle, which by standard kinship terms makes Ethan Alex's first cousin. The marriages of Beth to Carl and Carl's sister Diana to Ethan involve no blood connections, so they do not affect the blood relationship.

A and C are brothers, so they share the same parents. B and D are sisters, also sharing the same parents. P’s parents are A (brother) and B (sister); Q’s parents are C (the other brother) and D (the other sister). Thus P and Q are each the child of a sibling pair on both the paternal and maternal sides, meaning they share both sets of grandparents. This makes them first cousins through two distinct lines, i.e., double first cousins.

M and N are full siblings, so they share the same parents. Their children X and Y each inherit one set of grandparents from the paternal side (the parents of M and N). A and B are also full sisters, giving X and Y a second shared set of grandparents from the maternal side. Because X and Y are first cousins through both their fathers and their mothers, they are double first cousins.

M and N share both parents, making them full siblings. X and Y also share both parents, so they are full siblings. A’s father (M) is a full sibling of B’s father (N), giving A and B a first‑cousin relationship through their fathers. Simultaneously, A’s mother (X) is a full sibling of B’s mother (Y), giving another first‑cousin link through their mothers. Because the two cousin relationships arise from both parental lines, A and B are double first cousins, not half‑cousins or second cousins.

M and N are siblings, so their children O (M's daughter) and R (N's daughter) are first cousins. Q is R's child, placing Q one generation below O. A first cousin's child is a first cousin once removed relative to the cousin. Therefore O and Q are first cousins once removed.
Beth is Alex's sister, so her child Carl is Alex's nephew. Alex's child Dana marries Carl, making Carl Alex's son‑in‑law. Thus Carl simultaneously holds both relationships.

Lisa is John’s niece because she is the daughter of John’s brother Tom. Kevin is Lisa’s husband, so his connection to John is solely through marriage. No blood ties exist between Kevin and John, and standard kinship terms for blood relations do not include a term for a spouse of a niece. Therefore Kevin is related to John only affinally, i.e., without a blood relationship.

Each child’s father is the brother of the other child’s father, making them first cousins paternally. L's father and S are full siblings, making S L's paternal aunt. M is S's child, so M is the child of L's aunt, which by definition is L's first cousin. The other options do not fit the given strict monogamous, non‑adoptive relations.

R's mother has one sister (maternal aunt) and R's father has one sister (paternal aunt). The two aunts are unrelated, so they are distinct individuals. M and N share the same parents, and O and P share another set of parents. X is child of M (sibling of N) and O (sibling of P). Y is child of N and P. Therefore X and Y are each the child of two siblings, giving them both sets of grandparents in common. X's maternal aunt is the sister of X's mother; her child Y is the child of a sibling of X's parent, making Y a first cousin. Similarly, X's paternal uncle is the brother of X's father; his child Z is also a child of a sibling of X's parent, thus a first cousin. Since either choice S (Y or Z) is a first cousin, the relationship is uniquely first cousin.

Therefore M and N share both sets of grandparents—paternal and maternal—making them first cousins through two distinct parental sibling links. This is the definition of double first cousins.

Mary and Peter are John’s siblings, so their children Alex and Beth are John’s nephew and niece. Alex (nephew) and Beth (niece) are first cousins and have a child Sam. Sam is therefore the child of John’s nephew/niece, which is termed a great‑nephew or great‑niece (also called grandnephew). The other options describe cousin relationships, which do not apply.

A and B are siblings; C and D are siblings. A marries C and B marries D, so each child has one parent from each sibling pair. The two children therefore share both sets of grandparents (the parents of A/B and the parents of C/D). Sharing both grandparent pairs makes them double first cousins, not half‑cousins nor unrelated.

A is L's paternal aunt, making her child M a first cousin on L's father's side. B is L's maternal uncle, making his child M a first cousin on L's mother's side. Since L and M are first cousins through both parental lines—children of two sibling pairs—they are double first cousins, the most precise term.

Adam's father is Sam's great-grandparent because Sam is the child of Eva (Adam's granddaughter) and Frank (Brian's grandson). Sam's gender is not specified, so the gender‑neutral term 'great‑grandchild' is the most precise.

Adam and Beth are siblings (share parents F). Carl and Diana are siblings (share parents G). Adam marries Diana, Beth marries Carl. X is child of Adam (F side) and Diana (G side); Y is child of Beth (F side) and Carl (G side). X’s paternal grandparents are the F parents, maternal grandparents are the G parents. Y’s paternal grandparents are the G parents, maternal grandparents are the F parents. Therefore X and Y share both sets of grandparents, i.e., they are children of two pairs of siblings, which is the definition of double first cousins.
Mary is the mother of Peter. Peter is Lily's father, making Mary Lily's maternal grandmother. Therefore Lily is Mary's granddaughter.

Lisa's brother Mark is Kyle's father, making Kyle Lisa's nephew. Lisa's children Sam and Nina are Lisa's direct offspring. A nephew of a parent is a first cousin to that parent's children. Therefore Kyle is Nina's first cousin.

J's mother has a brother; his child L is the offspring of J's maternal uncle, which makes L a first cousin of J. Similarly, J's father has a sister; her child K is the offspring of J's paternal aunt, also a first cousin of J. With monogamy and no adoption/remarriage, no other relationships are possible, so whether X is L or K, X is J's first cousin.

A and C are full sisters, so they share the same parents. B and D are full brothers, sharing their own parents. X’s mother (A) and Y’s mother (C) have the same parents, making those parents X’s maternal grandparents and Y’s maternal grandparents. Likewise, X’s father (D) and Y’s father (B) share the same parents, which are X’s paternal grandparents and Y’s paternal grandparents. Thus X and Y share both sets of grandparents, a relationship defined as double first cousins.

M and S are full siblings, and W and N are full siblings. C is the child of M (sibling of S) and W (sibling of N). D is the child of S (sibling of M) and N (sibling of W). Thus C and D are each the offspring of two sibling pairs, which is the definition of double first cousins.

The father's sister is the man's paternal aunt. Her daughter is therefore his first cousin. The statement says this cousin is the man's wife's mother, meaning his wife's mother is his first cousin. Consequently, his wife is the child of his first cousin, which is the definition of a first cousin once removed (one generation apart). This matches a standard kinship term.

P's mother’s only brother is P’s maternal uncle. P's father’s only sister is P’s paternal aunt. These two siblings‑in‑law marry, and their child is the offspring of both P’s maternal uncle and paternal aunt. Therefore the child is a first cousin through the mother (child of maternal uncle) and also a first cousin through the father (child of paternal aunt). Being a cousin on both parental lines makes the child a double first cousin of P. The relationship is uniquely determined.

Adam and Ben are brothers, so Ethan and Fiona share a set of paternal grandparents. Clara and Diana are sisters, so they also share a set of maternal grandparents. Because the two children are related through both their fathers and their mothers, they are first cousins on two separate lines, i.e., double first cousins.

Y's father has exactly one sibling, who is Z's parent. If that sibling is a full sibling of Y's father, Y and Z share both grandparents, making them first cousins. If the sibling is only a half‑sibling (sharing one parent), Y and Z share only one grandparent, making them half‑first cousins. The puzzle does not specify whether the sibling is full or half, so the precise relationship cannot be uniquely determined.

X’s maternal uncle is X’s mother’s only brother; his child Y is the child of a sibling of X’s mother, making Y a first cousin of X. Similarly, X’s paternal aunt is X’s father’s only sister; her child Z is the child of a sibling of X’s father, also a first cousin of X. Selecting either Y or Z yields the same relationship: first cousin. The relation is uniquely determined.

Adam and Brian are brothers, so their children share the same paternal grandparents. Clara and Diana are sisters, so their children share the same maternal grandparents. Because the two children are related through both parental lines, they are first cousins on both sides, i.e., double first cousins. They are not half‑first cousins (which would require sharing only one set of grandparents) nor second cousins (which would require sharing great‑grandparents).

X's parents are M and O; Y's parents are N and P. M and N are siblings, so they share the same parents (grandparents of X and Y). O and P are also siblings, sharing another set of parents (the other grandparents of X and Y). Thus X and Y share both sets of grandparents, meaning their parents are two pairs of siblings. This relationship is defined as double first cousins.

L’s mother’s brother is L’s maternal uncle; his child is a first cousin on the maternal side. L’s father’s sister is L’s paternal aunt; her child is a first cousin on the paternal side. Since the two parents of Z are distinct individuals (the maternal uncle and the paternal aunt), Z is simultaneously a first cousin through both parents—i.e., a child of two sibling pairs who married each other. This relationship is precisely termed a double first cousin.

Aaron's father Liam and Bella's father Maya are siblings (Stone family). Aaron's mother Olivia and Bella's mother Peter are siblings (Lake family). Thus Aaron and Bella are each child of a pair of siblings, sharing both sets of grandparents (the Stones and the Lakes). This is the definition of double first cousins, who share both paternal and maternal grandparents.

L's sister and L's brother are siblings, sharing both parents. Their respective children (the sister's son and the brother's daughter) are therefore first cousins. M is the child of the sister's son, and N is the child of the brother's daughter. Thus M and N are the children of first cousins, which by standard kinship terminology makes them second cousins.

M’s maternal aunt (mother’s sister) and M’s paternal uncle (father’s brother) are married. Their child N is therefore the offspring of M’s mother’s sibling and M’s father’s sibling. N is a first cousin to M through the maternal line and also a first cousin through the paternal line. Because the cousin relationship occurs on both sides, they are double first cousins.

X's paternal grandmother is the sister of Y's mother, making them siblings. Their children—X's father and Y—are therefore first cousins. X is the child of X's father, placing X one generation below the cousin relationship, which is defined as first cousins once removed.

Adam and Beth are siblings, so they share the same parents. Dana and Carl are also siblings, sharing another set of parents. Ethan is the child of Adam (one sibling pair) and Dana (the other sibling pair). Fiona is the child of Beth (the first sibling pair) and Carl (the second sibling pair). Therefore Ethan and Fiona have both sets of grandparents in common, making them children of two sibling pairs. This relationship is defined as double first cousins.

M and N are siblings, so their children X (via M) and Y (via N) are first cousins. Likewise O and P are siblings, and they are the other parents of X and Y, making X and Y first cousins again through that side. Being first cousins through both parental lines makes them double first cousins.

M and N are siblings, so they share one set of grandparents. O and P are also siblings, sharing a second set of grandparents. X is child of M (from the first sibling pair) and O (from the second pair); Y is child of N (the other sibling of M) and P (the other sibling of O). Therefore X and Y have both sets of grandparents in common, making them double first cousins.

M and P are brothers, so their children S and R share one set of paternal grandparents, making them first cousins. N and Q are sisters, so S and R also share one set of maternal grandparents, giving another first‑cousin relationship. Because they are first cousins through both parents, they are double first cousins, the most precise term.

P and Q are half‑siblings because they share only their father G. R is P's child and S is Q's child. Children of siblings are first cousins; when the siblings are half‑siblings, their children share only one grandparent (G) and are thus half‑first cousins. Therefore R and S are half‑first cousins.

M and N are full siblings; O and P are full siblings. M marries O and N marries P. Their children X (of M + O) and Y (of N + P) each have the same two sets of grandparents: the parents of M/N and the parents of O/P. Hence X and Y are first cousins through both their mothers and fathers, i.e., they share both sets of grandparents. This is the definition of double first cousins.

Adam and Brian are brothers, so their children share the same paternal grandparents. Clara and Diana are sisters, so their children share the same maternal grandparents. Ethan and Fiona thus share both sets of grandparents, making them children of two sibling pairs. This fits the definition of double first cousins, the most precise term among the options.

John is father of both Lisa (with Mary) and Mark (with Anne), making Lisa and Mark half‑siblings. Lisa’s child is Emma. Therefore Mark is the half‑brother of Emma’s mother, which is the definition of a half‑uncle (an uncle who is a half‑sibling of the parent).

X's mother and A are siblings, making A X's maternal uncle. A's daughter Y is therefore X's first cousin. Y's child Z is one generation below Y, so Z is the child of X's cousin, which is defined as a first cousin once removed.

John and Mary share the same mother. John’s daughter Lisa and Mary’s son Tom are first cousins. Their child Emma is thus the grandchild of both John and Mary. Consequently Emma is the great‑grandchild of John’s mother through John’s line (John → Lisa → Emma) and also through Mary’s line (Mary → Tom → Emma). Hence Emma is John’s mother’s great‑granddaughter via two parallel lines, i.e., a double great‑granddaughter.

M's father has exactly one child; with monogamy and no adoption that sole child must be M. P is defined as the child of this only child, i.e., the child of M. The same reasoning applies to Q via M's mother. Therefore P and Q are each M's children. The kinship term is 'Child'.

Zoe is the daughter of Victor, who is Laura's brother. Laura is Paul's wife; Paul is Emma's son. Zoe's lineage contains no ancestors from Emma, John, Paul, Nina, Mark, or Daniel. Ethan is the son of Daniel, who is Mark's brother. Mark married Nina, but Daniel is not blood‑related to Nina; he is only Mark's sibling. Therefore Ethan's blood line comes from Daniel and his parents, unrelated to Zoe's line. No common ancestor exists, so there is no blood relationship.

M and N are full siblings, sharing grandparents GM1/GM2. O and P are full siblings, sharing grandparents GO1/GO2. X is child of M (a sibling of N) and O (a sibling of P). Y is child of N and P. Therefore X and Y each have the same two sets of grandparents (GM1/GM2 and GO1/GO2). Sharing both sets of grandparents makes them double first cousins, not just first cousins or any more distant kinship.

M and N are double first cousins, meaning they share both sets of grandparents. The children of first cousins are second cousins because they share great‑grandparents. Since M and N share two distinct grandparent pairs, their children A and B share two distinct great‑grandparent pairs, making them second cousins through both lines – i.e., double second cousins.

M is the child of N's paternal aunt (sister of N's father) and also the child of N's maternal uncle (brother of N's mother). Thus M is a first cousin on both the father's side and the mother's side, meaning the two cousins share both sets of grandparents. This relationship is called double first cousins.

P’s mother is sibling to Q’s father, and P’s father is sibling to Q’s mother, with the two sibling pairs being distinct. Thus each of P’s parents is a sibling of one of Q’s parents, meaning P and Q are the children of two sibling couples. This makes them double first cousins, sharing both sets of grandparents.

A and C are brothers; B and D are sisters. A marries B, C marries D. Thus X’s paternal grandparents are A and C’s parents, and maternal grandparents are B and D’s parents. Y has the same paternal and maternal grandparents. Sharing both sets of grandparents makes X and Y double first cousins, not merely first cousins (which share only one set) nor half‑first cousins (share one grandparent). They are not second cousins, which would require a generation gap. Hence the precise term is double first cousins.

John’s mother’s brother Tom is John’s maternal uncle, making Tom’s daughter Sarah John’s first cousin. John’s father’s sister Mary is his paternal aunt, so Mary’s son Kevin is also John’s first cousin. Sarah and Kevin (both John’s first cousins) have a child Lily. A child of one’s first cousin is a first cousin once removed. Therefore Lily is John’s first cousin once removed.

A is M's daughter, married to H (M's son‑in‑law). H's sister D is therefore the sister of M's son‑in‑law, a relation not covered by standard kin terms. D's daughter C is the niece of H, i.e., the niece of M's son‑in‑law. This does not correspond to granddaughter, niece, or daughter‑in‑law for M under the allowed terms, so only an affinal link exists.

From (1): Emma's mother’s brother is Liam’s maternal uncle, so Emma is the child of Liam’s uncle – making her Liam’s first cousin. From (2): Emma’s father’s sister is Liam’s mother, so Liam is the child of Emma’s aunt – also making them first cousins. Both statements describe the same cross‑generation sibling‑of‑parent relationship, confirming that Emma and Liam share a set of grandparents. Hence they are first cousins.

M and S are full sisters, sharing both parents. H shares only the mother with M, so H is also a half‑sibling of S (they share the same mother but not the father). C1 is H's child; C2 is S's child. Children of half‑siblings are half‑first cousins, as their parents are half‑siblings rather than full siblings. Therefore the precise kinship term is half‑first cousins.

Alan and Brian are full brothers, so their children share the same paternal grandparents. Clara and Diana are full sisters, so their children share the same maternal grandparents. Because X and Y share both sets of grandparents, they are first cousins through both parents, i.e., double first cousins.

M and N are siblings, so they share the same parents. M's son (father of X) and M's daughter (mother of Y) are siblings, and N's daughter (mother of X) and N's son (father of Y) are also siblings. Thus X and Y each have the same paternal grandparents (M's parents) and the same maternal grandparents (N's parents). Sharing both sets of grandparents makes them double first cousins, the most precise term.

M, N, and P are siblings. N's child O and P's child Q are therefore children of two siblings (N and P). Children of siblings share the same grandparents, making them first cousins in standard kinship terminology.

A and B are half‑siblings, sharing only mother M. Their children C (child of A) and D (child of B) therefore share one grandparent (M) but not the other. Children of half‑siblings are half‑first cousins. Hence C and D are half‑first cousins.

X is the child of N's father's sibling, making X a first cousin on the paternal side. X is also the child of N's mother's sibling, making X a first cousin on the maternal side. Because the same person X holds both cousin relationships simultaneously, X is a double first cousin of N.

M and N share the same parents, as do O and P. X’s grandparents are M/N’s parents and O/P’s parents. Y has the identical two sets of grandparents. Therefore X and Y are first cousins through both parental lines, i.e., double first cousins, the most precise term.

M and N are siblings, so their children are first cousins. O is M's daughter, R is N's daughter; thus O and R are first cousins. Q is R's child, one generation below R. Therefore O is the first cousin of Q's parent, making O and Q first cousins once removed.

M and N share the same parents, and X and Y share the same parents. A’s paternal grandparents are M/N’s parents, and his maternal grandparents are X/Y’s parents. B has the identical set of paternal and maternal grandparents. Thus A and B are first cousins through both parental lines, i.e., double first cousins – the most specific term among the options.

Alice's mother is the sister of Bob's father, making her Bob's aunt. Alice's father is the brother of Bob's mother, also making him Bob's uncle. Thus both of Alice's parents are siblings of Bob's parents. When two siblings from one family marry two siblings from another family, their children are double first cousins, sharing both sets of grandparents. Therefore Alice and Bob are double first cousins.

N's father has a sister; that sister is M's mother (or father). Thus M is N's paternal first cousin. N's mother has a brother; that brother is M's father (or mother). Thus M is also N's maternal first cousin. The two parents of M are respectively the sibling of N's father and the sibling of N's mother, meaning the parents are themselves first cousins. Consequently M and N share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins, a more precise relationship than simple first cousin.

A is the sister of P's mother, making A P's maternal aunt; B is the brother of P's father, making B P's paternal uncle. Their child C is therefore the child of P's aunt on the mother's side and the child of P's uncle on the father's side. In each case C is a first cousin of P. Because C is related to P as a first cousin through both parental lines, C is a double first cousin of P.

M is the child of N's father's brother (paternal uncle) making M a first cousin on the father's side. M is also the child of N's mother's sister (maternal aunt) making M a first cousin on the mother's side. Being a first cousin through both parental lines defines a double first cousin, which is possible without intermarriage among relatives.

E and F are half‑siblings, sharing only one parent (their mother). That mother is the sole common grandparent of X (child of E) and Y (child of F). Children of half‑siblings are therefore cousins who share only one grandparent, which is termed a half‑first cousin. Hence the most precise relation is half‑first cousins.

Let X be N’s mother. X’s father is N’s maternal grandfather (G). G’s only sister is G’s sibling, i.e., N’s great‑aunt. M is the child of that sister, making M a first cousin of X (they share grandparents). Since X is N’s mother, M is one generation apart from N, so M is N’s first cousin once removed. The relationship is uniquely determined.

John's son is Peter. Lily is the child of Peter (and Anna). Therefore Lily is the direct descendant of John through his son, making her John's granddaughter. The other relations involve siblings or in-laws, which are irrelevant for blood kinship.

M and N are half‑siblings, meaning they share exactly one parent and thus one grandparent for each of their children. X is the child of M and Y is the child of N, placing them in the same generation. Because their parents share only one parent, X and Y share only one grandparent, not both. Therefore they are cousins of the first degree but with a half‑relationship, i.e., half‑first cousins.

M and N share the same parents, as do X and Y. A’s paternal grandparents are M/N’s parents, and A’s maternal grandparents are X/Y’s parents. B has the same paternal and maternal grandparents because his father N and mother Y belong to the same sibling pairs. Therefore A and B share both sets of grandparents, making them first cousins through both parents – i.e., double first cousins, the most specific term.

M’s mother and N’s father are married to each other, forming a single household. M is the biological child of his mother only, and N is the biological child of his father only. Since they share no common biological parent but their respective parents are married, M and N are related as step‑siblings.
John is married to Emma. Emma’s father is also Victor’s father, making Victor Emma’s brother. Therefore Victor is the brother of John’s wife, which is the definition of a brother‑in‑law.

Anna's mother and Ben are siblings, making Ben Anna's maternal uncle. Ben's son Carl is therefore Anna's first cousin. Diana is Carl's daughter, i.e., the child of Anna's first cousin. The child of a first cousin is a first cousin once removed (one generation apart). Hence Diana is Anna's first cousin once removed.

John’s mother’s brother is his maternal uncle; his father’s sister is his paternal aunt. They are married, so their child Emma is the offspring of John’s maternal uncle (making her a first cousin on the mother’s side) and also the offspring of John’s paternal aunt (making her a first cousin on the father’s side). Being a first cousin through both parental lines makes Emma a double first cousin of John.

Robert and Linda are siblings. Linda's son Kevin is therefore the child of John’s paternal aunt, which makes Kevin John’s first cousin. The additional information about Mary and Tom does not affect this direct lineage.

Ben is Anna's maternal uncle, so his daughter Dana is Anna's first cousin on her mother's side. Claire is Anna's paternal aunt, and her son Dana is Anna's first cousin on her father's side. Because Dana is the same person, she is a double first cousin—still classified as a first cousin in standard kinship terminology.

A and C are sisters, sharing the same parents; B and D are brothers, sharing the same parents. Their children F (of A & B) and E (of C & D) thus have both sets of grandparents in common. This makes them first cousins through both parental lines, i.e., double first cousins.

C1’s father B1 and C2’s father B2 are brothers, so C1 and C2 share paternal grandparents. Likewise, C1’s mother S2 and C2’s mother S1 are sisters, so they also share maternal grandparents. Sharing both sets of grandparents makes them first cousins on both sides, i.e., double first cousins, the most precise standard term.

M and N are siblings, so their children O and P are first cousins. R is married to P, making R the spouse of O's cousin. This is an affinal (marriage) connection, not a blood relation. In English kinship, the term "cousin‑in‑law" is used to denote the spouse of one’s cousin, providing a standard label for this relationship.

M and N are siblings, sharing grandparents A. O and P are siblings, sharing grandparents B. M marries O, N marries P. X’s parents are M (child of A) and O (child of B); Y’s parents are N (child of A) and P (child of B). Thus X and Y each have the same two sets of grandparents (A and B). Children who share both sets of grandparents are double first cousins, the most precise term.

R's mother's only brother is R's maternal uncle; his child X is R's first cousin. Similarly, R's father's only brother is R's paternal uncle; his child Y is also R's first cousin. Since S is either X or Y, S is necessarily a first cousin of R, with no alternative kinship possible.

X and Y are each the child of a brother (Adam, Ben) and a sister (Clara, Diana). The brothers share the same parents, and the sisters share the same parents. Therefore X and Y have both sets of grandparents in common, making them first cousins on both the paternal and maternal sides. This relationship is called double first cousins.

Alan and Brian are brothers; Clara and Diana are sisters. Their children Emma and Frank therefore share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins. Grace is Emma's daughter and Henry is Frank's son, so each is one generation below the double first cousins. Children of first cousins are second cousins; when the parents are double first cousins, their children share both pairs of great‑grandparents, making them double second cousins. Hence the most precise term is double second cousins.

N's father (F) and M's mother (S) are half‑siblings, sharing one parent P. Thus P is a grandparent of both N (through F) and M (through S). They have only this single common grandparent; the other grandparents differ. Children of half‑siblings are half‑first cousins, i.e., cousins who share exactly one grandparent. Therefore M is N's half‑first cousin.

Alice's maternal uncle (her mother's brother) and her paternal aunt (her father's sister) are unrelated individuals. Their child Ben is therefore Alice's first cousin through her mother and also her first cousin through her father. Being first cousins on both parental lines makes them double first cousins.

Adam's son Ethan is Greg's father, making Greg Adam's grandson. Simultaneously, Fiona is Adam's niece (Brian's daughter), so Greg, as her child, is Adam's grand‑nephew (great‑nephew). Thus Greg has two distinct standard relations to Adam, and no single term encompasses both.

A is the child of P's paternal aunt, making A P's first cousin on the father's side. B is the child of P's maternal uncle, making B P's first cousin on the mother's side. A's grandparents are P's paternal grandparents, while B's grandparents are P's maternal grandparents. Since the paternal and maternal grandparents are unrelated (no marriage connections considered), A and B share no common ancestor, so they have no direct kinship.

R's mother has one brother; his son L is R's maternal first cousin. R's father has one sister; her daughter W is R's paternal first cousin. Marriage between L and W does not affect blood ties. Therefore W is a first cousin of R.

Mary’s brother Peter is John’s maternal uncle, making Peter’s daughter Lisa John’s first cousin. John’s brother Tom is therefore also Lisa’s first cousin. Anna is the child of Tom (John’s brother) and Lisa. In kinship terms, the child of one’s sibling is a niece or nephew, regardless of the other parent’s relation. Hence Anna is John’s niece.

A’s mother and B’s father are siblings, so they share one set of grandparents (call them G1). A’s father and B’s mother are siblings, sharing another set of grandparents (G2). Thus A’s maternal grandparents are B’s paternal grandparents, and A’s paternal grandparents are B’s maternal grandparents. A and B therefore share both sets of grandparents, making them children of two sibling pairs, i.e., double first cousins.

M is N's mother. T is M's sibling, making T N's aunt/uncle. S is T's son, so S is N's first cousin. Other links (O, P, Q, R) involve marriage or lateral relations but do not alter S‑N blood link. Hence the direct blood relationship is first cousins.

M and N are siblings, and O and P are siblings. M marries O, N marries P. Their children X (of M + O) and Y (of N + P) therefore each have the same two sets of grandparents: the parents of M/N and the parents of O/P. Hence X and Y are first cousins through both parental lines, i.e., double first cousins.

M and N are full siblings, sharing both parents. A is M's daughter, while D is N's daughter. Children of two full siblings are first cousins. There is no half relationship because the sibling link between M and N is full, and no adoption or remarriage alters the lineage.

J's mother’s brother is J's maternal uncle; his child (K) is J’s first cousin. J's father’s brother is J's paternal uncle; his child (L) is also J’s first cousin. Selecting either K or L yields a person who is a first cousin of J. Hence the relation is first cousin.

Mara and Nia are sisters, so their children Omar and Priya are first cousins. Sam is Priya's son, making him one generation below Priya. The relation between a person and the child of their first cousin is a first cousin once removed. Thus Sam is Omar's first cousin once removed.

L and K are siblings. Their children M and N are first cousins. S is N's daughter, making S one generation below N. Therefore S is one generation below M's first cousin, which defines a first cousin once removed relationship.

M and N are siblings, so they share the same parents. X and Y are also siblings, sharing another set of parents. A is the child of M (one of the first sibling pair) and X (one of the second sibling pair). B is the child of N (the other sibling of M) and Y (the other sibling of X). Therefore A and B have both sets of grandparents in common: the parents of M/N and the parents of X/Y. Children who share both paternal and maternal grandparents are called double first cousins, which is more precise than ordinary first cousins.

Adam and Ben are brothers and Clara and Diana are sisters, so their children Ethan and Felix are first cousins on both paternal and maternal sides – i.e., double first cousins. The children of double first cousins (Lily and Maya) are therefore second cousins through both lineages, making them double second cousins.

M is mother of both O and Q, but they have different fathers, making O and Q half‑siblings. O's child S is the niece/nephew of O's siblings. Since Q is a half‑sibling of O, Q is a half‑aunt (or half‑uncle) to S. The precise term among the choices is "Half‑aunt".

A and B share the same parents, as do C and D. The child of A and C inherits grandparents from both A's parents and C's parents. The child of B and D inherits the identical set of grandparents, because B shares A's parents and D shares C's parents.
