Thus M’s parents are N’s two aunts/uncles who are married to each other. M is therefore the child of both a paternal and a maternal sibling of N, i.e., the child of two sibling pairs. This defines a double first cousin relationship.

M and N are brothers, so they share the same parents (paternal grandparents of X and Y). S and T are sisters, sharing another set of parents (maternal grandparents of X and Y). X’s father is M and mother is S; Y’s father is N and mother is T. Thus X and Y have both sets of grandparents in common, making them children of two sibling pairs. This is the definition of double first cousins.

John and Mary share the same parents, and Lisa and Tom share a different pair of parents. Adam is the child of John (from the first family) and Lisa (from the second family). Beth is the child of Mary (same first family) and Tom (same second family). Thus Adam and Beth have both sets of grandparents in common, making them children of two sibling pairs. This relationship is called double first cousins, not half or second cousins.

M's mother and her sister (the aunt) are siblings, making N the child of M's maternal aunt – a first cousin on the maternal side. Likewise, M's father and his brother (the paternal uncle) are siblings, and N is the child of that uncle – a first cousin on the paternal side. Since N is simultaneously the child of both a maternal aunt and a paternal uncle, M and N share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins.

X is the biological child of Mary. Anna is the biological child of Peter. After John’s death, Mary marries Peter, making Peter X’s step‑father and Mary Anna’s step‑mother. Children of a married couple who are not biologically related are defined as step‑siblings. No blood parent is shared, so they are not half‑siblings, nor are their parents siblings, so they are not cousins. A standard term exists—step‑siblings—so the most precise choice is C.

P’s mother and Q’s father are siblings, so P and Q share the same grandparents and are first cousins. Q’s sister is also a child of those grandparents, making her another first cousin of P. R is the child of Q’s sister, i.e., the child of P’s first cousin. In kinship terms, the child of a first cousin is a first cousin once removed. Hence R’s precise relationship to P is first cousin once removed.

N is L's maternal uncle (mother's brother). N's daughter O is therefore L's first cousin. O's son P is one generation below L's cousin, making P L's first cousin once removed. The relationship is uniquely determined.

M and S are sisters, so they share parents. A is child of M; therefore S is A's maternal aunt. S and her husband H have a biological child E. Children of siblings are first cousins, so E is A's first cousin. No other blood ties affect this relation.

Lisa is John’s maternal first cousin (child of his mother’s brother). Tom is John’s paternal first cousin (child of his father’s brother). Their child Emily is thus the child of John’s first cousin on each side. In kinship terms, the child of a first cousin is a first cousin once removed, regardless of which side the link comes from. No closer relationship (nephew, half‑sibling) exists, and there is blood relation, so the correct choice is C.

R's spouse S has a brother T, making T R's brother-in-law. T's wife U is therefore R's sister-in-law. V is U's sister, i.e., a sibling of R's sister-in-law. This relationship is an affinal chain without a specific standard term; it is not brother‑in‑law, cousin‑in‑law, or nephew‑in‑law.

S is the sister of T's father, making S T's paternal aunt. U, as S's child, is T's first cousin. V, being U's child, is one generation below T's cousin, which is defined as a first cousin once removed. Hence the precise kinship term is "first cousin once removed".

X is the child of N's father's sister (paternal aunt) and also the child of N's mother's brother (maternal uncle). For X to be the same person, the aunt and uncle must be married to each other. Thus X is N's cousin through both the paternal and maternal sides, i.e., a double first cousin.

Mary's brother Tom is married to Linda, making Linda Mary's sister‑in‑law. Eva is Linda's sister by blood, not married to anyone in Mary's immediate family. Standard English in‑law terms cover a spouse, that spouse's siblings/parents, one's own siblings' spouses, and children's spouses, but do not include the sibling of a sister‑in‑law. Therefore there is no direct standard kinship term; the relation exists only as an affinal chain.

Alan and Brian are brothers, so their children X and Y are first cousins on the paternal side. Clara and Diana are sisters, so X and Y are also first cousins on the maternal side. Because the two children share both sets of grandparents (paternal and maternal), they are cousins through two sibling pairs, which is the definition of double first cousins. No half‑relationships or second‑cousin connections exist.

R's spouse S has a sister T; T's husband U is R's brother‑in‑law. U's brother V is thus sibling of R's brother‑in‑law, a relation not covered by standard in‑law terms. W, as V's spouse, is the spouse of that sibling, also outside the defined categories. Therefore no standard direct relation applies.

A and B are half‑siblings, sharing one parent. Their children X and Y each inherit that shared grandparent as a common ancestor. Therefore X and Y share exactly one grandparent, not both, which defines the relationship of half‑first cousins. Standard English kinship terminology distinguishes this from full first cousins, so the most precise term is "half‑first cousins".

Adam and Beth are siblings, as are Dana and Carl. Ethan is the child of Adam (Smith) and Dana (Jones); Fiona is the child of Beth (Smith) and Carl (Jones). Therefore Ethan and Fiona share both sets of grandparents—the parents of Adam/Beth and the parents of Dana/Carl. Sharing both grandparent pairs makes them double first cousins, the most precise term.

B is A's maternal uncle, so C (B's daughter) is A's first cousin on the mother's side. D is A's paternal aunt, so E (D's son) is A's first cousin on the father's side. C and E share no common ancestor because their only link is through A, whose parents are unrelated. Therefore C and E have no standard blood‑kinship term; they are related only affinally (cousins‑in‑law).

John's sister Mary makes Lisa his niece. John’s brother Mark makes Tom his nephew. Lisa and Tom’s child Anna is therefore the child of John’s niece (or nephew). In kinship terms the child of a niece or nephew is a grandniece (also called great‑niece). None of the other options fit this relationship.

Paul's father John and Anna's father Mark are brothers, so they share the same paternal grandparents. Paul's mother Mary and Anna's mother Lisa are sisters, sharing the same maternal grandparents. Consequently Paul and Anna share both sets of grandparents, making them first cousins through two sibling links—i.e., double first cousins.

L's mother (M) and R are siblings, making R L's maternal uncle. R's daughter S is therefore L's first cousin. S's son T is the child of L's cousin, which by standard kinship terminology is a first cousin once removed. No other relationships fit the given constraints, so the relation is uniquely determined.
Alex's father is Tom (mother Sara). Sam's father is also Tom (mother Linda). They share one parent (Tom) but have different mothers, making them half‑siblings.

M and N are half‑siblings, sharing one parent X. Their children P and Q each have X as a grandparent, but they do not share the other grandparent. Therefore P and Q share exactly one grandparent, making them half‑first cousins, the correct specific term.

B is A's father. B's sister C is A's paternal aunt. C's son D is therefore A's first cousin. E is D's daughter, i.e., the child of A's first cousin. In standard kinship terminology, the child of a first cousin is a first cousin once removed. No half‑relationship or other degree applies.

M is parent of D. D's daughter is C, making C M's biological granddaughter. Although C also marries B (M's nephew), that does not change the direct blood relation. Therefore the correct kinship term for C relative to M is Granddaughter.

Ethan's father Adam and Fiona's father Brian are brothers, so Ethan and Fiona share the same paternal grandparents. Their mothers Clara and Dana are sisters, so they also share the same maternal grandparents. Sharing both sets of grandparents makes them first cousins on both sides, i.e., double first cousins.

Y is described as the child of X’s father’s sister, i.e., the daughter of X’s paternal aunt. The child of a parent's sibling is a first cousin. The other statement about X’s maternal uncle marrying Y’s sister only creates an in‑law link and does not affect blood ties. Therefore X and Y share the standard first‑cousin relationship.

John and Anna are full siblings; Mary and Ben are full siblings. John marries Mary, Anna marries Ben. Emma (child of John & Mary) has paternal grandparents = John’s parents and maternal grandparents = Mary’s parents. Liam (child of Anna & Ben) has paternal grandparents = Ben’s parents (Mary’s parents) and maternal grandparents = Anna’s parents (John’s parents). Hence Emma and Liam share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins, the most precise term.

John’s brother Peter is married to Mary, making Mary John’s sister‑in‑law. Mary’s sister Lisa is not directly related to John by any standard in‑law term. However, Lisa marries Kevin, who is John’s only child. The spouse of one’s child is the child’s daughter‑in‑law (or son‑in‑law). Therefore Lisa’s relation to John is that of a daughter‑in‑law.

Alan and Beth are siblings. Their children, Dana and Carl, are first cousins. Eva is Dana's child, placing her one generation below Dana. Therefore Carl and Eva are separated by one generation while sharing a common ancestor (the grandparents of Alan and Beth), making them first cousins once removed.

A is X's maternal uncle; C is his spouse, making C X's aunt by marriage. B is C's brother, unrelated by blood to X. Y is B's daughter, i.e., the niece of C. Since the connection runs only through marriage (aunt by marriage's sibling's child), there is no recognized blood-based kinship term such as first or second cousin, nor a half‑cousin. Hence the relation has no standard term.

L's father has one brother (paternal uncle) and L's mother has one sister (maternal aunt). Each of those siblings has a single child, and both children are the same individual M. Therefore M is simultaneously the child of L's paternal uncle and the child of L's maternal aunt, meaning the uncle and aunt must be married to each other. M thus shares both sets of grandparents with L, making M a double first cousin rather than a regular or half cousin. The relationship is determinable.

M's father F and B are brothers; M's mother M1 and N are sisters. B (paternal uncle) married N (maternal aunt). Their child O therefore has as grandparents both the paternal grandparents of M (through B) and the maternal grandparents of M (through N). O and M share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins, the children of two sibling pairs who married each other.

R's mother and U share the same parents, making U R's maternal uncle. V is the sole child of that uncle. In standard blood‑relation terms, the child of one's uncle or aunt is a first cousin. No other information suggests a different relationship, so the precise term is first cousin.

M and N are siblings, so they share the same parents. O and P are siblings, sharing another set of parents. X is the child of M (who is sibling to N) and O (who is sibling to P). Y is the child of N and P. Therefore X and Y are first cousins through their fathers (M and N) and also first cousins through their mothers (O and P). Sharing both sets of grandparents makes them double first cousins, not half or unrelated.

Y, S, and B are siblings, sharing the same parents. S's son and B's daughter are thus children of two siblings, making them first cousins. X is the child of S's son, and Z is the child of B's daughter. Children of first cousins are second cousins, as they share the same great‑grandparents (the parents of Y, S, B) and are of the same generation. Therefore X and Z are second cousins.

L's father has one sister (paternal aunt). M is her child, making M L's paternal first cousin. L's mother has one brother (maternal uncle). M is also his child, making M L's maternal first cousin. Thus M is the child of both L's paternal aunt and maternal uncle, i.e., a double first cousin. This still falls under the standard term "first cousin," which is uniquely determined among the choices.

B is A's parent. B's sister C is A's aunt. C's child D is therefore A's first cousin (children of siblings). E is D's child, making E one generation below A's first cousin, which is the definition of a first cousin once removed. No other option fits more precisely.

M and N are half‑siblings because they share only their mother. Their children P (child of M) and Q (child of N) each have that common mother as a grandparent. Since they share only one grandparent rather than a full set of two, P and Q are cousins who share a single grandparent, i.e., half‑first cousins.

John and Linda are siblings, so Anna’s paternal grandparents are the same as Ben’s maternal grandparents. Mary and Tom are siblings, so Anna’s maternal grandparents are the same as Ben’s paternal grandparents. Hence Anna and Ben share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins.

A is the sister of X's mother, making A X's maternal aunt; her son P is X's maternal first cousin. B is the brother of X's father, making B X's paternal uncle; his daughter Q is X's paternal first cousin. Since X's parents are unrelated (no intermarriage), the two aunts (A and B) are from distinct families and share no common ancestors. Consequently P and Q share no blood relation; they are unrelated to each other.

B is A's parent. B and C are siblings, making C A's aunt/uncle. C's daughter D is therefore A's first cousin. D's son E is one generation below D, so E is the child of A's first cousin, which is defined as a first cousin once removed.

R's sibling's child is either a niece (if female) or a nephew (if male). Because the child's gender is unknown and no gender‑neutral standard term exists in common English kinship vocabulary, the exact relationship term cannot be uniquely determined.

A and B are half‑siblings, sharing only one parent. P is A's child and Q is B's child. The children of siblings are first cousins; when the siblings are half‑siblings, their children are half‑first cousins. No other marriages affect this relationship, so the precise term is half‑first cousins.

M and N share only one parent (their mother), making them half‑siblings. Their children, A and B, are each one generation down from M and N and thus share that common grandparent (the mother). Because they inherit only one shared grandparent rather than two, A and B are half‑first cousins. No generation difference exists, so 'once removed' does not apply, and they are not full first cousins nor second cousins.

Ben is Alex's maternal uncle (mother's brother) and Clara is Alex's paternal aunt (father's sister). Their daughter Dana is therefore Alex's child of his maternal uncle, making her a first cousin on his mother's side, and also the child of his paternal aunt, making her a first cousin on his father's side. Being a first cousin through both parental lines defines a double first cousin.

P and Q are brothers, so X and Y share the same paternal grandparents. R and S are sisters, so X and Y also share the same maternal grandparents. Thus X and Y have both sets of grandparents in common, making them first cousins through two sibling pairs. This is the definition of double first cousins.

M’s father’s sister N is his paternal aunt. If N is a full sister, her child P is M’s first cousin. If N is a half‑sister (sharing only one parent with the father), then P is a half‑cousin. The statement only says “sister” without specifying full or half, so both possibilities exist and the precise relationship cannot be uniquely determined.

John and Mary are siblings; Lisa and Paul are siblings. John marries Lisa and Mary marries Paul. Their children, Anna (John + Lisa) and Ben (Mary + Paul), each receive one set of grandparents from John/Mary (G1) and the other set from Lisa/Paul (G2). Thus Anna and Ben share both sets of grandparents, making them the children of two sibling pairs. This relationship is called double first cousins.

R's mother’s brother T is R’s maternal uncle. T’s daughter S is therefore R’s first cousin. R’s son U is one generation below R. A first cousin of a parent is a first cousin once removed to the child. Hence S is U’s first cousin once removed, which matches choice B.

Aaron's sister Beth's son Carl is Aaron's nephew. Carl's child Fiona is therefore the child of Aaron's nephew, making Fiona Aaron's grandniece (the daughter of a nephew). Dana adds no blood connection, but Fiona's relation via Carl is sufficient for a direct blood kinship term.

Mike is John’s maternal uncle (mother’s brother) and Anna is John’s paternal aunt (father’s sister). Their child Lily is therefore John’s cousin through his mother and also his cousin through his father, making her a first cousin on both sides – a double first cousin.

M and N share only their mother, making them half‑siblings. Their mother is the sole common grandparent of P and Q. First cousins share both grandparents; when only one grandparent is shared, the relationship is termed half‑first cousins. No other family connections are introduced, so the relation is determinable as half‑first cousins.

J’s father’s only sibling is his sister, making her J’s paternal aunt. J’s mother’s only sibling is her brother, making him J’s maternal uncle. Those two siblings marry each other and have a child M. M is therefore the child of J’s paternal aunt (first‑cousin relation) and also the child of J’s maternal uncle (another first‑cousin relation). Because the same two individuals are each a pair of siblings of J’s parents, M occupies the role of a cousin on both parental lines, i.e., a double first cousin.

M’s mother is the sister of N’s father, meaning the two parents are siblings. The children of siblings are first cousins. M is the sole child of his mother, and N is the sole child of his father, but that does not change the cousin relationship. Therefore M and N are first cousins.

M and N are double first cousins, meaning they share both sets of grandparents. Their children X and Y each inherit those grandparents as great‑grandparents. Since X and Y share both sets of great‑grandparents, they are second cousins through two distinct lines, i.e., double second cousins. This is more precise than simply second cousins.

M is the child of P's mother's only brother, making M a maternal first cousin. M is also the child of P's father's only sister, making M a paternal first cousin. Since the same individual M is simultaneously a cousin on both maternal and paternal sides, the parents of M are a brother (maternal uncle) and a sister (paternal aunt) who are married to each other. This situation creates a double first cousin relationship.

Emma and Carl are siblings. Carl's wife Diana is the daughter of Emma's maternal aunt, making Diana Emma's first cousin. Sam is Emma's son, one generation below Emma. In standard kinship, Diana would be Sam's first cousin once removed, but that term is not among the choices and the allowed in‑law terms do not cover this relationship. Therefore no listed standard relation applies.

X's mother’s brother (maternal uncle) and X's father’s sister (paternal aunt) are married and have a daughter Y. Y is therefore the child of X's maternal uncle (making her X's first cousin on the mother's side) and also the child of X's paternal aunt (making her X's first cousin on the father's side). Sharing both sets of grandparents makes Y a double first cousin of X.

John and Mary are full siblings, so Lily and Mark share the same paternal grandparents (John's parents). Anna and Ben are also full siblings, giving Lily and Mark the same maternal grandparents (Anna's parents). Thus Lily and Mark have both sets of grandparents in common, making them first cousins through two sibling pairs. This is the definition of double first cousins, not half‑first or second cousins.

M and N are siblings, so their children O (M's daughter) and R (N's daughter) are first cousins. Q is R's child, making Q one generation below R. Therefore O and Q are separated by one generation while sharing a common ancestor (the parents of M and N), which defines a first‑cousin‑once‑removed relationship.

W's mother has a sibling, who is W's aunt or uncle. Z is described as the child of that sibling. The child of an aunt or uncle is a first cousin to W. Niece/nephew refer to children of one's own sibling, not of one's parent’s sibling, so those options are incorrect. The relationship is uniquely determined as first cousin.

M and N are brothers; O and P are sisters. Their children A and B are each the product of a brother-sister marriage, so A and B share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins. C and D are the children of A and B respectively. Children of first cousins are second cousins; because A and B are double first cousins, their children share both sets of great‑grandparents, i.e., they are double second cousins. The most precise term among the choices is therefore double second cousins.

M and N share both parents, as do X and Y. A’s father M is sibling to B’s father N, making A and B first cousins on the paternal side. Likewise, A’s mother X is sibling to B’s mother Y, making them first cousins on the maternal side as well. Because they are cousins through both parents, they are double first cousins, not half‑first cousins or second cousins.

John and Michael are brothers, sharing parents. Mary is described as John’s sister, so she is also their sibling. Mary’s son Peter is the child of Michael’s sister, making Peter Michael’s nephew/niece. Susan is Michael’s daughter. Children of siblings are first cousins, so Peter and Susan are first cousins.

M and N are half‑siblings, sharing only one parent (their mother). That mother is the sole common grandparent of A (through M) and B (through N). Children of half‑siblings share exactly one grandparent, making them half‑first cousins, the most precise standard term.

M and N are full siblings, so they share the same parents (grandparents of X and Y on that side). O and P are also full siblings, sharing another set of parents (the other set of grandparents). X is child of M and O; Y is child of N and P. Hence X and Y are first cousins through both parental lines, sharing both sets of grandparents, which is the definition of double first cousins.

M is N's mother. M's brother Q is N's maternal uncle. Q's daughter P is therefore N's first cousin by blood. Additionally, P is O's sister and O is N's spouse, making P N's sister‑in‑law, but the direct blood relationship is first cousin, which is the standard kinship term used.

X is the daughter of R's maternal uncle (mother's brother) making X a first cousin on the maternal side. X is also the daughter of R's paternal aunt (father's sister) making X a first cousin on the paternal side. Thus R's parents are married to each other's siblings, and R and X share both sets of grandparents. This relationship is a double first cousin.

Tom is the brother of John’s father, making Tom John’s paternal uncle (blood). Nina is Tom’s wife, i.e., the spouse of John’s parent’s sibling. Under the allowed in‑law definitions (siblings’ spouses), Nina is an aunt‑in‑law, not a blood aunt.

M and N are siblings, so they share the same parents. O and P are siblings, sharing another set of parents. M marries O, producing X; N marries P, producing Y. X and Y therefore have the same two sets of grandparents: the parents of M/N and the parents of O/P. Because they are first cousins through both parental lines, they are double first cousins, not half‑first or second cousins.

A’s mother’s only brother is A’s maternal uncle. A child of that uncle is A’s first cousin on the mother’s side. A’s father’s only sister is A’s paternal aunt. A child of that aunt is A’s first cousin on the father’s side. For X to satisfy both statements, the maternal uncle and paternal aunt must be X’s two parents (a married couple), making X a double first cousin of A. Thus X is a first cousin, not a nephew/niece or half‑cousin, and the relationship is uniquely determined.

Adam and Brian are brothers, so they share the same parents. Clara and Diana are sisters, sharing another set of parents. Ethan is the child of Adam and Clara; Fiona is the child of Brian and Diana. Therefore Ethan and Fiona are first cousins through their fathers (Adam and Brian) and also first cousins through their mothers (Clara and Diana). Sharing both sets of grandparents makes them double first cousins, the most precise term.

M and N are siblings (share parents A). O, P, Q are siblings (share parents B). M marries O and N marries Q, so X (child of M+O) and Y (child of N+Q) have the same paternal grandparents (A) and the same maternal grandparents (B). Sharing both sets of grandparents makes them double first cousins, the most specific term.

W is the paternal aunt of M, making M W's niece/nephew. D is M's daughter, i.e., the child of W's niece/nephew. The standard term for the child of a niece/nephew is grandniece (or grandnephew). Hence D is W's grandniece.

Emma and Lily share the same mother but have different fathers, because Emma's father had only Emma and the mother later had Lily with another partner. Sharing one parent defines a half‑sibling relationship.

Alice and Bob are siblings. Bob's daughter Diana is Alice's niece. Diana's son Frank is therefore the child of Alice's niece, making Frank Alice's grandnephew (also called great‑nephew). The other options do not match this direct lineage.

M and N are siblings, so they share the same two parents (grandparents of their children). O and P are also siblings, sharing another pair of parents (the other set of grandparents). X is child of M (a sibling of N) and O (a sibling of P); Y is child of N and P. Therefore X and Y each have the same four grandparents: the parents of M/N and the parents of O/P. Sharing both sets of grandparents makes them double first cousins, the precise kinship term.

L's father has one sibling who marries L's mother's sibling. Their child M is the offspring of L's paternal aunt/uncle and maternal aunt/uncle. Therefore M is L's first cousin through the father's side and also first cousin through the mother's side, making M a double first cousin of L.

L and M are half‑siblings, sharing only one parent (their mother). Their children A and B each inherit that shared grandparent through their respective parent. Because A and B share a single grandparent rather than a full pair of grandparents, they are cousins of the first degree but only half‑related, i.e., half‑first cousins.

Anna and Beth are sisters. Beth's daughter Clara is Anna's niece. Clara's son Daniel is the child of Anna's niece, making Daniel the grandchild of Anna's sibling's line. In kinship terms, the child of a niece/nephew is called a great‑nephew or grandnephew. Thus Daniel is Anna's great‑nephew (or great‑niece if female).

Mary is John's sister, so her son Tom is John's nephew. Tom marries Anna, who is John's daughter, making Tom also John's son‑in‑law and Anna's first cousin. Their child Lily is therefore the child of John's daughter, i.e., his granddaughter. Simultaneously Lily is the child of John's nephew, making her his great‑niece. Hence Lily holds both relations, and the most precise single description is that she is both granddaughter and great‑niece.

M and N are siblings, so they share the same two grandparents. O and P are siblings, sharing another pair of grandparents. X is child of M (one set) and O (the other set); Y is child of N (first set) and P (second set). Thus X and Y share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins.

Adam and Brian are full brothers, so Ethan and Fiona share the same paternal grandparents. Clara and Diana are full sisters, so Ethan and Fiona also share the same maternal grandparents. Sharing both sets of grandparents makes them double first cousins, not half‑cousins.

M and N are siblings, making their children (D and S) first cousins. J is S's son, one generation below S. Therefore D and J are separated by one generation but share the same first-cousin ancestor level, which defines a first cousin once removed relationship.

M's maternal grandmother and N's paternal grandmother are sisters, making M's mother and N's father first cousins. The children of first cousins (M and N) are second cousins. No other shared ancestors are present, confirming the precise relation.

M and N are half‑siblings, sharing one parent. Their children X and Y each have that shared parent as a grandparent, but they do not share both grandparents. Thus X and Y are first cousins, but only through half‑blood, which is termed half‑first cousins.
Peter's sister is Lisa. Carl is married to Lisa, making him the spouse of Peter's sibling. Under the allowed in-law definitions (siblings' spouses), this relationship is termed brother-in-law.

Adam and Ben are brothers, so they share the same parents. Clara and Diana are sisters, sharing their own parents. X is the child of Adam (father) and Clara (mother); Y is the child of Ben (father) and Diana (mother). Therefore X and Y share both sets of grandparents—the paternal grandparents (parents of Adam and Ben) and the maternal grandparents (parents of Clara and Diana). Sharing both grandparent pairs makes them double first cousins, not just first cousins or any other degree.

Bob's father's sister is Bob's paternal aunt. Her child (Alice) is Bob's first cousin. Since Bob is Carol's parent, Alice is one generation above Carol, making her Bob's cousin's child relative to Carol: a first cousin once removed.

M's brother U is R's maternal uncle; U's child C is R's maternal first cousin. F's sister S is R's paternal aunt; S's child D is R's paternal first cousin. Marriage between C and D does not alter blood ties. Therefore D is R's first cousin.

O is mother of N and P, making N and P half‑siblings. P's daughter Q is therefore the child of N's half‑sibling, which in English is called a niece (the "half" qualifier is not used for the niece relationship). M is married to N, so M is the spouse of Q's aunt/uncle. The in‑law term for a spouse's niece is "niece‑in‑law". Hence Q is the niece‑in‑law of M.

M and N share only one parent (their mother), making them half‑siblings. Their children X and Y each descend from a different parent of M and N, so X and Y share only that one common grandparent (the mother of M and N). First cousins require both grandparents in common; with only one grandparent shared, the correct term is half‑first cousins.

Aaron and Ben are brothers, so their children share the same paternal grandparents. Clara and Dana are sisters, so their children share the same maternal grandparents. Thus X and Y have both sets of grandparents in common, making them first cousins on both the father's and mother's sides. The standard term for such a relationship is “double first cousins.”

L's mother’s brother M is L’s maternal uncle. M’s daughter N is L’s first cousin. N’s son O is the child of L’s first cousin, which is defined as a first cousin once removed. Hence O is L’s first cousin once removed.

John and Mary are siblings, so they share both parents. Their children, Lisa (John's daughter) and Peter (Mary's son), each descend from one of those siblings. Therefore Lisa and Peter each have one grandparent in common, making them first cousins. The marriage of Lisa to Alan does not affect blood relations, so the correct classification is first cousin.

John’s mother’s brother Mark is John’s maternal uncle. Mark’s daughter Anna is therefore John’s first cousin. Anna’s son Ben is one generation below that cousin, making Ben the child of John’s first cousin. In kinship terminology, the child of a first cousin is a first cousin once removed. Hence Ben is John’s first cousin once removed.

S and D are half‑siblings, sharing only parent M. Their children C1 and C2 each have M as a grandparent, but their other grandparents differ.
