That child is simultaneously P’s cousin through the father’s line and through the mother’s line, i.e., a double first cousin.

C's father's sister (E) is C's paternal aunt, making E's son D C's first cousin. B is married to C, so D is the cousin of B's spouse. Standard English kinship terms limited to direct in-law relations (spouse, spouse's parents/siblings, siblings' spouses, children's spouses) do not include a term for a spouse's cousin. Thus there is no standard direct kin term for D's relation to B.

M is the child of P's paternal aunt (sister of P's father) making M a first cousin on the father's side. M is also the child of P's maternal uncle (brother of P's mother) making M a first cousin on the mother's side. Being first cousins through both parental lines defines a double first cousin. Hence the precise kinship term is double first cousin.

M and N share only a mother, making them half‑siblings. The children of siblings are first cousins. When the siblings are half‑siblings, their children share only one grandparent (the common mother) rather than two, which defines a half‑first cousin relationship. Thus X and Y are half‑first cousins, the most precise term.

M is his mother's only child, so any sister N must be a half‑sister (sharing only a father). N's son O is therefore M's half‑nephew, and O's daughter P is M's half‑grandniece (great‑niece). This specific kinship term is not among the listed options, so the relation cannot be matched to any choice.

John and Anna are siblings; Mary and Ben are siblings. Kevin is child of John and Mary. Lily is child of Anna (John's sister) and Ben (Mary's brother). Thus Lily and Kevin are children of two pairs of siblings, sharing both sets of grandparents. This makes them double first cousins.

M and N share one set of grandparents, and O and P share another set. X’s parents are M (from the first set) and O (from the second set); Y’s parents are N (from the first set) and P (from the second set). Therefore X and Y share both pairs of grandparents, making them first cousins through both parental lines—i.e., double first cousins.

A's father’s sister is A’s paternal aunt. She is B’s mother, making B the child of A’s aunt—i.e., A’s first cousin. B’s son C is the next generation down from that cousin relationship. The child of one’s first cousin is defined as a first cousin once removed. Hence C is A’s first cousin once removed.

Adam is the father of Ethan, making Ethan his son. Ethan’s child Grace is therefore Adam’s grandchild. Adam is also the brother of Ben, so Ben’s daughter Fiona is Adam’s niece. Grace is Fiona’s daughter, making Grace the child of Adam’s niece, i.e., his grandniece (also called great‑niece). Thus Grace holds both relationships: grandchild (through Ethan) and great‑niece (through Fiona).

L's father’s only sister is L’s paternal aunt; L's mother’s only brother is L’s maternal uncle. They marry each other, so their child M is simultaneously the child of L’s paternal aunt and maternal uncle. Therefore M is L’s first cousin on both the paternal and maternal sides—a double first cousin, uniquely determined.

A and B are siblings, sharing parents P1 and P2. C and D are siblings, sharing parents Q1 and Q2. A marries C, B marries D. X is child of A (descended from P1,P2) and C (descended from Q1,Q2). Y is child of B (descended from P1,P2) and D (descended from Q1,Q2). Therefore X and Y have the same four grandparents (P1,P2,Q1,Q2). Sharing both sets of grandparents makes them double first cousins, i.e., first cousins through two sibling pairs.

M and N are full siblings, sharing the same parents. O and Q are also full siblings, sharing the same parents. R is child of M (father) and O (mother); S is child of N (father) and Q (mother). Hence R and S have the same paternal grandparents (parents of M/N) and the same maternal grandparents (parents of O/Q). Sharing both sets of grandparents makes them double first cousins.

R and S are each the child of a brother (P and Q) and a sister (their wives). Their fathers are brothers, making them first cousins on the paternal side; their mothers are sisters, making them first cousins on the maternal side as well. Sharing both sets of grandparents defines double first cousins, the most precise term.

M is the child of L's paternal aunt, making M a first cousin of L on the father's side. N is the child of L's maternal uncle, making N a first cousin of L on the mother's side. The two sides of L's family are unrelated, so M and N have no common ancestor. Therefore they share no blood relation.
M's mother and her sister are siblings. The sister's child N is M's first cousin. N's child P is therefore the child of M's cousin, which by kinship terminology is a first cousin once removed.

Adam and Brian are brothers, so Ethan and Fiona are first cousins through their fathers. Clara and Diana are sisters, making Ethan and Fiona also first cousins through their mothers. Because they share both sets of grandparents, they are double first cousins, the most precise term.

M is the brother of R's mother, making M R's maternal uncle. C is M's child, so C is the child of R's uncle, i.e., R's first cousin on the maternal side. The marriage to a child of S (R's paternal aunt) does not affect the blood relationship between C and R. Therefore C's precise blood relation to R is that of a first cousin.

Mary and Tom are siblings. Mary’s child John is Tom’s nephew/niece. Emma is John’s daughter, making her Mary’s grandchild. Therefore Emma is the grandchild of Tom’s sibling, i.e., Tom’s grandniece (also called great‑niece). This matches option A.

B is sister of C's mother, making B C's maternal aunt. A, as B's son, is C's first cousin. C is D's father, so D is one generation below C. A is therefore the first cousin of D's parent, which is the definition of a first cousin once removed.

Y is X's sister, so Y's son Z is X's nephew. X's daughter W is X's child. Their child V is therefore the child of X's daughter, making V a grandchild of X. V is also the child of X's nephew, which would label V as a great‑niece, but the direct descendant term grandchild is more precise and unambiguous.

A is C's mother, so she is E's grandmother via C. Since A is B's sister, A is aunt of B's child D; as D is E's other parent, A is great‑aunt of E via D. Both relations hold simultaneously, giving a double relationship.

R's mother has one brother S, making S R's maternal uncle. S's only child T is R's first cousin. T's only child U is the child of R's cousin, which is defined as a first cousin once removed. No alternative kinship fits given the constraints, so the relation is uniquely determined.

A's father P and B's father Q are brothers, so A and B share paternal grandparents. A's mother R and B's mother S are sisters, so they also share maternal grandparents. Thus they share both sets of grandparents, which defines double first cousins – a more specific term than just first cousins. No half‑relationship exists because the sibling links are full, not half, and they are not second cousins.

A and B are half‑siblings, sharing only their mother. Their children X and Y each have that mother as a grandparent, but have different other grandparents. Therefore X and Y share exactly one grandparent, making them half‑first cousins.

M is the child of N's paternal aunt (the only sister of N's father) and also the child of N's maternal uncle (the only brother of N's mother). Thus M's parents are the sister of N's father and the brother of N's mother—two siblings from opposite sides marrying each other. Their offspring are first cousins to N through both the paternal and maternal lines, i.e., double first cousins.

Mx (X's mother) and Fy (Y's father) are siblings, so they share the same parents (the paternal grandparents of Y and maternal grandparents of X). Likewise Fx (X's father) and My (Y's mother) are siblings, sharing another set of parents (the maternal grandparents of Y and paternal grandparents of X). Therefore X and Y each receive one set of grandparents from Mx/Fy and another set from Fx/My, meaning they share both sets of grandparents. This is the definition of double first cousins, who are first cousins through both parental lines.

N's spouse is P. Q is P's sister, making Q N's spouse's sibling, which is the standard term sister‑in‑law. Although Q also marries N's nephew, that relation (niece‑in‑law) is not a direct standard term under the allowed categories, whereas sister‑in‑law is directly permitted.

A is married to B. B’s brother C is A’s brother‑in‑law. C’s wife D is A’s sister‑in‑law. E is D’s brother, i.e., the sibling of A’s sister‑in‑law. Standard English kinship terms do not include a direct term for the sibling of a sister‑in‑law; the relationship exists only through an affinal chain.

M's mother’s brother is M’s maternal uncle; his daughter A is M’s first cousin. Similarly, M’s father’s sister is M’s paternal aunt; her son B is also M’s first cousin. A and B (both first cousins of M) have a child C. The child of your first cousin is your first cousin once removed. Since M is a first cousin to both parents of C, M is a first cousin once removed to C.

M is mother of N and O, so N and O are siblings. O's child R is therefore the child of N's sibling, which makes R N's niece or nephew. The marriage of O to Q and P's relation to N do not change this direct blood line. Hence the correct kinship term is niece/nephew.

X and Y are children of two sibling pairs: Adam and Brian are brothers, and Clara and Diana are sisters. Thus X and Y are first cousins through their fathers and also first cousins through their mothers, sharing both sets of grandparents. This makes them double first cousins, the most precise term.

Emma and Fiona share only one parent (their mother), making them half‑siblings. Their respective children, Greg and Hannah, each descend from one of these half‑siblings. Consequently, Greg and Hannah share a single grandparent (the common mother) but not both grandparents. This relationship is defined as half‑first cousins, i.e., cousins who share only one grandparent. The other options do not fit: they are not full first cousins, not siblings, and the relationship is determinable.

M and N share one parent (their mother) and are therefore half‑siblings. Their respective children, A and B, are one generation removed from M and N. In kinship terminology, the children of full siblings are first cousins. When the siblings are half‑siblings, their children are termed half‑cousins, i.e., half‑first cousins. This is the most precise standard English term; "first cousins" would be less specific, and the relationship is determinable.

M and N share only a mother, making them half‑siblings. Their respective children, P and Q, are therefore the offspring of half‑siblings. Children of full siblings are first cousins; children of half‑siblings are half‑first cousins. No double‑cousin situation arises because there is no intermarriage between the two families beyond the single half‑sibling link.

L and S are siblings. L's daughter D is thus S's niece. S's son T is D's first cousin (children of siblings). M is D's child and N is T's child. Children of first cousins are second cousins. Therefore M and N are second cousins.

Emma and Liam are half‑siblings, sharing only one parent (their mother). Their children, Noah and Zoe, therefore share only that one grandparent (the mother of Emma and Liam). Cousins who share both grandparents are first cousins; sharing just one grandparent makes them half‑first cousins. Hence the precise term is half‑first cousins.

M and N are maternal half‑siblings, sharing only their mother. That mother is a grandparent of both X (through M) and Y (through N). Because X and Y’s parents are half‑siblings, X and Y share only one grandparent, not the full set of grandparents required for ordinary first cousins. The correct term for children of half‑siblings is “half‑first cousins.” Hence the most precise relation is half‑first cousins.

M and N are siblings, so their children O and R are first cousins. Q is R's child, making Q one generation below R. Therefore O and Q are first cousins separated by one generation, i.e., first cousins once removed.

N's father has one sibling; that sibling's child is N's paternal first cousin. Likewise, N's mother has one sibling; that sibling's child is N's maternal first cousin. M is described as the child of both the father's sibling and the mother's sibling, meaning the two siblings are married to each other. Hence M is simultaneously N's first cousin on both parental sides, which is the definition of a double first cousin.

John and Mary are siblings, so Mary's child Bob is John's nephew. Bob marries Carol, who is Alice's sibling; Alice is John's spouse, making Carol John's sister‑in‑law. Their child Dave is the child of John's nephew, which makes Dave John's grandnephew (great‑nephew), a standard kinship term.

John's sister Mary has daughter Lily, making Lily John's niece. John’s brother David has son Tom, making Tom John's nephew. Lily and Tom are first cousins (children of siblings) who marry and have Sam. Sam is therefore the child of John’s niece (Lily) and nephew (Tom). The child of a niece or nephew is called a grandniece or grandnephew (also great‑niece/nephew). This matches option A.

M and N are siblings, so their children O and P are first cousins. O (M's daughter) and P (N's son) marry and have child Q. Since Q is the child of P, who is N's son, Q is N's grandchild. No other listed term fits this direct descent relationship.

Mary and Peter are siblings, so Peter is the uncle of Mary's children John and Anna. Lisa, Peter's daughter, is therefore a first cousin of Anna. Tom is Anna's son, making him the child of Lisa's first cousin. The relationship between a person and the child of their first cousin is "first cousin once removed." Hence Lisa is Tom's first cousin once removed.

L's father’s sister is L’s paternal aunt; L's mother’s brother is L’s maternal uncle. Those two relatives marry and have a child M. M is therefore the child of L’s aunt on the father's side and the child of L’s uncle on the mother’s side, making M a first cousin to L on both sides (a double first cousin). The appropriate kinship term is first cousin.

Alice's paternal aunt is her father's sister. Evelyn is the daughter of that aunt, making Evelyn the child of Alice's father's sibling. Children of siblings are first cousins, so Evelyn is Alice's first cousin. Other marriage links do not change this blood relationship.

John and Mary share only one parent, making them half‑siblings. Their children (Alice and Bob) are thus the offspring of half‑siblings. In kinship terminology, the children of full siblings are first cousins; when the siblings are half‑siblings, their children are called half‑first cousins. This is the most precise standard term.

M and N share only one parent, making them half‑siblings. First cousins are the children of full siblings. Since M and N are not full siblings, their children X and Y are not full first cousins. The appropriate term distinguishes the half‑sibling relationship of their parents, yielding "half‑first cousins" (also called half‑cousins). This is the most precise standard kinship term.

S is R's paternal aunt's daughter, making S R's first cousin. T is R's maternal uncle's son, also a first cousin. C is the child of S and T. The child of one's first cousin is defined as a first cousin once removed (one generation apart). No half‑blood or second‑cousin relationship exists, and a standard term does apply.

George and Helen share only their mother, making them half‑siblings. Their children each inherit that one shared grandparent, so Alan and Beth share a single grandparent rather than both. Hence they are half‑first cousins.

M and N are full siblings; P and Q are full siblings. A's parents are M (sibling of N) and Q (sibling of P). B's parents are N and P. Therefore A and B are first cousins through their fathers (M and N) and also first cousins through their mothers (Q and P). Sharing both sets of grandparents makes them double first cousins, which is more specific than plain first cousins.

John and Mark are brothers, so their parents are the paternal grandparents of both Carl and Dana. Anna and Beth are sisters, so their parents are the maternal grandparents of both children. Thus Carl and Dana share both sets of grandparents, making them first cousins through both the father’s side and the mother’s side. The precise term for such a relationship is double first cousins.

My father's sister's only son is my paternal first cousin. His child M is therefore my first cousin once removed. Similarly, my mother's brother's only daughter is my maternal first cousin, and her child is also my first cousin once removed. Both descriptions refer to the same individual, so M is uniquely identified as my first cousin once removed.

Adam and Brian are brothers; Clara and Diana are sisters. Their children Ethan and Fiona are therefore double first cousins (they share both paternal and maternal grandparents). Ethan Jr. and Fiona Jr. are the children of these double first cousins. Children of first cousins are second cousins; because the parent relationship is double, the offspring share both sets of great‑grandparents, making them double second cousins. Hence the precise relation is double second cousins.

John is Mary's biological son from her first marriage; Lisa is Robert's biological daughter from his previous marriage. After Mary and Robert marry, each becomes the other's step‑parent, making John and Lisa step‑siblings. They share no blood relation and no adoption occurred, so the appropriate term is step‑sibling.

A and B are brothers, so their children X and Y share the same paternal grandparents. C and D are sisters, so X and Y also share the same maternal grandparents. Since X and Y have both sets of grandparents in common, they are first cousins on the father's side and also first cousins on the mother's side. The precise term for cousins who share both parental lineages is “double first cousins.”

A and B are half‑siblings, sharing only father M. Their children C (of A) and D (of B) therefore share a single grandparent (M) but not the other grandparent. Children of half‑siblings are called half‑first cousins, as they are first cousins through one common grandparent only. No other ties affect this relationship.

R is the child of T's maternal uncle (the only brother of T’s mother), making R a first cousin on the mother’s side. R is also described as the sibling of the child of T's paternal aunt (the child of T’s father’s sister). Being a sibling means they share the same parents, so R must also be the child of T’s paternal aunt. This occurs when T’s maternal uncle marries T’s paternal aunt, making R the offspring of both, i.e., a child of two siblings from opposite sides. Such a person is a double first cousin of T.

D is the biological mother of E, who is one of F's parents. Therefore D is F's maternal grandmother, making F the grandchild of D. No step or in‑law qualifier is needed because the direct parent‑child link exists through E.

Susan's brother Tom is married to Emma. The spouse of one's sibling is the sibling's sister- or brother-in-law. Therefore Emma is Susan's sister-in-law. Since 'sister‑in‑law' is not among the given options, none of the listed terms correctly describe the relationship.

X's father Aaron and Y's father Ben are brothers, making X and Y first cousins on their paternal side. Likewise, X's mother Clara and Y's mother Dana are sisters, making X and Y first cousins on their maternal side. Because they are first cousins through both parents, they are double first cousins, not half‑first or second cousins.

M and N are siblings (family A) and S and T are siblings (family B). M marries S and N marries T. Their children X (M+S) and Y (N+T) each have the same two sets of grandparents: the parents of M/N and the parents of S/T. Sharing both sets of grandparents defines double first cousins, distinct from ordinary first cousins (one set), half‑first cousins (one grandparent), or second cousins (great‑grandparents).

M is sibling of S, and W is sibling of B. C is child of M and W; D is child of S and B. Thus C’s father is sibling of D’s mother, and C’s mother is sibling of D’s father. They are the children of two distinct sibling pairs, sharing both sets of grandparents. This makes them double first cousins, the most specific term.

M and N are siblings. Their children R (of M) and S (of N) are first cousins. T is S's child, one generation below S. Therefore R is one generation above T but shares the same ancestral level as T's grandparent, making R a first cousin once removed to T.

John and Mark are full brothers, so Sam and Lily share the same paternal grandparents. Alice and Beth are full sisters, so Sam and Lily also share the same maternal grandparents. Sharing both sets of grandparents makes them first cousins on both sides, i.e., double first cousins, not half or second cousins.

M and N are brothers, so X and Y share the same paternal grandparents. A and B are sisters, so X and Y also share the same maternal grandparents. Consequently X and Y are first cousins through both parents, i.e., double first cousins, not half or unrelated.

M is the sole child of his father, but his father has a sister. That sister is M's paternal aunt. Her child Q is M's first cousin. P is the child of M (and N). The child of one's first cousin is a first cousin once removed. Therefore Q is P's first cousin once removed.

M and N share the same parents, and X and Y share the same parents. A’s father (M) is sibling of B’s father (N), and A’s mother (X) is sibling of B’s mother (Y). Thus A and B are first cousins through both paternal and maternal lines, i.e., double first cousins.

Alex is child of John and Mary. Emma is child of Lisa (John's sister) and Tom (Mary's brother). Lisa and John share the same parents, and Tom and Mary share the same parents. Therefore Alex and Emma share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins, the precise term.

Emma and Liam are siblings; Noah and Grace are siblings. Emma (child of grandparents P1) marries Noah (child of grandparents P2) producing Ava. Liam (child of P1) marries Grace (child of P2) producing Ben. Ava’s maternal grandparents are P1 and paternal grandparents are P2; Ben’s paternal grandparents are P1 and maternal grandparents are P2. Thus Ava and Ben share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins.

U is X's maternal uncle because he is the brother of X's mother. Therefore V, U's daughter, is X's first cousin. Y, being V's son, is one generation below that cousin, making Y X's first cousin once removed. The relationships are uniquely defined given standard kinship rules.

N’s father’s sister is N’s paternal aunt; N’s mother’s brother is N’s maternal uncle. They marry and have M. M is the child of N’s paternal aunt, making M a first cousin to N on the father’s side, and also the child of N’s maternal uncle, making M a first cousin on the mother’s side. Because M is first cousin through both parental lines, M and N are double first cousins.

L is M's mother. K is L's brother, making K M's maternal uncle. N is K's son, so N is the child of M's uncle. In kinship terms, the child of one's aunt or uncle is a first cousin. Therefore N is M's first cousin.

L and K are half‑siblings, sharing only one parent. Their children R and S therefore share only one grandparent (the common father of L and K). First cousins share both grandparents; when only one grandparent is common, the relationship is termed half‑first cousins. Hence the most precise term is half‑first cousins.

N's father has one sister (paternal aunt). N's mother has one brother (maternal uncle). The puzzle says the child of that sister and the child of that brother are the same person, M. Therefore M is the child of N's paternal aunt and also the child of N's maternal uncle, meaning the aunt and uncle are married and have a shared child. Consequently M is N's first cousin through the father and also N's first cousin through the mother, making M a double first cousin.

Q is the sister of P, who is married to N (M's daughter). Thus Q is N's sister‑in‑law. For M, Q is the sibling of a child’s spouse, which English kinship does not give a specific term; she is not a spouse, child, parent, or sibling of M, nor a direct in‑law such as daughter‑in‑law or niece‑in‑law. Therefore no standard direct relation applies.

A and B are siblings. Their children, C (child of A) and D (child of B), are first cousins. E is D's child, one generation below D. Therefore E is one generation removed from C, making the precise relation a first cousin once removed.

Mia and Noah share both parents, making them full siblings. Their respective children, Zoe (Mia's daughter) and Ryan (Noah's son), are therefore the children of two full siblings. This relationship defines first cousins. There is no half‑relationship because the sibling link is not half, and no extra generational gap to make second cousins. Hence the precise kinship is first cousins.

John’s mother Mary’s sister Linda is John’s maternal aunt. Linda’s husband Peter is John’s uncle‑in‑law (sibling’s spouse). Victor is Peter’s brother, i.e., the brother of John’s uncle‑in‑law. This makes Victor the brother of an uncle‑by‑marriage, which has no direct term in standard kinship (the allowed in‑law relations do not cover a sibling of a sibling’s spouse). Therefore Victor has no standard direct relation to John.

A and B are half‑siblings, sharing only one parent. Their children X and Y are the offspring of half‑siblings. By definition, children of siblings are first cousins; when the sibling relationship is half, the cousins are termed half‑first cousins. Therefore the most precise standard term is half‑first cousins.

Y’s father’s only sister is Y’s paternal aunt; her only child is X. Y’s mother’s only brother is Y’s maternal uncle; his only child is also X. Therefore X is the child of Y’s paternal aunt and Y’s maternal uncle, meaning those two siblings are married and have a child together. X is thus both a child of a paternal aunt and a child of a maternal uncle, making X a first cousin to Y on the father’s side and also a first cousin on the mother’s side. Being first cousins through both parental lines defines a double first cousin.

A is X's mother, so A's brother B is X's maternal uncle. B's daughter C is therefore X's first cousin. C's son D is the child of X's cousin, which makes D X's first cousin once removed according to standard kinship terminology.

M and N are brothers, so they share the same paternal grandparents. O and Q are sisters, sharing the same maternal grandparents. X is the child of M (brother) and O (sister); Y is the child of N (brother) and Q (sister). Thus X and Y have both sets of grandparents in common, making them first cousins through both parents. This situation is called double first cousins, the most specific term for cousins who share both paternal and maternal grandparents.

M and N are siblings, sharing one pair of grandparents. O and Q are another set of siblings, sharing a different pair of grandparents. Each child (A and B) inherits one grandparent pair from the M/N side and the other from the O/Q side. Thus A and B share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins, the most precise term.

M’s mother’s brother is M’s maternal uncle. He is married to N’s sister, making N’s sister M’s aunt by marriage. N is the sibling of that aunt‑in‑law. English kinship terminology has no standard term for the sibling of an aunt‑by‑marriage; it is purely an affinal connection with no direct blood or marital label. Therefore the correct choice is that there is no standard direct relation.

Tom is Mike's father, so Mike's child Nina is Tom's grandchild. Tom is also Sue's brother; Sue is Nina's mother, making Nina Tom's niece (or nephew). Hence Nina simultaneously holds both relationships to Tom.

A's mother has exactly one brother; his child (X) is the child of A's maternal uncle, which is A's first cousin. A's father has exactly one sister; her child (Y) is the child of A's paternal aunt, also A's first cousin. Thus whichever person is chosen as Z, Z is a first cousin of A. The relationship is uniquely determined.

Mary and Michael are siblings of John, making them brother and sister to each other. Their children, Peter (Mary's son) and Anna (Michael's daughter), are thus the children of two siblings. Children of siblings are first cousins.

P and R are brothers, sharing the same parents, and Q and S are sisters, also sharing the same parents. M is the child of P and Q, while N is the child of R and S. Because each child’s father is a brother of the other’s father and each child’s mother is a sister of the other’s mother, M and N share both sets of grandparents. This makes them first cousins on both the paternal and maternal sides, i.e., double first cousins.
Mary is Peter's mother. Peter and Susan's child Emma is therefore Mary's direct descendant: Emma is the daughter of Mary's son, making Emma Mary's granddaughter. No other kinship term fits.

Lisa is Mary's sister. Since Mary is John's spouse, Mary's sibling is John's sister‑in‑law by the definition that includes a spouse's siblings. Although Lisa is also Tom's wife and Tom is John's cousin, the allowed in‑law categories do not include a cousin's spouse, so "cousin‑in‑law" is not a standard term here. Therefore the correct standard relation is sister‑in‑law.

L is parent of D; D is mother of M, so M is L's grandchild. L's sister S is mother of N; N is parent of O, making O S's grandchild. L and S are sisters, sharing both parents, so D and N are first cousins. The children of first cousins (M and O) are second cousins, sharing great‑grandparents. No half‑sibling relationship is indicated, so the correct term is second cousins.

E's mother is the sister of F's father, making E's mother and F's father siblings. Therefore E and F are children of siblings, i.e., first cousins. G is the child of F, so G is the child of E's first cousin, which is the definition of a first cousin once removed.

Y is X's mother. Y's brother Z is X's maternal uncle. Z's daughter W is therefore X's first cousin (children of siblings). V is W's son, i.e., the child of X's cousin. In kinship terms, the child of a cousin is a first cousin once removed. No other relationship fits, so the relation is uniquely determined as first cousin once removed.

M and N are siblings; O and P are siblings. M marries O, N marries P. Their children X (M·O) and Y (N·P) each have the same two sets of grandparents: the parents of M/N and the parents of O/P. Sharing both sets of grandparents makes X and Y double first cousins, i.e., first cousins through both parental lines.

John and Mary are siblings. Their children Paul (John's son) and Lisa (Mary's daughter) are first cousins. Emma is Lisa's daughter, one generation below Lisa. Therefore Emma is the child of Paul's first cousin, making Paul and Emma first cousins once removed. This matches option B.

M and N are siblings, sharing a set of parents. X and Y are siblings, sharing another set of parents. A’s parents are M (child of the first set) and X (child of the second set); B’s parents are N (child of the first set) and Y (child of the second set). Therefore A and B share both sets of grandparents, making them cousins through two sibling connections. The specific term for cousins who share both pairs of grandparents is double first cousins, which is more precise than plain first cousins or any other listed category.

M is the child of P's maternal aunt, and N is the child of P's paternal uncle. The aunt (mother's sister) and the uncle (father's brother) are not blood‑related to each other; they are linked only through marriage to P's parents. Therefore M and N share no common ancestor, so there is no standard blood kinship term for their relationship.

X is the child of Y's father's only sister, making X a child of Y's paternal aunt – a first cousin of Y. Z is the child of Y's mother's only brother, making Z a child of Y's maternal uncle – also a first cousin of Y. The paternal aunt and maternal uncle are unrelated, as they belong to different parental lines. Consequently X and Z share no common grandparent or ancestor, so they have no blood relation. They are not siblings, first cousins, or half‑cousins.

X's mother is sister of Y's father, so they share the same maternal grandparents. X's father is brother of Y's mother, so they share the same paternal grandparents. Thus X and Y each have both sets of grandparents in common, each set via a different parent. This is exactly the definition of double first cousins (children of two pairs of siblings). No other relationship fits, so the correct term is double first cousins.

Alice and Bob are siblings, so their children Carol and Dave are first cousins. Eve is Carol's child, placing her one generation below Carol. A first cousin's child is a first cousin once removed relative to the original cousin, so Eve and Dave are first cousins once removed.

M and N are full siblings, as are O and P. X's parents are M (family A) and O (family B); Y's parents are N (family A) and P (family B). Therefore X and Y each have the same four grandparents: the parents of M/N and the parents of O/P. Sharing both sets of grandparents makes them double first cousins, i.e., first cousins through both parental lines.

A and B are full brothers; C and D are full sisters. E is child of A (brother) and C (sister). F is child of B (the other brother) and D (the other sister). Therefore E and F share both paternal grandparents (parents of A and B) and maternal grandparents (parents of C and D). Sharing both sets of grandparents makes them double first cousins, the most precise term.

Susan is Lisa's niece (daughter of Lisa's brother Tom). Lisa is John’s spouse, so Susan is the daughter of John’s brother‑in‑law. The allowed in‑law terms include spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, and children’s spouses, but do not include a brother‑in‑law’s child. Therefore there is no standard direct kinship term under the given constraints; the relation exists only via an affinal chain.

John is Peter's father, so Kevin (Peter's child) is John’s grandson. John is also Mary's brother, making Mary’s daughter Susan John’s niece. Kevin, as Susan’s child, is the child of John’s niece, which is termed a great‑nephew (or grandnephew). Hence Kevin fits both definitions simultaneously.

C is A's brother, so any child of C is A's niece/nephew by blood. D, being B's sister, adds no blood connection to A. Therefore E, the child of C and D, is the child of A's sibling, making E A's niece/nephew.

John, Tom, and Mary share the same parents, making them full siblings. Mary’s son Paul is therefore the grandchild of those parents. Tom’s daughter Lisa is also a grandchild of the same parents, as Tom is another child of them. Since Paul and Lisa share both grandparents, they are first cousins.

L’s mother is the sister of K’s father, making L’s mother an aunt of K through K’s paternal line. Likewise, K’s mother is the sister of L’s father, making K’s mother an aunt of L through L’s paternal line. Thus two siblings from one family married two siblings from another family, causing L and K to share both sets of grandparents. This is the definition of double first cousins.

A and C are brothers, sharing the same parents, and B and D are sisters, also sharing the same parents. X is the child of A (father) and B (mother); Y is the child of C (father) and D (mother). Therefore X and Y are first cousins through their fathers (A and C) and also first cousins through their mothers (B and D). Having two independent lines of first‑cousin relationship makes them double first cousins, the most specific standard term.

R is married to S. S's mother’s brother T is S’s maternal uncle, making T R’s uncle‑in‑law. T’s spouse U is R’s aunt‑in‑law. V is U’s sister, i.e., the sister of R’s aunt‑in‑law. English kinship terminology does not have a standard direct term for the sister of an aunt‑in‑law; it is merely an affinal link through multiple marriages. Therefore V has no standard direct relation to R.

John and Michael share both parents, making them full brothers. Mary is their sister, so she is Michael's sibling. Peter is Mary's son, making Michael his maternal uncle. Susan is Michael's daughter, so she is the child of Peter's uncle. Children of siblings are first cousins, so Peter and Susan are first cousins.

Carl's father Adam and Dana's father Brian are brothers, making Carl and Dana paternal first cousins. Likewise, Carl's mother Anna and Dana's mother Beth are sisters, making them maternal first cousins. Because they are first cousins through both parents, they share both sets of grandparents, which is precisely described as double first cousins.

M and N are full siblings, as are P and Q. X's parents are M (from family A) and P (family B); Y's parents are N (family A) and Q (family B). Therefore X and Y each have the same two sets of grandparents: the parents of M/N and the parents of P/Q. Sharing both sets of grandparents makes them first cousins through both parental lines, i.e., double first cousins, which is the most specific term.

A's mother and B's mother are sisters, making A and B first cousins. B's child is C, so A is one generation above C relative to the cousin relationship, which defines a first cousin once removed. The paternal‑side cousin D married C, but marriage does not create blood ties, so it does not affect the relationship.

Y is X's mother. Y's brother Z is X's maternal uncle. Z's daughter W is therefore X's first cousin. W's son V is the child of X's first cousin, making V X's first cousin once removed. The relation is uniquely determined.

M is parent of S, making S's child C M's grandchild. M is also aunt/uncle of D, so D's child C would be M's great‑niece/nephew, a more distant relation. The closest and most precise standard term is therefore "grandchild".

Ethan's father Adam and Fiona's father Brian are brothers, making them first cousins through the paternal line. Ethan's mother Clara and Fiona's mother Diana are sisters, also making them first cousins through the maternal line. Because they share both sets of grandparents (paternal and maternal), they are double first cousins.

Robert is Alex’s father. Before marrying Alex’s mother, Robert fathered Kate, making Kate Alex’s half‑sister. Alex’s daughter Mia therefore regards Kate as the sister of her parent, but because the sibling relationship is half‑blood, Kate is Mia’s half‑aunt. The option that matches this specific relation is ‘Half-aunt.’

Adam's son Carl is Ethan's father, making Ethan Adam's grandson. Dana, Ethan's mother, is Brian's daughter, i.e., Adam's niece; thus Ethan is also the child of Adam's niece, making him Adam's grandnephew. Both relations hold simultaneously, and the only option that captures this dual relationship is the combined term "Grandson‑nephew (double relation)".

John and Michael are brothers. John’s daughter Emma is Michael’s niece; Michael’s son David is John’s nephew. Emma and David are first cousins who marry and have Lily. Since David is Michael’s son, Lily is Michael’s direct descendant – his granddaughter. Therefore Michael is Lily’s grandfather.

A is Y's paternal aunt (father's sister) and B is Y's maternal uncle (mother's brother). Their child X is therefore Y's first cousin through the father's side (child of the father's sister) and also Y's first cousin through the mother's side (child of the mother's brother). Since X occupies both cousin positions simultaneously, X is a double first cousin of Y. No half‑relationship exists because A and B are full siblings of Y's parents and are not blood‑related to each other.

Ethan's father Adam and Fiona's father Brian are brothers, giving them the same paternal grandparents. Ethan's mother Clara and Fiona's mother Diana are sisters, giving them the same maternal grandparents. Thus Ethan and Fiona share both sets of grandparents, making them first cousins through both parental lines, i.e., double first cousins.

Mary's brother Tom is Emma's maternal uncle; John’s sister Lisa is Emma's paternal aunt. Alex is the child of Tom and Lisa, so he is the child of Emma's maternal uncle and paternal aunt. Consequently Alex and Emma share both sets of grandparents (Mary’s parents and John’s parents), making them first cousins on both sides – i.e., double first cousins.

M and N are siblings; O and P are siblings. Their marriages create two sibling couples, so X (child of M+O) and Y (child of N+P) share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins. The children of first cousins are second cousins; likewise, the children of double first cousins share both sets of great‑grandparents, thus they are double second cousins. Therefore Z and W are double second cousins.

A and B are full brothers, sharing the same parents. C and D are full sisters, also sharing the same parents. X is the child of A (father) and C (mother); Y is the child of B (father) and D (mother). Because A and B have the same parents, X and Y are first cousins on their fathers' side. Likewise, because C and D have the same parents, X and Y are first cousins on their mothers' side. Sharing both sets of grandparents makes them double first cousins, not half or second cousins.

M and N are siblings, so their children O and P are first cousins (they share grandparents). Q is O's child and R is P's child. Children of first cousins share the same great‑grandparents (the parents of M and N), which defines a second‑cousin relationship. No closer kinship term applies.

A and B are half‑siblings, sharing only mother M. Their children X and Y therefore share only one grandparent (M). Cousins who share a single grandparent are termed half‑first cousins. They are in the same generation, so no "removed" applies. Hence the precise term is half‑first cousins.

Mary and Michael are siblings, sharing the same parents. Peter is Mary's son, and Lisa is Michael's daughter. Children of siblings are first cousins. No other family links alter this relationship, so Peter and Lisa are first cousins.

Adam and Brian are brothers; Clara and Diana are sisters. Their children Ethan and Felix therefore share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins. Lily and Maya are the next generation, each being the child of one of those double first cousins. Children of first cousins are second cousins; because the parents are double first cousins, Lily and Maya share both sets of great‑grandparents, giving them the status of double second cousins.

A's mother’s brother is A's maternal uncle; his daughter X is A's first cousin. A's father's sister is A's paternal aunt; her son Y is also A's first cousin. Since Z is either X or Y, Z is always A's first cousin, making the relationship uniquely determined as a first cousin.

L's mother and S are sisters, making S L's maternal aunt. L's father and B are brothers, making B L's paternal uncle. S and B's child M is therefore the child of L's maternal aunt (first‑cousin relationship) and also the child of L's paternal uncle (another first‑cousin relationship). M is thus L's first cousin on both sides, i.e., a double first cousin.
M's mother’s brother is M’s maternal uncle. The child of an uncle (or aunt) is a first cousin to the niece/nephew. Since L is the child of M’s maternal uncle, L is M’s first cousin.

M and N are full siblings, both children of L. A is M's child and B is N's child. Children of siblings are first cousins. There is no shared second set of grandparents (double) nor only one shared grandparent (half), so the precise term is first cousins.

M and N are full siblings, and O and P are full siblings. X is child of M (sibling of N) and O (sibling of P). Y is child of N and P. Therefore X and Y each have the same two sets of grandparents: the parents of M/N and the parents of O/P. Sharing both grandparent pairs makes them double first cousins, the most specific term among the choices.

L's mother has one brother, making that brother L's maternal uncle. His only child K is therefore L's maternal first cousin. Similarly, L's father has one brother, making that brother L's paternal uncle, and his only child M is L's paternal first cousin. Thus whether X is K or M, X is a first cousin of L.

L's father and K are siblings (the father's sister). K's child R is therefore the child of L's paternal aunt, making R and L the children of two siblings. In standard kinship, children of siblings are first cousins. No half‑sibling or generational offset is indicated, so the relation is a direct first cousin.

R's mother has a single brother (maternal uncle). X is that brother's child, making X a maternal first cousin. R's father has a single sister (paternal aunt). X is also that sister's child, making X a paternal first cousin. The only way X can satisfy both conditions is if the maternal uncle and paternal aunt are a married couple, producing a double cousin. Hence X is R's cousin.

Anna is Tom's paternal uncle's daughter, making her Tom's first cousin. Ben is Tom's maternal aunt's son, also Tom's first cousin. Their marriage produces Claire, who is the child of Tom's first cousin on both sides. A child of one's first cousin is a first cousin once removed. Since both parental lines give the same degree, the precise term is "first cousin once removed."

M is R's maternal uncle, so his daughter A is R's first cousin. N is R's paternal aunt, so her son B is also R's first cousin. A and B have a child C. The child of a first cousin is one generation apart from the original cousin, making C a first cousin once removed of R (both via A and via B). No half‑relationship or second‑cousin link exists.

John and Lily share the same father but have different mothers, making them half‑siblings. The only option that captures a half‑sibling relationship is "Half‑sister," which correctly describes Lily's relation to John.

M is the child of N's paternal aunt (the father's only sister) and also the child of N's maternal uncle (the mother's only brother). For M to have both parents, those two relatives must be married to each other (monogamy, no adoption). Their child is therefore a first cousin of N through the father's side and also a first cousin through the mother's side, making M a double first cousin of N.

John, Mary, and Tom are siblings sharing both parents. Mary’s son Peter is the child of one sibling; Tom’s daughter Linda is the child of another sibling. Children of two full siblings are first cousins. No half‑sibling relationship exists, so they are not half first cousins, nor are they more distant. The relation is determinable as first cousins.

X is the sole brother of Y's father, making X Y's paternal uncle. Z, as X's child, is Y's first cousin. W, being Z's child, is the child of Y's cousin, which is the definition of a first cousin once removed. The relationship is uniquely determined by the given constraints.

X’s mother is the sister of Y’s father, so they share one set of grandparents. X’s father is the brother of Y’s mother, giving a second shared set of grandparents. Thus X and Y are the children of two distinct sibling pairs, meaning they share both parental lineages. This is precisely the definition of double first cousins, not merely first cousins or half‑first cousins.

X and Y are brothers; S1 and S2 are sisters. Their children A and B are double first cousins (they share both sets of grandparents). The next generation, C (child of A) and D (child of B), therefore share both sets of great‑grandparents, making them double second cousins. This matches option D.

Linda is Mary's sister, making her John’s aunt. Her son Paul is therefore John’s first cousin. Emma is Paul’s daughter, i.e., the child of John’s first cousin. The child of a first cousin is a first cousin once removed, not a grandniece (which would require a sibling’s descendant). Hence Emma is John’s first cousin once removed.

R's mother has exactly one brother; his child P is the offspring of R's maternal uncle, making P R's first cousin on the mother's side. Similarly, R's father has exactly one brother; his child Q is the offspring of R's paternal uncle, making Q R's first cousin on the father's side. The two uncles are distinct (parents are not siblings), so P and Q are each first cousins to R. Selecting either yields the same kinship term: first cousin.

J’s mother’s brother is J’s maternal uncle. His son is J’s first cousin. I is defined as the child of that son, i.e., the child of J’s first cousin. The child of a first cousin is a first cousin once removed. Therefore I is J’s first cousin once removed.

Michael is Anna's father, making him Lily's maternal grandfather, i.e., Lily is Michael's granddaughter. Michael is also John’s brother, and John is Lily's father, so Michael is Lily's paternal uncle, making Lily his niece. Both relations apply, and there is no single standard term that combines them, so the correct choice is that Lily is both granddaughter and niece.

N's mother and O are siblings, making O N's maternal uncle. O's daughter P is therefore N's first cousin. M is N's spouse, so P is the spouse's cousin. English kinship has no standard direct term for a spouse's cousin; it is an affinal relation (cousin‑in‑law). Hence the correct choice is that there is no standard direct kinship term.

Lily's father Peter is Mary's brother, making Mary's parents Lily's paternal grandparents. Lily's mother Anna is John's sister, making John's parents Lily's maternal grandparents. Mark's parents are John and Mary, so his paternal grandparents are John's parents (Lily's maternal grandparents) and his maternal grandparents are Mary's parents (Lily's paternal grandparents). Thus Lily and Mark share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins.

Ethan's father Adam and Fiona's father Brian are brothers, making Ethan and Fiona first cousins on their paternal side. Their mothers Clara and Diana are sisters, making them first cousins on their maternal side as well. Because they are first cousins through both parents, they share both sets of grandparents, which is the definition of double first cousins.

John and Mary are siblings, making their children Paul (John's son) and Linda (Mary's daughter) first cousins. Kevin is Linda's son, placing him one generation below Paul. A child of your cousin is your first cousin once removed, reflecting the one‑generation difference.

A and B are siblings, so their children C and D are first cousins (they share the same grandparents). E is C's child and F is D's child. Children of first cousins share the same great‑grandparents, making them second cousins. Therefore E and F are second cousins.

M and N are siblings, sharing one set of grandparents. O and Q are also siblings, sharing another set of grandparents. M marries O and N marries Q, so their children X and Y each have one parent from each sibling pair. Consequently X and Y share both sets of grandparents, making them first cousins through both parents, i.e., double first cousins.

John's maternal uncle's daughter is Emily, making Emily John's first cousin on his mother's side. John's paternal aunt's son is Mark, making Mark John's first cousin on his father's side. If Emily and Mark are the same individual, that person is the child of both John’s maternal uncle and paternal aunt, meaning the two siblings (the uncle and aunt) married each other. Consequently, the person is a first cousin to John through both parental lines, i.e., a double first cousin.

John and Mary are siblings. Mary's son Peter is John's nephew. John’s son Michael is Peter’s first cousin (children of siblings). Lisa is Michael’s daughter, making her Peter’s cousin's child. A child of one's first cousin is a first cousin once removed. Hence Peter and Lisa are first cousins once removed.

X’s mother is the sister of Y’s father, making her Y’s paternal aunt; X’s father is the brother of Y’s mother, making him Y’s maternal uncle. Hence X’s parents are respectively the siblings of Y’s parents on both sides, meaning X and Y share both sets of grandparents. This is the definition of double first cousins.

Alex and Brian are full brothers, sharing both paternal grandparents. Clara and Diana are full sisters, sharing both maternal grandparents. Ethan’s father is Alex and mother is Clara; Felix’s father is Brian and mother is Diana. Consequently, Ethan and Felix have the same paternal grandparents (through their fathers) and the same maternal grandparents (through their mothers). Sharing both sets of grandparents makes them double first cousins, not merely first cousins or any half‑cousin variant.

R's mother (M) has a brother U, making U R's maternal uncle. S is U's daughter, so she is the child of R's uncle. In standard kinship, the child of one's uncle or aunt is a first cousin. Therefore S is R's first cousin.

John's siblings are Tom and Mary. Mary's son Peter is John's nephew; Tom's daughter Sarah is John's niece. Peter and Sarah (John's nephew and niece) are first cousins who have a child, Emma. The child of a niece or nephew is a grandniece (or great‑niece). Therefore Emma is John's grandniece.

P and R share only one parent, making them half‑brothers. Their children M and N are therefore the children of half‑siblings. The offspring of siblings are first cousins; when the siblings are half‑siblings, the offspring are called half‑first cousins (or half‑cousins). Thus M and N are half‑first cousins, not full cousins, siblings, nor unrelated.

M and S are siblings; W and B are siblings. C’s parents are M (child of grandparents P1) and W (child of grandparents P2). D’s parents are B (child of P2) and S (child of P1). Hence C and D share both sets of grandparents (P1 and P2). Sharing both grandparent couples makes them double first cousins, not just ordinary first cousins.

Aaron and Ben are brothers, so Emma and Felix share the same paternal grandparents. Clara and Diana are sisters, so Emma and Felix also share the same maternal grandparents. Sharing both sets of grandparents makes them first cousins through both parents, i.e., double first cousins.

M and N are siblings sharing the same parents. O and Q are also siblings sharing another set of parents. M marries O and N marries Q, so their children X and Y each have one set of grandparents from M/N and the other set from O/Q. Therefore X and Y share both sets of grandparents, making them first cousins through both parents – i.e., double first cousins.

M is mother of O. T is described as the sister of O, so T shares the same mother, M. T is the mother of S. Therefore M is the mother of S's mother, i.e., S's maternal grandmother. The precise kinship term is Grandmother.

Adam and Ben are brothers, so X and Y share the same paternal grandparents. Clara and Diana are sisters, so X and Y also share the same maternal grandparents. Thus the two children are first cousins through both parents, i.e., double first cousins, which is more precise than simply first cousins.

Adam and Brian are full brothers, sharing the same parents. Clara and Diana are full sisters, also sharing the same parents. Ethan is the child of Adam (brother) and Clara (sister), while Felix is the child of Brian (the other brother) and Diana (the other sister). Thus Ethan and Felix have both sets of grandparents in common: the paternal grandparents (parents of Adam and Brian) and the maternal grandparents (parents of Clara and Diana). Sharing both grandparents makes them double first cousins, not just single first cousins or any half‑cousin relationship.

Y’s father’s only sister is Y’s paternal aunt; Y’s mother’s only brother is Y’s maternal uncle. Their child X is the offspring of Y’s paternal aunt and maternal uncle. Consequently X is Y’s cousin on the father’s side and also on the mother’s side, sharing both sets of grandparents. This makes X a double first cousin of Y, not merely a single first cousin, half‑cousin, or second cousin.

M and N share the same parents, and O and P share the same parents. X is child of M (sibling of N) and O (sibling of P); Y is child of N and P. Hence X and Y share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins, the most precise term.

Y's mother has exactly one brother, who is Y's maternal uncle. Z is his child, so Z is Y's maternal first cousin. Y's father has exactly one sister, Y's paternal aunt. Z is also her child, making Z Y's paternal first cousin. The two parents (maternal uncle and paternal aunt) must be married to each other, giving Z the same set of grandparents on both sides. Hence Z is a first cousin through both maternal and paternal lines – a double first cousin. The relation is uniquely determined as such.

Emma's father Adam and Frank's father Ben are brothers, making Emma and Frank first cousins on the paternal side. Their mothers, Clara and Diana, are sisters, so Emma and Frank are also first cousins on the maternal side. Sharing both sets of grandparents means they are double first cousins, not half or second cousins.

M and N are siblings, so they share the same parents (paternal grandparents for X and Y). O and P are also siblings, sharing another set of parents (maternal grandparents for X and Y). X’s parents are M (paternal side) and O (maternal side); Y’s parents are N (paternal side) and P (maternal side). Consequently X and Y share both sets of grandparents, making them children of two sibling pairs. This relationship is defined as double first cousins.

A and B are half‑siblings, sharing one parent P. Their children C and D each have P as a grandparent, but their other grandparents differ. Cousins are defined by shared grandparents; first cousins share both grandparents, while half‑first cousins share only one. Therefore C and D are half‑first cousins, a precise standard term.
Ethan is Adam's son, making George his grandson. Fiona is Adam's niece (Brian's daughter), so her child George is Adam's great‑nephew. Hence George holds both roles simultaneously.

N is L's maternal uncle, so O (N's daughter) is L's maternal first cousin. Q is L's paternal aunt, so P (Q's son) is L's paternal first cousin. R is the child of O and P. In each line, R is the child of L's first cousin, which makes R a first cousin once removed to L. The two lines do not change the degree of removal; they simply reinforce the same relationship. Hence R is L's first cousin once removed.

K’s paternal grandmother (G) and the woman S are sisters. S is therefore the aunt of K’s father (F). L is S’s son, making L a first cousin of F. A first cousin of one’s parent is a first cousin once removed to the child. No half‑sibling information is given, so it isn’t a half‑first cousin, and the generational gap is one, not two, so it isn’t a second cousin. Hence L is K’s first cousin once removed.
A and B are brothers, so their children D and C are first cousins. E is D's child, one generation below D. Therefore C is the first cousin of E's parent, making C and E first cousins once removed.

X and Y are first cousins, meaning they share a pair of grandparents. Their children M and N each descend one generation further, so they share the same great‑grandparents. Sharing great‑grandparents defines a second‑cousin relationship. No half‑cousin or removal applies because the generational levels are equal and the original cousins are full, not half. Hence the relationship is uniquely second cousins.

A's father's sister is A's paternal aunt. Her child B is therefore A's first cousin. C is married to B, making C the spouse of A's first cousin. Standard English kinship terms do not include a specific term for a cousin's spouse, and the allowed in‑law extensions (spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses) do not cover this case. Hence C has no standard direct relation to A, only an affinal connection.

L's father's sister is L's paternal aunt; L's mother's brother is L's maternal uncle. Their child M is simultaneously the child of L's paternal aunt (making M a first cousin on the father's side) and the child of L's maternal uncle (making M a first cousin on the mother's side). Hence M shares both sets of grandparents with L, which is the definition of a double first cousin.

Emma is John's mother. Emma's sister Susan is John's maternal aunt. Susan's sole child Paul is therefore the child of John's aunt, making Paul John's first cousin. The marriage of John’s child Mary to Paul does not affect blood relations, so the correct blood‑kinship term is first cousin.

M and N share the same parents, and O and P share another set of parents. X’s paternal grandparents are M’s parents, and maternal grandparents are O’s parents. Y’s paternal grandparents are N’s parents (the same as M’s) and maternal grandparents are P’s parents (the same as O’s). Therefore X and Y have both sets of grandparents in common, making them the children of two sibling pairs. This is the definition of double first cousins, the most precise term among the choices.

X’s mother is the sister of Y’s mother, making her Y’s maternal aunt. X’s father is the brother of Y’s father, making him Y’s paternal uncle. Thus X is the child of both Y’s maternal aunt and paternal uncle. Consequently X shares both sets of Y’s grandparents (maternal and paternal). Sharing both grandparent pairs defines a double first‑cousin relationship.

N’s father’s sister is N’s paternal aunt, and N’s mother’s brother is N’s maternal uncle. They marry each other and have a child M. M is therefore the child of N’s aunt on the father's side and also the child of N’s uncle on the mother’s side. Consequently M is a first cousin through the father and a first cousin through the mother, making M a double first cousin of N.
Y is X's maternal uncle, making Y's daughter Z X's first cousin. W is Z's son, i.e., the child of X's first cousin. The child of a first cousin is a first cousin once removed.

Emma is Liam's mother. Emma's brother Noah is Liam's maternal uncle. Noah's daughter Zoe is therefore Liam's first cousin. Zoe's son Maya is one generation below Zoe, making Maya the child of Liam's first cousin. The kinship term for a person and the child of their cousin is "first cousin once removed".

L’s brother and sister are siblings, so their children X and Y are first cousins (they share L’s parents as grandparents). M is X’s child and N is Y’s child. Children of first cousins are second cousins, sharing the same great‑grandparents. Thus M and N are second cousins.

M's father has a sister S, making S M's paternal aunt. L is S's son, so L is M's first cousin. B is L's brother, thus also S's child and another first cousin of M. N is B's daughter, placing N one generation below M's cousin, which is the definition of a first cousin once removed.

M and O are brothers; N and P are sisters. X is child of M + N, Y is child of O + P. Thus X and Y are first cousins through their fathers (who are brothers) and also first cousins through their mothers (who are sisters). Sharing both paternal and maternal grandparent sets makes them double first cousins, the most precise term.

S is the child of R's mother's only brother, i.e., the child of R's maternal uncle. T is the child of R's father's only brother, i.e., the child of R's paternal uncle. In both cases the person is the child of an uncle, which by definition is a first cousin of R. The two uncles cannot be the same person because that would make R's parents siblings, violating the no intermarriage rule. Therefore any arbitrarily chosen U (either S or T) is uniquely a first cousin of R.

X's father M is sibling of Y's parent N, making X and Y first cousins through the paternal line. Simultaneously, X's mother O is sibling of Y's other parent P, making them first cousins through the maternal line as well. Being first cousins via both parents defines double first cousins, the most precise term.

M is G's maternal uncle (mother's brother) and F is G's paternal aunt (father's sister). Their child C is therefore the child of G's maternal uncle, making C a first cousin on the mother's side, and also the child of G's paternal aunt, making C a first cousin on the father's side. Since C shares both sets of grandparents with G, the relationship is a double first cousin.

B and C are first cousins, sharing the same grandparents. A is B's child, so A is one generation below B. The child of a first cousin is a first cousin once removed relative to the original cousin. Thus A is C's first cousin once removed.

M and N are full siblings, as are P and Q. A’s parents are M (child of grandparents G1,G2) and P (child of grandparents G3,G4). B’s parents are N (same G1,G2) and Q (same G3,G4). A and B share only a mother, making them half‑siblings. Their children C and D each have that mother as a grandparent, but they do not share the other grandparent. L and S are siblings, making their children D and T first cousins. M is D's child and N is T's child. Children of first cousins share the same great‑grandparents (the parents of L and S), so M and N share great‑grandparents and are therefore second cousins.
