Their child Sam is therefore John's cousin through his mother and also his cousin through his father. This makes Sam a double first cousin, the term for children who share both sets of grandparents.

M and N are full siblings, sharing both parents. P and Q are also full siblings, sharing their own parents. X is child of M and P; Y is child of N and Q. Therefore X’s four grandparents are the parents of M/N and the parents of P/Q. Y has exactly the same four grandparents. Sharing both sets of grandparents makes X and Y double first cousins, the most precise term.

M and N are siblings, so X and Y are first cousins through their fathers. O and P are also siblings, so X and Y are first cousins through their mothers as well. Because they share both sets of grandparents (the parents of M/N and the parents of O/P), they are first cousins on two separate lines, i.e., double first cousins.

M and N are siblings (family A). O and P are siblings (family B). M marries O, N marries P. X is child of M (A) and O (B); Y is child of N (A) and P (B). Therefore X and Y each have the same two sets of grandparents: the parents of M/N and the parents of O/P. Sharing both paternal and maternal grandparents makes them children of two sibling pairs, i.e., double first cousins, which is more precise than plain first cousins.

John and Mark are full brothers, sharing both paternal grandparents. Anna and Beth are full sisters, sharing both maternal grandparents. Carl is the child of John (paternal side) and Anna (maternal side); Diana is the child of Mark (paternal side) and Beth (maternal side). Thus Carl and Diana are first cousins through their fathers and also first cousins through their mothers, sharing both sets of grandparents. This makes them double first cousins, the most precise term.

L and N are siblings. M is L's child; O is N's child, making M and O first cousins. P is O's daughter, one generation below O. Therefore P is the child of M's first cousin, which is defined as a first cousin once removed.

A and C share the same mother but have different fathers, making C A's half‑sister. C is the mother of E, so E is the child of A's half‑sister. In English kinship, the child of a full sibling is a niece/nephew; the child of a half‑sibling is termed a half‑niece/nephew. Therefore E is A's half‑niece.

The two children each have fathers who are brothers, making them first cousins on the paternal side. Their mothers are sisters, making them first cousins on the maternal side as well. Sharing both sets of grandparents means they are first cousins through two distinct sibling pairs, which is the definition of double first cousins. They are not half‑first cousins (which would involve only one shared grandparent set) nor second cousins.

Lisa is John’s niece (daughter of his sister Mary). She marries Mark, John’s son, making Anna the child of John’s son – thus John’s grandchild (granddaughter). Simultaneously, Anna is the child of John’s niece, which makes her John’s great‑niece. Both relations are valid, so the correct choice is D.

E and F share only one parent (their father), making them half‑siblings. The children of half‑siblings are classified as half‑first cousins, since they share a set of grandparents only through the common parent. Therefore G (E's daughter) and H (F's son) are half‑first cousins.

Ethan's father Adam and Fiona's father Brian are brothers, making Ethan and Fiona first cousins on their paternal side. Likewise, Ethan's mother Clara and Fiona's mother Diana are sisters, making them also first cousins on their maternal side. Sharing both sets of grandparents means they are related through two distinct lines, which is defined as double first cousins.

Y and Z are sisters, making Z X's maternal aunt. V and U are brothers, making U X's paternal uncle. Their child W is therefore the child of X's aunt and uncle on both sides, giving X two independent first‑cousin links. This is the definition of a double first cousin.

Alice and Bob share a single parent, making them half‑siblings. The children of siblings are first cousins. When the siblings are half‑siblings, their children are first cousins who share only one grandparent, i.e., half‑first cousins. Thus Clara and David are half‑first cousins.

Clara’s parents (John and Anna) are a brother-sister pair, and Daniel’s parents (Jim and Amy) are the other brother-sister pair. Since John and Jim share both parents, and Anna and Amy also share both parents, Clara and Daniel share both sets of grandparents. This makes them double first cousins, not just regular first cousins or any half/second cousin relationship.

N's mother has one brother, who is N's maternal uncle. N's father has one sister, who is N's paternal aunt. M is the child of that uncle and that aunt. Therefore M is the child of N's maternal uncle (making M a first cousin on the mother's side) and also the child of N's paternal aunt (making M a first cousin on the father's side). Since the two parents are siblings of N's parents, M and N share both sets of grandparents, which is the definition of a double first cousin.

Mary's brother's son is John; Mary's sister's son is Paul, making John and Paul first cousins. Paul’s daughter Susan is one generation below John, so Susan is John’s first cousin once removed. Susan’s son Tim is another generation down, placing Tim two generations apart from John. Therefore Tim is John’s first cousin twice removed.

Mary is John’s sister, so her son Peter is John’s nephew. Peter’s child Lily is therefore John’s great‑niece (the child of a nephew). John’s own daughter Anne is Lily’s mother, making Lily John’s granddaughter. Lily thus holds both relations simultaneously.

P’s father’s sister is P’s paternal aunt; her child is a first cousin on the paternal side. P’s mother’s brother is P’s maternal uncle; his child is a first cousin on the maternal side. Since M is the child of both the aunt and the uncle, they must be married (monogamy, no adoption). Thus M is a first cousin to P through both parental lines, i.e., a double first cousin.

M and N are full siblings, so their children P and Q are first cousins (they share grandparents). R is the child of Q, placing R one generation below Q. Therefore R is a first cousin once removed relative to P, as they are separated by one generation from the first-cousin relationship.

John's father Peter has a brother Mark. Mark is John's paternal uncle. Mark's daughter Emma is therefore the child of John's uncle, making Emma John's first cousin. Other connections (through Mary’s brother Tom and his wife Linda) are by marriage only and do not affect blood kinship.

The man's mother's brother is his maternal uncle; his daughter is the man's maternal first cousin. The man's father's brother is his paternal uncle; his son is the man's paternal first cousin. The maternal cousin descends from the mother's family, the paternal cousin from the father's family. Assuming the parents are unrelated, the two cousins share no common ancestors, so there is no blood relationship between them.

My mother’s sister is my maternal aunt. Her son Tom is thus my first cousin. Tom’s daughter Lily is one generation below my cousin, making her my first cousin once removed according to standard kinship terminology.

M and N are siblings, so they share the same paternal (or maternal) grandparents. P and Q are also siblings, sharing another set of grandparents. X is the child of M and P; Y is the child of N and Q. Therefore X and Y share both sets of grandparents—one through their fathers (M and N) and another through their mothers (P and Q). This makes them first cousins on both parental sides, i.e., double first cousins, which is the most precise term.

M and N are siblings, so their children O and Q are first cousins. R is O's daughter, making R the child of Q's cousin, which is the definition of a first cousin once removed. Since R also marries Q, the relationship is both blood (first cousin once removed) and spouse.

M and N are full siblings, and P and Q are full siblings from a different family. X is child of M and P; Y is child of N and Q. Thus X and Y share two distinct sets of grandparents (the parents of M/N and the parents of P/Q). They are first cousins through both parental lines, i.e., double first cousins, which is more specific than any other listed term.

John and Mary are siblings, so their children Michael and Peter are first cousins. Lisa is Michael's daughter, one generation below Michael. A person who is a first cousin of someone's parent is a first cousin once removed. Therefore Peter’s relation to Lisa is that of a first cousin once removed.

Adam and Brian are brothers, so their children share the same paternal grandparents. Clara and Diana are sisters, so their children share the same maternal grandparents. Ethan (Adam + Clara) and Fiona (Brian +  Diana) therefore are first cousins on both sides, i.e., double first cousins.

Mary and Susan share the same mother but have different fathers, making them half‑sisters. Susan is therefore John’s half‑aunt, and her son Tom is John’s half‑first cousin. Lily is John’s daughter, one generation below John. The relationship between Tom (same generation as John) and Lily (one generation down) is a half‑first cousin once removed.

M and N are siblings, so their children O and R are first cousins. R is Q's mother, making O a first cousin of Q's parent. Therefore O is one generation removed from Q, i.e., a first cousin once removed.

M's mother and N's father are siblings, making them share one set of grandparents. Likewise M's father and N's mother are siblings, giving a second shared set of grandparents. Thus M and N share both couples of grandparents, the definition of double first cousins.

Y's mother has one brother; X is that brother's child, making X Y's maternal first cousin. Y's father has one sister; X is also that sister's child, making X Y's paternal first cousin. For X to be both, the maternal uncle and paternal aunt must be married (monogamy, no adoption). Thus X is the child of two siblings of Y who married each other, which is the definition of a double first cousin.

John and Mary are siblings, so their children Tom and Lisa are first cousins. Lisa’s husband (H) has a mother who is Tom’s sister, making H the child of Tom’s sister. Therefore Tom is the brother of H’s mother, i.e., Tom is H’s uncle.

M's mother’s brother is M’s maternal uncle; M’s father’s sister is M’s paternal aunt. Their child N is thus the child of M’s maternal uncle (making N a first cousin on the mother’s side) and also the child of M’s paternal aunt (making N a first cousin on the father’s side). Because N is a first cousin through both parental lines, they share both sets of grandparents with M, which is the definition of a double first cousin.

M is mother of O, making O her child. O's child Q is M's grandchild. S is child of Q, so S is one generation further: M's great‑grandchild. Other parent P is not a blood relative, but S’s blood line through Q gives the great‑grandchild relation.

M and N are half‑siblings, sharing only one parent (their mother). Their children P and Q each inherit that shared grandparent from the mother of M and N. Since P and Q have only one common grandparent, they are cousins who share a single grandparent, i.e., half‑first cousins. They do not share both grandparents, so they are not full first cousins, nor are they second cousins. The relationship is therefore determinable as half‑first cousins.

M and N share only a mother, making them half‑siblings. Their children A and B are thus the offspring of half‑siblings. In kinship terminology, the children of full siblings are first cousins; when the siblings are half‑siblings, their children are termed half‑first cousins (often just half‑cousins). Therefore the precise standard English term for A and B is half‑first cousins.

L's father and P are brothers, so P is L's paternal uncle. L's mother and Q are sisters, so Q is L's maternal aunt. Their child M is therefore the child of L's paternal uncle and maternal aunt. Consequently M is L's first cousin through the father's side and also L's first cousin through the mother's side, sharing both sets of grandparents. This is the definition of a double first cousin.

P's father's sister (paternal aunt) and P's mother's brother (maternal uncle) marry each other. Their child M is first cousin to P through the father's side (child of his aunt) and also first cousin through the mother's side (child of his uncle). Because M is related to P via two distinct sibling pairs, they are double first cousins.

R's father has one brother (paternal uncle) who marries R's mother's sister (maternal aunt). Their child X is therefore the offspring of R's paternal uncle, making X a first cousin on the father's side, and also the offspring of R's maternal aunt, making X a first cousin on the mother's side. Since X is a first cousin through both parental lines, X is a double first cousin of R.

M and N share the same parents, and O and P share another set of parents. X’s paternal grandparents are M/N’s parents, and X’s maternal grandparents are O/P’s parents. Y has the same paternal and maternal grandparents, because his father N shares the first set and his mother P shares the second. Thus X and Y are first cousins through both their fathers and their mothers, i.e., double first cousins, which is more specific than plain first cousins.

S's mother has one brother (her only brother). That brother is S's maternal uncle. The child of that uncle (R) is therefore the child of S's parent's sibling, which by standard kinship terms is a first cousin of S.

M's father has a sister, who is M's paternal aunt. She is N's mother, making N M's first cousin. P is described as the son of N's mother, i.e., also a child of the same aunt. Therefore P is another child of M's paternal aunt, which makes P also a first cousin of M. The relationship is thus first cousin.

N's mother’s brother is N’s maternal uncle; N's father’s brother is N’s paternal uncle. Their child M is therefore the offspring of N’s maternal uncle, making M a first cousin on the mother’s side, and also the offspring of N’s paternal uncle, making M a first cousin on the father’s side. Being a first cousin through both parental lines classifies M as a double first cousin of N.

M and N share only one parent (their mother), making them half‑siblings. Their children, A and B, therefore share only one grandparent (the mother of M and N). Children of half‑siblings are called half‑first cousins, distinct from full first cousins who share both grandparents. Hence the precise kinship term is half‑first cousins.

Peter is the son of Mary, who is John’s sister, while Susan is the daughter of Tom, who is Lisa’s brother. John and Lisa are spouses, but they have no blood connection. Thus Mary and Tom are connected only through their siblings' marriage, and their children share no common ancestor. Therefore Peter and Susan have no blood relationship; any connection is affinal only.

M and N are siblings, so their children share the same paternal grandparents. X and Y are siblings, so their children share the same maternal grandparents. A and B therefore share both sets of grandparents, making them children of two sibling pairs, which is the definition of double first cousins.

Linda and Kevin are siblings of Paul, making Linda and Kevin also siblings to each other. Their children Tom (Linda's son) and Sara (Kevin's daughter) are therefore first cousins, sharing the same set of grandparents. Maya is Tom's child, and Noah is Sara's child. Children of first cousins are second cousins because they share the same great‑grandparents. No half‑relations are indicated, so the precise kinship is second cousins.

First cousins are children of siblings. Second cousins are children of first cousins. M and N are double first cousins (their parents are two sets of siblings), so they are first cousins through two separate lines. Therefore their children, A and B, are second cousins through both lines, i.e., double second cousins.

Mary and David are John's siblings. Their children, Peter (Mary's son) and Anna (David's daughter), are John's nephew and niece respectively. Lily is the child of Peter and Anna. The child of a niece or nephew is the grandniece or grandnephew of the original sibling. Therefore Lily is John's grandniece.

M and N are full siblings, so they share the same parents. X and Y are also full siblings, sharing their own parents. A’s parents are M (child of the first set of grandparents) and X (child of the second set). B’s parents are N (the sibling of M) and Y (the sibling of X). Thus A and B are related through both parental lines: they are first cousins via M‑N and also first cousins via X‑Y. Sharing both pairs of grandparents makes them double first cousins, the most precise term.

M and N are siblings, so their children O and P are first cousins. O marries Q; Q's sister is R, who is married to P. Thus R is the wife of O's cousin P. This makes R the cousin's spouse, which is not covered by standard kinship terms such as aunt, cousin, or sister‑in‑law. Therefore the correct choice is that there is no standard relation.

John and Mary share the same parents, and Anna and Ben share another set of parents. Carl’s father John and Dana’s father Mary are siblings, making Carl and Dana first cousins on their fathers’ side. Likewise, Carl’s mother Anna and Dana’s mother Ben are siblings, making them first cousins on their mothers’ side. Since they are first cousins through both parents, the precise term is double first cousins.

B and S are siblings (brother and sister) of M, thus they share both parents. Their children, John (B's child) and Susan (S's child), are therefore children of two full siblings, which makes them first cousins.

M is the brother of R's mother, making M R's maternal uncle. N is the sister of R's father, making N R's paternal aunt. Both M and N are each the sole parent of S, so S is the child of R's maternal uncle and paternal aunt. Consequently S shares both sets of grandparents with R, fitting the definition of a double first cousin (children of two sibling pairs). Hence the precise kinship term is double first cousin.

M and N share only one parent (their mother), so they have only one grandparent in common. Their children X and Y each inherit that shared grandparent through their respective parent. Hence X and Y share exactly one grandparent, not a full set of two. This matches the definition of half‑first cousins, which are the offspring of half‑siblings. Therefore the most precise term is half‑first cousins.

M and N share the same parents, and S and T share the same parents. Each child inherits one set of grandparents from their father’s family and another set from their mother’s family. Since A’s paternal grandparents are M/N’s parents and maternal grandparents are S/T’s parents, and B’s grandparents are the same two sets, A and B share both pairs of grandparents. This is the definition of double first cousins.

P and Q are siblings, so their children X (of P) and Y (of Q) are first cousins. Z is the son of Y, making Z one generation below Y. Therefore X is the first cousin of Z's parent, which is the definition of a first cousin once removed. Hence Z is X's first cousin once removed.

R's father is Q. P is stated to be Q's brother, so P is the brother of R's father. In standard kinship terms, the brother of one's parent is an uncle (specifically paternal uncle). This is a direct kinship term, so the correct choice is Uncle.

B is C's daughter, making A C's grandson. E is C's brother, so D (E's son) is C's nephew. Thus B and D are first cousins (children of siblings C and E). A, being B's son, is one generation below B, so A is D's first cousin once removed. Therefore the correct choice is C.

Lisa is the daughter of Peter, who is Mary’s brother. Mary is Thomas’s spouse, so Peter is Thomas’s brother‑in‑law. Therefore Lisa is the child of Thomas’s spouse’s sibling, i.e., his spouse’s niece. The standard term for a spouse’s niece is "niece‑in‑law". None of the other options fit this relationship.

A and B are full siblings, so they share both grandparents. D and F are also full siblings, sharing another pair of grandparents. C is the child of A (one sibling) and D (the other sibling pair), while E is the child of B and F. Therefore C and E each receive the same two sets of grandparents from both sides. They share both sets of grandparents, which defines double first cousins, as opposed to regular first cousins (one shared grandparent set) or half‑first cousins (one shared grandparent set due to half‑siblings).

Adam’s maternal uncle Ben’s daughter Clara is Adam’s first cousin. Adam’s paternal aunt Diana’s son Frank is also Adam’s first cousin. Grace is the child of Clara and Frank. In kinship terms, the child of your first cousin is your first cousin once removed. Since Grace is the child of both of Adam’s first cousins, the relationship is still first cousin once removed. Hence the correct choice is C.

M and N share only one parent, making them half‑siblings. Their children X and Y therefore share only the one grandparent common to M and N (the mother). Full first cousins share both grandparents; when only one grandparent is shared, the correct term is half‑first cousins. Thus the most precise standard English term is half‑first cousins.

M and N share the same parents, and O and P share another set of parents. A is the child of M (a child of the first set) and O (a child of the second set). B is the child of N (also a child of the first set) and P (also a child of the second set). Consequently A and B have both sets of grandparents in common, meaning they are first cousins through two sibling pairs. This relationship is called double first cousins.

John’s father and Mary’s father are brothers, so John and Mary share the same paternal grandparents. John’s mother and Mary’s mother are sisters, so they also share the same maternal grandparents. Sharing both sets of grandparents makes them first cousins on both parental lines, which is the definition of double first cousins.

N and O are full siblings (same parents M and A). P and Q are full siblings (same parents B and C). R is child of N (child of M&A) and P (child of B&C). S is child of O (child of M&A) and Q (child of B&C). Thus R and S share both sets of grandparents: M&A (maternal) and B&C (paternal). Sharing both grandparent pairs makes them double first cousins, not just first cousins or half‑cousins.

L’s mother’s only brother is L’s maternal uncle. L’s father’s only sister is L’s paternal aunt. Their child M is therefore the child of L’s maternal uncle (making M a first cousin on the mother’s side) and also the child of L’s paternal aunt (making M a first cousin on the father’s side). When the same person is a first cousin through both parental lines, the relationship is a double first cousin. No half‑relation or ambiguity is introduced by the given constraints.

X’s father Adam and Y’s father Ben are brothers, making X and Y first cousins on their paternal side. Likewise, X’s mother Clara and Y’s mother Diana are sisters, making X and Y first cousins on their maternal side. Because they are first cousins through both parents, they are double first cousins, the most specific term.

X's mother is the sister of Y's father, and X's father is the brother of Y's mother. This means each child's mother is sibling to the other's father, and each child's father is sibling to the other's mother. Thus the two children are born from two sibling pairs marrying each other, causing them to share both sets of grandparents. That relationship is known as double first cousins.

M and N are full brothers, sharing the same parents. X and Y are sisters, also sharing the same parents. A’s parents (M and X) are a brother–sister pair, and B’s parents (N and Y) are the other brother–sister pair. Thus A and B share both sets of grandparents – the paternal grandparents (parents of M and N) and the maternal grandparents (parents of X and Y). Sharing two lines of descent makes them double first cousins, which is more specific than ordinary first cousins. Hence the most precise term is double first cousins.

F is N's father's only sibling, making her N's paternal aunt. G is N's mother's only sibling, making him N's maternal uncle. Their child M is therefore N's cousin through the father's side (child of paternal aunt) and also through the mother's side (child of maternal uncle). Being first cousin on both parental lines defines a double first cousin.

P is the child of Q's maternal uncle (the only brother of Q's mother) and also the child of Q's paternal uncle (the only brother of Q's father). In either case, a child of an uncle is a first cousin. Being the child of both uncles makes P a double first cousin, but the kinship term remains "first cousin". Hence the precise term is first cousin.

P's mother’s brother (A) is P’s maternal uncle, making A’s child a first cousin on the maternal side. P's father’s sister (B) is P’s paternal aunt, so B’s child is a first cousin on the paternal side. Since A and B are married, their single child C is simultaneously the child of P’s maternal uncle and paternal aunt, sharing both sets of grandparents with P. This dual shared lineage defines a double first cousin relationship.

Anna and Sophie are sisters. Anna's child is Clara; Sophie's child is Ethan. Children of siblings are first cousins. No other relationship (e.g., half‑cousin) applies because the siblings share both parents. Thus Ethan is Clara's first cousin.

Y's two children are siblings. X is the child of Y's son, and Z is the child of Y's daughter. Therefore X and Z are each the child of one of Y's siblings, making them the children of siblings. In standard kinship terms, children of siblings are first cousins, with no generational offset, so the correct term is first cousins.

P and Q are first cousins, so they share a set of grandparents. P’s child X is directly descended from P. When X and Y (Q’s child) have a child Z, Z is the offspring of X. Therefore Z is one generation below X, making Z the grandchild of P. The other options describe lateral or more distant relations, which do not apply here.
M and N are siblings. N's child Q is M's niece/nephew. Q's daughter R is the child of M's niece/nephew, making R the grandniece (or great‑niece) of M. Thus the correct kinship term is great‑niece.

Z is married to P, who is the brother of M's father. The spouse of one's parent's sibling is the parent's sibling's spouse, which is the standard term for an aunt (by marriage). Hence Z is M's aunt-in-law.

P and Q are brothers, so they share the same parents. R and S are sisters, sharing their own parents. M is the child of P and R; N is the child of Q and S. Therefore M and N share both sets of grandparents: the paternal grandparents (parents of P and Q) and the maternal grandparents (parents of R and S). Sharing both grandparent pairs makes them double first cousins, the most specific term among the choices.

Ethan and Fiona are double first cousins, sharing both sets of grandparents. The children of first cousins are second cousins; similarly, the children of double first cousins are double second cousins, retaining the doubled relationship across one generation. George (Ethan's child) and Hannah (Fiona's child) therefore are double second cousins.

John and Mary are siblings, so their children Ben and Anna are first cousins. Clara is Ben's daughter and David is Anna's son. Children of first cousins share the same great‑grandparents (John and Mary's parents), making them second cousins. Therefore Clara and David are second cousins.

L and K are sisters, so their children M and N are first cousins. F and B are brothers, so their children M and O are also first cousins. Since M and O are related as first cousins through both their mothers' and fathers' lines, they have a double first‑cousin relationship, which is the most precise description.

M and N are siblings, so they share the same parents (paternal grandparents for X and Y). O and P are also siblings, sharing another set of parents (maternal grandparents for X and Y). X is child of M and O; Y is child of N and P. Therefore X and Y have both sets of grandparents in common, making them children of two sibling pairs. This relationship is defined as double first cousins, not merely first cousins, half‑first cousins, or second cousins.

Mark and Neil are brothers, making their children first cousins on the paternal side. Anna and Beth are sisters, so their children are also first cousins on the maternal side. Because the two cousins share both sets of grandparents, they are double first cousins.

Mary is the mother of Lisa, making Lisa Mary's daughter. Anna is Lisa's child, so Anna is Mary's granddaughter. Mary is also the sister of John, making John’s son Tom her nephew. Anna is Tom's child, which makes her Mary’s great‑niece (child of a nephew). Since both relationships apply, the most precise description combines them.

P is child of S1 (who is sister of S2) and A (brother of B). Q is child of S2 and B. Since S1 and S2 are full sisters and A and B are full brothers, P and Q share both maternal grandparents and paternal grandparents. This makes them double first cousins, the most precise term.

Alan is Tom's maternal uncle (mother's brother) and Beth is Tom's paternal aunt (father's sister). Since Claire is both Alan's daughter and Beth's child, Alan and Beth must be married and share Claire as their child. Thus Claire is Tom's cousin on his mother's side and also on his father's side—a double first cousin, which is still classified as a first cousin.

Ethan's father Adam and Fiona's father Brian are brothers, so they share paternal grandparents. Ethan's mother Clara and Fiona's mother Diana are sisters, so they share maternal grandparents. The children share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins.

M and N share the same parents, and X and Y share another set of parents. A’s father (M) and B’s father (N) are siblings, so A and B share their paternal grandparents. Likewise, A’s mother (X) and B’s mother (Y) are siblings, so they also share their maternal grandparents. Thus A and B are first cousins through both parental lines, i.e., double first cousins, which is more specific than the other options.

Sam's mother and Tom are siblings, making Tom Sam's maternal uncle. Tom's daughter Lily is therefore Sam's first cousin. The marriage between Sam's sister Emma and Lily's brother Michael is an affinal link and does not alter the blood relationship. Hence Sam and Lily are first cousins.

Y is the child of A and B. X is the child of C (A's brother) and D (B's sister). Therefore X's father C shares the same parents as A, and X's mother D shares the same parents as B. Consequently X and Y have both sets of grandparents in common, making them first cousins through both parental lines. This relationship is called double first cousins.

Y and Z are siblings. Their children X (of Y) and W (of Z) are first cousins. V is W's child, making V one generation below W. Thus X is a first cousin of V's parent, which is the definition of a first cousin once removed.

M is R's maternal uncle (mother's brother) and F is R's paternal aunt (father's sister). Their daughter S is child of both R's maternal uncle and paternal aunt, meaning S's grandparents are exactly R's maternal grandparents (through M) and paternal grandparents (through F). Hence R and S share both sets of grandparents but have different parents, making them double first cousins.

M is the child of L's maternal uncle (brother of L's mother) and also the child of L's paternal aunt (sister of L's father). Thus M is a first cousin to L through both the maternal and paternal lines, making them double first cousins.

John and Mark are brothers, so John is the sibling of Mark. Lisa is explicitly stated to be Mark's daughter, giving her a direct blood link to Mark. Therefore Lisa is John’s brother's child, which makes her John’s niece. No other blood connections alter this straightforward uncle‑niece relationship.

Tom is John's maternal uncle (mother's brother) and Mary is John's paternal aunt (father's sister). Their daughter Lily is thus the child of John's maternal uncle and paternal aunt. Lily is therefore John's first cousin through his mother and also his first cousin through his father, making her a double first cousin. The other options do not fit the described connections.

A is L's father's sister, making her L's paternal aunt. B is L's mother's brother, making him L's maternal uncle. Their child C is therefore the child of L's paternal aunt and maternal uncle. C is a first cousin to L through the father's side and also a first cousin through the mother's side, sharing both sets of grandparents with L. This dual relationship defines a double first cousin.

M and N are half‑siblings, sharing only one parent (their mother).
