A's mother is sibling to B's father, giving them one shared set of grandparents. A's father is sibling to B's mother, giving a second shared set of grandparents. Thus A and B share both paternal and maternal grandparents, making them double first cousins, the most precise term.

M and N share both parents, as do P and Q. X is child of M (sibling of N) and Q (sibling of P). Y is child of N and P. Therefore X and Y each have the same two sets of grandparents: the parents of M/N and the parents of P/Q. Sharing both sets of grandparents makes them first cousins through two sibling pairs, i.e., double first cousins.

A and B are siblings, C and D are siblings. A marries C, B marries D. Their children E (A+C) and F (B+D) each have the same two sets of grandparents: the parents of A/B and the parents of C/D. Thus E and F share both pairs of grandparents, making them double first cousins, the most precise term.

M's father's sister is M's paternal aunt; her husband N is therefore M's uncle by marriage (uncle‑in‑law). N's mother is the sister of M's mother, making N the child of M's maternal aunt, i.e., M's first cousin. Hence N holds both relationships simultaneously.

R's paternal grandfather's brother is R's great‑uncle. The child of that brother is the great‑uncle's child, which is the first cousin of R's father. Therefore, to R, that person is one generation removed from a first cousin, i.e., a first cousin once removed.

John and Mary are siblings, so their children Alice and Bob are first cousins (they share the same grandparents). Carol is Bob's daughter, placing her one generation below Bob. Alice, being the first cousin of Carol's parent, is therefore a first cousin once removed to Carol.

A is Q's paternal aunt (father's sister) and B is Q's maternal uncle (mother's brother). Their child P is therefore the offspring of Q's aunt on his father's side and uncle on his mother's side. P's maternal grandparents are Q's paternal grandparents, and P's paternal grandparents are Q's maternal grandparents, so P and Q share both sets of grandparents. Sharing both sets of grandparents makes them double first cousins, the most precise term.

M’s father (F) and B are brothers, so B is M’s paternal uncle. M’s mother and S are sisters, so S is M’s maternal aunt. B and S are married and have a daughter D. Therefore D is the child of M’s paternal uncle (making D a first cousin on the father’s side) and also the child of M’s maternal aunt (making D a first cousin on the mother’s side). Sharing both sets of grandparents, M and D are double first cousins.

A's mother’s brother is A’s maternal uncle; his daughter B is A’s first cousin. B’s husband C is not blood‑related to A. C’s mother D makes D C’s mother, and D’s brother E is C’s maternal uncle; E’s son F is C’s first cousin. Hence F is the cousin of A’s cousin’s spouse, a relation by marriage with no direct blood term. The standard English kinship system has no specific term for this, so the correct choice is ‘No standard direct relation.’

Peter is Mary's son, making him John's nephew. Lisa is John's daughter. Their child Emma is simultaneously the child of John's daughter (grandchild) and the child of John's nephew (grandniece). Since two distinct standard kinship terms apply, Emma's relation to John is not uniquely determined by a single term.
Lisa is married to Kevin, who is John’s son. By definition, the spouse of one’s child is a daughter‑in‑law. No other listed in‑law categories apply, so the correct term is daughter‑in‑law.

X is the child of Y's maternal uncle (brother of Y's mother) and Y's paternal aunt (sister of Y's father). Thus X's father is Y's maternal uncle and X's mother is Y's paternal aunt. The two parents are a married couple, each being a sibling of one of Y's parents. Consequently X shares both sets of grandparents with Y, making X and Y double first cousins—their relationship is more specific than a regular first cousin.

M and N are full siblings, so they share the same parents. O and P are also full siblings, sharing another set of parents. X is the child of M (father) and O (mother); Y is the child of N (father) and P (mother). Thus X and Y have the same paternal grandparents (parents of M and N) and the same maternal grandparents (parents of O and P). Sharing both sets of grandparents makes them double first cousins, the most precise term among the choices.

M is the child of N's paternal aunt (the father's only sister) and also the child of N's maternal uncle (the mother's only brother). Those two are married, so M is the offspring of both N's aunt and uncle. Hence M is N's first cousin through the father's side and also through the mother's side, making the relationship a double first cousin, the precise standard term.

M’s mother has exactly one brother – M’s maternal uncle. M’s father has exactly one sister – M’s paternal aunt. The child N is described as the child of both the maternal uncle and the paternal aunt, which can only happen if those two are married to each other. Their offspring is therefore the child of M’s uncle and aunt, making N a first cousin of M on both sides. No other relationship fits the description, so N is uniquely a first cousin.

A and B are full brothers sharing the same parents, and C and D are full sisters sharing their own parents. X’s paternal grandparents are the parents of A and B, and X’s maternal grandparents are the parents of C and D. Y has the same paternal and maternal grandparents, because his parents are B (brother of A) and D (sister of C). Hence X and Y share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins.

John’s maternal uncle Tom’s daughter Lily is John’s first cousin. John’s paternal aunt Mary’s son Peter is also John’s first cousin. Lily and Peter (two first cousins of John) marry and have Sam. Sam is therefore the child of John’s first cousin, making Sam John’s first cousin once removed. No closer standard kin term applies.

Laura and Mark are siblings, so their children (Anna and Beth) are first cousins. Carl is Anna's child, placing him one generation below Anna. Therefore Carl is one generation removed from the first‑cousin relationship with Beth, making him Beth's first cousin once removed.

M and N are full siblings, so they share the same parents (paternal grandparents of X and Y). O and P are also full siblings, sharing another set of parents (maternal grandparents of X and Y). X is child of M (one sibling) and O (the other sibling), while Y is child of N (M's sibling) and P (O's sibling). Therefore X and Y have both sets of grandparents in common, making them the children of two sibling pairs. This is the definition of double first cousins, more specific than regular first cousins.

John's father's brother is his paternal uncle. The uncle's daughter Emily is John's first cousin. Emily's son Victor is one generation below Emily, making Victor the child of John's first cousin. In standard kinship terms, the child of a first cousin is a first cousin once removed (removed by one generation). No half‑relation is indicated, and the relationship is fully determinable.

John and Mark are brothers, so their children Lily and Peter are first cousins (they share grandparents). Sam is Lily's child, placing Sam one generation below Lily. A person’s child’s relationship to that person’s first cousin is a first cousin once removed—"once removed" denotes the single‑generation gap. Therefore Sam is Peter’s first cousin once removed.

X's father's brother is X's paternal uncle; his wife Y is X's paternal aunt by marriage. Y's brother Z is therefore the brother of X's paternal aunt-in-law. Z is married to the sister of X's mother, i.e., to X's maternal aunt (blood relation). Hence Z is the husband of X's maternal aunt, making him an uncle by marriage on the maternal side – an uncle‑in‑law. This matches choice B.

N’s father’s sister is N’s paternal aunt; N’s mother’s brother is N’s maternal uncle. Their child M is the offspring of N’s aunt and uncle, making M a first cousin of N through the father’s side and also a first cousin through the mother’s side. Because M shares both sets of grandparents with N, the relationship is that of a double first cousin.

R's mother’s only brother is R’s maternal uncle; his child P is R’s first cousin. R's father's only sister is R’s paternal aunt; her child Q is also R’s first cousin. Whether S is P or Q, the relationship to R is the same: first cousin. Hence the relation is uniquely determined as first cousin.

M is the child of P's paternal aunt (sister of P's father) and also the child of P's maternal uncle (brother of P's mother). These two relatives are married, so M is simultaneously P's first cousin on the father's side and on the mother's side, making them double first cousins.

M and Z are siblings. Y is Z's daughter, making Y the child of one sibling. X is M's son, making X the child of the other sibling. Children of siblings are first cousins to each other. Therefore X is Y's first cousin.

Lily is the daughter of Emma's maternal uncle (mother's brother) and also the daughter of Emma's paternal aunt (father's sister). For the same Lily to fulfill both roles, the uncle and aunt must be married to each other. Consequently Lily is Emma's first cousin on both the maternal and paternal sides, which is precisely the definition of a double first cousin.

John is sibling to Mary (Lily's maternal grandmother) and to David (Lily's paternal grandfather). Thus he is a great‑uncle on both sides of Lily's family. The most precise term reflecting his dual great‑uncle status is "double great‑uncle".

L's father has one sister, who is L's paternal aunt. L's mother has one brother, who is L's maternal uncle. M is the child of exactly one of these two relatives. The child of an aunt or an uncle is, by definition, a first cousin of the person whose parent is the sibling. Whether M is the aunt's child or the uncle's child, the kinship term remains "first cousin". Therefore M's relation to L is uniquely determined as a first cousin.

Emma is the child of John’s daughter Lisa, making her John’s granddaughter. She is also the child of John’s nephew Peter (Mary’s son), which makes her John’s great‑niece (or grand‑niece). No single standard term covers both relationships, so the most precise description is to state both relations.

John and Mary are siblings, so their children Peter and Tom are first cousins. Anna is Peter's daughter, placing her one generation below Peter. Thus Tom, being Peter's first cousin, is one generation above Anna, making Tom and Anna first cousins once removed.

Ethan and Fiona are first cousins because their mother Clara and father David are siblings, sharing the same grandparents. Their children Greg and Hannah are therefore one generation removed, sharing those grandparents as great‑grandparents. That makes Greg and Hannah second cousins. No double or half relationship applies.

John and Peter share both parents, making them full brothers. Mary and Anna also share both parents, making them full sisters. Lisa’s father is John and mother is Mary; Mark’s father is Peter and mother is Anna. Therefore Lisa and Mark share the same paternal grandparents (parents of John and Peter) and the same maternal grandparents (parents of Mary and Anna). Sharing both sets of grandparents makes them double first cousins, a more specific term than regular first cousins.

X's mother and B are siblings, making B X's maternal uncle. X's father and S are siblings, making S X's paternal aunt. B and S marry and have Y. Y is therefore the child of X's maternal uncle (first‑cousin relationship) and also the child of X's paternal aunt (another first‑cousin relationship). Since the two cousin links are through both parental lines, Y is X's double first cousin, not a half or indeterminate relation.

M and N are brothers, so they share the same paternal grandparents. A and B are sisters, sharing the same maternal grandparents. X is child of M (brother) and A (sister); Y is child of N (brother) and B (sister). Thus X and Y have both sets of grandparents in common, making them first cousins through both parents—i.e., double first cousins.

Q is the sibling of M's mother, making Q the aunt/uncle of M. Since O is M's child, Q is one generation above O's parent, i.e., the sibling of O's grandparent. The standard term for a sibling of a grandparent is great-aunt or great-uncle.

M and N are siblings, so they share the same parents. Their children A and B are therefore first cousins, sharing those grandparents. C is A's child and D is B's child; thus C and D are each one generation removed from the first cousins. They share the great‑grandparents (the parents of M and N). Sharing great‑grandparents defines a second‑cousin relationship. Marriage between C and D does not alter the blood relation.

M has two first cousins: the child of his mother's only brother and the child of his father's only brother. Both are equally first cousins to M. Selecting one of these cousins (K) yields the same relation regardless of which cousin is chosen. Hence K is M's first cousin.

Mary and Anna are full sisters, sharing the same parents. Peter and Michael are full brothers, sharing the same parents. John is the child of Mary (sister of Anna) and Peter (brother of Michael). Lily is the child of Anna (sister of Mary) and Michael (brother of Peter). Consequently John and Lily have both sets of grandparents in common – the parents of Mary/Anna and the parents of Peter/Michael. Sharing both maternal and paternal grandparents makes them double first cousins, not merely half‑first or second cousins.

Ethan's father Adam and Fiona's father Brian are brothers, making Ethan and Fiona first cousins paternally. Likewise, Ethan's mother Clara and Fiona's mother Diana are sisters, making them first cousins maternally. Sharing both sets of grandparents qualifies them as double first cousins.

J and K are siblings, sharing the same parents (M and her spouse). L and N are also siblings, sharing their own parents. P is child of J and L; Q is child of K and N. Therefore P and Q each inherit one set of grandparents from J/K (the M side) and a second set from L/N. They share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins.

Mary is Tom's biological mother. Lily is Tom's child, making Lily the direct descendant of Mary through her son. This matches the standard term "granddaughter". No step or half relation applies because the lineage is biological on Mary's side.

K's father's sister is K's paternal aunt; K's mother's brother is K's maternal uncle. L is the child of that aunt and that uncle. Thus L is K's child of a paternal aunt (first cousin) and also child of a maternal uncle (first cousin). Because the two cousin relationships arise through both of K's parents, L is a double first cousin of K.

M's mother’s brother is M’s maternal uncle; his child is M’s first cousin. Likewise, M's father’s brother is M’s paternal uncle; his child is also M’s first cousin. Both possibilities give the same relationship, which is a standard first cousin. The other options do not match these definitions.

Alex's father has a sister Clara. Clara is Alex's paternal aunt. Clara's daughter Emma is therefore the child of Alex's aunt, making Emma Alex's first cousin. Emma is not a sibling (Alex's mother has only Alex) nor an aunt, and there is no half‑sibling relationship.

Adam and Ben are brothers, so they share the same paternal grandparents. Claire and Diana are sisters, sharing the same maternal grandparents. Ethan is the child of Adam (father) and Claire (mother); Fiona is the child of Ben (father) and Diana (mother). Therefore Ethan and Fiona share both sets of grandparents (paternal and maternal), making them first cousins on both sides. The precise term for this relationship is double first cousins.

My father's brother is my paternal uncle. His daughter is my first cousin. X is described as the son of that daughter, i.e., the child of my first cousin. The child of a first cousin is a first cousin once removed (one generation down). Hence X is my first cousin once removed.

M and N are siblings, so their children are first cousins. O is M's son and R is N's son, making O and R children of siblings. Marriage to Q does not change their blood relationship, which remains first cousins.

M's brother A is M's sibling, so A's child is M's niece or nephew. The child C is born to A (M's brother) and B, making C directly the offspring of M's sibling. Therefore, C is M's niece/nephew. This matches choice B.

M is parent of D. D is father of C, making C the child of M's son, i.e., M's grandchild. The marriage to B (M's nephew) does not change the biological relationship. Among the choices, only "Granddaughter" matches this relationship.

M’s mother and N’s father are siblings, so they share one pair of grandparents. Likewise, M’s father and N’s mother are siblings, sharing a second pair of grandparents. Thus M and N have both sets of grandparents in common, meaning they are first cousins through both parental lines – the definition of double first cousins.

M’s mother is the sister of L’s father, making M a first cousin of L on the paternal side. M’s father is the brother of L’s mother, making M a first cousin of L on the maternal side. Because the two cousins are related through both parents, M is a double first cousin of L.

Tom and Sam are brothers, so they share the same parents. Lily and Maya are sisters, sharing the same parents. Peter is the child of Tom (brother) and Lily (sister), while Paula is the child of Sam (brother) and Maya (sister). Thus Peter and Paula are first cousins through their fathers and also first cousins through their mothers. Because they are first cousins on both paternal and maternal sides, they are double first cousins.

Tom and Sam are brothers, so they share the same parents (paternal grandparents of Mike and Nina). Anne and Beth are sisters, sharing the same parents (maternal grandparents of Mike and Nina). Each child’s father is the brother of the other child’s father, and each child’s mother is the sister of the other child’s mother. Thus Mike and Nina share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins, the most precise term.

R's mother has one brother, making him R's maternal uncle. P, as his child, is R's first cousin. R's father has one sister, his paternal aunt. Q, as her child, is also R's first cousin. Since S is either P or Q, S is necessarily R's first cousin. The relationship is uniquely determined.

A and B share the same mother (M). A’s son C and B’s daughter D are M’s grandchildren. C and D’s child E is therefore a generation below C and D, making M a generation above E by three steps: M → A/B → C/D → E. This is the definition of a great‑grandparent relationship. Hence the precise term for E’s relation to A’s mother is great‑grandmother.

S is P's maternal aunt (mother's sister) and B is P's paternal uncle (father's brother). Their child M is therefore the child of P's aunt on the mother's side and also the child of P's uncle on the father's side. M is thus a first cousin through the maternal line and simultaneously a first cousin through the paternal line. Sharing both sets of grandparents makes them double first cousins.
M’s father’s sister is M’s paternal aunt. The aunt’s children are the children of the father’s sibling, making them M’s first cousins. Therefore P, as another child of the aunt, is M’s first cousin.

John, Mary, and Tom are siblings. Mary’s son Peter is the child of John’s sister, making Peter John’s nephew. Tom’s daughter Lisa is the child of John’s brother, making Lisa John’s niece. Since Peter and Lisa are each the children of two siblings (Mary and Tom), they are each other's first cousins.

X’s mother and Y are siblings, making Y X’s maternal uncle. Z is Y’s daughter, i.e., the child of X’s uncle. In standard kinship terms, the child of one’s uncle/aunt is a first cousin. No other relationships fit given monogamy and no adoptions.

Tom is Emma's maternal uncle (her mother's brother) and Lucy is Emma's paternal aunt (her father's sister). Their son Victor is therefore Emma's child of her maternal uncle (first cousin) and also the child of her paternal aunt (another first cousin). Being first cousins through both parental lines makes Victor a double first cousin of Emma.

X and Y are first cousins through their fathers, who are brothers, and also first cousins through their mothers, who are sisters. Sharing both paternal and maternal grandparents makes them double first cousins, the most precise standard term.

L's mother’s brother is L’s maternal uncle, so M (his child) is L’s maternal first cousin. L's father’s sister is L’s paternal aunt, so N (her child) is L’s paternal first cousin. The two parents (maternal uncle and paternal aunt) are from separate families and have no blood connection, so their children M and N share no common ancestor. Hence M and N have no blood relation.

R is married to S. S’s sister T is R’s sister‑in‑law. T’s husband U is therefore also R’s brother‑in‑law (spouse of his sister‑in‑law). V is U’s brother, i.e., the brother of R’s brother‑in‑law. This makes V related to R only through a chain of affinal connections; there is no standard direct term such as brother‑in‑law, cousin‑in‑law, or nephew‑in‑law for this relationship.

R's father's sister is R's paternal aunt; her son S is R's first cousin. R's mother's brother is R's maternal uncle; his daughter T is also R's first cousin. Thus S and T are each R's first cousins from different sides. The child C of S and T is the offspring of R's first cousins. By standard kinship, the child of one's first cousin is a first cousin once removed. No other special term applies, so C is R's first cousin once removed.

Adam and Brian are brothers, so their children X and Y share the same paternal grandparents. Clara and Diana are sisters, so X and Y also share the same maternal grandparents. Sharing both sets of grandparents makes X and Y double first cousins, the most precise term.

Alex’s mother’s brother is Alex’s maternal uncle; his daughter Maya is the child of Alex’s uncle, making Maya a first cousin. Alex’s father’s sister is Alex’s paternal aunt; her son Noah is the child of Alex’s aunt, also a first cousin. Whether Sam is Maya or Noah, the relationship to Alex is the same: first cousin. Hence the kinship is uniquely determined as a first cousin.

R's maternal uncle's child X is the child of R's mother's brother, making X a first cousin of R. Similarly, R's paternal uncle's child Y is the child of R's father's brother, also a first cousin of R. Whether Z is X or Y, Z is always R's first cousin. Hence the relation is uniquely first cousin.

John and Mary are half‑siblings, sharing a single parent. Their children, Alan and Beth, each inherit that shared parent as a grandparent. Because they have only one common grandparent (instead of a full pair), they are cousins who share half of the grandparental lineage, i.e., half‑first cousins. The relationship is determinable, so the correct choice is A.

John's mother Mary and Anna's father Tom are siblings, making Anna John’s first cousin through Mary’s side. Likewise, John's father Peter and Anna's mother Lisa are siblings, making Anna John’s first cousin through Peter’s side. Because the two cousins are related through both parental lines, they share both sets of grandparents, which is the definition of double first cousins. Hence the most precise term is double first cousin.

Greg is Adam's grandson because Adam's son Ethan is Greg's father. He is also Adam's great‑nephew because Adam's brother Brian's daughter Fiona (Adam's niece) is Greg's mother, making Greg the child of Adam's niece. Both relations hold, so the most precise term must reflect the double relationship.

A and B are described only as "siblings"; they may be full siblings or half‑siblings. If they are full siblings, their children L and M are first cousins. If they are half‑siblings, L and M are half‑first cousins. Because the information does not specify which case holds, the precise relationship cannot be uniquely determined.

A and B are full brothers, so X and Y each have a father who is a sibling of the other's father, making them first cousins paternally. C and D are full sisters, so X and Y also have mothers who are sibling to each other's mother, making them first cousins maternally as well. Because they are first cousins through both parents, they are double first cousins, the most specific term.

R’s paternal aunt is his father’s sister. R’s maternal uncle is his mother’s brother. The son is described as both the aunt’s son and the uncle’s son, meaning the aunt and the uncle are the child’s parents. Thus the father’s sister married the mother’s brother. Their child shares both sets of grandparents with R, making him a double first cousin (cousin through both the paternal and maternal lines).

John and Mary are siblings, so their children (Peter and Lisa) are first cousins. Tom is Lisa's son, placing him one generation below Lisa. Therefore Peter is a generation above Tom and is the first cousin of Tom's parent, making Peter and Tom first cousins once removed. The uncle‑nephew relationship would require Peter to be a sibling of Tom's parent, which he is not.

John and Peter are brothers; Mary and Anna are sisters. John marries Mary, and Peter marries Anna. Their children, Mark (John & Mary) and Lily (Peter & Anna), share both sets of grandparents: the parents of John/Peter and the parents of Mary/Anna. Sharing both paternal and maternal grandparents makes them double first cousins, not just regular first cousins.

M and N are siblings, so they share the same two parents (grandparents of X and Y). O and P are also siblings, sharing another two parents (the other set of grandparents). X is child of M and O; Y is child of N and P. Therefore X and Y have both sets of grandparents in common. This matches the definition of double first cousins, who share all four grandparents, unlike regular first cousins (one set) or half‑first cousins (one parent in common). Hence the most precise term is double first cousins.

A's mother’s brother is A's maternal uncle; his son B is A's maternal first cousin. A's father’s sister is A's paternal aunt; her daughter C is A's paternal first cousin. Both B and C are first cousins of A, regardless of which is chosen as D. Hence D's relation to A is a first cousin.

Adam and Brian are full brothers, sharing the same parents. Clara and Diana are full sisters, sharing the same parents. Ethan's parents are Adam (brother) and Clara (sister), while Fiona's parents are Brian (brother) and Diana (sister). Thus Ethan and Fiona share both sets of grandparents—the grandparents of Adam/Brian and the grandparents of Clara/Diana—making them cousins through two distinct sibling links. This is the definition of double first cousins, more specific than regular first cousins.

X's father A and Y's father C are brothers, making X and Y first cousins through their fathers. Likewise, X's mother B and Y's mother D are sisters, also making X and Y first cousins through their mothers. Being first cousins on both paternal and maternal sides defines a double first‑cousin relationship, the most precise term.

M and N are siblings, so they share the same parents. O and P are also siblings, sharing another set of parents. X is the child of M (one sibling) and O (the other sibling pair). Y is the child of N (the sibling of M) and P (the sibling of O). Hence X and Y have both sets of grandparents in common, making them first cousins through both parental lines—i.e., double first cousins.

K's father’s sister is K’s paternal aunt; K's mother’s brother is K’s maternal uncle. Their child M is therefore the offspring of K’s aunt and uncle, making M a first cousin on the paternal side and also a first cousin on the maternal side (a double first cousin). The appropriate standard term is first cousin.

M is R's maternal uncle (mother's brother) and S is R's paternal aunt (father's sister). Their child C is the offspring of both an uncle and an aunt of R, each from opposite parental lines. C therefore shares R's maternal grandparents (through M) and R's paternal grandparents (through S). Sharing both sets of grandparents makes C a double first cousin of R, the most precise kinship term.

M and N are full siblings, so they share the same set of grandparents. A and B are also full siblings, sharing another set of grandparents. X’s father M is sibling to Y’s father N, making X and Y first cousins through their fathers. Simultaneously, X’s mother A is sibling to Y’s mother B, making X and Y first cousins through their mothers as well. Because they are first cousins on both parental lines, they share both sets of grandparents, which is the definition of double first cousins.

L’s father’s sister is L’s paternal aunt. Her only son is L’s first cousin. The child of that cousin (M) is one generation below L, making M the child of L’s cousin. In standard kinship terminology, a cousin’s child is a first cousin once removed.

G and H share only one parent (their mother), making them half‑siblings. Their children, I and J, each descend from one of those half‑siblings. Therefore I and J share exactly one grandparent (the mother of G and H) but not both grandparents. In kinship terminology, children of half‑siblings are called half‑first cousins. This matches option C.

A is father of B and C, so A's spouse is C's mother. D's mother‑in‑law is the mother of D's spouse C, thus D's mother‑in‑law (E) is C's mother, i.e., A's wife. E's brother (F) is therefore the brother of A's wife, making F A's brother‑in‑law.

M is the mother of A, making M the grandparent of C through A. M is also the sister of N, making M the aunt of B, and thus the great‑aunt of C through B. The direct line (grandparent) is more precise than the collateral line, so the most specific standard term is Grandmother (also great‑aunt).

M is mother of O. O’s child is R, making M R’s grandmother. Q is married to R, so Q’s spouse’s grandmother is M. In kinship terms, the parent of one’s spouse is a mother‑in‑law; analogously, the grandparent of one’s spouse is a grandmother‑in‑law. Therefore M is Q’s grandmother‑in‑law.

Beth is the daughter of John and Linda; Carl is the son of Mary and Peter. John and Mary were previously married but share no blood with each other's new spouses. Beth and Carl have no common parent or grandparent, so they are not cousins or half‑cousins. They are not step‑siblings because step‑siblings are children of a parent's current spouse, and John is not married to Mary now. Therefore there is no blood relation.

P and Q are children of two brothers who married two sisters. Their fathers are siblings, making them first cousins paternally, and their mothers are siblings, making them first cousins maternally. Sharing both sets of grandparents yields the doubled version of first cousins, i.e., double first cousins.

M and N are half‑siblings, sharing one parent. Each child inherits two grandparents: one from the shared parent and one from the other parent. Thus P and Q share only the single grandparent that M and N share, not both grandparents. Children who share exactly one grandparent are termed half‑first cousins. Therefore the precise kinship term is half‑first cousins.

M and N are full siblings; O and P are full siblings. X is child of M (parent from first sibling pair) and O (parent from second sibling pair). Y is child of N (the other sibling of M) and P (the other sibling of O). Thus X and Y each have the same two sets of grandparents: the parents of M/N and the parents of O/P. Sharing both sets of grandparents makes them double first cousins, the most precise term.

M and N are siblings, so they share the same parents. O and P are also siblings, sharing another set of parents. X is child of M (one sibling) and O (the other sibling), while Y is child of N (the first sibling) and P (the second sibling). Thus X and Y have the same paternal grandparents (the parents of M and N) and the same maternal grandparents (the parents of O and P). Sharing both sets of grandparents makes them double first cousins, the most specific term.

Carl and Dan each have a father who is a brother of the other's father, and a mother who is a sister of the other's mother. Thus they share both sets of grandparents (paternal and maternal). Sharing both grandparents makes them first cousins on two separate lines, i.e., double first cousins.

M and N share the same parents, and X and Y share another set of parents. Each child inherits one set of grandparents from the M/N side and the other set from the X/Y side. Therefore A and B share both pairs of grandparents, making them double first cousins, the most precise term.

M's mother has one brother (maternal uncle) who is married to X's mother. Thus X is the child of M's maternal uncle, making X a first cousin on the maternal side. M's father has one sister (paternal aunt) who is X's other parent, so X is also the child of M's paternal aunt, making X a first cousin on the paternal side as well. Since X is a first cousin to M through both parents, the precise term is "double first cousin."

John and Mary are siblings, so their children are first cousins. Lisa and Mark are also siblings, making their children first cousins as well. Since X’s father (John) is sibling to Y’s mother (Mary) and X’s mother (Lisa) is sibling to Y’s father (Mark), X and Y share both sets of grandparents. This dual link makes them double first cousins, the most precise term among the choices.

L's paternal uncle (father's brother) and L's maternal aunt (mother's sister) are the parents of M. Thus M is the child of L's father's sibling, making M a first cousin on the paternal side, and simultaneously the child of L's mother's sibling, making M a first cousin on the maternal side. Because the two cousin relationships involve both sets of grandparents, M and L are double first cousins, the most specific term.

M and N are siblings, sharing grandparents A and B. P and Q are siblings, sharing grandparents C and D. X is child of M (child of A&B) and P (child of C&D). Y is child of N (child of A&B) and Q (child of C&D). Therefore X and Y share both sets of grandparents, making them first cousins through each parental line. This is the definition of double first cousins, not half or second cousins.

Tom and Jerry are brothers, and Anna and Beth are sisters. Their children, Peter (Tom + Anna) and Paula (Jerry + Beth), therefore have both sets of grandparents in common: the parents of Tom/Jerry and the parents of Anna/Beth. This makes them double first cousins, the most precise term.

John and Mary are siblings. Mary’s daughter Susan and John’s son Tom are therefore first cousins. Lily is Tom’s daughter, one generation below Tom. A child of a first cousin is a first cousin once removed. Hence Susan is Lily’s first cousin once removed.

N’s father’s sister (F) is N’s paternal aunt; her child X is N’s paternal first cousin. N’s mother’s brother (M) is N’s maternal uncle; his child X is N’s maternal first cousin. Since X is the same individual, X is the child of both F and M, meaning X is related to N through both the paternal and maternal lines. This situation—children of two siblings who marry each other—creates a double first‑cousin relationship.

M and S are siblings, sharing the same parents. W and N are siblings, sharing another set of parents. D is child of M (one sibling) and W (the other sibling), while C is child of S (the first sibling) and N (the other sibling). Thus D and C each descend from both sets of grandparents: the parents of M/S and the parents of W/N. Sharing both pairs of grandparents makes them first cousins on two distinct lines, i.e., double first cousins.

A is the daughter of M's maternal uncle (mother's brother), making her M's first cousin on the maternal side. B is the daughter of M's paternal uncle (father's brother), making her M's first cousin on the paternal side. Both relationships are standard first cousin connections; no half‑sibling or generational differences are indicated. Therefore, whichever individual (A or B) is considered X, X is M's first cousin.

K’s father (F) has a sister (S). L is described as the mother of S. Since S is the sister of F, they share the same parents. Therefore L is the mother of both F and S, i.e., the mother of K’s father. That role is K’s grandmother.

Adam and Brian are brothers, so their children share the same paternal grandparents. Clara and Diana are sisters, so their children share the same maternal grandparents. Thus Ethan and Fiona share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins, the most precise term among the options.
Alice's brother Tom is Emma's maternal uncle. Tom's son Ben is Emma's first cousin. Ben's daughter Clara is one generation below Emma's cousin, making her Emma's first cousin once removed.

P’s mother is sibling of Q’s father, making P and Q first cousins through that line. Likewise, P’s father is sibling of Q’s mother, giving another first‑cousin link. With both parental pairs being siblings, P and Q share both sets of grandparents, which is exactly the definition of double first cousins. No other relationship (e.g., half‑sibling) fits, so the most precise term is double first cousins.

Y’s father’s brother Z is Y’s paternal uncle, making Z’s daughter W Y’s first cousin. X is married to Y, so X is the spouse of Y’s cousin. Standard kinship terms for in‑law relations are limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, and children’s spouses; there is no accepted term for a spouse’s cousin. Therefore W is related to X only via an affinal chain, with no direct standard term.

U is X's maternal uncle. W, U's spouse, is X's aunt by marriage. W's brother B is therefore sibling of X's aunt-in-law. Separately, B is married to the sister of X's father, i.e., to X's paternal aunt. The husband of one's father's sister is conventionally called an uncle-in-law (paternal uncle by marriage). This gives a standard kinship term, so B is an uncle-in-law to X.

Mary has two children: John’s mother and Peter. Therefore Peter is John’s maternal uncle. Peter’s daughter Susan is thus John’s first cousin. Tom is Susan’s son, making him the child of John’s first cousin. In kinship terms, the child of a first cousin is a first cousin once removed.

Ethan’s father Adam and Fiona’s father Brian are brothers, making Ethan and Fiona first cousins on their paternal side. Likewise, Ethan’s mother Clara and Fiona’s mother Diana are sisters, making them first cousins on their maternal side as well. Sharing both sets of grandparents, they are cousins through two sibling pairs, i.e., double first cousins, which is the most specific kinship term.

A and B share the same mother but have different fathers, making them half‑siblings. B's child C is therefore the child of A's half‑sibling. In kinship terminology the child of a half‑sibling is called a half‑niece or half‑nephew. Hence C's relation to A is a half‑niece/nephew.

John and Mary are double first cousins, meaning they share both sets of grandparents. Their children (Alan and Brian) therefore share both sets of great‑grandparents, which is the definition of double second cousins. Hence the most precise term is double second cousins.

B is A's parent. B's sister C is A's aunt. C's daughter D is therefore A's first cousin. D's son E is the child of A's first cousin, which makes E A's first cousin once removed. No half‑sibling or in‑law relationships are involved.

M and N are half‑siblings because they share exactly one parent. Their children P and Q each inherit that shared parent as a grandparent. Thus P and Q have one common grandparent but not the other, making them first cousins who share only half of the grandparental lineage. The standard term for this relationship is "half‑first cousins".

John and Mark are brothers, so their children share one set of paternal grandparents. Anna and Beth are sisters, so their children share one set of maternal grandparents. Carl and Dana thus share both paternal and maternal grandparents, making them first cousins through two distinct sibling pairs. The term that captures this doubled relationship is "double first cousins," which is more precise than simply first cousins.

Lily's father John and Mark's mother Mary are full siblings, making Lily and Mark first cousins through that side. Simultaneously, Lily's mother Anna and Mark's father Ben are also full siblings, creating a second first‑cousin link. Because the two children are related as first cousins on both parental lines, they are double first cousins.
M's son D is a child of M. C is described as D's daughter, making C a child of M's child. Therefore C is a grandchild of M. Since C is female, the precise kinship term is "granddaughter".

H and J share only their father G, making them half‑siblings. Their children X (child of H) and Y (child of J) therefore share only one grandparent (G). Cousins who share both grandparents are first cousins; when only one grandparent is shared, they are called half‑first cousins. Hence X and Y are half‑first cousins.

Y’s mother has an only sister – a maternal aunt. X is her child, making X Y’s first cousin on the maternal side. Y’s father has an only brother – a paternal uncle. X is also that uncle’s child, making X Y’s first cousin on the paternal side. Since the same X is child of both the maternal aunt and the paternal uncle (a married couple), X shares both sets of grandparents with Y, which is the definition of a double first cousin.

Half‑siblings share one parent. That parent is a grandparent to each of their children. The children therefore share exactly one grandparent, not both. In kinship terminology, children of half‑siblings are called half‑first cousins (they are first cousins through a single shared grandparent). Thus the precise term is half‑first cousins.

L's mother’s brother is L’s maternal uncle. His only daughter is L’s first cousin. That daughter’s child M is the child of L’s first cousin, which by standard kinship terminology is a first cousin once removed.

X and Y are each the child of a pair of siblings: A and B are brothers, C and D are sisters. Therefore X and Y share both sets of grandparents (the parents of A/B and the parents of C/D). This makes them first cousins through two distinct lines, i.e., double first cousins, not half or second cousins.

Aaron and Ben are brothers, so they share the same parents. Clara and Diana are sisters, sharing the same parents. Each child of Aaron has as grandparents the parents of Aaron (paternal) and the parents of Clara (maternal). Each child of Ben has the same paternal grandparents (parents of Aaron/Ben) and the same maternal grandparents (parents of Clara/Diana). Thus the two children share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins, the precise term for cousins whose parents are siblings on both sides.

M and N share the same parents, and X and Y share another set of parents. Each child inherits one parent from each sibling pair. Thus A and B have both sets of grandparents in common, making them double first cousins, the most precise term.

M and S are siblings; W and N are siblings. M marries W, while S marries N. C is the child of M + W; D is the child of S + N. C’s paternal grandparents are M’s parents, which are also D’s paternal grandparents (since S shares those parents). C’s maternal grandparents are W’s parents, which are also D’s maternal grandparents (since N shares those parents). Thus C and D share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins.

X's mother’s brother is X's maternal uncle. His spouse Y together have a son Z, who is the uncle's biological child, making Z X's first cousin. Z's daughter W is the child of X's first cousin, which by standard kinship terminology is a first cousin once removed. Hence the correct choice is A.

John and Mary are siblings, so their children Alice and Carol are first cousins. Dave is Carol's child, one generation below Carol. Therefore Alice is the first cousin of Dave's parent, making her Dave's first cousin once removed.

Q is P's mother. Q's brother R is P's maternal uncle. R's daughter S is the child of P's uncle, making S P's first cousin. S's son T is the child of P's first cousin, which defines a first cousin once removed relationship (one generation down). Therefore T is P's first cousin once removed.

A's mother and B's father are siblings, making A and B first cousins (children of siblings). A's daughter C is one generation down from A, so C is the child of B's first cousin. In kinship terms, the child of a cousin is a first cousin once removed. The relationship is uniquely determined.

N's father’s brother is N’s paternal uncle; his child X is a first cousin of N. N's mother’s sister is N’s maternal aunt; her child Y is also a first cousin of N. Since X and Y are the same individual, that child must be the offspring of the paternal uncle and the maternal aunt, i.e., the two siblings from opposite parental families married each other. Consequently the child shares both sets of grandparents with N, making the relationship a double first cousin rather than a simple first cousin or a more distant cousin.

Sam is the child of Lily, who is John’s daughter, making Sam John’s grandchild. Though Sam is also the child of Peter (John’s nephew), the direct line relation (grandchild) is the primary standard term used.

M is the child of N's father's only sister, making M a paternal first cousin. Simultaneously, M is the child of N's mother's only brother, making M a maternal first cousin. Being both a paternal and maternal first cousin means M and N share both sets of grandparents, which is precisely a double first cousin relationship.

M and N are full siblings, and X and Y are full siblings. A is the child of M (one sibling) and X (the other sibling), while B is the child of N (M's sibling) and Y (X's sibling). Thus A and B are first cousins through both their fathers and their mothers, making them double first cousins, the most precise term.

M's mother is the sister of N's father, making M N's paternal first cousin. M's father is the brother of N's mother, making M N's maternal first cousin. Since M is a first cousin to N through both parental lines, they are double first cousins.

Statement 1 says P's parent is the only brother of Q's mother, i.e., P's father is Q's maternal uncle. Statement 2 says Q's mother is the only sister of P's father, i.e., Q's mother is P's paternal aunt. In both cases each is the child of the other's parent's sibling, which defines first cousins. No other relationship fits given the constraints.

X's mother's brother is X's maternal uncle; his daughter Y is X's first cousin. X's father's sister is X's paternal aunt; her son Z is also X's first cousin. The marriage between Y and Z does not change the blood relationship between X and Z. Therefore Z is X's first cousin.

A and B are siblings, sharing both parents P1 and P2. C and D are siblings, sharing both parents Q1 and Q2. X is child of A (parent from P1‑P2) and C (parent from Q1‑Q2). Y is child of B (also from P1‑P2) and D (also from Q1‑Q2). Therefore X and Y have the same paternal grandparents (P1, P2) and the same maternal grandparents (Q1, Q2). Sharing both sets of grandparents makes them double first cousins, the most precise term among the options.

The only sibling of N’s father is N’s paternal aunt/uncle; their child would be N’s paternal first cousin. Likewise, the only sibling of N’s mother is N’s maternal aunt/uncle; their child would be N’s maternal first cousin. M is the child of both those siblings, meaning the paternal sibling and maternal sibling are married to each other and have a child together. Thus M is simultaneously N’s first cousin on the father’s side and on the mother’s side – a double first cousin.

M and N are siblings, sharing the same parents. O, P, and Q are siblings, sharing another set of parents. X is the child of M (from the first family) and O (from the second family). Y is the child of N (M's sibling) and Q (O's sibling). Therefore X and Y each have the same paternal grandparents (parents of M and N) and the same maternal grandparents (parents of O and Q). Sharing both sets of grandparents makes them double first cousins, not merely first cousins or half‑first cousins.

Nina is married to Mark, who is Peter's brother, making Mark John's paternal uncle by blood. The spouse of an uncle is conventionally referred to as an aunt (by marriage). Since the relationship is through marriage rather than blood, the precise term is aunt-in-law.

M and N are siblings, so their children (A, D, and B) are first cousins. D is the father of C, making C the niece of D's sister A. Thus A and C are related by blood as aunt and niece. The marital link between B and C does not affect the blood relationship, and there is no half‑relationship indicated, so the correct term is aunt/niece.

M and N are siblings, and O and P are siblings. X is child of M (sibling of N) and O (sibling of P). Y is child of N (sibling of M) and P (sibling of O). Hence X and Y are first cousins through the O‑P sibling pair and also first cousins through the M‑N sibling pair. Sharing both sets of grandparents makes them double first cousins, not merely first, half‑first, or second cousins.

R’s mother’s sister is R’s maternal aunt; her son is R’s maternal first cousin. R’s father’s brother is R’s paternal uncle; his daughter is R’s paternal first cousin. The two cousins (one maternal, one paternal) have a child X. A child of any first cousin is a first cousin once removed of the original person, regardless of which cousin is the parent. Therefore X is R’s first cousin once removed.

M and N are half‑siblings, sharing only one parent (their mother). Their respective children A and B each inherit that shared parent as a grandparent. Thus A and B have exactly one common grandparent, not a full set of two. Cousins who share both grandparents are first cousins; those who share only one are termed half‑first cousins. No other relationship can be inferred, so the precise term is half‑first cousins.

Adam and Ben are brothers, so their children share the same paternal grandparents. Clara and Diana are sisters, so their children also share the same maternal grandparents. Thus the two children are related through both parental lines, making them cousins who are first cousins on both sides—a relationship known as double first cousins.

John is Michael's sibling and Emma is David's sibling. John marries Emma, Michael marries David. Their children Alice and Bob each have one parent from each sibling pair, making Alice and Bob double first cousins. Carl, as Alice's son, is one generation below Alice, so he is the child of Bob's first cousin, i.e., first cousin once removed.

John and Mark are brothers sharing the same parents, and Anna and Beth are sisters sharing the same parents. Their children X and Y thus share both sets of grandparents (paternal and maternal). This makes them first cousins on both sides, i.e., double first cousins, the most precise kinship term among the options.

M and N are siblings. Their children D and B are first cousins. C is D's daughter, i.e., one generation below D. A first cousin once removed is defined as the child of one's cousin (or the cousin of one's parent). Since B is the cousin of C's parent D, B is C's first cousin once removed.

Emma and Liam have the same mother but different fathers, making them half‑siblings. Their children, Zoe and Noah, are the offspring of half‑siblings, so they share only one grandparent (the common mother). Children of half‑siblings are termed half‑first cousins, distinguishing them from full first cousins who share both grandparents.

M and N are siblings, so their children X and Y are first cousins through that side. P and Q are also siblings, making X and Y first cousins through the other side as well. Because the two children share both sets of grandparents, they are cousins on two distinct parental lines, i.e., double first cousins.

M's mother is the only sister of N's father, making her N's paternal aunt. M's father is the only brother of N's mother, making him N's maternal uncle. Therefore M is the child of both N's paternal aunt and maternal uncle, meaning M and N are children of two pairs of siblings. This yields the relationship of double first cousins, the most precise term.

X's paternal aunt's child (C1) and maternal uncle's child (C2) are each X's first cousins. Y is the son of those first cousins. The child of a first cousin is a first cousin once removed. This holds for both parental lines, and no closer relationship (e.g., sibling) applies.

X is the child of Y's maternal uncle (the only brother of Y's mother) and also the child of Y's paternal aunt (the only sister of Y's father). These two are X's parents, meaning X's father is Y's maternal uncle and X's mother is Y's paternal aunt. Consequently X shares both sets of grandparents with Y, making them first cousins on both the maternal and paternal sides—a double first cousin relationship.

Adam is Ethan's father, making Greg (Ethan's child) Adam's grandson. Adam is also Ben's brother, so Ben's daughter Fiona is Adam's niece. Fiona's child Greg is therefore Adam's great‑nephew (child of a niece). Both blood relations hold simultaneously, so Greg is both grandson and great‑nephew.

A is X's mother's brother, i.e., X's maternal uncle. B is A's daughter, making B the child of X's uncle. In standard kinship terms, the child of one's uncle or aunt is a first cousin. The later marriage between B and D (X's paternal cousin) does not alter the blood relationship between B and X.

A's father and B's father are half‑brothers, sharing only one parent (their father). Therefore A and B share only that one grandparent, not a full pair of grandparents. Children of half‑siblings are termed half‑first cousins, reflecting the single common grandparent. Hence the most precise kinship term is half‑first cousins.

M’s mother’s sister is M’s maternal aunt. She is married to a man who is the brother of M’s father. The brother of one’s father is a paternal uncle. Hence the man’s kinship to M is that of a paternal uncle, matching choice A.

Brian is Ethan's father’s father, making Ethan his grandson. Although Ethan is also the child of Brian's niece (a great‑nephew relationship), the direct line through his son defines the precise relationship as grandson.

M is X's maternal uncle, so his daughter Y is X's first cousin. S is X's paternal aunt, so her son Z is also X's first cousin. W is the child of X's first cousins (both Y and Z). The child of a first cousin is a first cousin once removed. Hence W is X's first cousin once removed.

M and F are siblings, sharing the same parents. W1 and M2 are also siblings, sharing another set of parents. C1 is the child of M (one of the siblings) and W1 (one of the other siblings). C2 is the child of F (the other sibling) and M2 (the other sibling). Therefore C1 and C2 have the same paternal grandparents (parents of M and F) and the same maternal grandparents (parents of W1 and M2). Sharing both sets of grandparents makes them double first cousins, not siblings because they have different parents.

M and N are siblings, so they share the same paternal grandparents. O and P are siblings, sharing the same maternal grandparents. X is child of M (paternal side) and O (maternal side); Y is child of N (paternal side) and P (maternal side). Therefore X and Y share both sets of grandparents, making them first cousins through both parental lines—i.e., double first cousins.

M and N share the same parents (A & B). O and P share another set of parents (C & D). X is child of M (A&B) and O (C&D); Y is child of N (A&B) and P (C&D). Thus X and Y have both A&B as paternal grandparents and C&D as maternal grandparents. They are first cousins through both parental lines, i.e., double first cousins, the most precise term among the choices.

L has one brother and one sister, each with one child. The brother's child is L's niece/nephew; that child's child (M) is the grandchild of the brother, making M L's grandniece/grandnephew. Similarly, the sister's child is L's niece/nephew; that child's child (N) is also L's grandniece/grandnephew. Thus whether X is M or N, X holds the same precise kinship: grandniece or grandnephew.

M's maternal uncle T's daughter L is M's first cousin. M's paternal aunt S's son K is also M's first cousin. L and K (both first cousins of M) have a child Z. The child of a first cousin is a first cousin once removed. Since Z is the child of two of M's first cousins, the appropriate standard term remains first cousin once removed.

M is the child of P's paternal aunt (father's sister) and also the child of P's maternal uncle (mother's brother). Since those two parents are married, M is linked to P through both the father's side and the mother's side, each relationship being that of first cousins. Being first cousins on both parental lines makes M a double first cousin of P. The other options do not match this configuration.
A is parent of C, making E the grandchild of A via C. A is also sibling of B, so B's son D is A's nephew; D's child E is therefore A's grand‑nephew/niece. Hence E holds both relationships to A.

R's spouse is S. S's brother is T, making T R's brother-in-law. T's wife U is therefore R's sister-in-law (spouse's sibling's spouse). V is U's sister, i.e., the sister of R's sister-in-law. English kinship does not have a standard term for the sibling of an in‑law; it is not an aunt, cousin, or half‑sibling by any conventional definition. Hence the relation falls outside standard direct kinship terms.

Alex's mother’s brother is Alex’s maternal uncle; his daughter Diana is the child of that uncle, making Diana a first cousin of Alex. Alex’s father’s sister is Alex’s paternal aunt; her son Edward is the child of that aunt, also a first cousin of Alex. Regardless of whether S is Diana or Edward, S is Alex’s first cousin. The relationship is uniquely determined as first cousin.

M's mother’s brother is M’s maternal uncle. His wife (the woman) is M’s aunt by marriage. The woman’s sister is identified as M’s father’s sister, i.e., M’s paternal aunt. The question asks for the kinship term of that sister (the paternal aunt) to M. The correct term is "aunt" (specifically, father’s sister).

Let S be N’s spouse. S’s mother (M1) has a brother B, who is S’s maternal uncle. M is described as the brother of B, so M is also a sibling of M1, i.e., another brother of S’s mother. Therefore M is also a maternal uncle of S. To N, this makes M the uncle of N’s spouse, which is the standard term “uncle‑in‑law”. The other options do not match this relationship.

L’s sister’s son X is L’s nephew; L’s brother’s daughter Y is L’s niece. X and Y are first cousins (children of L’s siblings). Their child M is the grandchild of L’s sister and brother, making M the child of L’s nephew/niece. The child of one’s niece or nephew is a great‑niece or great‑nephew. Hence M is L’s great‑niece/nephew.

Alan is Beth's maternal uncle (brother of her mother) and Clara is Beth's paternal aunt (sister of her father). Their child Dana is therefore the child of Beth's maternal uncle, making Dana a first cousin on the mother's side, and also the child of Beth's paternal aunt, making Dana a first cousin on the father's side. Because Dana is first cousin to Beth through both parental lines, they share all four grandparents, which defines a double first cousin relationship.

Lisa is John’s daughter, so her son Sam is John’s grandson. Peter is Mary’s son, making him John’s nephew; Peter’s child is therefore John’s great‑nephew (grandnephew). Sam is simultaneously John’s grandson (through Lisa) and great‑nephew (through Peter). Because two distinct standard kinship terms apply, no single term uniquely captures the relationship.

R's mother has exactly one brother, making that brother R's maternal uncle. The uncle's only child, A, is the child of R's aunt/uncle, which by definition is a first cousin of R. Similarly, R's father has exactly one sister, the paternal aunt, whose only child B is also the child of R's aunt/uncle, making B a first cousin of R. Since both possible choices (A or B) are first cousins, X's relation to R is uniquely a first cousin.

R's mother’s brother is R’s maternal uncle. His daughter is R’s first cousin. The child of that cousin is one generation down, making it R’s first cousin once removed. The relationship is uniquely determined.

S and B are siblings, so their children C₁ and C₂ are first cousins. M is the child of C₁ and N is the child of C₂. Children of first cousins are second cousins, because they share the same great‑grandparents (the parents of L). Therefore M and N are second cousins.

X’s mother is the sister of Y’s mother, making X and Y first cousins on the maternal side. X’s father is the brother of Y’s father, making them first cousins on the paternal side as well. Since both of X’s parents are the respective siblings of Y’s parents, X is related to Y through both lines, which is the definition of a double first cousin. No other intermarriages are allowed, so this is the most precise term.

X's father's sister is X's paternal aunt. Her daughter Y is X's first cousin. Z is Y's son, i.e., the child of X's first cousin. In English kinship, the child of a first cousin is a first cousin once removed. The relationship is uniquely determined under the given constraints.

Y’s father’s sister is Y’s paternal aunt; Y’s mother’s brother is Y’s maternal uncle. X is the child of both the aunt and the uncle, meaning they are married. X therefore shares Y’s paternal grandparents (through the aunt) and Y’s maternal grandparents (through the uncle). Sharing both sets of grandparents makes X a double first cousin of Y, the most specific term among the choices.

Emily's mother and Carl are siblings, making Carl Emily's maternal uncle. Carl's daughter Fiona is therefore Emily's first cousin. Greg is Fiona's son, placing him one generation below Emily's first cousin. The appropriate term for a child of one's cousin is "first cousin once removed."

M and N are full siblings, so X and Y share the same paternal grandparents. O and P are also full siblings, so X and Y share the same maternal grandparents. Thus X and Y have both sets of grandparents in common, making them children of two sibling pairs – the definition of double first cousins, which is more specific than regular first cousins.
John, Michael, and Mary are siblings. Peter is Mary's son, Susan is Michael's daughter. Children of siblings are first cousins. No half‑relationship is indicated, so they are standard first cousins.

Maya’s parent and Nikhil’s parent are half‑siblings, meaning they share exactly one grandparent. Their children (Maya and Nikhil) therefore share only that one grandparent, not a full pair of grandparents. In standard kinship terminology, children of half‑siblings are called half‑first cousins. The relationship is therefore determinable and is not a full first‑cousin nor a second cousin.

M is the sister of N and O, making M the aunt of N's daughter Q and O's son S. Q and S are M's niece and nephew, respectively. Their child T is therefore the child of M's niece/nephew, which standard terminology calls a grandniece or grandnephew. This matches option B.

John and Mary are siblings, making John Susan's uncle and Mary Susan's mother. John’s son Peter is Susan’s first cousin. Lily is Peter’s daughter, i.e., the child of Susan’s first cousin. A child of a first cousin is a first cousin once removed, reflecting a one‑generation difference. No other standard term fits.

A's paternal aunt (father's sister) is A's first cousin parent on the paternal side, and A's maternal uncle (mother's brother) is the first cousin parent on the maternal side. Their child B is therefore the child of A's first cousin on both sides, making B a double first cousin of A. This is the standard term that captures the doubled ancestry.

M’s mother and N’s father are siblings, meaning they are the parents of M and N respectively. Children of siblings are first cousins. No other relationships (e.g., sibling, uncle/niece) fit this configuration, so the precise term is first cousins.

X's father's sister is X's paternal aunt; X's mother's brother is X's maternal uncle.
