R's mother’s brother is R's maternal uncle; his daughter D is R's first cousin. C is R's child. A first cousin of a parent is a first cousin once removed to that parent's child. Hence D is C's first cousin once removed, uniquely determined.

M's mother is the sister of N's father (paternal aunt), and M's father is the brother of N's mother (maternal uncle). Thus M's parents are respectively siblings of each of N's parents, meaning M and N share both sets of grandparents. This makes them double first cousins, not merely first cousins or half‑first cousins.

M has two children, J and K. J marries L, making L M's daughter‑in‑law. L’s sister S is therefore J’s sister‑in‑law. S marries K, who is M’s son. The spouse of a child is that child's parent’s daughter‑in‑law. Hence S is M’s daughter‑in‑law.

M and N are siblings, making their children O and R first cousins. R's child Q is one generation below R, so Q is the child of O's first cousin. The relationship between O and Q is therefore first cousin once removed, which is a standard kinship term.

E’s father A and F’s father B are brothers, making E and F first cousins on their fathers’ side. Likewise, E’s mother C and F’s mother D are sisters, making them first cousins on their mothers’ side as well. Sharing both sets of grandparents qualifies them as double first cousins, the most precise term.

John's paternal uncle (his father's brother) Alan marries John’s maternal aunt (his mother's sister) Beth. Their child Clara is therefore John’s first cousin through his father's side and also his first cousin through his mother's side. When the same two families provide both sets of parents, the cousins share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins.

M is the child of L's nephew (the sister's son) and also the child of L's niece (the brother's daughter). Thus M is the grandchild of both of L's siblings, making M the grandniece/nephew of L through two separate lines. This is exactly a double grandniece/nephew relationship.

Y's father’s sister is Y’s paternal aunt. Her child is Y’s first cousin. X is the grandchild of that aunt, meaning X is the child of that cousin. Thus X is one generation below Y’s cousin, making X Y’s first cousin once removed. The relationship is uniquely determined.

Mary is John’s sister, so her son Tom is John’s nephew. Tom marries John’s daughter Anna, who is Tom’s first cousin. Their child Lily is therefore John’s granddaughter through Anna, and simultaneously John’s grand‑niece (the child of his nephew) through Tom. Since Lily fits two distinct kinship categories, a single standard term does not uniquely describe her relationship to John.

X’s mother and Y’s father are full siblings, making X and Y first cousins (they share the same grandparents). Y’s daughter Z is the child of Y. The relationship between a person and the child of their cousin is defined as a first cousin once removed. No other kinship ties affect this direct line, so X is Z’s first cousin once removed.

M is father of O. O is married to P. P's mother Q is not blood related to M; she is M's daughter‑in‑law's mother. Q's brother R is P's maternal uncle, and R's daughter S is P's cousin. Therefore S is the cousin of M's son‑in‑law, giving no direct blood or standard affinal term for S's relation to M.

M and N are siblings, so their children A and B are first cousins. B's spouse D has a sister C, making C B's sister‑in‑law. The standard in‑law definitions only cover a person's spouse, that spouse's parents/siblings, one's own siblings' spouses, and children's spouses. C does not fit any of these categories relative to A, nor is she a first cousin. Hence there is no standard direct kinship term for C's relation to A.

Emma and Liam share only a mother, making them half‑siblings. Their children, Sara and Tom, are therefore the offspring of half‑siblings. In kinship terminology, children of half‑siblings are called half‑first cousins, distinguishing them from first cousins (children of full siblings). Hence the correct relation is half‑first cousins.

John’s wife is Mary. Mary’s brother is Tom, making Tom John’s brother‑in‑law by the definition (spouse’s sibling). The additional fact that Tom is married to Susan (John’s niece) does not change that primary relation. Thus the standard kinship term is brother‑in‑law.

R's mother and S are siblings, making S R's maternal uncle. T is S's daughter, so T is the child of R's uncle. Children of a person's uncle/aunt are first cousins, sharing the same set of grandparents. No half‑sibling or more distant relation applies.

John and Mary are siblings (share Grandparents A). Anna and Peter are siblings (share Grandparents B). John marries Anna, Mary marries Peter. Lily’s parents are John (A‑descendant) and Anna (B‑descendant); Mark’s parents are Mary (A‑descendant) and Peter (B‑descendant). Therefore Lily and Mark share both sets of grandparents (A and B), making them first cousins through each parental line. Sharing two grandparent sets defines double first cousins.

John and Mary are full siblings, and Anna and Ben are full siblings. Clara is child of John (from the first sibling pair) and Anna (from the second pair); David is child of Mary (the other sibling from the first pair) and Ben (the other sibling from the second pair). Hence Clara and David share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins.

A and B share only one parent, making them half‑siblings. Their children, X and Y, each inherit that half‑shared lineage. First cousins share a set of grandparents; here X and Y share only one grandparent (the common mother of A and B). Therefore they are cousins of the first degree but with only half the typical genetic overlap, termed "half‑first cousins" in standard kinship nomenclature.

J and M are brothers, so their children K and N are first cousins. L is K's son, placing him one generation below K. A first cousin's child is a first cousin once removed to the cousin of the parent. Therefore, L is a first cousin once removed of N.

B's mother's mother is B's maternal grandmother. The sister of that grandmother is one generation above B's parents, making her B's great-aunt, which is called a grand‑aunt in standard English kinship.

Anna and Ben are siblings, so their children David (Anna's son) and Clara (Ben's daughter) are first cousins. Ethan is Clara's son, making him the child of David's first cousin. In kinship terms, the child of your cousin is your first cousin once removed. Therefore Ethan is David's first cousin once removed.

R's father and P are brothers, so P is R's uncle. P's daughter S is therefore R's first cousin. R's daughter T is one generation below R. Thus S is the first cousin of T's parent, making S T's first cousin once removed.

R is married to S. S’s brother T is R’s brother‑in‑law. T’s wife U is S’s sister‑in‑law (and also R’s sister‑in‑law). V is U’s brother, i.e., the brother of R’s sister‑in‑law. This relationship is a second‑order affinal link with no commonly used term; it is not a direct brother‑in‑law, cousin‑in‑law, or nephew‑in‑law.

John's sister Anna is his full sibling. The child of a sibling is a niece or nephew, regardless of whom the sibling marries. Anna marries Ben, who is John’s brother‑in‑law, but that does not alter the direct blood relationship. Therefore Clara, as Anna’s daughter, is John’s niece.

A and B share the same parents, as do C and D. When A marries C, their child has grandparents from A's parents and C's parents. Likewise, B and D's child has the same two sets of grandparents. Thus the two children share both sets of grandparents, making them first cousins through two sibling pairs. The precise term for such a relationship is “double first cousins.”

R's paternal aunt's daughter S and R's maternal uncle's son T are each R's first cousins. Their child C is thus the child of R's first cousin, which by standard kinship terminology is a first cousin once removed (one generation down from the cousin). Hence C's relation to R is first cousin once removed.

Emma's father John and Noah's mother Mary are siblings, making Emma and Noah first cousins on the paternal side. Likewise, Emma's mother Linda and Noah's father Peter are siblings, creating a second first‑cousin link on the maternal side. Since they are first cousins through both parents, they are double first cousins, not half or second cousins.

M’s mother is the mother‑in‑law of N (since N is married to M). N’s father is the father‑in‑law of M. The two grandparents are linked only through these affinal (in‑law) connections; there is no single standard English kinship term that directly describes the relation between a mother‑in‑law and a father‑in‑law. Hence the correct choice is that no standard direct relation exists.

M is N's father. N is married to O, making M O's father‑in‑law. O's mother P has brother Q, who is O's maternal uncle. Q's daughter R is O's first cousin. Thus R is the cousin of M's child’s spouse, i.e., a cousin of M’s son‑in‑law/daughter‑in‑law. This is an affinal link beyond the allowed direct in‑law terms, so no standard direct kinship term applies.

A's mother is the sister of B's father, making B's father A's maternal uncle. B is the child of A's uncle, so A and B are children of siblings. Children of siblings are first cousins (even if the siblings were half‑siblings, they are still first cousins). Hence the precise relation is first cousin.

John's sister Mary is Paul's mother, making Paul John’s nephew. John’s brother Tom is Susan’s father, making Susan John’s niece. Paul and Susan (first cousins) have Lily. Lily is therefore the child of John’s nephew and niece, i.e., the child of his sibling’s grandchildren. The child of a niece or nephew is called a grandniece (also great‑niece). Among the options, this matches choice D.

N’s father has one sibling (a paternal aunt/uncle) and N’s mother has one sibling (a maternal aunt/uncle). M is described as the child of the father’s sibling and also the child of the mother’s sibling, meaning those two siblings are married to each other and have a child together. Consequently M is a first cousin to N through the paternal line and also a first cousin through the maternal line, making M a double first cousin of N.

A and B are half‑siblings, sharing only one parent (their mother). Their children C and D each descend from that shared parent through A and B respectively, giving C and D a single common grandparent. First cousins share both grandparents; when only one grandparent is common, the relationship is qualified as "half‑first cousins." Thus the precise term is half‑first cousins.

Bob is Paul’s son. Paul is sibling to John and Mary, whose children are Alice and Charles respectively. Thus Bob is first cousin to both Alice and Charles. Diana is the child of Alice and Charles, so she is one generation down from Bob’s first cousins. A person’s first cousin’s child is a first cousin once removed, making Bob and Diana first cousins once removed.

P’s mother’s brother Q is P’s maternal uncle. Q’s daughter R is therefore P’s first cousin. R’s child S is the child of P’s first cousin, which makes S a first cousin once removed to P (the “once removed” indicates a one‑generation difference). This relationship is uniquely defined under standard blood kinship terms.

L's maternal uncle G's child P and L's paternal uncle H's child Q are each the child of one of L's parents' siblings, making both P and Q first cousins of L. Since Z is either P or Q, Z must also be L's first cousin. The relation is uniquely determined as first cousin.

M's mother is the sister of N's father, making M a first cousin of N on the paternal side. M's father is the brother of N's mother, making M a first cousin on the maternal side as well. Thus M and N share both sets of grandparents, which is the definition of double first cousins.

M and N are siblings, so they share the same parents. O and P are also siblings, sharing another set of parents. X is child of M (one sibling) and O (the other sibling), while Y is child of N (the first sibling) and P (the second sibling). Consequently X and Y have both sets of grandparents in common: the parents of M/N and the parents of O/P. Sharing both paternal and maternal grandparents defines double first cousins, not just regular first cousins or half‑first cousins.

M's mother and her brother are full siblings, so the brother's daughter (D) is M's maternal first cousin. The fact that D is married to M's paternal cousin does not alter the blood relationship between M and D; marriage only creates in‑law ties. Therefore M and D are directly related as first cousins.

Ethan's parents are Adam (brother of Ben) and Clara (sister of Diana). Fiona's parents are Ben and Diana. Thus each child’s father is the brother of the other child’s father, and each child’s mother is the sister of the other child’s mother. This means Ethan and Fiona share both sets of grandparents (paternal and maternal), making them double first cousins, the most precise term among the choices.

A is X's maternal uncle (mother's brother) and B is X's paternal aunt (father's sister). Their child C is therefore X's child of a maternal uncle (first cousin) and also child of a paternal aunt (first cousin). Being a first cousin through both parental lines makes C a double first cousin of X, the most precise standard term.

Ethan and Fiona are children of two sets of sibling parents (Adam–Ben and Clara–Diana), making them double first cousins. Their children, Liam and Maya, are therefore the offspring of double first cousins, which defines them as double second cousins.

Peter is John’s half‑brother because they share only their mother. Anna is Peter’s daughter, making her the child of John’s half‑sibling. In standard English kinship, the child of any sibling (full or half) is called a niece or nephew. The term "half‑niece" is not a standard kinship term, so the precise standard relation is niece.

John, Mary, and Michael are siblings. Michael’s daughter Anna is John’s niece. John marries Anna, making Anna both his niece and his wife. Their child Sam is therefore Michael’s grandson through Anna (the daughter) and simultaneously Michael’s nephew because Sam’s father John is Michael’s brother. The only option that captures both applicable relations is A.

John and Mary are siblings. John’s daughter Lisa and Mary’s son Peter are therefore first cousins (children of siblings). Tom is Peter’s son, making him one generation below Peter. The relation between a person and the child of their cousin is defined as first cousin once removed. Hence Tom is Lisa’s first cousin once removed.

Mary and Linda are sisters. Mary’s children are John and Tom, making Tom a child of Mary. Linda’s children, including Sarah, are the offspring of Mary’s sister, thus they are Tom’s maternal cousins. First cousins share grandparents, which applies here.

M and N are siblings; X and Y are siblings. Their marriages produce A (child of M and X) and B (child of N and Y). A and B share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins. C is A's child, D is B's child. Therefore C and D share both sets of great‑grandparents, i.e., they are second cousins through two distinct lines. The most precise term is double second cousins.

M's spouse is R. R's brother Q is M's brother‑in‑law (spouse’s sibling). P is Q's spouse, i.e., the spouse of M's spouse’s sibling. Standard English kinship terms allow in‑law labels only for a spouse, that spouse’s parents/siblings, a sibling’s spouse, or a child’s spouse. The spouse of a spouse’s sibling is not covered by any standard term, so P has no direct standard relation to M; the connection is only an affinal chain.

X’s father’s sister is X’s paternal aunt. Her child Y is therefore X’s first cousin. Y’s child Z is one generation below Y, making Z the child of X’s first cousin. In kinship terms, the child of a cousin is a first cousin once removed. No half‑sibling relation is involved, so other options do not apply.

My paternal aunt's son is my first cousin (paternal). My maternal uncle's daughter is also my first cousin (maternal). Their child is the offspring of my first cousin, which makes that child my first cousin once removed. The double‑cousin parentage does not change the standard term.

John and Thomas are brothers, sharing the same parents. Mary is John’s sister, thus also Thomas’s sister. Mary’s son Peter is therefore Thomas’s nephew. Thomas’s daughter Lisa is Thomas’s child. Children of a sibling (Peter) and a child of the sibling’s sibling (Lisa) are first cousins. Hence Peter and Lisa are first cousins, regardless of their marriage.

Mia and Nora share the same parents, making them sisters; Tom and Sam share the same parents, making them brothers. Alex is the child of Mia (sister) and Tom (brother), while Bella is the child of Nora (sister) and Sam (brother). Therefore Alex and Bella have both sets of grandparents in common – the maternal grandparents (parents of Mia and Nora) and the paternal grandparents (parents of Tom and Sam). Sharing both grandparents makes them double first cousins, the most specific term among the choices.

X is the child of Y's father's only sibling, making X a first cousin on the paternal side. X is also the child of Y's mother's only sibling, making X a first cousin on the maternal side. Since the two siblings (the father's sibling and the mother's sibling) are distinct individuals, they are a pair of siblings who married each other, producing children who are related to each other through both parental lines. This relationship is precisely defined as a double first cousin.

Lara’s mother (M) and Nora’s father (F) are half‑siblings, meaning they share exactly one parent (call this common parent P). Therefore P is a grandparent of both Lara (through M) and Nora (through F). Since M and F are not full siblings, Lara and Nora share only one grandparent, not both. Children of half‑siblings are termed half‑first cousins, reflecting that they are first cousins through a single shared grandparent. No other intermarriages affect this relationship, so the precise term is half‑first cousins.

M is the child of P's paternal aunt (sister of P's father) making M a first cousin on the father's side. M is also the child of P's maternal uncle (brother of P's mother) making M a first cousin on the mother's side. Since the aunt and uncle are married, M shares both sets of grandparents with P, which is the definition of a double first cousin.

C is A's maternal first cousin (child of A's maternal uncle). E is A's paternal first cousin (child of A's paternal uncle). F is the child of C and E. A is therefore the first cousin of each of F's parents. The child of one's first cousin is a first cousin once removed. This holds through both parental lines, but the relation remains first cousin once removed, not sibling, second cousin, or double first cousin.

A's father's only sister is A's paternal aunt; her child P is the child of A's father's sibling, making P a first cousin of A. A's mother's only brother is A's maternal uncle; his child Q is the child of A's mother's sibling, also a first cousin of A. Whether R is P or Q, R is always a first cousin of A. Hence the relationship is uniquely a first cousin.

Mary is John's sister. John is Emma's father, making Mary Emma's aunt. Emma is Lily's mother, so Lily is the child of Mary's niece. The child of a niece/nephew is a great‑niece, making Mary Lily's great‑aunt.

Y is the brother of X's mother, making Y X's maternal uncle. Y's daughter Z is therefore X's first cousin. W is X's son, one generation below X. The relationship between a first cousin and the cousin's child is first cousin once removed, which is uniquely determined under the given constraints.

A and E are sisters, making them siblings. B is A's child, and D is E's child. Children of siblings are first cousins. Therefore B and D share grandparents but are not siblings, aunts/uncles, or unrelated.

A and B are brothers; X and Y are sisters. C is child of A + X, D of B + Y. Since C’s father and D’s father are full siblings, and C’s mother and D’s mother are full siblings, C and D are cousins through both parental lines. This matches the definition of double first cousins (children of two pairs of siblings).

Adam and Brian are brothers, so X and Y share the same paternal grandparents. Clara and Diana are sisters, so X and Y also share the same maternal grandparents. Thus X and Y are first cousins through both their fathers and their mothers, making them double first cousins, the most precise term.

M and N are half‑siblings, sharing only one parent (their mother). Their children A (M’s daughter) and B (N’s son) each have that shared parent as a grandparent. Because they share only one grandparent, they are not full first cousins, which require both grandparents in common. The precise English term for cousins who share a single grandparent is “half‑first cousins.” Therefore the most accurate designation is half‑first cousins.

M and N are full siblings (share the same parents). O and P are also full siblings (share the same parents). X is the child of M and O; Y is the child of N and P. Therefore X and Y are each the child of a sibling from the first family and a sibling from the second family. They share both sets of grandparents, making them first cousins through two independent sibling links – the definition of double first cousins.

R's mother has a brother U, making U R's maternal uncle. U's daughter V is therefore the child of R's maternal uncle, i.e., R's first cousin. The marriage of V to X (R's paternal cousin) does not alter the blood relationship between V and R. Hence V is R's first cousin.

Alex and Emma are siblings; Lily and Tom are siblings. Alex marries Lily, Emma marries Tom. Their children Sam and Kate each have one parent from each sibling pair. Thus Sam and Kate share both sets of grandparents (Alex/Emma's parents and Lily/Tom's parents). Children of two sibling pairs are double first cousins.

A's mother’s brother B is A’s maternal uncle. B’s daughter C is therefore A’s first cousin. C’s son D is the child of A’s first cousin, which in kinship terminology is a first cousin once removed (one generation down). Hence D’s precise relation to A is first cousin once removed.

P's parents are Alex (child of X's parents) and Dana (child of Y's parents). Q's parents are Bella (Alex's sibling, also child of X's parents) and Carl (Dana's sibling, also child of Y's parents). Therefore both P and Q have the same four grandparents—those of families X and Y—making them first cousins through both parental lines. This precise relationship is called double first cousins.

X's mother has a brother (X's maternal uncle). That brother is married to Y, making Y the spouse of X's maternal uncle. The kinship term for the spouse of an uncle is an aunt by marriage, i.e., an aunt‑in‑law. The additional information about Y's sister and Z does not change Y's relationship to X; it only links Y's sister to X's spouse. Y is not a blood aunt nor a great‑aunt, and the relation is uniquely determined as an aunt‑in‑law.

M and N are half‑siblings, meaning they share exactly one parent. Their children P and Q each inherit that shared grandparent (the parent of M and N) as a common grandparent, but they have different other grandparents. First cousins share both grandparents; half‑first cousins share only one. Therefore P and Q are half‑first cousins.

M is the child of A's maternal uncle (the only brother of A's mother), making M a first cousin on the mother's side. M is also the child of A's paternal aunt (the only sister of A's father), making M a first cousin on the father's side. Since both parental siblings are distinct individuals, M is simultaneously a maternal and paternal first cousin, i.e., a double first cousin.
Tom is Mary's son from a previous marriage. John, as Mary's husband, is Tom's stepfather. The relationship is not a blood son, brother‑in‑law, or nephew. The appropriate standard term is step‑son.

Tom is father of both Mia and Sam, but they have different mothers, making them half‑siblings. Sam is Eva's father, so Mia is the sister of Eva's parent. In kinship terms, a sibling of a parent is an aunt/uncle; because the sibling relationship is half, the precise term is half‑aunt (or half‑uncle). Therefore the exact relationship is half‑aunt.

A's mother’s only brother is A's maternal uncle; his daughter B is A's first cousin. A's father’s only sister is A's paternal aunt; her son C is also A's first cousin. Selecting either B or C yields a first cousin relationship, and there is no scenario where the relation changes. Hence X is a first cousin of A.

M's paternal aunt's daughter N is M's first cousin. M's maternal uncle's son O is also M's first cousin. N and O each have a child C. In kinship, the child of a first cousin is a first cousin once removed from the original person. Since both parental lines give the same relationship, C is M's first cousin once removed.

F is L's paternal uncle (father's brother) and M is L's maternal uncle (mother's brother). Their sole child is both X and Y, making that child the child of L's paternal uncle and also of L's maternal uncle. Hence the child is L's first cousin through the father's side and also a first cousin through the mother's side, i.e., a double first cousin.

Y and Z are sisters. Their children X and W are therefore first cousins. V is the child of W, making V the next generation down from X's cousin. A child of one’s first cousin is termed a first cousin once removed (one generation removed). Hence V is X's first cousin once removed.

X is the child of Y's paternal aunt (father's sister) and Z is the child of Y's maternal uncle (mother's brother). The aunt and uncle belong to different families and are not related, so X and Z share no common ancestor. Therefore they have no blood relationship.
Peter and Linda are siblings. Linda's daughter Emma is therefore Peter's brother's (or sister's) daughter, which is the definition of a niece. No other generational link changes this relationship.

W's mother’s sibling is either her brother (uncle) or sister (aunt). Regardless of that sibling’s gender, the child of that sibling is a first cousin to W. The specific gender of the sibling does not affect the cousin relationship, so Z is uniquely determined to be W’s cousin.

P is mother of Q. Q's spouse R and R's brother S are both child‑in‑laws of P. S's spouse T is also a child‑in‑law of P. T's sister U is merely the sibling of a child‑in‑law; there is no standard English kinship term for that relationship, only an affinal chain.

Anna and Ben are siblings. Their children Clara and David are therefore first cousins. Ethan is Clara's child, placing him one generation below Clara. The relationship between a person and the child of their first cousin is defined as a first cousin once removed, reflecting a one‑generation difference.

R's mother and S are sisters, so S is R's maternal aunt. R's father and T are brothers, so T is R's paternal uncle. S and T marry and have child X. X's parents are R's aunt (maternal) and uncle (paternal), meaning X shares both sets of R's grandparents: the maternal grandparents (parents of R's mother and S) and the paternal grandparents (parents of R's father and T). Sharing both grandparent pairs makes X a double first cousin of R, the most precise term.

M’s mother and N’s father are half‑siblings, i.e., they share exactly one parent. The children of two siblings are first cousins; when the siblings are half‑siblings, their children are half‑first cousins. Since M and N have no other shared ancestors, their relationship is precisely that of half‑first cousins.

Mary and Peter are siblings. Peter's daughter Lisa is therefore Mary's niece and John's first cousin. Tom is Lisa's son, making him the child of John's first cousin. In kinship terminology, the child of a first cousin is a first cousin once removed.

M and N are half‑siblings, sharing only a mother. The children of siblings are first cousins. When the siblings are half‑siblings, their children are called half‑first cousins (often just "half‑cousins"). Thus X and Y are half‑first cousins. The other options do not match this definition, and the relationship is determinable.

Linda is Mary's mother. She later marries Tom, making Tom her husband. Tom's son Kevin is from a previous marriage, so Kevin is Linda's step‑son, not her biological child. Emma is Kevin's daughter, thus Emma is Tom's biological granddaughter but only Linda's step‑granddaughter. Since the question restricts answers to blood‑kinship terms only, there is no direct blood relationship between Linda and Emma.

John and Mary are siblings. Mary’s child Ben is John’s nephew. Ben’s child Carl is one generation below Ben, making Carl the child of John’s nephew. The child of a nephew is a great‑nephew (or grand‑nephew) to the original sibling. Therefore Carl is John’s great‑nephew.

Mark is John’s maternal uncle, so his daughter Lisa is John’s first cousin. Sarah is John’s paternal aunt (father’s sister). Tom is Sarah’s son, and Lisa is married to Tom. Therefore Lisa is the spouse of Sarah’s child, which makes her Sarah’s daughter‑in‑law, an allowed in‑law term (children’s spouse).

R's mother’s brother is R’s maternal uncle; his daughter S is R’s maternal first cousin. R's father’s sister is R’s paternal aunt; her son T is R’s paternal first cousin. S and T are unrelated to each other, so their child U is the child of two of R’s first cousins. In kinship terms, the child of a first cousin is a first cousin once removed. This holds regardless of the two separate lines, and no double‑cousin condition exists because S and T are not siblings. Thus U’s precise relation to R is first cousin once removed.

R's mother’s brother is R’s maternal uncle; his child is R’s first cousin. R’s father’s sister is R’s paternal aunt; her child is also R’s first cousin. Since S is the child of both the maternal uncle and the paternal aunt, the two must be married (monogamy, no adoption). Thus S is simultaneously the child of an uncle and an aunt, making S a first cousin of R on both sides. No other kinship fits the given constraints, so the relationship is uniquely determined as a first cousin.

R's father's sister's daughter (A) is R's paternal first cousin. R's mother's brother's son (B) is R's maternal first cousin. A and B each are R's first cousins, so their child C is the child of R's first cousin. In kinship terms, the child of a first cousin is a first cousin once removed. The double connection does not change the designation; C is R's first cousin once removed.

Mary and John are siblings. Mary’s children are Peter and Michael; John’s child is Lisa. Therefore Peter and Michael are brothers, and both are first cousins of Lisa. Lisa marries Michael, her first cousin, and they have a daughter Anna. Since Peter is Michael’s brother, he is Anna’s father's brother, i.e., her uncle. No half‑relationship or cousin‑once‑removed applies.

X's father M and Y's father N are siblings, giving X and Y a shared set of paternal grandparents. Likewise, X's mother O and Y's mother P are siblings, giving them a shared set of maternal grandparents. Thus X and Y share both sets of grandparents, which defines double first cousins.

A's mother is sibling of B's father, and A's father is sibling of B's mother. Thus each of A's parents is a sibling of one of B's parents, meaning the two families consist of two sibling pairs. Consequently A and B share both sets of grandparents, which is the definition of double first cousins.

M's mother’s brother is M's maternal uncle; M's father’s sister is M's paternal aunt. They marry and have child N. N is the child of M's maternal uncle, making N a first cousin on the mother's side, and also the child of M's paternal aunt, making N a first cousin on the father's side. Being a first cousin through both parental lines makes N a double first cousin of M.

B and C are siblings. A (child of B) and D (child of C) are therefore first cousins. E is D's daughter, one generation below D. A's relationship to a first cousin's child is "first cousin once removed". Hence E is A's first cousin once removed.

A and B are half‑siblings, sharing only one parent (their father). That father is the paternal grandfather of both X (child of A) and Y (child of B). X and Y therefore share a single grandparent, not a full set of grandparents. The correct term for children of half‑siblings—who share exactly one grandparent—is “half‑first cousins.”

Lily's father Tom and Noah's father Tim are brothers, so Lily and Noah share the same paternal grandparents. Lily's mother Anna and Noah's mother Amy are sisters, so they also share the same maternal grandparents. Thus the cousins share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins, the most precise term.

L's paternal aunt (father's sister) and L's maternal uncle (mother's brother) each produce a first cousin for L. Since they marry each other, their single child M is simultaneously the child of L's paternal aunt and the child of L's maternal uncle, making M L's first cousin on both parental lines. This is the definition of a double first cousin.

Ethan's father Adam and Fiona's father Brian are brothers, making them first cousins on the paternal side. Ethan's mother Clara and Fiona's mother Diana are sisters, also making them first cousins on the maternal side. Because they share both sets of grandparents, they are first cousins through two sibling pairs, i.e., double first cousins.

T is L's maternal uncle (mother's brother) and S is L's paternal aunt (father's sister). Their shared child M is therefore the child of L's maternal uncle and also the child of L's paternal aunt. Each relationship alone makes M a first cousin of L, and because the same person fulfills both roles, M is a double first cousin of L.

N's father and P's mother are siblings (paternal side) and N's mother and P's father are siblings (maternal side). Thus N and P are first cousins through both parental lines, making them double first cousins, the most precise term.

John and Mary are siblings. Their spouses, Anna and Tom, are also siblings. Lily is the child of John (who shares parents with Mary) and Anna (who shares parents with Tom). Sam is the child of Mary and Tom. Therefore Lily and Sam share both sets of grandparents: the parents of John/Mary and the parents of Anna/Tom. Sharing both paternal and maternal grandparents makes them double first cousins, a specific term beyond ordinary first cousins.

John and Mary are siblings. Mary’s child is David; John’s child is Michael, making David and Michael first cousins. Sarah is Michael’s daughter, i.e., one generation below Michael. A first cousin’s child (or a first cousin’s parent’s child) is a first cousin once removed. Hence David is a first cousin once removed to Sarah.

C is married to B's father, making her B's step‑mother. After B marries C's daughter D, C also becomes B's mother‑in‑law. Since two distinct standard kinship terms both apply, the relation cannot be uniquely identified by a single term.

Z and W are full brothers, so their children Y and V are first cousins (they share the same grandparents). X is the child of Y, making X the next generation relative of V. A child of one’s first cousin is defined as a first cousin once removed. Hence X is V’s first cousin once removed.

U is the brother of R's mother, making U R's maternal uncle. V is the sister of R's father's brother, so V is R's paternal aunt. The child of U and V is therefore the child of R's maternal uncle and paternal aunt, which makes that child R's first cousin (through both sides).

Emma is the child of Tom and Lily. Sam is the child of Anna (Tom's sister) and Ben (Lily's brother). Thus Emma and Sam are each the child of a sibling pair: Emma's father is sibling to Sam's mother, and Emma's mother is sibling to Sam's father. They share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins, the precise term.

N is the child of M's father's sister, making N M's paternal aunt's child – a first cousin. P is the child of M's mother's brother, making P M's maternal uncle's child – also a first cousin. Whether Q refers to N or P, the kinship term is the same: first cousin. No other option fits, and the relation is uniquely determined.

John and Mary are siblings. John’s daughter Anna is Mary’s niece. Mary’s son Peter is Anna’s first cousin. Lisa is Anna’s daughter, one generation below Anna. Therefore Peter is one generation above Lisa but is first cousin to Lisa’s parent, making Peter and Lisa first cousins once removed.

M and N share the same two parents, and P and Q share another pair of parents. X’s parents (M and P) and Y’s parents (N and Q) are each formed by a sibling pair from the two families. Therefore X and Y have both sets of grandparents in common, making them first cousins through two distinct sibling lines – the definition of double first cousins.

Adam and Ben are brothers; Clara and Diana are sisters. Their children Ethan and Felix therefore share both paternal and maternal grandparents, making them double first cousins. Maya is Ethan's child and Noah is Felix's child. The children of first cousins are second cousins; when the parents are double first cousins, their children share both sets of great‑grandparents, i.e., they are double second cousins. Hence Maya and Noah are double second cousins.

N's father's only sister is N's paternal aunt; her child is N's first cousin. N's mother's only brother is N's maternal uncle; his child is also N's first cousin. For the same person M to satisfy both, the aunt and uncle must be married, making M a double first cousin. This is still classified as a first cousin, not a half‑cousin, and the relationship is uniquely determined.

M's mother and U are siblings, making U M's maternal uncle. U's son V is therefore M's first cousin. V's daughter W is one generation below V, so W is the child of M's first cousin, which is defined as a first cousin once removed.

Maya and Nina are sisters, making their children Sara and Tom first cousins. Alex is Sara's son, so Tom is a first cousin of Alex's mother, which makes Tom Alex's first cousin once removed. No adoption or half relations apply, and uncle‑in‑law does not describe this connection.
M and Q are siblings. Q's daughter P is therefore the child of M's sibling, making P the niece of M. Marriage of P to O does not alter the blood relationship. Hence the correct kin term is niece.

John and Mary are half‑siblings, sharing only their mother. That mother is the sole common grandparent of Lily (John's daughter) and Ethan (Mary's son). Since first cousins share both grandparents and half‑first cousins share only one, Lily and Ethan are half‑first cousins.

V is the child of T's maternal uncle (U) and also the child of T's paternal aunt (W). For V to be the same person, U and W must be married, making V the child of two siblings of T's parents. Thus V is simultaneously a first cousin on the mother’s side and a first cousin on the father’s side, i.e., a double first cousin.

Ava and Ben are each the child of a sibling pair: Mia and Noah are siblings, and their spouses Lily and Leo are also siblings. Thus Ava and Ben share both sets of grandparents (their parents’ parents). This makes them first cousins through two distinct lines, i.e., double first cousins.

P is the daughter of Q. Q is the brother of R, making Q and R siblings. R is the father of S, so S is the child of R. Children of siblings are first cousins, so P (child of Q) and S (child of R) are first cousins. No other blood ties alter this relationship.

Alan and Brian are full brothers, and Clara and Diana are full sisters. Ethan is the child of Alan and Clara; Fiona is the child of Brian and Diana. Ethan and Fiona share the same paternal grandparents (parents of Alan and Brian) and the same maternal grandparents (parents of Clara and Diana). Sharing both sets of grandparents makes them first cousins on both sides, i.e., double first cousins.

Alice and Ben are siblings, so their mother is the common parent. Alice’s child Carla and Ben’s child David are each grandchildren of that mother. Ethan is the child of Carla and David, making him the child of the mother’s grandchildren. In standard kinship terms, the child of a grandchild is a great‑grandchild. Hence Ethan is a great‑grandchild of Alice’s mother.

R’s mother’s brother U is R’s maternal uncle. U’s daughter V is therefore the child of R’s uncle, making V R’s first cousin by blood. The additional fact that V is married to R’s paternal cousin Y does not alter the blood relationship; it only adds a cousin‑in‑law connection, which is not a separate direct kin term among the options. Hence the precise kinship term is first cousin.

M and N are full siblings, so they share one set of grandparents. X and Y are also full siblings, sharing another set of grandparents. A is the child of M and X; B is the child of N and Y. Therefore A and B are first cousins through both parental lines, i.e., they are first cousins on two separate sides. The precise term for this relationship is double first cousins.

X's mother’s brother’s daughter (Y) and X's father’s brother’s daughter (Z) are each X’s first cousins. Y and Z have a child W. The child of your first cousin is your first cousin once removed. Therefore W is X’s first cousin once removed.

Mary's brothers are Peter and Mark. Lily is Peter's daughter; Sam is Mark's son (by his marriage to Anna). Since Peter and Mark are siblings, their children Sam and Lily share the same grandparents (the parents of Mary, Peter, and Mark). Hence Sam and Lily are first cousins. No other standard term applies.

R's mother and M are siblings, making M R's maternal uncle. M's daughter D is therefore R's first cousin. D's son S is the child of R's cousin, which is the definition of a first cousin once removed (one generation down). The other options do not match this relationship.

John and Mary are half‑siblings, sharing only one parent. Their children, Alan and Beth, are therefore the children of half‑siblings. The children of full siblings are first cousins; when the siblings are half‑siblings, the cousins are termed half‑first cousins (or simply half‑cousins). This matches the standard kinship terminology. Hence the correct choice is half‑first cousins.

U's mother has exactly one brother, making him U's maternal uncle. T is described as the child of that brother. The child of one's uncle (or aunt) is a first cousin. No other relationship fits, and the term is uniquely determined.

John and Mark are brothers, so Mark is John’s sibling. Mark and his wife Lisa have a daughter Anna. The child of one’s sibling is a niece or nephew. No other blood or marriage link changes this basic relationship, and standard kinship terminology includes 'niece' for a brother’s daughter. Therefore Anna is John’s niece.

M is A's mother. M's brother B is A's maternal uncle. B's child C is A's first cousin. C's child D is one generation down from that cousin, making D A's first cousin once removed. No half-sibling or other relationships are indicated, so the relation is uniquely determined.

Adam and Brian are brothers, so their fathers are the same. Clara and Diana are sisters, so their mothers are the same. Ethan’s paternal grandparents are Adam’s parents; Fiona’s paternal grandparents are Brian’s parents – the same set. Likewise, Ethan’s maternal grandparents are Clara’s parents; Fiona’s maternal grandparents are Diana’s parents – also the same set. Thus Ethan and Fiona share both sets of grandparents, making them first cousins on both sides, i.e., double first cousins.

Alex is the son of Maya’s brother, so Maya’s brother is Alex’s father. Maya is therefore the sister of Alex’s father. In standard kinship terms, the sister of one’s parent is called an aunt. The fact that Maya is married to a man unrelated by blood simply confirms she is not Alex’s mother, and does not affect the aunt relationship.

Alan’s mother is sister to Beth’s father, so they share one set of grandparents (call them G1). Beth’s mother is sister to Alan’s father, so they share another set of grandparents (G2). Thus Alan’s paternal grandparents are G2 and maternal grandparents are G1; Beth’s paternal grandparents are G1 and maternal grandparents are G2. They share both pairs of grandparents, meaning they are children of two sibling pairs. This is the definition of double first cousins, not half‑first or second cousins.

S₁ is the sibling of Y's father, so X, as S₁'s child, is Y's paternal first cousin. Likewise S₂ is the sibling of Y's mother, so X is also Y's maternal first cousin. Because X shares both sets of grandparents with Y, the kinship is a double first cousin.

N's father and M's father are brothers, making N and M first cousins on the paternal side. Likewise, N's mother and M's mother are sisters, making them first cousins on the maternal side as well. Because the two cousin relationships involve both parents, N and M share all four grandparents, which is the definition of double first cousins.

Y's paternal grandfather (G) has a sister, who is Y's great‑aunt. X is the child of that sister, making X the child of Y's great‑aunt. The child of a great‑aunt is first cousin to Y's father, because they share the same grandparents (the parents of G). Since X is first cousin to Y's father, X is one generation removed from Y, giving the relationship of first cousin once removed.

Z and W are full sisters, so their children Y and V are first cousins. X is Y's child and U is V's child. Children of first cousins are second cousins to each other because they share the same great‑grandparents (the parents of Z and W). No half‑sibling information is given, so the relation is not a half‑cousin, and it is determinable. Hence the precise term is second cousins.

Peter and John are siblings. Peter’s daughter Anna is John’s wife, making Anna both Peter’s daughter and John’s spouse. Their child Sam is therefore (1) the child of Peter’s daughter, i.e., Peter’s grandchild, and (2) the child of Peter’s brother John, i.e., Peter’s nephew/niece. Both kinship links exist simultaneously.

Tom is M's maternal uncle (mother's brother) and Anne is M's paternal aunt (father's sister). Their child Lily is therefore the child of M's maternal uncle and paternal aunt. Lily shares both sets of grandparents with M: the maternal grandparents through Tom and the paternal grandparents through Anne. Thus Lily is M's cousin on both the mother's side and the father's side, making her a double first cousin.

M and N are siblings. Their children R and S are first cousins. C is R's child, making C one generation below R. The child of your first cousin is your first cousin once removed, so C is S's first cousin once removed (and vice‑versa). This matches a standard kinship term.

X is the child of Z's mother's only brother, making X the child of Z's maternal uncle—a first cousin. Y is the child of Z's father's only sister, the child of Z's paternal aunt—also a first cousin. Hence, regardless of whether we pick X or Y as W, W is Z's first cousin.

M’s mother and N’s father are siblings, making M and N first cousins through the maternal line of M and paternal line of N. Likewise, M’s father and N’s mother are siblings, creating another first‑cousin link through the paternal line of M and maternal line of N. Because both of M’s parents are each a sibling of one of N’s parents, the two individuals share both sets of grandparents, which is the definition of double first cousins. No half‑relations or generational gaps are involved, so the precise term is double first cousins.

A and B share only one parent, making them half‑siblings. First cousins are the children of two siblings. When the parents are half‑siblings, their children are cousins with a half‑relationship, commonly termed half‑first cousins. Thus X and Y are half‑first cousins.

Michael and Laura are siblings (Laura is Michael's sister). Laura's child is Emma; Michael's child is John. Children of siblings are first cousins. The statement "Emma’s mother’s brother is Michael" confirms Michael is Emma's maternal uncle, making John her cousin. No half‑sibling indication is given, so the standard precise term is first cousins.

The mother’s sister is an aunt; her child X is a first cousin if the aunt is a full sibling, otherwise a half‑first cousin. Likewise the father’s brother is an uncle; his child Y is a first cousin if the uncle is a full sibling, otherwise a half‑first cousin. Since the problem allows each sibling to be either full or half, X and Y may each be either a first cousin or a half‑first cousin. Therefore Z’s exact kinship to M cannot be uniquely determined.

L and N are siblings. L's daughter is M's mother, making M L's grandchild. N's son O is the parent of P, making P N's granddaughter. Grandchildren of siblings are children of first cousins, which are classified as second cousins. Hence P and M are second cousins.

P and R are full brothers, sharing both parents. Q and S are full sisters, also sharing both parents. M is child of P (son of the brothers) and Q (daughter of the sisters). N is child of R and S. Thus M and N have the same paternal grandparents (parents of P and R) and the same maternal grandparents (parents of Q and S). Sharing both sets of grandparents makes them double first cousins, not just regular first cousins or any other degree.

M's father and N are siblings (N is the sister of M's father). Since L's mother is N, L is the child of M's father's sister. Therefore, M and L are children of siblings, making them first cousins. Marital ties are ignored, so the correct blood relation is first cousin.

M's mother’s brother J is M’s maternal uncle; his child K is therefore M’s first cousin. M's father’s sister L is M’s paternal aunt; her child N is also M’s first cousin. Both K and N are first cousins of M (they happen to be the same age, but that does not change the kinship term). Hence P, whether K or N, is M’s first cousin.

Eve and Frank have the same mother but different fathers, making them maternal half‑siblings. Their children, Greg and Hannah, are therefore the offspring of half‑siblings. Such offspring share only one grandparent (the common mother) rather than a full set of grandparents, which defines the relationship as half‑first cousins.

M and N are siblings, so they share the same parents (set G1). O and P are siblings, sharing another set of parents (set G2). X's parents are M (from G1) and O (from G2); Y's parents are N (from G1) and P (from G2). Therefore X and Y each have the same two sets of grandparents: G1 via M/N and G2 via O/P. Sharing both sets of grandparents makes them first cousins through both parental lines, i.e., double first cousins.

Emily's mother and Fiona's mother are sisters, making Emily and Fiona first cousins. Greg is Fiona's son, i.e., the child of Emily's first cousin. In kinship terms, the child of a first cousin is a first cousin once removed. Therefore Greg is Emily's first cousin once removed.
S’s mother has a brother, i.e., S’s maternal uncle. T is described as the child of that brother. The child of one’s uncle or aunt is a first cousin. Therefore T is S’s first cousin.

M and N are brothers, so they share the same parents. O and Q are sisters, sharing their own parents. A is the child of M (brother) and O (sister), while B is the child of N (the other brother) and Q (the other sister). Thus A and B have both sets of grandparents in common – the parents of M/N and the parents of O/Q. Children who share both paternal and maternal grandparents are called double first cousins. Hence the most precise term is double first cousins.

Mary's sister Linda is John’s maternal aunt. Linda’s husband Peter is John’s uncle by marriage. Thomas is Peter’s brother, i.e., the brother of John’s aunt’s husband. English kinship terminology does not provide a specific term for the sibling of an uncle‑by‑marriage; he is not a blood uncle, nor a brother‑in‑law or father‑in‑law. Hence there is no direct kinship term.

M is parent of N. N’s spouse is O. O’s mother is P, whose brother Q is O’s maternal uncle. Q’s daughter R is O’s first cousin. Thus R is the cousin of M’s child’s spouse. The given kinship rules cover only spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, and children’s spouses; they do not define a term for a parent’s relation to a spouse’s cousin. Hence there is no standard direct relation, only an affinal chain.

A is the child of R's paternal aunt (father's sister), making A a first cousin on the father's side. B is the child of R's maternal uncle (mother's brother), also a first cousin on the mother's side. If A and B are the same person, that individual is simultaneously a paternal and maternal first cousin – a double first cousin – which still falls under the general category of first cousin. Thus the precise kinship term is "first cousin".

Emma is John’s daughter, making John her father. The child of Emma (and her husband Alan) is therefore the child of John’s daughter, i.e., John’s grandchild. No other relationship supersedes this direct line.

P and Q are siblings, but we are not told whether they share both parents (full siblings) or only one parent (half‑siblings). If they are full siblings, their children R and S are first cousins; if they are half‑siblings, R and S are half‑first cousins. Because the information does not specify which case holds, the exact kinship term cannot be uniquely determined.

M and N are siblings, and O and P are siblings. A’s parents are M (child of grandparents G) and O (child of grandparents H). B’s parents are N (same grandparents G) and P (same grandparents H). Therefore A and B share both sets of grandparents, making them the children of two sibling pairs, i.e., double first cousins.
V is the sister of W, who is Y's parent. Therefore V is the sibling of Y's mother/father, making V Y's aunt by blood. No other standard term fits more precisely.

U is the brother of M’s mother, making U M’s maternal uncle. L is U’s daughter, so L is the child of M’s uncle, i.e., M’s first cousin on the maternal side. The additional fact that L marries the son of M’s father’s sister (a paternal first cousin) does not change L’s own blood tie to M; it only describes her spouse. Therefore L’s precise blood relationship to M is that of a first cousin.

X's mother has a single brother (maternal uncle) and X's father has a single brother (paternal uncle). Y is the child of one of these two brothers, i.e., of an uncle of X. The child of an uncle is a first cousin. The alternative of the two brothers being the same person would imply X's parents are siblings, which is not a standard kinship scenario, so the relation is uniquely a first cousin.

Emma becomes John’s relation through her marriage to Mark, who is John’s son. In kinship terms, the spouse of one’s child is a daughter‑in‑law. Although Emma was previously Lily’s stepdaughter, that does not change her primary relation to John after she marries Mark. Hence Emma is John’s daughter‑in‑law.

R is M's paternal aunt, making M and R's child Q first cousins. P is married to Q, so P is the spouse of M's cousin. English lacks a standard kinship term for the spouse of a cousin; it is merely an affinal link without a specific name. Therefore the correct choice is D.

John and Mark are full brothers, so they share the same parents. Anna and Beth are full sisters, sharing their own parents. X’s father (John) is the brother of Y’s father (Mark), making X and Y first cousins on their paternal side. Likewise, X’s mother (Anna) is the sister of Y’s mother (Beth), making them first cousins on their maternal side. Because they are first cousins through both parental lines, they are double first cousins, the most precise term.

M and N share the same parents, and O and P share another set of parents. X’s paternal grandparents are M/N’s parents, and X’s maternal grandparents are O/P’s parents. Y has the same paternal grandparents (M/N’s parents) and the same maternal grandparents (O/P’s parents). Thus X and Y share both sets of grandparents, making them first cousins through two sibling links – the definition of double first cousins.

M and N are siblings, so they share the same two parents. X and Y are also siblings, sharing another pair of parents. A’s paternal grandparents are the parents of M (same as N’s), and A’s maternal grandparents are the parents of X (same as Y’s). B has the same set of paternal and maternal grandparents. Thus A and B share all four grandparents, making them first cousins through both parental lines—a double first‑cousin relationship.

Lily is Emma's maternal first cousin (child of Emma's maternal uncle). Mark is Emma's paternal first cousin (child of Emma's paternal aunt). The child of a first cousin is a first cousin once removed. Alex is the child of both Lily and Mark, so through each line Alex is Emma's first cousin once removed. No half‑sibling or other relation applies, making the precise term "first cousin once removed".

A and B share only one parent, making them half‑siblings. The children of half‑siblings are termed half‑first cousins, distinguishing them from the children of full siblings (first cousins). Therefore X and Y are half‑first cousins.

Alan and Beth share one parent (their mother) but have different fathers, making them half‑siblings. Their children, Carl and Dana, each descend from one of those half‑siblings. Because Carl and Dana share only one grandparent (the mother of Alan and Beth) rather than a full set of grandparents, they are cousins whose parents are half‑siblings. The precise term for that relationship is "half‑first cousins".

Tom and Sam are brothers, so Maya and Kyle are first cousins through their fathers. Lisa and Nina are sisters, so Maya and Kyle are also first cousins through their mothers. Sharing both sets of grandparents makes them double first cousins, the most precise term.

M and N are siblings, so they share the same parents (Grandparents A). O and P are siblings, sharing another set of parents (Grandparents B). X is child of M (child of A) and O (child of B). Y is child of N (child of A) and P (child of B). Therefore X and Y have both Grandparents A and Grandparents B in common, meaning they share both lines of first‑cousin relationships. This is the definition of double first cousins.

Half‑siblings share one parent. Each half‑sibling's child inherits that shared parent as a grandparent, but only one grandparent is common to both children. Consequently, the children share exactly one grandparent, making them half‑first cousins, the precise term for cousins who share a single grandparent.

L’s mother’s brother G is L’s maternal uncle, making any of G’s children L’s first cousin on the maternal side. L’s father’s sister H is L’s paternal aunt, so any of H’s children are L’s first cousin on the paternal side. Since G and H are married, their child X is simultaneously the child of L’s maternal uncle and paternal aunt, giving X the status of a first cousin through both parental lines – a double first cousin.

M and N are full siblings, and X and Y are full siblings. Each child receives one parent from each sibling pair, so P and Q share both sets of grandparents (the parents of M/N and the parents of X/Y). This makes them cousins through both parental lines, i.e., double first cousins, which is more specific than ordinary first cousins.

M and N share the same parents, as do X and Y. A’s father (M) and B’s father (N) are siblings, making A and B first cousins on their fathers’ side. Likewise, A’s mother (X) and B’s mother (Y) are siblings, making A and B first cousins on their mothers’ side. Because they are first cousins through both parents, they are double first cousins, the most precise term.

M is the child of the sister of P's father, making M P's paternal first cousin. M is also the child of the brother of P's mother, making M P's maternal first cousin. Since the same individual is a first cousin on both the father's and mother's sides, M and P are double first cousins, a recognized kinship term.

A and B are half‑siblings, sharing one parent. Their children (C and D) are the offspring of half‑siblings. In kinship terminology, the children of full siblings are first cousins; when the siblings are half‑siblings, the correct term is half‑first cousins (sometimes called first cousins, half‑blood). This is the most precise standard English term, making option A the correct choice.

Emma and Liam share both parents, making them full siblings. Their respective children, Noah (Emma's son) and Zoe (Liam's daughter), are therefore the children of two full siblings. Children of full siblings are first cousins. No half‑relationship or further generational gap exists.

M and N are siblings, so their children O (M's daughter) and R (N's daughter) are first cousins. R's child Q is one generation below R. A first cousin's child is a first cousin once removed. Therefore O and Q are first cousins once removed, regardless of their marriage.

John is the sibling of both Lily's father Ben and Alex's mother Mary, making him the uncle of Lily and Alex. Lily and Alex each are John's niece and nephew respectively. The child of a niece or nephew is one generation further down, which is termed a grandniece or grandnephew (sometimes called great‑niece/nephew). Therefore Sam, the child of Lily and Alex, is John's grandniece/grandnephew.

R's maternal uncle (mother's brother) and R's paternal aunt (father's sister) each have a child, and those children are the same person. This can only occur if the uncle and aunt are married, making their child a cousin of R on both the maternal and paternal sides. In standard kinship terms, such a child is simply a first cousin (a double cousin), not a nephew/niece or a removed cousin.

Anna's brother Peter makes Lisa John’s maternal first cousin. John’s father’s sister Mary makes Mark John’s paternal first cousin. Their child Sam is therefore the child of John’s first cousin (through either parent). In kinship terms, the child of a first cousin is a first cousin once removed. No other listed relation fits.

John's daughter is Anna, making Lily, Anna's child, John's granddaughter by blood. Lily is also the child of Tom, who is John's nephew (Mary's son), which would make Lily a great‑niece. However, the direct blood term for a child of one's daughter is granddaughter, which is the standard and closest generational term. Hence Lily is John's granddaughter.

Emily is John’s sister, making her children John’s nieces/nephews. Sarah is Emily’s daughter, so by blood she is John’s niece. The fact that Sarah is also Tom’s wife (John’s sister‑in‑law’s brother) is a marital link, not a blood relation, and does not affect the direct blood kinship term.

Maya and Olivia are sisters, so X and Y share the same maternal grandparents. Nathan and Peter are brothers, so X and Y also share the same paternal grandparents. Because they are first cousins through both their mothers and their fathers, they are double first cousins—the most precise term.

Tom and Sam are full brothers, so their children share the same paternal grandparents. Lily and Rose are full sisters, so their children share the same maternal grandparents. Thus A and B are first cousins through both their fathers and their mothers, making them double first cousins, the most precise term.

R's father's sister's son is R's paternal first cousin. R's mother's brother's son is R's maternal first cousin. If they are the same person, that individual is simultaneously the child of R's paternal aunt and maternal uncle, making him a double first cousin of R. The standard term is still "first cousin".

M and N are siblings, sharing one set of grandparents. O and P are siblings, sharing another set of grandparents. X is child of M (from the first sibling pair) and O (from the second sibling pair). Y is child of N (the other sibling from the first pair) and P (the other sibling from the second pair). Therefore X and Y share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins, the most precise term among the choices.

B is the brother of R's mother, making B R's maternal uncle. A is the sister of R's father, making A R's paternal aunt. Their only child S is therefore the child of R's maternal uncle and paternal aunt, giving S the status of a first cousin on both sides (a double first cousin). A and B are brothers, so their children D (son of A) and C (daughter of B) are first cousins. X is the child of C, placing X one generation below C. Therefore X is one generation apart from D, making their relationship a first cousin once removed.

M and N are half‑siblings, sharing only their mother. That mother is a grandparent of both P and Q. Since the children of full siblings share two grandparents (first cousins), children of half‑siblings share only one grandparent, making them half‑first cousins. No other relationship fits.

A is M's maternal uncle (mother's brother) and B is M's paternal aunt (father's sister). Their child C is therefore M's first cousin on the mother's side (through A) and also M's first cousin on the father's side (through B). Sharing both sets of grandparents makes them double first cousins, a standard kinship term.

X’s father (A) and Y’s father (B) are brothers, giving them the same paternal grandparents. X’s mother (C) and Y’s mother (D) are sisters, giving them the same maternal grandparents. Sharing both sets of grandparents makes X and Y double first cousins, the most precise term.

N’s father has a sister (paternal aunt). N’s mother has a brother (maternal uncle). M is the child of that aunt and that uncle. E’s father (A) and F’s father (B) are brothers, and E’s mother (C) and F’s mother (D) are sisters. Thus E and F share both sets of grandparents – the parents of A/B and the parents of C/D. Sharing both grandparent pairs makes them double first cousins, the most precise term.

M and N are siblings, so X and Y each have the same set of paternal grandparents (M/N's parents). O and P are also siblings, giving X and Y the same set of maternal grandparents (O/P's parents). Sharing both sets of grandparents makes X and Y double first cousins, the most precise term.

John is Alice's father, making Clara his grandchild via Alice. John is also Mary's brother; Mary is Bob's mother, so John is Bob's maternal uncle. Bob's child Clara is therefore John's great‑niece. Both relations coexist, so the most precise description includes both.

Adam and Brian are brothers, so their children share the same paternal grandparents. Clara and Diana are sisters, so their children share the same maternal grandparents. Ethan and Felix therefore share both sets of grandparents, making them first cousins through both parents, i.e., double first cousins.

R's mother's only brother is R's maternal uncle; his child P is R's first cousin. Similarly, R's father's only brother is R's paternal uncle; his child Q is also R's first cousin. Hence, whether S is P or Q, S is a first cousin of R.

A and B are full siblings, sharing both parents. C and D are full siblings, sharing a different pair of parents. X is child of A (one sibling) and C (one sibling). Y is child of B (the other sibling) and D (the other sibling). Therefore X and Y each have the same two sets of grandparents: the parents of A/B and the parents of C/D. They are first cousins through both parental lines, which the precise term for is “double first cousins.” They are not half‑first cousins (which would require sharing only one set of grandparents) nor second cousins (which would involve a generation gap).

S and D are the two children of P and share both parents, making them full siblings. X is S's child and Y is D's child. Children of two full siblings are first cousins by standard kinship terminology. No half‑sibling or other relation is possible under the given assumptions, so the term is uniquely determined.

Alan and Beth share both parents (P1). Diana and Carl share both parents (P2). Alan (P1 child) marries Diana (P2 child) and they have Ethan. M and N are siblings, so M is aunt/uncle of N's child Q. Q's child R is therefore M's grand‑niece by blood. R also marries P, who is M's daughter; a spouse of one's child is a daughter‑in‑law. Thus R holds both relations simultaneously, making "both grand‑niece and daughter‑in‑law" the most precise description.

M and N are siblings, so they share the same parents (grandparents A for their children). P and Q are siblings, sharing another set of parents (grandparents B). X’s parents are M (child of A) and P (child of B); Y’s parents are N (child of A) and Q (child of B). M and B are brothers, so they share the same parents. W and S are sisters, sharing another set of parents. C1 is the child of M (son of the first set) and W (daughter of the second set). L’s mother and M are siblings, so L (child of the mother) and C (child of M) are first cousins. D is C’s son, i.e., one generation down from L’s first cousin. M and N are siblings, so their children X and Y are first cousins through that line. U is R's maternal uncle, so his child X is R's first cousin. V is R's paternal aunt, so her child Y is also R's first cousin. X and Y (both R's first cousins) have a child Z. The child of one's cousin is a first cousin once removed. Therefore Z is R's first cousin once removed.

Peter is John’s brother, making him Lily’s paternal uncle, so Lily is his niece. John's mother Mary and Sophie's mother Laura are sisters, so they share maternal grandparents. John's father Peter and Sophie's father Mark are brothers, so they share paternal grandparents. Alan and Brian are brothers; Clara and Diana are sisters. Their children Ethan and Fiona therefore share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins. The next generation—Ethan's child George and Fiona's child Hannah—are the children of double first cousins. Mary and Tom are siblings. Peter is Mary’s son, making Tom Peter’s maternal uncle. Lisa is Tom’s daughter, so she is the child of Peter’s uncle. Children of siblings are first cousins, so Peter and Lisa are first cousins.

John and Mark are brothers, so Tom and Sam share the same paternal grandparents. Alice and Beth are sisters, so Tom and Sam also share the same maternal grandparents. L and S are siblings, making D (L's daughter) and S1 (S's son) first cousins. The children of first cousins are second cousins, so M (child of D) and N (child of S1) are second cousins.

M and N are siblings, sharing grandparents G1 and G2. O and P are siblings, sharing grandparents H1 and H2. X is child of M (a G‑grandchild) and O (an H‑grandchild). R’s paternal aunt is the sister of R’s father; her child (S) shares a grandparent with R, making S a first cousin. Y's mother has exactly one brother; his child is Z, making Z Y's first cousin on the maternal side. M and N are siblings, so their children X and Y are first cousins on the paternal side. O and P are also siblings, making X and Y first cousins on the maternal side as well. John, Mary, and Mark are all siblings, sharing the same parents. Mary’s child Lisa is therefore the child of Mark’s sister. John and Mary are siblings, so they share the same parents. Anna and Tom are also siblings, sharing another set of parents. Lily is child of John (from the first set) and Anna (from the second set). L’s mother’s brother is L’s maternal uncle; L’s father’s sister is L’s paternal aunt. These two siblings‑in‑law marry and have a child M. A and B are full brothers; C and D are full sisters. X is child of A (brother) and C (sister), while Y is child of B (brother) and D (sister). X's father and Y's mother are siblings (paternal aunt), and X's mother and Y's father are siblings (maternal uncle). M is N's mother; O is N's father. O's sister P is N's paternal aunt. P's son Q is therefore N's cousin. Q marries R, who is S's daughter. Hence Q is the husband of S's daughter, making Q S's son‑in‑law. No other direct kinship term applies.

L’s mother’s only brother is L’s maternal uncle. His son M is the child of L’s maternal uncle, making M the child of L’s parent’s sibling. That defines a first‑cousin relationship. The information about L’s father’s sister is irrelevant to the L‑M connection. Hence L and M are first cousins.

L's brother K is M's maternal uncle. K's daughter X is M's first cousin. X's son Y is M's first cousin once removed (one generation down). Y's daughter Z is one more generation down, making Z M's first cousin twice removed. Therefore the precise term is first cousin twice removed.

Adam and Ben are brothers; Clara and Dana are sisters. Their children Ethan and Fiona therefore share both paternal and maternal grandparents, making them double first cousins. A and B share one parent, making them half‑siblings. Their children, C and D, are the next generation down from those half‑siblings. M and S are full sisters; F and B are full brothers. M marries F and has child X; S marries B and has child Y. X and Y are thus children of two sibling pairs who married each other, sharing both sets of grandparents. This relationship is defined as double first cousins.

P's father is the brother of Q's mother, meaning they are siblings. The child of one sibling (P) and the child of the other sibling (Q) are first cousins. The additional conditions (only children, no adoption or remarriage) do not alter this standard relationship.

M is N's mother. M's brother R is N's maternal uncle. R's daughter Q is the child of N's uncle, making Q N's first cousin. No in‑law relationships are involved.

Emma and Noah share both parents, making them full siblings. Their children, Liam (Emma's son) and Maya (Noah's daughter), are each one generation removed from the common grandparents. Children of siblings are first cousins, so Maya is Liam's first cousin.

R's mother’s brother is R's maternal uncle. His daughter S is therefore R's first cousin. S's son T is the child of R's first cousin, which makes T R's first cousin once removed (the "once removed" denotes a generational difference).

Emma’s mother’s brother Carl is Emma’s maternal uncle. Carl’s daughter Nina is therefore Emma’s first cousin. Nina’s son Leo is one generation below Nina, making him the child of Emma’s first cousin. Lara and Mark share only one parent, making them half‑siblings. The children of half‑siblings are called half‑first cousins. Therefore Sam (Lara's child) and Tina (Mark's child) are half‑first cousins.

Alan and Brian are brothers, so their children share the same paternal grandparents. Claire and Denise are sisters, so their children share the same maternal grandparents. Ethan and Fiona therefore share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins, the most specific term.

M and N are siblings, so their children O and P are first cousins (they share the same grandparents). Q is O's child and R is P's child. Children of first cousins share the great‑grandparents of O and P, making Q and R second cousins. Therefore the precise relation is second cousins.

M and N are first cousins, meaning they share a set of grandparents. N's daughter D is one generation below N.
