In kinship terms, a child of a nephew or niece is called a great‑nephew or great‑niece (also grandnephew/grandniece). This matches option A.

M and N are full siblings, so they share the same parents (paternal grandparents of X and maternal grandparents of Y). O and P are also full siblings, sharing their own parents (maternal grandparents of X and paternal grandparents of Y). X’s parents (M and O) each come from one of the sibling pairs, and Y’s parents (N and P) come from the opposite members. Consequently X and Y share both sets of grandparents, not just one. This makes them double first cousins, the most precise term among the choices.

P is M's brother, so A and B share M's parents as paternal grandparents. Q is N's sister, so A and B share N's parents as maternal grandparents. Thus A and B have both sets of grandparents in common, making them the children of two sibling pairs. This is the definition of double first cousins.

A is mother of B. Since B and C are siblings, they share the same parents, so A is also mother of C. C is married to D, who is parent of E; therefore C is also parent of E. E and F are siblings, so F shares the same parents C and D. Thus A, as mother of C, is the grandparent of F. Being female, A is F's grandmother.

A's father M and B's father N are brothers, so A and B share the same paternal grandparents. Likewise, A's mother O and B's mother P are sisters, giving them the same maternal grandparents. Thus the two children share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins—the precise term for children of two sibling pairs.

Dana and Frank share the same mother, Alice, but have different fathers (Charles and Edward). This makes them share one parent only, which defines a half‑sibling relationship. No other kinship ties alter this classification.

L's father's sister is L's paternal aunt; L's mother's brother is L's maternal uncle. Their child M is the offspring of both the aunt and the uncle, making M simultaneously the child of L's paternal aunt and maternal uncle. Hence M shares both sets of L's grandparents, which defines a double first cousin relationship.

George and Helen have the same mother but different fathers, making them half‑siblings. Their children, Lily and Mark, thus share only that one common grandparent (the mother of George and Helen). Children of half‑siblings are half‑first cousins, i.e., cousins who share a single grandparent. Therefore Lily and Mark are half‑first cousins.

Adam and Ben share the same mother (M). Adam’s son Ethan is M’s grandchild, and Ethan’s daughter Grace is M’s great‑grandchild. Likewise, Ben’s daughter Fiona is also M’s grandchild, and Fiona’s child Grace is again M’s great‑grandchild. Thus Grace is a great‑granddaughter of Adam’s mother, with both parental lines descending from her (double descent). The precise standard term is “great‑granddaughter.”

M’s father is the brother of N’s mother, making M a first cousin of N through the maternal line. M’s mother is the sister of N’s father, making M a first cousin of N through the paternal line as well. Since the two parental lines are unrelated (no other intermarriage), M is both a maternal and a paternal first cousin – a double first cousin. This matches choice A.

X's maternal uncle's daughter Y is X's first cousin. X's paternal aunt's son Z is also X's first cousin. Y and Z (both first cousins of X) marry and have child W. The child of a first cousin is a first cousin once removed from the original person. Since W is the child of X's first cousin (both Y and Z), the relationship between X and W is first cousin once removed.

Mary’s mother is the sister of John’s mother, making them siblings. Therefore John (child of his mother) and Mary (child of her mother) are children of two sisters, which defines a first‑cousin relationship. The other condition—John’s paternal aunt married to Mary’s brother—creates only an affinal link and does not add any blood connection between John and Mary. Hence the precise blood relation is first cousins.
K and L are siblings, making L J's aunt. L's child M is therefore J's first cousin. N is M's child, i.e., the child of J's cousin, which is defined as a first cousin once removed.

Emma’s father Adam and Frank’s father Brian are brothers, making Emma and Frank first cousins through their paternal line. Likewise, Emma’s mother Clara and Frank’s mother Diana are sisters, making Emma and Frank first cousins through their maternal line as well. Because they are first cousins on both sides, they share both sets of grandparents, which is the definition of double first cousins.

M is R's maternal uncle (mother's brother) and N is R's paternal aunt (father's sister). Their child S is therefore the offspring of R's maternal uncle and paternal aunt. S is a first cousin to R on the mother's side and also a first cousin on the father's side, sharing both sets of grandparents. This makes S a double first cousin of R.

John's sister Mary makes her son Peter John’s nephew. Peter marries John’s daughter Anna, making Peter also John’s son‑in‑law. Their child Lily is therefore John’s grandchild via Anna, i.e., his granddaughter. At the same time Lily is the child of John’s nephew, which makes her John’s great‑niece (or grand‑niece). Thus Lily holds two distinct kinship ties to John, and no single standard term covers both.

Mary is John's sister, so her son Peter is John's nephew. Peter marries John's daughter Anna, making Anna both John's daughter and Peter's spouse. Their child Lily is therefore John's granddaughter through Anna, and also the child of his nephew Peter, making her his grandniece (also called great‑niece). The only choice that captures both relations is D.

M’s mother (A) and N’s father (B) are siblings, so M and N are first cousins (same generation, sharing grandparents). O is N’s son, i.e., one generation below N. The child of your cousin is your first cousin once removed. Therefore O is M’s first cousin once removed.

Emma and Fiona are sisters, so their parents are Maya's maternal grandparents and Kai's maternal grandparents. Liam and Noah are brothers, so their parents are Maya's paternal grandparents and Kai's paternal grandparents. Thus Maya and Kai share both sets of grandparents, making them children of two sibling pairs. This defines double first cousins, the most precise term.

John and Mark are brothers, making their children (Emma and Sara) first cousins. Sara's son Noah is one generation below Sara, so Emma is one generation above Noah but related through the cousin line. The correct kinship term for a person who is the child of one's cousin (or the cousin of one's parent) is "first cousin once removed".

Mary and Tom are siblings, making Tom John’s maternal uncle. Paul and Linda are siblings, making Linda John’s paternal aunt. Emma is the daughter of Tom and Linda, so she is John’s cousin through his mother (first cousin) and also his cousin through his father (first cousin). Being a cousin on both parental sides makes Emma a double first cousin of John.

M and N are siblings, so their children D and B are first cousins. C is the daughter of D, making C one generation below D. Therefore B, who is a first cousin of C's parent, is C's first cousin once removed.

A and B are siblings, so their children C and D are first cousins. The children of first cousins (E, child of C, and F, child of D) are one generation further removed, making them second cousins. Therefore the precise relationship between E and F is that they are second cousins.

B is the brother of A's mother, making B A's maternal uncle. A's mother is D's grandmother, so B is the sibling of D's grandmother. In kinship terms, a sibling of a grandparent is a great‑uncle (or great‑aunt). Therefore D's precise relation to B is great‑uncle.

A and B share only their mother, making them half‑siblings. Their children, C and D, each inherit one of those half‑siblings as a parent. Therefore C and D share a single grandparent—the mother of A and B—while their other grandparents are distinct. Cousins who share only one grandparent are classified as half‑first cousins. Hence the most precise term is half‑first cousins.

M and N are half‑siblings, sharing only one parent. Their children X and Y each have that shared parent as a grandparent, but they do not share the other grandparent. Therefore X and Y are cousins who share only one grandparent, i.e., half‑first cousins.

Anna is Clara's mother, and Clara is Ethan's mother, making Ethan a direct descendant one generation below Clara. Therefore Ethan is Anna's grandchild. The other lineage via Ben does not change this direct relationship.
M and P are sisters, so they share the same parents. P is Q's mother (by marriage to R). Therefore M is the sister of Q's mother, which makes M Q's maternal aunt. This is a direct blood relation.

John and Mary share only one parent (their mother), making them half‑siblings. Their children, Lily and Mark, each descend from one of those half‑siblings. Because they share a single grandparent (the mother) but not both, Lily and Mark are first cousins through that one shared grandparent, i.e., half‑first cousins.

P and R are brothers, so they share the same parents (paternal grandparents of both A and B). Q and S are sisters, sharing the same parents (maternal grandparents of both A and B). A’s parents are P and Q; B’s parents are R and S. Thus A and B have both sets of grandparents in common, making them double first cousins, the most precise term.

Kevin and Mary are siblings, making Mary the aunt of Kevin’s son Peter. Lisa is married to Peter, so she is the spouse of Mary's nephew. The standard term for the aunt of one's spouse is "aunt‑in‑law". Therefore Mary’s relation to Lisa is aunt‑in‑law.

M's father is N's father's brother (paternal uncle) and M's mother is N's mother's sister (maternal aunt). Since these two are M's parents, they are a brother–sister pair from opposite families who married. Their child M is therefore a first cousin of N on both the paternal and maternal sides, i.e., a double first cousin. The other options do not fit.

P is the child of Q's father's sister, making P Q's paternal first cousin. R is the child of Q's mother's brother, making R Q's maternal first cousin. The two parents (Q's aunt and uncle) are siblings of different parents and have no blood relation to each other. Consequently P and R share no common ancestor; they are not cousins or any other kinship term in standard English. Thus the most precise description is that they have no standard direct relation by blood.

Sarah and Laura are half‑sisters, sharing one parent. Their children (Emma and Nina) therefore share only that one grandparent. Children of half‑siblings are classified as half‑first cousins. They are not full first cousins (which require full siblings) nor aunt/niece, and they do have a blood connection, so 'No blood relation' is incorrect.

John's parents are Michael and Mary. Mary's brother is Peter, making Peter John's maternal uncle. Peter's daughter Lisa is thus Mary's niece and John’s first cousin. Michael's sister Sarah is John's paternal aunt. Since Sarah is related only to Michael's side and Lisa is related only to Mary's side, they share no common ancestor. Therefore Lisa and Sarah have no blood relationship.

M, N, and Q are siblings. N's daughter O is the child of N; Q's son P is the child of Q. Since N and Q are siblings, O and P are first cousins. They also marry each other, making O both P's first cousin and his spouse. No other option fits: she is not an aunt, half‑sibling, or merely a cousin‑in‑law (which would imply only a marital link). The most precise term is therefore "first cousin and spouse".

K’s mother has one brother; his child is L, making L K’s maternal first cousin. K’s father has one sister; her child is also L, making L K’s paternal first cousin. Thus L is the child of both K’s maternal uncle and paternal aunt, meaning K and L share both sets of grandparents. This is the definition of double first cousins.

L's mother and her sister are siblings, making the sister L's maternal aunt. The aunt's son T is therefore L's first cousin. T's daughter S is the child of L's first cousin, which is defined as a first cousin once removed. Hence S is L's first cousin once removed.

Peter is the brother of John and Mary, so Anna and Michael are John’s niece and nephew. John marries his niece Anna; their child is therefore the child of Michael’s sister (Anna). In kinship terms, the child of one’s sibling is a niece or nephew. Hence the child of John and Anna is Michael’s niece/nephew.

X's mother is the sister of Y's paternal grandfather, making her Y's father's aunt (Y's great-aunt). X is the child of that aunt, so X is the first cousin of Y's father. A first cousin of one's parent is a first cousin once removed to the child. Since X's father is unrelated, no other blood ties affect the term. Therefore X is Y's first cousin once removed.

A and B share only one parent, making them half‑siblings. Their children C and D are the offspring of half‑siblings. In kinship terminology, the children of full siblings are first cousins; when the parents are half‑siblings, their children are termed half‑first cousins. Thus the most precise standard term is half‑first cousins.

M and N are siblings, so they share the same parents. O and P are siblings, sharing another set of parents. M marries O, N marries P. Therefore X’s paternal grandparents are M/N’s parents, and Y’s paternal grandparents are the same set. Likewise, X’s maternal grandparents are O/P’s parents, which are also Y’s maternal grandparents. X and Y thus share both sets of grandparents, which is the definition of double first cousins.

John and Mary are half‑siblings, sharing one parent (their mother). Their children, Lily and Mark, each have that shared parent as a grandparent. Since they share only one grandparent, they are cousins of the first degree but only through a single line, which is termed "half‑first cousins" in genealogical nomenclature.

A's mother and C are sisters, so C is A's maternal aunt. C's son D is therefore A's first cousin. D's daughter E is the child of A's first cousin, which makes E A's first cousin once removed (the "once removed" indicates the generational difference). The relationship is uniquely determined.

Because R’s mother has exactly one child, that child must be R (no adoptions or other births). Likewise, R’s father’s only child is also R (monogamous marriage). S is defined as the child of that sole child, i.e., the child of R. Hence S is R’s son or daughter.

M's mother’s only brother is M’s maternal uncle; his child A is M’s first cousin. M’s father’s only sister is M’s paternal aunt; her child B is also M’s first cousin. Selecting either A or B (named C) yields a person who is a first cousin of M. The relation is uniquely determined as first cousin.

M is the child of N's father's only sister (paternal aunt) and also the child of N's mother's only brother (maternal uncle). Each relationship makes M a first cousin of N on that side. Because the two parents are siblings of N's parents, M is simultaneously a first cousin through both the paternal and maternal lines, which is the definition of a double first cousin.

R’s father’s sister A is R’s paternal aunt. A’s son B is therefore R’s first cousin. B’s daughter C is one generation below that cousin, making C the child of R’s first cousin. In kinship terms, the child of a first cousin is a first cousin once removed.

John’s mother’s brother Mike is John’s maternal uncle, making Mike’s daughter Sarah John’s first cousin. Sarah’s marriage to Tom creates no blood link; Tom is unrelated by blood to John. Tom’s sister Lily is Tom’s blood sibling, and Lily’s son Kevin is Tom’s nephew. Since Kevin’s lineage traces only through Tom’s family, and there is no shared ancestor between John’s family (John, his mother, Mike) and Tom’s family, Kevin and John share no blood relationship. Therefore, using only blood‑kinship terms, they are unrelated.

X’s paternal grandparents are the parents of A and B, while its maternal grandparents are the parents of C and D. Y shares the same paternal grandparents (through B) and the same maternal grandparents (through C). Thus X and Y have both sets of grandparents in common, making them first cousins on both parental lines – i.e., double first cousins.

Anna's parents are Peter and Lucy. Sam's parents are Peter and Mary. They share one biological parent (Peter) but have different mothers, making them half‑siblings. The other options do not fit: they are not cousins, not step‑siblings (they share a parent), and Sam is not an aunt/uncle.

Ethan’s father Adam and Fiona’s father Brian are brothers, giving Ethan and Fiona a paternal first‑cousin link. Their mothers Clara and Diana are sisters, providing a maternal first‑cousin link as well. Because they share both sets of grandparents, they are double first cousins, the most precise term.

M and O are brothers, so their children share the same paternal grandparents. N and P are sisters, so their children share the same maternal grandparents. X and Y therefore have both sets of grandparents in common, making them first cousins through both parents—a double first‑cousin relationship. They are not half‑cousins (which would lack one set of shared grandparents) nor second cousins (which would share great‑grandparents).

Peter is Mary’s brother, making him John’s maternal uncle. Peter’s children Lisa and Tom are therefore John’s first cousins. Tom’s daughter Anna is the child of John’s cousin, which by standard kinship terminology is a first cousin once removed (the “once removed” indicates a difference of one generation). The marital link of Lisa to John’s son does not affect Anna’s blood relationship to John.

A is the father's only brother, making A P's paternal uncle. B is the mother's only sister, making B P's maternal aunt. Their child C is therefore the child of P's paternal uncle and also the child of P's maternal aunt. C is consequently a first cousin of P on both the father's side and the mother's side, which is the definition of a double first cousin. The other options do not capture this dual relationship.

M's children J and K are M's direct children. Their children N and Q are M's grandchildren. R is the child of N and Q, who are both grandchildren of M, making R a child of a grandchild, i.e., a great‑grandchild. Because both of R's parents are grandchildren of M, R occupies the great‑grandchild role twice, so the most precise term is "double great‑grandchild".

X’s father A and Y’s father B are brothers, making X and Y first cousins through their fathers. Likewise, X’s mother C and Y’s mother D are sisters, making X and Y first cousins through their mothers. Because they are first cousins on both parental lines, they share both sets of grandparents, which is the definition of double first cousins.

Q’s mother’s brother is Q’s maternal uncle; Q’s father’s sister is Q’s paternal aunt. They marry each other, so their child P is the offspring of Q’s maternal uncle and paternal aunt. Hence P is a first cousin to Q through the mother’s side and also a first cousin through the father’s side, making them double first cousins.

M and N are full siblings, and O and Q are full siblings. A is the child of M (sibling of N) and O (sibling of Q), while B is the child of N and Q. Therefore A and B are cousins through both parental lines, sharing both sets of grandparents, which is the definition of double first cousins.

M’s father has a sister N, making N M’s paternal aunt. O is the child of N, so O is the child of M’s aunt. In standard kinship terms, the child of an aunt or uncle is a first cousin. No other relationships apply given monogamy and no remarriage.

Emma and Noah share only a mother, making them half‑siblings. Their children, Carl and Dana, are the offspring of half‑siblings, which in kinship terminology are called half‑first cousins. This is more precise than simply first cousins, and a standard term exists.

R’s mother’s brother (U) is R’s maternal uncle; his only child X is therefore R’s first cousin on the mother’s side. Similarly, R’s father’s brother (V) is R’s paternal uncle; his only child Y is R’s first cousin on the father’s side. Whichever child (X or Y) we label S, S is a child of an uncle of R, which by definition makes S a first cousin of R. The relation is uniquely determined as first cousin.

John and Mary are full siblings; Anna and Peter are full siblings. Sam is child of John (from family X) and Anna (from family Y). Lily is child of Mary (family X) and Peter (family Y). Thus Sam and Lily share both sets of grandparents (the X grandparents via their fathers and the Y grandparents via their mothers). Sharing both grandparent pairs makes them double first cousins, not merely first cousins or half‑first cousins.

P and Q are each the child of a sibling pair: A and B are brothers, C and D are sisters. Through their fathers, P and Q are first cousins (children of brothers). Through their mothers, they are also first cousins (children of sisters). Because they are first cousins on both paternal and maternal sides, they share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins, the most specific term.

X's mother’s brother is X’s maternal uncle. Y is married to that uncle, making Y the uncle’s spouse. In standard English kinship, the spouse of an uncle is called an aunt (by marriage). No other listed term fits, so the correct choice is Aunt.

M and N are siblings, sharing both parents. P and Q are also siblings, sharing both parents. X is the child of M (who is sibling of N) and P (who is sibling of Q). Y is the child of N and Q. Therefore X and Y each have the same two sets of grandparents: the parents of M/N and the parents of P/Q. Sharing both sets of grandparents makes them double first cousins, not just first cousins (which share only one set) nor half‑first cousins (share one grandparent). They are not second cousins because they are closer than that.

M's mother is the sister of N's father, making her N's paternal aunt. M's father is the brother of N's mother, making him N's maternal uncle. Thus M is the child of N's paternal aunt and maternal uncle. This means M is N's cousin on both the father's side and the mother's side, i.e., a double first cousin.

L's father and his brother P share the same paternal grandparents; L's mother and her sister Q share the same maternal grandparents. P and Q marry and have a child R. R is the child of L's paternal uncle and maternal aunt, thus R shares both sets of grandparents with L, making them first cousins through both parental lines—a double first cousin.

Tom is John's maternal uncle, making Tom's daughter Lily John's first cousin. Mary is John's paternal aunt, making Mary's son Sam also John's first cousin. Lily and Sam's child Alex is therefore the child of John's first cousins. The child of a first cousin is a first cousin once removed relative to the original person.

J’s mother’s new husband is K’s father, but J and K have no common ancestors. Therefore they are not blood relatives. The only standard blood‑kinship term that fits is that they have no blood relation.

Carla’s father Alan and Derek’s father Brian are brothers, making Carla and Derek first cousins on their fathers’ side. Likewise, Carla’s mother Maya and Derek’s mother Nora are sisters, making them first cousins on their mothers’ side. Being first cousins through both parents defines them as double first cousins.

Mary and Lisa are sisters, so Anna and Ben share the same maternal grandparents. Tom and Sam are brothers, so they also share the same paternal grandparents. Thus the children share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins.
B is A's parent. B's sibling C is A's aunt/uncle, making C's child D A's first cousin. E is D's son, i.e., the child of A's first cousin. The child of a first cousin is a first cousin once removed.

Mother's brother is M's maternal uncle; his son is M's maternal first cousin. The extra clause about him being married to M's paternal cousin does not change his direct kinship to M. He remains a first cousin, not a double cousin or any other relation.

Mary is John’s sister, making her son Peter John’s nephew. Peter’s son David is therefore the child of John’s nephew, i.e., the grandson of John’s sister. The appropriate kinship term for the son of a nephew is great‑nephew (also called grandnephew). Hence David is John’s great‑nephew.

M and S are siblings; W and N are siblings. D is child of M (sibling of S) and W (sibling of N). E is child of S (sibling of M) and N (sibling of W). Thus D and E are first cousins through both parental lines, sharing both sets of grandparents, which defines double first cousins.

M's mother is the sister of N's father, making her N's paternal aunt. M's father is the brother of N's mother, making him N's maternal uncle. Thus M is the child of N's paternal aunt and maternal uncle. Consequently, M and N share both sets of grandparents: the parents of M's mother are N's paternal grandparents, and the parents of M's father are N's maternal grandparents. Sharing both grandparent pairs defines double first cousins, not just ordinary first cousins.

B1 and B2 are brothers, sharing both parents. S1 and S2 are sisters, also sharing both parents. X is the child of B1 + S1; Y is the child of B2 + S2. Therefore X and Y share the same paternal grandparents (parents of B1/B2) and the same maternal grandparents (parents of S1/S2). They are first cousins through both parental lines, i.e., double first cousins, the most specific term among the choices.

Mary and Peter are siblings. Mary’s children are John and Emma. Peter’s child is Lisa. Therefore Lisa and Emma are children of siblings, making them first cousins. The marriage of Lisa to Emma’s son Tom creates a legal relationship, but does not affect their blood relation.

A's mother’s brother B is A’s maternal uncle, making B’s daughter C A’s first cousin. A’s father’s sister D is A’s paternal aunt, making D’s son E also A’s first cousin. C and E each are A’s first cousin, so their child F is one generation below A’s cousins. The child of a first cousin is defined as a first cousin once removed. This relationship is consistent regardless of the two separate cousin lines, so the relation is uniquely determined as first cousin once removed.

M is the child of N's paternal aunt (the only sister of N's father) and also the child of N's maternal uncle (the only brother of N's mother). Therefore M is the offspring of two siblings of N's parents, meaning M is a first cousin to N on both the father's and mother's sides. Being a first cousin through both parental lines makes M a double first cousin of N.
Y and Z are siblings. X is Y's child, W is Z's child. Children of siblings are first cousins by standard kinship terminology. No other relationship applies.

Peter is John’s brother, so Peter’s son Tom is John’s nephew by blood. Lucy, John’s daughter, marries Tom, making Tom John’s son‑in‑law by marriage. Both relationships are valid under the allowed kinship categories, so Tom is simultaneously John’s nephew and son‑in‑law.

Emma and Fiona are half‑sisters, sharing only one parent. Their children, George and Hannah, each descend from one of those half‑siblings, so they share exactly one grandparent. That makes them first cousins, but only through one shared grandparent, i.e., half‑first cousins.

Alice → Carol (child) → Eve (grandchild) → George (great‑grandchild). The lineage is a direct maternal line of three generations, making George Alice’s great‑grandchild. The alternative options describe different cousin relationships, which do not apply to this direct descent.

Ethan's mother Alice and Fiona's father Bob are full siblings, making Ethan and Fiona first cousins through that side. Likewise, Ethan's father Charles and Fiona's mother Diana are full siblings, making them first cousins through the other side as well. Sharing both sets of grandparents defines double first cousins, which is more precise than plain first cousins.

John’s father and Mary’s mother are half‑siblings, sharing only one parent (their mother). That shared parent is the grandmother of both John and Mary. Thus John and Mary share a single grandparent, making them first cousins, but because the shared grandparent is only one of each’s two grandparents, the precise term is half‑first cousins.

N's father has one sibling, whose child is N's paternal first cousin. N's mother also has one sibling, whose child is N's maternal first cousin. M is defined as the child of either the father's sibling or the mother's sibling. In both cases M is the child of an aunt or uncle of N, which by standard kinship terminology is a first cousin. Thus the relationship is uniquely determined as a first cousin.

Linda is George's mother; her sister Martha is George's aunt. Martha's son Peter is therefore George's first cousin. Sophie's mother is Peter, making Sophie the child of George's first cousin, which is defined as a first cousin once removed.

Tom's father and Carl are siblings, making Carl Tom's paternal uncle. Carl's daughter Emma is therefore Tom's first cousin. Emma's son Leo is the child of Tom's first cousin, which is defined as a first cousin once removed (one generation down). Hence Leo is Tom's first cousin once removed.

A and B are brothers, sharing the same parents. C and D are sisters, sharing the same parents. X is child of A (brother) and C (sister); Y is child of B (brother) and D (sister). Therefore X and Y have both sets of grandparents in common – the parents of A/B and the parents of C/D. This is precisely the definition of double first cousins, children of two sibling pairs who marry each other.

Z is the daughter of Y, who is X's maternal uncle, making Z X's maternal first cousin. V is the son of W, who is X's paternal aunt, making V X's paternal first cousin. Y and W belong to separate families with no intermarriage, so Z and V have no common ancestors. Hence they are unrelated by blood.

P’s father A and Q’s father B are brothers, so P and Q share the same paternal grandparents. Likewise, P’s mother C and Q’s mother D are sisters, giving them the same maternal grandparents. Sharing both sets of grandparents makes them first cousins on both sides, i.e., double first cousins, the most precise term.

M and N are siblings. M's daughter O is therefore N's niece. O's daughter Q is the child of N's niece, making Q the daughter of a niece. In standard kinship terminology, the child of a niece/nephew is called a grandniece (also termed great‑niece). Thus Q is N's grandniece.

Sarah is the daughter of John’s maternal uncle, making her John’s first cousin on his mother’s side. David is the son of John’s paternal uncle, making him John’s first cousin on his father’s side. Their only potential common ancestors would be John’s grandparents, but Sarah’s grandparents are John’s maternal grandparents while David’s grandparents are John’s paternal grandparents, which are unrelated unless the parents are themselves related. Assuming no intermarriage, Sarah and David share no blood relation.

X is married to Y. Y’s sister A is X’s sister‑in‑law. A’s husband B is therefore X’s brother‑in‑law (the husband of his sister‑in‑law). B’s sister C is the sister of X’s brother‑in‑law. No standard English kinship term directly describes the sister of one’s brother‑in‑law; it is an affinal chain without a specific label. Hence the correct choice is the option stating there is no standard direct relation.

John, Mary, and Paul are siblings. Mary’s son Tom is therefore the nephew of Paul. Lisa’s brother Kevin is Paul’s child, making Kevin Paul’s son. Thus Kevin is the child of Tom’s uncle (Paul), which defines a first‑cousin relationship. No other standard term fits.

P's paternal uncle (father's only brother) and P's maternal aunt (mother's only sister) are the parents of Q. These two are not siblings, so they must be married, making Q the child of both a paternal uncle and a maternal aunt. That relationship yields a double first cousin, which is more precise than a simple first cousin.

A is X's maternal uncle (mother's brother) and B is X's paternal aunt (father's sister). Their marriage makes Y the child of X's maternal uncle, giving Y a first‑cousin relationship through X's mother. Simultaneously, Y is the child of X's paternal aunt, giving another first‑cousin relationship through X's father. Because Y is first cousin to X via both parental lines, Y is a double first cousin.
